2ee2178120cdb937.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Canada

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Since 2013 the Criminal Code (s. 34) allows force, including deadly force, if the person reasonably believes force or a threat of force is being used against them or someone else, acts to defend against it, and the act is reasonable in the circumstances. The Code does not mention retreat; instead the court must weigh a list of factors, including "whether there were other means available to respond" and the proportionality of the response. In R v Khill (2021 SCC 37) the Supreme Court said this is a "multifactorial reasonableness assessment" that also considers the accused's own role in the incident. So there is no fixed duty to retreat, but the chance to avoid the attack counts against the defender. The sources opened here do not address a reduced-liability rule for excessive force.

At home

Courts have held there is "a very strong line of authority that a person is not required to retreat in the face of an attack in his or her own home" (R. v. Docherty, Ontario Court of Appeal, 2012, para. 21, as quoted by Robichaud Law). Defence of property is a separate rule (Criminal Code s. 35).

What the law says
Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 34(1)-(2)
34 (1) A person is not guilty of an offence if (a) they believe on reasonable grounds that force is being used against them or another person or that a threat of force is being made against them or another person; (b) the act that constitutes the offence is committed for the purpose of defending or protecting themselves or the other person from that use or threat of force; and (c) the act committed is reasonable in the circumstances. (2) In determining whether the act committed is reasonable in the circumstances, the court shall consider the relevant circumstances of the person, the other parties and the act, including, but not limited to, the following factors: (a) the nature of the force or threat; (b) the extent to which the use of force was imminent and whether there were other means available to respond to the potential use of force; (c) the person's role in the incident; ... (g) the nature and proportionality of the person's response to the use or threat of force ...
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Criminal Code, section 34 (Justice Laws Website, Government of Canada)
  • Broadening the Scope of Self-defence: Accused's "Role in the Incident" in R v Khill (TheCourt.ca, Osgoode Hall Law School (Jennifer Laws, 2021))
  • Self Defence Law in Canada: Retreat or Not to Retreat? (Robichaud Law (2012, discussing R. v. Docherty, Ont. C.A.))

705b0da59d5a34dc.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Russia

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Article 37 of the Criminal Code says harming an attacker is not a crime when defending against an attack that involves violence dangerous to life, or an immediate threat of such violence; against such attacks there is no proportionality limit. Against less dangerous attacks, defence is lawful unless the defender 'exceeded the limits of necessary defence', meaning deliberate acts clearly out of line with the nature and danger of the attack; acts caused by surprise that prevented the defender from judging the danger are not an excess (added 2003). Part 3 of article 37 states expressly that the right applies regardless of whether the person could have avoided the attack or called others or the authorities for help, so there is no duty to retreat. Killing while exceeding the limits is a separate, lighter offence (article 108) punished by up to two years.

At home

The Criminal Code has no separate home-defence rule; article 37 applies wherever the attack happens.

What the law says
Criminal Code of the Russian Federation, art. 37(1)
Не является преступлением причинение вреда посягающему лицу в состоянии необходимой обороны, то есть при защите личности и прав обороняющегося или других лиц, охраняемых законом интересов общества или государства от общественно опасного посягательства, если это посягательство было сопряжено с насилием, опасным для жизни обороняющегося или другого лица, либо с непосредственной угрозой применения такого насилия.
Criminal Code, art. 37(2) and 37(2.1)
Защита от посягательства, не сопряжённого с насилием, опасным для жизни обороняющегося или другого лица, либо с непосредственной угрозой применения такого насилия, является правомерной, если при этом не было допущено превышения пределов необходимой обороны, то есть умышленных действий, явно не соответствующих характеру и опасности посягательства. 2¹. Не являются превышением пределов необходимой обороны действия обороняющегося лица, если это лицо вследствие неожиданности посягательства не могло объективно оценить степень и характер опасности нападения.
Criminal Code, art. 37(3)
Положения настоящей статьи в равной мере распространяются на всех лиц независимо от их профессиональной или иной специальной подготовки и служебного положения, а также независимо от возможности избежать общественно опасного посягательства или обратиться за помощью к другим лицам или органам власти.
Criminal Code, art. 108(1)
Убийство, совершённое при превышении пределов необходимой обороны, — наказывается исправительными работами на срок до двух лет, либо ограничением свободы на срок до двух лет, либо принудительными работами на срок до двух лет, либо лишением свободы на тот же срок.

b3ee499185601bfc.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Greenland

Part of Denmark, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Greenland has its own Criminal Code (Kriminallov for Grønland, Act no. 306 of 30 April 2008), separate from Denmark's, which uses "measures" rather than ordinary punishments. Under § 9, no measures are imposed on a person who acted in self-defence, to the extent the acts were necessary to resist or avert an unlawful attack that has begun or is imminent, and did not obviously go beyond what is justifiable given how dangerous the attack was, who the attacker was, and the importance of the interest attacked. The Code does not mention retreat. A person who exceeds the limits is still free of measures if the excess was reasonably caused by fear or agitation provoked by the attack (§ 9(2)); otherwise exceeding the limits is a ground for a milder measure or none at all (§ 123). No separate home rule appears in § 9.

What the law says
Kriminallov for Grønland (lov nr. 306 af 30/04/2008), § 9
§ 9. Over for personer, der har handlet i nødværge, finder denne lovs foranstaltninger ikke anvendelse, i det omfang handlingerne har været nødvendige for at modstå eller afværge et påbegyndt eller overhængende uretmæssigt angreb og ikke åbenbart går ud over, hvad der under hensyn til angrebets farlighed, angriberens person og det angrebne retsgodes betydning er forsvarligt. Stk. 2. Overskrider nogen grænserne for lovligt nødværge, finder denne lovs foranstaltninger dog ikke anvendelse, hvis overskridelsen er rimeligt begrundet i den skræk eller ophidselse, som angrebet fremkaldte.
Kriminallov for Grønland, § 123 nr. 2
§ 123. Som forhold, der kan begrunde, at der idømmes en mindre indgribende foranstaltning, eller at der efter omstændighederne ikke idømmes nogen foranstaltning, regnes, ... 2) at gerningsmanden har overskredet grænserne for lovligt nødværge eller for nødret
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

4b5dd094a37b30ec.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Chile

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 10 No. 4 of the Penal Code, a person who acts in defence of their person or rights is exempt from criminal liability if there is an unlawful aggression, "rational necessity of the means used" to prevent or repel it, and no sufficient provocation by the defender; defence of relatives and strangers follows similar rules (Nos. 5 and 6). The Code does not mention retreat, and the sources opened here did not address whether flight is expected. If not all requirements are met, art. 11 No. 1 turns the defence into a mitigating circumstance that reduces the sentence. The Naín-Retamal law (Ley 21.560, published April 2023) added a presumption of self-defence for police, prison guards and the armed forces performing public-order duties when they repel an aggression that could seriously harm life or physical integrity, with a sentence reduction where use of the weapon was not rationally necessary.

At home

Art. 10 No. 6 creates a legal presumption that self-defence applies, "whatever the harm caused to the aggressor", to a person who repels climbing-in (escalamiento) into an inhabited house, flat or office or its outbuildings, or at night into a commercial or industrial premises, and to a person who prevents certain serious crimes (including kidnapping, rape, homicide and violent robbery).

What the law says
Código Penal, art. 10 No. 4 and No. 6 (2nd para.)
Están exentos de responsabilidad criminal: ... 4.° El que obra en defensa de su persona o derechos, siempre que concurran las circunstancias siguientes: Primera.-Agresión Ilegítima. Segunda.- Necesidad racional del medio empleado para impedirla o repelerla. Tercera.-Falta de provocación suficiente por parte del que se defiende. ... Se presumirá legalmente que concurren las circunstancias previstas en este número y en los números 4° y 5° precedentes, cualquiera que sea el daño que se ocasione al agresor, respecto de aquel que rechaza el escalamiento en los términos indicados en el número 1° del artículo 440 de este Código, en una casa, departamento u oficina habitados, o en sus dependencias o, si es de noche, en un local comercial o industrial y del que impida o trate de impedir la consumación de los delitos señalados en los artículos 141, 142, 361, 362, 365 bis, 390, 391, 433 y 436 de este Código.
Código Penal, art. 10 No. 6 (police presumption, Ley 21.560)
Se presumirá legalmente que concurren las circunstancias previstas en los números 4°, 5° y 6° de este artículo, respecto de las Fuerzas de Orden y Seguridad Pública, Gendarmería de Chile, las Fuerzas Armadas y los servicios bajo su dependencia, cuando éstas realicen funciones de orden público y seguridad pública interior; en dichos casos se entenderá que concurre el uso racional del medio empleado si ... repele o impide una agresión que pueda afectar gravemente su integridad física o su vida o las de un tercero, empleando las armas o cualquier otro medio de defensa.
Código Penal, art. 11 No. 1
Son circunstancias atenuantes: 1.° Las expresadas en el artículo anterior, cuando no concurren todos los requisitos necesarios para eximir de responsabilidad en sus respectivos casos.

4f1db1ed30303ab2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Norway

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Under section 18 of the Norwegian Penal Code (2005), an otherwise punishable act is lawful when it is done to avert an unlawful attack, goes no further than necessary, and does not 'obviously' go beyond what is justifiable given how dangerous the attack is, what interest it violates and the attacker's guilt. The statute does not mention retreat, but because force must be 'necessary', a lawyer answering for the state youth-information service ung.no wrote in 2023 that if there were other ways to avert the attack, 'such as calling for help or running away', a killing cannot be claimed as self-defence; the Supreme Court's appeals committee has also upheld a conviction where the defendant had 'several alternative courses of action' and had partly provoked the fight (HR-2022-1377-U). Someone who goes too far can still be acquitted where 'special reasons' justify it, and the sentence can in any case be reduced (sections 80 and 81, as described by the national encyclopedia). Lawful self-defence is not just unpunished but lawful, so the Supreme Court held in 2018 (HR-2018-2427-A) that the defender cannot be ordered to pay damages when the attack was real.

At home

No separate home-defence rule was found; section 18 applies to attacks on persons and on property alike.

What the law says
Straffeloven (Penal Code 2005), § 18 første ledd (as quoted by the Supreme Court in HR-2022-1377-U)
En handling som ellers ville være straffbar, er lovlig når den a. blir foretatt for å avverge et ulovlig angrep, b. ikke går lenger enn nødvendig, og c. ikke går åpenbart ut over hva som er forsvarlig under hensyn til hvor farlig angrepet er, hva slags interesse som angrepet krenker, og angriperens skyld.

57057d3454bb62e9.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

China

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

China's Criminal Law (art. 20) treats an act to stop an ongoing unlawful infringement of the state, public, or a person's rights as justifiable defence with no criminal responsibility. If the defence obviously exceeds the limits of necessity and causes serious damage, the defender is criminally responsible but must receive a mitigated punishment or be exempted. Against an ongoing assault, murder, robbery, rape, kidnap or other violent crime seriously endangering personal safety, causing injury or death is never 'undue defence'. The code does not mention retreat; the 2020 judicial guiding opinions on justifiable defence could not be opened from here, so the retreat question is left unsettled in this entry.

At home

No home-specific rule in art. 20; the third paragraph lets a person defending against an ongoing violent crime that seriously endangers personal safety (assault, murder, robbery, rape, kidnap) cause injury or death without it being excessive.

What the law says
Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China (1997), art. 20 (NPC English translation)
An act that a person commits to stop an unlawful infringement in order to prevent the interests of the State and the public, or his own or other person's rights of the person, property or other rights from being infringed upon by the on-going infringement, thus harming the perpetrator, is justifiable defence, and he shall not bear criminal responsibility. If a person's act of justifiable defence obviously exceeds the limits of necessity and causes serious damage, he shall bear criminal responsibility; however, he shall be given a mitigated punishment or be exempted from punishment. If a person acts in defence against an on-going assault, murder, robbery, rape, kidnap or any other crime of violence that seriously endangers his personal safety, thus causing injury or death to the perpetrator of the unlawful act, it is not undue defence, and he shall not bear criminal responsibility.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

cab6b1f696ec9bd5.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Australia

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Most criminal law in Australia is made by the six states and two territories, each with its own self-defence rule; this national entry describes the Commonwealth Criminal Code, which covers federal offences. Under s 10.4 a person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them. No Australian statute found imposes a duty to retreat; in jury directions (NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book) the availability of retreat is listed as one matter the jury may weigh in deciding whether the response was reasonable. Deadly or really serious force cannot be justified solely to protect property or deal with trespassers. Whether excessive force reduces murder to manslaughter depends on the state or territory (e.g. NSW s 421, WA s 248(3), SA s 15(2)).

At home

Varies by state and territory (see the AUS-xx files). Under the Commonwealth Criminal Code, force intended to kill or cause really serious injury may not be used only to protect property or to stop or remove a trespasser (s 10.4(3)); several states have specific home-defence provisions (e.g. Queensland s 267, Western Australia s 244, South Australia s 15C, Tasmania s 40).

What the law says
Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth), Schedule (Criminal Code), s 10.4 Self-defence
(1) A person is not criminally responsible for an offence if he or she carries out the conduct constituting the offence in self-defence. (2) A person carries out conduct in self-defence if and only if he or she believes the conduct is necessary: (a) to defend himself or herself or another person; or (b) to prevent or terminate the unlawful imprisonment of himself or herself or another person; or (c) to protect property from unlawful appropriation, destruction, damage or interference; or (d) to prevent criminal trespass to any land or premises; or (e) to remove from any land or premises a person who is committing criminal trespass; and the conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as he or she perceives them. (3) This section does not apply if the person uses force that involves the intentional infliction of death or really serious injury: (a) to protect property; or (b) to prevent criminal trespass; or (c) to remove a person who is committing criminal trespass.
NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book, Self-defence [6-460] (suggested jury direction)
[It may be necessary to give directions on such matters as arise on the evidence relating to, for example, the imminence of a threatened attack or the availability of other remedies to the accused, such as retreat. It should, however, be made emphatically clear to the jury that it is the accused’s perception of the circumstances which must be considered.]

0be660216abeb5fe.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Brazil

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 25 of the Penal Code, a person acts in self-defence when, "using the necessary means in moderation", they repel an unjust aggression, current or imminent, against their own or another's right. Unlike necessity (art. 24), which requires that the danger could not be avoided another way, self-defence has no avoidance requirement: Brazilian legal teaching holds that flight is not required even when it is possible, and that the "commodus discessus" (easier way out) is required only in necessity. Force must still be necessary and moderate, and under art. 23 the defender is liable for intentional or negligent excess. A 2019 law (Lei 13.964) added that police who repel aggression against hostages act in self-defence. In August 2023 the Supreme Federal Court (ADPF 779) unanimously ruled the "legitimate defence of honour" argument unconstitutional in femicide cases.

At home

The Penal Code's general part (arts. 23-25) contains no separate rule for defending the home; the general self-defence rule of art. 25 applies.

What the law says
Código Penal (Decreto-Lei 2.848/1940), art. 25
Art. 25 - Entende-se em legítima defesa quem, usando moderadamente dos meios necessários, repele injusta agressão, atual ou iminente, a direito seu ou de outrem. Parágrafo único. Observados os requisitos previstos no caput deste artigo, considera-se também em legítima defesa o agente de segurança pública que repele agressão ou risco de agressão a vítima mantida refém durante a prática de crimes.
Código Penal, art. 23 (excesso punível)
Art. 23 - Não há crime quando o agente pratica o fato: ... II - em legítima defesa; ... Parágrafo único - O agente, em qualquer das hipóteses deste artigo, responderá pelo excesso doloso ou culposo.
Código Penal, art. 24 (estado de necessidade, for contrast)
Art. 24 - Considera-se em estado de necessidade quem pratica o fato para salvar de perigo atual, que não provocou por sua vontade, nem podia de outro modo evitar, direito próprio ou alheio...

f824a7c9c301b56c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Japan

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Japan's Penal Code (art. 36) makes an act not punishable if the person was compelled to take it ('yamu wo ezu ni shita') to protect their own or another's rights against an imminent and unlawful infringement. Force beyond the limits of self-defence (excessive self-defence) is still a crime but the court may reduce the sentence or waive punishment depending on the circumstances (art. 36(2)). A 1930 law extends self-defence for burglary and home intrusion, including a person who kills an intruder out of fear or panic. The code text does not mention retreat, and no court decision on retreat was opened for this entry, so whether escape must be preferred is left unsettled here.

At home

Act on Prevention and Disposition of Robbery and Theft (Act No. 9 of 1930), art. 1: killing or injuring an offender to remove a present danger to life, body or chastity is deemed self-defence under Penal Code art. 36(1) when preventing theft or recovering stolen goods, stopping someone entering a home or guarded building armed or by breaking in, or expelling an unlawful intruder; and even without such a present danger, a person who kills or injures the offender on the spot out of fear, surprise, excitement or panic is not punished.

What the law says
Penal Code (Act No. 45 of 1907), art. 36 (official translation)
Article 36 (1) An act a person was compelled to take to protect the rights of oneself or any other person against imminent and unlawful infringement is not punishable. (2) An act exceeding the limits of self-defense may lead to the punishment being reduced or may exculpate the offender in light of the circumstances. [第三十六条 急迫不正の侵害に対して、自己又は他人の権利を防衛するため、やむを得ずにした行為は、罰しない。２ 防衛の程度を超えた行為は、情状により、その刑を減軽し、又は免除することができる。]
盗犯等ノ防止及処分ニ関スル法律 (Act No. 9 of 1930), art. 1
左ノ各号ノ場合ニ於テ自己又ハ他人ノ生命、身体又ハ貞操ニ対スル現在ノ危険ヲ排除スル為犯人ヲ殺傷シタルトキハ刑法第三十六条第一項ノ防衛行為アリタルモノトス ... 前項各号ノ場合ニ於テ自己又ハ他人ノ生命、身体又ハ貞操ニ対スル現在ノ危険アルニ非ズト雖モ行為者恐怖、驚愕、興奮又ハ狼狽ニ因リ現場ニ於テ犯人ヲ殺傷スルニ至リタルトキハ之ヲ罰セズ

9a0512eb124ef89b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

India

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Since the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replaced the Indian Penal Code 1860, private defence is in BNS ss 34–44, which keep the IPC wording. Deadly force is allowed against assaults reasonably causing fear of death or grievous hurt, and against assaults intended to rape, abduct or wrongfully confine, or acid attacks (s 38); the harm must not exceed what is necessary, and there is no right where there is time to seek protection from the authorities (s 37). The Supreme Court in Darshan Singh v State of Punjab (2010) ruled that the law of private defence does not impose a duty to retreat (as described by Prof. Stanley Yeo, NUJS Law Review 2011; the judgment itself could not be opened from here). A person who in good faith exceeds the right of private defence and kills without premeditation commits culpable homicide not amounting to murder (Exception 2 to murder, BNS s 101 / IPC s 300).

At home

BNS s 41: the right of private defence of property extends to causing death against robbery, house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise, arson or explosives on a building used as a dwelling, and theft, mischief or house-trespass that reasonably causes fear of death or grievous hurt.

What the law says
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s 37
(1) There is no right of private defence,- ... (c) in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities. (2) The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence.
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s 38
The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions specified in section 37, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the assailant, if the offence which occasions the exercise of the right be of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely:- (a) such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that death will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; (b) such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; (c) an assault with the intention of committing rape; ... (g) an act of throwing or administering acid or an attempt to throw or administer acid which may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such act.
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, murder, Exception 2 (text from Bill No. 121 of 2023 as introduced)
Exception 2.—Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation, and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.
S. Yeo, 'Staying True to the Indian Penal Code' (2011) 4 NUJS L Rev 163, on Darshan Singh v State of Punjab (2010) 2 SCC 333
The Court in Darshan Singh could also have referred to cases from these jurisdictions possessing the IPC to further support its ruling that our law of private defence does not impose a duty to retreat. ... the IPC provisions are sufficiently clear that there is no legal duty to retreat

11b5cea38bad1024.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Alaska

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Alaska allows deadly force in self-defence when a person reasonably believes it is necessary against death, serious physical injury, kidnapping, first- or second-degree sexual assault, first-degree sexual abuse of a minor, or robbery of any degree (Alaska Stat. § 11.81.335(a)). The statute keeps a basic retreat rule (deadly force is not allowed if the person knows they can avoid it by leaving with complete safety for themselves and anyone they are protecting) but then lists exceptions so broad that there is no duty to leave on premises they own, lease, live in or visit as a guest, in a building where they work, when protecting a child or household member, when acting as or assisting a peace officer, or 'in any other place where the person has a right to be' (§ 11.81.335(b)). That last exception was added by House Bill 24 (ch. 51 SLA 2013, effective 18 September 2013); before then Alaska had a duty to retreat outside the home and workplace. Deadly force is also allowed to stop arson of a dwelling or occupied building, a burglary of an occupied dwelling or building, or a carjacking (§ 11.81.350). Self-defence is not available to a person in mutual combat, a person who provoked the other with intent to injure, or an initial aggressor, unless they withdrew and clearly communicated it; nor where the force came from a deadly weapon possessed while furthering a felony, during a drug transaction, or in gang-style retaliation (§ 11.81.330). A person who used force as the law permits is not civilly liable to the person they used it against (except police, firefighters, emergency medical and health workers on duty), and a court must award fees and costs to a defendant found not liable (Alaska Stat. § 09.65.330); there is no statutory pretrial immunity hearing for criminal charges.

At home

Alaska Stat. § 11.81.335(b)(1): there is no duty to leave premises the person owns or leases, where they live (temporarily or permanently), or where they are a guest or agent of the owner or resident. Under § 11.81.350(c)(2), a person in possession or control of premises (or their guest or agent) may use deadly force when reasonably believed necessary to stop a burglary of an occupied dwelling or building. Alaska has no statutory presumption of reasonable fear for home intrusions.

What the law says
Alaska Stat. § 11.81.335(b)
A person may not use deadly force under this section if the person knows that, with complete personal safety and with complete safety as to others being defended, the person can avoid the necessity of using deadly force by leaving the area of the encounter, except there is no duty to leave the area if the person is (1) on premises (A) that the person owns or leases; (B) where the person resides, temporarily or permanently; or (C) as a guest or express or implied agent of the owner, lessor, or resident; ... (3) in a building where the person works in the ordinary course of the person's employment; (4) protecting a child or a member of the person's household; or (5) in any other place where the person has a right to be.
Alaska Stat. § 11.81.335(a)
a person who is justified in using nondeadly force in self-defense under AS 11.81.330 may use deadly force in self-defense upon another person when and to the extent the person reasonably believes the use of deadly force is necessary for self-defense against (1) death; (2) serious physical injury; (3) kidnapping ...; (4) sexual assault in the first degree; (5) sexual assault in the second degree; (6) sexual abuse of a minor in the first degree; or (7) robbery in any degree.
Alaska Stat. § 11.81.330(a)–(b)
unless (1) the person used the force in mutual combat not authorized by law; (2) the person claiming self-defense provoked the other's conduct with intent to cause physical injury to the other; (3) the person claiming self-defense was the initial aggressor ...
Alaska Stat. § 09.65.330(a)
A person who uses force in defense of self, other persons, or property as permitted in AS 11.81 is not liable for the death of or injury to the person against whom the force was intended to be used ...

6d0a3d2b0c438c82.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Philippines

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Under the Revised Penal Code, self-defense is a full justification when three things are present: unlawful aggression by the other person, reasonable necessity of the means used to prevent or repel it, and no sufficient provocation by the defender. The code itself says nothing about retreat. The Supreme Court adopted the American 'stand ground when in the right' rule in United States v. Domen (1917): a person who did not provoke the attack and was where he had a right to be is not required to retreat from an assailant advancing with a deadly weapon. Courts measure 'reasonable necessity' by 'rational equivalence' (People v. Olarbe, 2018), not by matching weapons. If some but not all requirements are met and most are present ('incomplete self-defense'), the act is still a crime but the penalty is lowered by one or two degrees (Articles 13 and 69).

At home

The Supreme Court held in United States v. Rivera (G.R. No. 16443, 1921) that a person attacked in his own house 'is not obliged to retreat, but may pursue his adversary until he has secured himself from danger', though a reasonable necessity for killing must still be shown. Article 11 also protects defense of one's 'rights', which courts have applied to the home.

What the law says
Revised Penal Code (Act No. 3815), art. 11(1)
The following do not incur any criminal liability: 1. Anyone who acts in defense of his person or rights, provided that the following circumstances concur: First. Unlawful aggression; Second. Reasonable necessity of the means employed to prevent or repel it; Third. Lack of sufficient provocation on the part of the person defending himself.
Revised Penal Code, art. 13(1)
The following are mitigating circumstances: 1. Those mentioned in the preceding chapter, when all the requisites necessary to justify the act or to exempt from criminal liability in the respective cases are not attendant.
Revised Penal Code, art. 69
A penalty lower by one or two degrees than that prescribed by law shall be imposed if the deed is not wholly excusable by reason of the lack of some of the conditions required to justify the same or to exempt from criminal liability in the several cases mentioned in articles 11 and 12, provided that the majority of such conditions be present.
United States v. Domen, G.R. No. L-12963 (Supreme Court, 25 Oct 1917)
The accused did not provoke the assault. The accused was where he had a right to be. The law did not require him to retreat when his assailant was rapidly advancing upon him in a threatening manner with a deadly weapon.
United States v. Rivera, G.R. No. 16443 (Supreme Court, 21 Mar 1921), syllabus
When a person is attacked in his own house, he has a right to protect it, and those within it, from the intrusion or attack. He may repel force by force in defense of person, habitation, or property, against one who manifestly intends or endeavors by violence or surprise to commit a felony, such as arson, upon either. In such case one is not obliged to retreat, but may pursue his adversary until he has secured himself from danger.
People v. Olarbe, G.R. No. 227421 (Supreme Court, 23 Jul 2018)
It is settled that reasonable necessity of the means employed does not imply material commensurability between the means of attack and defense. What the law requires is rational equivalence...

e34e025f550961bb.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Mexico

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under the Federal Penal Code (art. 15 IV), a person may repel a real, current or imminent unlawful attack on their own or another's legal interests if the defence is necessary and the means used are reasonable, and the defender did not deliberately provoke it. There is no statutory duty to retreat; a Supreme Court (SCJN) thesis holds that the possibility of flight should not be imposed as a condition on the person attacked, although older theses deny the defence where the person could easily have avoided the attack by other means. Anyone who tries to break into a home is presumed to be a lawful target of defence, unless shown otherwise. Excessive self-defence is still punished as an intentional offence, but at one quarter of the normal penalty (art. 16). Each of Mexico's 32 states also has its own penal code; this entry covers the federal code only.

At home

Federal Penal Code art. 15(IV) presumes legitimate defence, unless proven otherwise, when harm is caused to someone who tries to enter the home of the agent or their family without right, or who is found there in circumstances showing a probable attack.

What the law says
Código Penal Federal, art. 15, fracción IV
Se repela una agresión real, actual o inminente, y sin derecho, en protección de bienes jurídicos propios o ajenos, siempre que exista necesidad de la defensa y racionalidad de los medios empleados y no medie provocación dolosa suficiente e inmediata por parte del agredido o de la persona a quien se defiende. Se presumirá como defensa legítima, salvo prueba en contrario, el hecho de causar daño a quien por cualquier medio trate de penetrar, sin derecho, al hogar del agente, al de su familia, a sus dependencias, o a los de cualquier persona que tenga la obligación de defender, al sitio donde se encuentren bienes propios o ajenos respecto de los que exista la misma obligación; o bien, lo encuentre en alguno de aquellos lugares en circunstancias tales que revelen la probabilidad de una agresión;
Código Penal Federal, art. 16
En los casos de exceso de legítima defensa o exceso en cualquier otra causa de justificación se impondrá la cuarta parte de la sanción correspondiente al delito de que se trate, quedando subsistente la imputación a título doloso.
SCJN, Primera Sala, tesis aislada, Quinta Época, registro 814826 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA. EVITABILIDAD DEL PELIGRO)
no debe imponerse como condición al injustamente agredido la posibilidad de la fuga, pues en esas condiciones el ejercicio de la legítima defensa se tornaría en imposible en la mayoría de los casos
SCJN, tesis registro 806596 (LEGITIMA DEFENSA)
no puede aceptarse la defensa legítima, si el procesado no estuvo en inminente peligro de perder la vida o en condiciones de suponer este peligro, y pudo muy bien evitar la agresión de que fue víctima por otros medios, o en último extremo, preverla.

87db0e242b92a44d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Greece

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Article 22 of the Greek Penal Code (Law 4619/2019) says an act done in self-defence is not unlawful; self-defence is the 'necessary' harm done to an attacker to defend oneself or another against a present and unjust attack. How much defence is necessary is judged by how dangerous the attack is, the kind of harm threatened, the manner and intensity of the attack and the other circumstances. The code does not mention retreat or the home, and no Greek court decision or commentary on a duty to retreat was found within this search. Under Article 23, exceeding the limits intentionally is punished with a reduced penalty, and negligently under the negligence provisions; there is no punishment if the excess came from fear or agitation caused by the attack. A person who deliberately provoked the attack to commit a crime under the pretext of self-defence is not excused (Article 24). The text quoted is the 2019 code as enacted; later amendments were not checked.

What the law says
Ποινικός Κώδικας (Law 4619/2019, ΦΕΚ Α' 95/11.6.2019), άρθρα 22-24
Άρθρο 22 Άμυνα 1. Δεν είναι άδικη η πράξη που τελείται σε κατάσταση άμυνας. 2. Άμυνα είναι η αναγκαία προσβολή του επιτιθεμένου στην οποία προβαίνει το άτομο προς υπεράσπιση του εαυτού του ή άλλου από παρούσα και άδικη επίθεση που στρέφεται εναντίον τους. 3. Το αναγκαίο μέτρο της άμυνας κρίνεται από τον βαθμό επικινδυνότητας της επίθεσης, από το είδος της προσβολής που απειλείται, από τον τρόπο και την ένταση της επίθεσης και από τις υπόλοιπες περιστάσεις. Άρθρο 23 Υπέρβαση άμυνας Όποιος υπερβαίνει τα όρια της άμυνας τιμωρείται, αν η υπέρβαση έγινε με πρόθεση, με ποινή ελαττωμένη, και αν έγινε από αμέλεια, σύμφωνα με τις σχετικές με αυτήν διατάξεις. Μένει ατιμώρητος και δεν του καταλογίζεται η υπέρβαση, αν ενέργησε με αυτόν τον τρόπο εξαιτίας του φόβου ή της ταραχής που του προκάλεσε η επίθεση. Άρθρο 24 Υπαίτια κατάσταση άμυνας Δεν απαλλάσσεται από την ποινή που ορίζει ο νόμος όποιος με πρόθεση προκάλεσε την επίθεση άλλου για να διαπράξει εναντίον του αξιόποινη πράξη με το πρόσχημα της άμυνας.

dd7977b6e384a7c7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Sweden

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under chapter 24, section 1 of the Swedish Penal Code (Brottsbalken), an act done in self-defence is a crime only if it is 'manifestly indefensible' (uppenbart oförsvarlig) given the nature of the attack, the importance of what is attacked and the circumstances in general. The code does not mention retreat. A 2025 government inquiry directive (Dir. 2025:82) reports public criticism, following court cases about people attacked at their homes (the Vallåkra and Rättvik cases), that individuals have 'too great a duty to flee' even when fleeing is risky, which shows the chance to escape is weighed by courts. Under section 6 (excess), an act that was manifestly indefensible can still go unpunished if the person 'could hardly have kept their composure', judging the danger, the time available and the person's own characteristics. The inquiry was asked to propose a stronger right of self-defence for people attacked in their home, near their family, or when outnumbered or physically weaker, with a final report due by 10 September 2027.

At home

Chapter 24, section 1 gives a right of self-defence against anyone who has unlawfully forced or is trying to force entry into a room, house, yard or vessel, and against anyone who refuses to leave a dwelling when told to. The government's 2025 inquiry directive notes the Council on Legislation found it unclear how far this covers intruders in gardens after the 2022 trespass reform.

What the law says
Brottsbalken (Penal Code), chapter 24, section 1 (English translation, 1999 version)
An act committed by a person in self-defence constitutes a crime only if, having regard to the nature of the aggression, the importance of its object and the circumstances in general, it is clearly unjustifiable. A right to act in self-defence exists against, 1. an initiated or imminent criminal attack on a person or property, 2. a person who violently or by the threat of violence or in some other way obstructs the repossession of property when caught in the act, 3. a person who has unlawfully forced or is attempting to force entry into a room, house, yard or vessel, or 4. a person who refuses to leave a dwelling when ordered to do so. (Law 1994:458)
Brottsbalken 24 kap. 1 § (as summarised in Dir. 2025:82)
En gärning som någon begår i nödvärn utgör brott endast om den med hänsyn till angreppets beskaffenhet, det angripnas betydelse och omständigheterna i övrigt är uppenbart oförsvarlig.

76ca545f591ac13a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

New Zealand

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

New Zealand's Crimes Act 1961 (s 48) justifies such force as, in the circumstances as the person believes them to be, it is reasonable to use in defence of themselves or another; the prosecution must disprove self-defence. There is no stated duty to retreat, but according to the Law Commission (Report 139, 2016) courts judging reasonableness have required an imminent threat and look closely at whether the defendant had an alternative to force, 'such as leaving or seeking help from Police' (confirmed in R v Wang, Court of Appeal). There is no partial defence of excessive self-defence: the Commission reports it has been disavowed by New Zealand courts, so force found unreasonable gives no defence, though reduced blame may be reflected at sentencing. The official legislation website could not be opened from here; s 48 is quoted from the Law Commission report.

At home

No separate home-defence rule found in the sources opened; the general test in s 48 applies.

What the law says
Crimes Act 1961, s 48 (as quoted in Law Commission Report 139, para 5.11)
Everyone is justified in using, in the defence of himself or herself or another such force as, in the circumstances as he or she believes them to be, it is reasonable to use.
Law Commission, Report 139 (2016), para 6.16
In judging the reasonableness of the force used by a defendant, courts have traditionally required there to be an immediacy of life-threatening violence to justify the killing of another in self-defence. This is known as the requirement for “imminence”. Closely related to the concept of imminence is whether the defendant had an alternative to the use of force, such as leaving or seeking help from Police.

c2565f466e06d0d7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Argentina

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 34(6) of the Penal Code exempts from punishment a person who acts in defence of themselves or their rights if three conditions are met: an unlawful aggression, "rational necessity of the means used" to prevent or repel it, and no sufficient provocation by the defender. The Code does not mention retreat, and the sources opened here did not settle whether flight is expected. Under art. 35, a person who exceeds the limits imposed by law or necessity is punished with the penalty for the negligent (culpable) version of the offence, which is lighter than the intentional one. Defence of others is allowed on similar terms (art. 34(7)).

At home

Art. 34(6) presumes the conditions of self-defence are met for a person who, at night, repels the climbing over or breaking of the fences, walls or entrances of their house or inhabited flat, "whatever the harm caused to the aggressor", and likewise for a person who finds a stranger inside their home, provided there is resistance.

What the law says
Código Penal de la Nación (Ley 11.179), art. 34 inc. 6 y 7
ARTICULO 34.- No son punibles: ... 6º. El que obrare en defensa propia o de sus derechos, siempre que concurrieren las siguientes circunstancias: a) Agresión ilegítima; b) Necesidad racional del medio empleado para impedirla o repelerla; c) Falta de provocación suficiente por parte del que se defiende. Se entenderá que concurren estas circunstancias respecto de aquel que durante la noche rechazare el escalamiento o fractura de los cercados, paredes o entradas de su casa, o departamento habitado o de sus dependencias, cualquiera que sea el daño ocasionado al agresor. Igualmente respecto de aquél que encontrare a un extraño dentro de su hogar, siempre que haya resistencia; 7º. El que obrare en defensa de la persona o derechos de otro, siempre que concurran las circunstancias a) y b) del inciso anterior y caso de haber precedido provocación suficiente por parte del agredido, la de que no haya participado en ella el tercero defensor.
Código Penal, art. 35 (exceso)
ARTICULO 35.- El que hubiere excedido los límites impuestos por la Ley, por la autoridad o por la necesidad, será castigado con la pena fijada para el delito por culpa o imprudencia.

b1f910158e430063.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Kazakhstan

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Kazakhstan's Criminal Code of 2014 (art. 32) gives everyone the right of necessary defence and states that this right exists 'regardless of the possibility of avoiding the socially dangerous attack or of seeking help from other persons or state bodies' — so there is no duty to retreat. Defence is unlawful only if it is clearly out of proportion to the nature and danger of the attack, causing clearly excessive harm, and such excess is punishable only if intentional. Since a 2022 amendment, harm caused against someone attacking a person's life, or repelling an armed or life-threatening attack, a violent intrusion into a home or premises, or arson of a home, or when surprise prevented the defender from judging the danger, is not an excess. Killing in excess of necessary defence is a separate, lighter offence (art. 102: restriction of liberty or imprisonment up to two years).

At home

Art. 32(2) lists defence of the dwelling (жилище) among protected interests; since 2022 (Law No. 136-VII of 11 July 2022) harm caused while repelling a violent intrusion into a dwelling or premises, or arson of a dwelling, is by statute not an excess of necessary defence.

What the law says
Criminal Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 226-V of 3 July 2014, art. 32(1) (Russian)
Необходимой обороной признается правомерная защита личности и прав обороняющегося и других лиц, а также охраняемых законом интересов общества и государства от общественно опасного посягательства, в том числе путем причинения вреда посягающему лицу. Право на необходимую оборону имеют в равной мере все лица независимо от их профессиональной или иной специальной подготовки и служебного положения. Это право принадлежит лицу независимо от возможности избежать общественно опасного посягательства либо обратиться за помощью к другим лицам или государственным органам.
Criminal Code (Kazakhstan), art. 32(3) (Russian)
Превышением пределов необходимой обороны признается явное несоответствие защиты характеру и степени общественной опасности посягательства, в результате чего посягающему причиняется явно чрезмерный, не вызываемый обстановкой вред. Такое превышение влечет за собой уголовную ответственность лишь в случаях умышленного причинения вреда. Не является превышением пределов необходимой обороны причинение вреда лицу, посягающему на жизнь человека, либо при отражении иного посягательства, сопряженного с вооруженным нападением или насилием, опасным для жизни обороняющегося или других лиц, либо с непосредственной угрозой такого насилия, либо с насильственным вторжением в жилище, помещение, либо с поджогом жилища, помещения, а также если обороняющийся вследствие внезапности посягательства не мог объективно оценить степень и характер опасности нападения.
Criminal Code (Kazakhstan), art. 102 (Russian)
Убийство, совершенное при превышении пределов необходимой обороны, – наказывается ограничением свободы на срок до двух лет либо лишением свободы на тот же срок.

Vietnam

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 22 of the 2015 Criminal Code says 'legitimate defence' (phòng vệ chính đáng) means fighting back in a necessary way against a person who is attacking one's own or another's legitimate rights or interests, or those of the state or an organisation, and it is not a crime. The code does not mention retreat. Supreme People's Court Resolution No. 02 on the 1985 Criminal Code (expired but, per LuatVietnam, not yet replaced and still cited) says defence may not only fend off the attack but actively fight the attacker, and the response must not be grossly out of proportion to the attack, though it need not cause equal or lesser harm. Fighting back clearly beyond what was necessary ('exceeding the limits of legitimate defence') is a crime but a mitigating circumstance, and killing in that situation is a separate offence (article 126) carrying non-custodial reform or 3 months to 2 years in prison (2 to 5 years if two or more people are killed).

What the law says
Criminal Code 2015 (No. 100/2015/QH13), art. 22(1)-(2)
1. Phòng vệ chính đáng là hành vi của người vì bảo vệ quyền hoặc lợi ích chính đáng của mình, của người khác hoặc lợi ích của Nhà nước, của cơ quan, tổ chức mà chống trả lại một cách cần thiết người đang có hành vi xâm phạm các lợi ích nói trên. Phòng vệ chính đáng không phải là tội phạm. 2. Vượt quá giới hạn phòng vệ chính đáng là hành vi chống trả rõ ràng quá mức cần thiết, không phù hợp với tính chất và mức độ nguy hiểm cho xã hội của hành vi xâm hại. Người có hành vi vượt quá giới hạn phòng vệ chính đáng phải chịu trách nhiệm hình sự theo quy định của Bộ luật này.
Supreme People's Court Judicial Council Resolution No. 02 (guidance on the 1985 Criminal Code), section II, as summarised by LuatVietnam
Phòng vệ chính đáng không chỉ gạt bỏ sự đe dọa, đẩy lùi sự tấn công, mà còn có thể tích cực chống lại sự xâm hại, gây thiệt hại cho chính người xâm hại. ... Hành vi phòng vệ phải tương xứng với hành vi xâm hại, tức là không có sự chênh lệch quá đáng giữa hành vi phòng vệ với tính chất và mức độ nguy hiểm của hành vi xâm hại.
Criminal Code 2015, art. 126 (as summarised by Lawyers of Vietnam journal)
người nào giết người trong trường hợp vượt quá giới hạn phòng vệ chính đáng hoặc trong trường hợp vượt quá mức cần thiết khi bắt giữ người phạm tội, thì bị phạt cải tạo không giam giữ đến 02 năm hoặc phạt tù từ 03 tháng đến 02 năm.

be6b39a58e4fdfab.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Svalbard

A Norwegian archipelago governed under the Svalbard Treaty. Shown with the entry for Norway, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Under section 18 of the Norwegian Penal Code (2005), an otherwise punishable act is lawful when it is done to avert an unlawful attack, goes no further than necessary, and does not 'obviously' go beyond what is justifiable given how dangerous the attack is, what interest it violates and the attacker's guilt. The statute does not mention retreat, but because force must be 'necessary', a lawyer answering for the state youth-information service ung.no wrote in 2023 that if there were other ways to avert the attack, 'such as calling for help or running away', a killing cannot be claimed as self-defence; the Supreme Court's appeals committee has also upheld a conviction where the defendant had 'several alternative courses of action' and had partly provoked the fight (HR-2022-1377-U). Someone who goes too far can still be acquitted where 'special reasons' justify it, and the sentence can in any case be reduced (sections 80 and 81, as described by the national encyclopedia). Lawful self-defence is not just unpunished but lawful, so the Supreme Court held in 2018 (HR-2018-2427-A) that the defender cannot be ordered to pay damages when the attack was real.

At home

No separate home-defence rule was found; section 18 applies to attacks on persons and on property alike.

What the law says
Straffeloven (Penal Code 2005), § 18 første ledd (as quoted by the Supreme Court in HR-2022-1377-U)
En handling som ellers ville være straffbar, er lovlig når den a. blir foretatt for å avverge et ulovlig angrep, b. ikke går lenger enn nødvendig, og c. ikke går åpenbart ut over hva som er forsvarlig under hensyn til hvor farlig angrepet er, hva slags interesse som angrepet krenker, og angriperens skyld.

ae1d208fd1268805.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Finland

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Chapter 4, section 4 of the Finnish Criminal Code allows an act necessary to defend against an ongoing or imminent unlawful attack, unless it 'manifestly exceeds' what is justifiable when the nature and strength of the attack, the people involved and other circumstances are weighed as a whole. According to a 2022 peer-reviewed article citing the government bill (HE 44/2002) and Supreme Court case law, the mere fact that the defender could have escaped does not by itself make the defence unlawful, especially when the attacker is not a child or mentally ill person. The same article reports, however, that the courts of appeal often stress the defender's chance to flee or leave when judging whether the defence was justifiable. If the defence goes beyond the limits (excessive self-defence), the person is still exempt from liability when they could not reasonably have been expected to act otherwise, given the danger and suddenness of the attack.

At home

No separate home-defence rule in the Criminal Code; the general self-defence section applies.

What the law says
Criminal Code (Rikoslaki 39/1889), chapter 4, section 4 (515/2003) (unofficial English translation)
An act that is necessary to defend against an ongoing or imminent unlawful attack is permissible as self-defence, unless the act manifestly exceeds what is to be deemed justifiable when assessed as a whole, taking into consideration the nature and strength of the attack, the personal characteristics of the defender and the attacker, and the other circumstances. If the defence exceeds the limits of self-defence (excessive self-defence), the perpetrator is, nonetheless, exempt from criminal liability if the circumstances were such that the perpetrator could not have reasonably been expected to act otherwise, taking into consideration the dangerousness and unexpected nature of the attack and the situation also in other respects.

0997adfdd927cab7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

France

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 122-5 of the Penal Code, a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same time in a way required by the necessity of self-defence, unless the means used are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack. The defence must be simultaneous with the attack; a blow struck after the attacker has left is treated as ordinary violence. Neither art. 122-5 nor art. 122-6 mentions retreat, and the sources opened here did not address whether flight is expected. Defence of property can never justify intentional homicide. Judges decide whether the defence was disproportionate; Encyclopaedia Universalis notes that an excessive response may lead to mitigating circumstances or a conviction for a lesser offence rather than full exoneration.

At home

Art. 122-6 of the Penal Code presumes self-defence for a person who acts "to repel, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place", and against perpetrators of violent theft or looting. The presumption is rebuttable and does not cover daytime intrusions, which fall under the general rule of art. 122-5.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 122-5
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal, art. 122-6
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

b3bd2bc06d65c229.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Venezuela

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 65(3) of Venezuela's Penal Code, a person who acts in defence of their own person or rights is not punishable if there was an unlawful attack by the person harmed, the means used were necessary to prevent or repel it, and the defender did not sufficiently provoke it. Article 66 says that someone who exceeds the defence, or the means used, 'doing more than necessary', is punished with the normal penalty reduced by one to two thirds. The code does not mention retreat or contain a home-defence rule in the text found, and no Venezuelan court decision on retreat was found. The text used is the version published in Gaceta Oficial No. 5494 Extraordinario of 20 October 2000 (WIPO Lex copy); later reforms were not checked.

What the law says
Código Penal (Gaceta Oficial N° 5494 Extraordinario, 20 Oct. 2000), art. 65(3)
No es punible: [...] 3. El que obra en defensa de su propia persona o derecho, siempre que concurran las circunstancias siguientes: a Agresión ilegítima por parte del que resulta ofendido por el hecho. b. Necesidad del medio empleado para impedirla o repelerla. c. Falta de provocación, suficiente de parte del que pretenda haber obrado en defensa propia
Código Penal (2000), art. 66
El que traspasare los límites impuestos por la Ley en el caso del número 1º del artículo anterior, y por la autoridad que dio la orden en el caso del número 2º del mismo, y el que se excediere en la defensa, o en los medios empleados para salvarse del peligro grave e inminente, haciendo más de lo necesario, será castigado con la pena correspondiente, disminuida desde uno a dos tercios. La pena pecuniaria se aplicará con disminución de la mitad.

bc644bcb6e716759.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Italy

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Article 52 of the Italian Penal Code exempts from punishment a person forced to act by the need to defend their own or another's right against a present danger of an unjust offence, 'provided that the defence is proportionate to the offence'. The code does not mention retreat, but the annotated code commentary on Brocardi.it reports that prevailing legal doctrine allows self-defence by someone who could have fled only where flight would itself expose them or others to harm equal to or greater than the harm caused by defending, so a safe escape is expected (the Latin maxim cited is 'commodus discessus', a convenient withdrawal). Inside a home or workplace, statutory presumptions introduced in 2006 and strengthened in 2019 (Law 26 April 2019 no. 36) treat the defence as proportionate and an intrusion with violence or threats as always justifying defence. If a person negligently exceeds the limits of self-defence, they are punished under the rules for negligent crimes (Article 55); since 2019 there is no punishment for excess in the home cases when the person acted in grave disturbance caused by the danger.

At home

Article 52(2)-(4) of the Penal Code (added 2006, amended 2019): when someone lawfully present in a home (or a shop, office or other workplace) uses a lawfully held weapon or other suitable means to defend their own or another's safety, or property where there is no withdrawal by the intruder and a danger of aggression, the defence is always deemed proportionate; and a person who repels an intrusion carried out with violence or threat of weapons or other physical coercion 'always' acts in legitimate defence. Article 55(2) excludes punishment for excess in these home cases when the person acted in 'grave disturbance' caused by the danger.

What the law says
Codice penale, art. 52 (Difesa legittima)
Non è punibile chi ha commesso il fatto per esservi stato costretto dalla necessità di difendere un diritto proprio od altrui contro il pericolo attuale di un'offesa ingiusta, sempre che la difesa sia proporzionata all'offesa. Nei casi previsti dall'articolo 614, primo e secondo comma, sussiste sempre il rapporto di proporzione di cui al primo comma del presente articolo se taluno legittimamente presente in uno dei luoghi ivi indicati usa un'arma legittimamente detenuta o altro mezzo idoneo al fine di difendere: a) la propria o la altrui incolumità; b) i beni propri o altrui, quando non vi è desistenza e vi è pericolo d'aggressione. Le disposizioni di cui al secondo e al quarto comma si applicano anche nel caso in cui il fatto sia avvenuto all'interno di ogni altro luogo ove venga esercitata un'attività commerciale, professionale o imprenditoriale. Nei casi di cui al secondo e al terzo comma agisce sempre in stato di legittima difesa colui che compie un atto per respingere l'intrusione posta in essere, con violenza o minaccia di uso di armi o di altri mezzi di coazione fisica, da parte di una o più persone.
Codice penale, art. 55 (Eccesso colposo)
Quando, nel commettere alcuno dei fatti preveduti dagli articoli 51, 52, 53 e 54, si eccedono colposamente i limiti stabiliti dalla legge o dall'ordine dell'Autorità ovvero imposti dalla necessità, si applicano le disposizioni concernenti i delitti colposi, se il fatto è preveduto dalla legge come delitto colposo. Nei casi di cui ai commi secondo, terzo e quarto dell'articolo 52, la punibilità è esclusa se chi ha commesso il fatto per la salvaguardia della propria o altrui incolumità ha agito nelle condizioni di cui all'articolo 61, primo comma, n. 5) ovvero in stato di grave turbamento, derivante dalla situazione di pericolo in atto.

ffb7990564e64eee.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Maldives

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

The Maldives Penal Code (Law No. 9/2014) has a chapter on justification defences, with self-defence in s 45. Only the Dhivehi text could be opened, and the following is a rough unofficial reading: force is allowed against a person who is using, or is believed about to use, unlawful force against oneself or another, if it is not disproportionate to the expected harm (s 45(a)); force likely to kill or cause serious bodily injury is allowed only to defend against a threat of death, serious bodily injury or rape (s 45(b)). No retreat requirement was found in s 45 as read, but because the reading relies on a non-official interpretation of the Dhivehi text, the retreat question is marked unsettled. Section 1108 lowers the sentence by one or two grades when an offender believed a justification applied or came close to meeting its conditions (imperfect justification).

What the law says
Penal Code (Law No. 9/2014), s 45(a)–(b) (Dhivehi)
(ހ) މި މާއްދާގެ (ށ) ގައި ބަޔާންކޮށްފައިވާ އުސޫލުތަކަށް އުނިކަން ނާންނާނެ ގޮތުގެމަތިން، މީހަކު ބާރުގެ ބޭނުންކުރުން ހުއްދަވެގެންވަނީ އަންނަނިވި ޙާލަތްތަކުގައި އަންނަނިވި ސަބަބުތަކަށްޓަކައެވެ: (1) އަންނަނިވި ފަރާތްތަކާ ދެކޮޅަށް އެހެން މީހަކު ހުއްދަނޫން ގޮތެއްގައި ބާރުގެބޭނުން ކުރާ ހިނދުގައި ނުވަތަ ބާރުގެ ބޭނުންކޮށްފާނެ ކަމަށް ބެލެވޭ ހިނދުގައި ބޭނުންކުރަންޖެހޭ ބާރަކަށްވުން؛ (i) ތިމާގެ އަމިއްލަ ނަފުސު؛ ނުވަތަ (ii) އެހެން މީހެއްގެ ނަފުސު؛ އަދި (2) ބޭނުންކުރާ ބާރަކީ ކުރިމަތިވާނެކަމަށް ބެލެވޭ ގެއްލުމާ އަޅައިބަލާއިރު ނިސްބަތުން އިތުރަށް ބޭނުންކުރެވުނު ބާރަކަށް ނުވުން. (ށ) މި މާއްދާގެ (ހ) ގެ ދަށުން ހިންގޭ ޢަމަލެއްގައި ބާރުގެ ބޭނުންކުރުމުގައި މީހަކު މަރުވެދާ ފަދަ ނުވަތަ މީހަކަށް ޖިސްމާނީ ބޮޑު އަނިޔާ ލިބިދާ ފަދަ ގޮތަކަށް ބާރުގެ ބޭނުންކުރުން ހުއްދަވެގެންވާނީ އެފަދަ ބާރެއްގެ ބޭނުންކުރަނީ މީހަކު މަރުވެދާނެކަމުގެ ނުރައްކާ ކުރިމަތިވާ ހިނދުގައި އެކަމުން ދިފާޢުވުމަށާއި، ބޮޑެތި ޖިސްމާނީ އަނިޔާ ފޯރުކޮށްފާނެ ކަމުގެ ނުރައްކާ ކުރިމަތިވާ ހިނދުގައި އެކަމުން ދިފާޢުވުމަށާއި، ރޭޕްކޮށްފާނެކަމުގެ ނުރައްކާ ކުރިމަތިވާ ހިނދުގައި އެކަމުން ދިފާޢުވުމަށެވެ.
Penal Code (Law No. 9/2014), s 1108 (Dhivehi)
ކުށްވެރިޔާ، ކުށުގެ ޢަމަލު ހިންގީ، އޭނާއަށް މި ޤާނޫނުގެ 40 ވަނަ ބާބު (ހުއްދަ ކުރެވިގެންވާ ދިފާޢު) ގައި ބަޔާންކޮށްފައިވާ ހުއްދަ ކުރެވިފައިވާ ދިފާޢެއް އޮތްކަމަށް ޤަބޫލުކުރެވިގެން ކަމަށްވާނަމަ، އޭނާގެ މައްޗަށް ކަނޑައަޅަންޖެހޭ އަދަބު، އަންނަނިވި ގޮތުގެމަތިން، އަދަބު ކަނޑައެޅުމުގެ އަސާސީ މިންގަނޑަށްވުރެ ދަށްވާނެއެވެ. (ހ) އެއްދަރަޖަ، ނުވަތަ (ށ) ... ހުއްދަ ކުރެވިފައިވާ ދިފާޢުގެ ޙާލަތެއް ފުރިހަމަވުމާ ކައިރިވެފައިވާނަމަ، އަދަބު ކަނޑައެޅުމުގެ އަސާސީ މިންގަނޑަށްވުރެ 2 ދަރަޖަ.

f5acc691a88e4c1e.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Iceland

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Article 12 of Iceland's General Penal Code (no. 19/1940) says an act done in self-defence is not punishable if it was necessary to prevent or avert an unlawful attack that has begun or is imminent, provided the defence was not clearly more dangerous than the attack and the harm it threatened. If a person goes beyond the limits of lawful self-defence because they were so frightened or confused that they could not keep full control of themselves, they are not punished. The code does not mention retreat or the home, and no Icelandic court decision or commentary on a duty to retreat could be opened (an Icelandic university thesis repository was blocked). The official consolidated text (October 2026) shows no amendments to Article 12.

What the law says
Almenn hegningarlög nr. 19/1940 (General Penal Code), Article 12 (unofficial English translation)
This work is unpunished by emergency response, insofar as it has been necessary to prevent or avert an unlawful attack that is initiated or imminent, provided that no defenses have been used that are clearly more dangerous than the attack and damage what could be expected of her gave reason. If a person has exceeded the limits of permissible emergency protection, and the reason for this is that he has become so frightened or astonished that he could not take full care of himself, he shall not be punished.
Almenn hegningarlög nr. 19/1940, 12. gr. (opening words, official Icelandic text)
Það verk er refsilaust, sem menn vinna af neyðarvörn

ae7b80ff0bb07a99.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

South Korea

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 21 of the Criminal Act says an act to prevent an impending and unjust attack on one's own or another's legal interests is not punishable 'if there are reasonable grounds'. The Act does not mention retreat. According to a Seoul law-firm explainer, courts read 'reasonable grounds' to require a means adequate to stop the attack and, where several means exist, the one causing the least harm, and judge this more strictly for minor attacks. If the defence goes beyond normal limits ('excessive self-defence'), the punishment may be reduced or waived, and it is not punishable at all if done at night or in other alarming conditions out of fear, surprise, excitement or confusion. In decision 2021Hunma994 (31 August 2023), discussed by the firm D&A LLC on Mondaq, the Constitutional Court treated force used 'solely to defend oneself and to escape' from an assault as socially acceptable.

At home

No separate home-defence rule in the Criminal Act. In the Wonju 'braindead burglar' case, a homeowner was convicted (with probation) because the court saw his second round of blows against an intruder as 'more offensive than defensive in nature'; the Supreme Court affirmed on 12 May 2016 (reported by K Law Guru).

What the law says
Criminal Act, art. 21 (Korean)
제21조(정당방위) ①자기 또는 타인의 법익에 대한 현재의 부당한 침해를 방위하기 위한 행위는 상당한 이유가 있는 때에는 벌하지 아니한다. ②방위행위가 그 정도를 초과한 때에는 정황에 의하여 그 형을 감경 또는 면제할 수 있다. ③전항의 경우에 그 행위가 야간 기타 불안스러운 상태하에서 공포, 경악, 흥분 또는 당황으로 인한 때에는 벌하지 아니한다.
Criminal Act, art. 21 (KLRI English translation, unofficial)
(1) An act which is performed in order to prevent impending and unjust infringement of one's own or another person's legal interest shall not be punishable if there are reasonable grounds for that act. (2) When a preventive act has exceeded normal limits, the punishment may be mitigated or remitted according to the extenuating circumstances. (3) In the case of the preceding paragraph, an act performed through fear, surprise, excitement, or confusion in the night or under other extraordinary circumstances shall not be punishable.

6104e0ed2a2b1be0.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Thailand

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Section 68 of the Criminal Code says a person who must act to protect his own or another's rights from an imminent, unlawful attack acts in lawful defence and commits no offence if the act was reasonable under the circumstances ('พอสมควรแก่เหตุ'). The code does not mention retreat. The Secretary-General of the Lawyers Council, quoted by Daily News, explains that the defender should use the least harmful means available and keep the response in proportion to the danger, and that a person who started the trouble or freely joined a fight cannot claim defence (Supreme Court decisions 2154/2519, 1961/2528, 6630/2562). Under section 69, if the defence went beyond what was reasonable or necessary, the court may impose less than the normal punishment, or none at all if the act came from excitement, fright or fear.

At home

No separate home-defence rule. A Payap University journal article cites Supreme Court Decision 1923/2519 (1976), where a man whose storehouse had been burgled before strung an electrified wire that killed an intruding thief; the court held this was lawful defence of property, proportionate to the circumstances.

What the law says
Criminal Code, s. 68 (Thai)
ผู้ใดจำต้องกระทำการใดเพื่อป้องกันสิทธิของตนหรือผู้อื่นให้พ้นอันตรายซึ่งเกิดจากการประทุษร้ายอันละเมิดต่อกฎหมาย และเป็นภยันตรายที่ใกล้จะถึง ถ้าได้กระทำพอสมควรแก่เหตุ การกระทำนั้นเป็นการป้องกันโดยชอบด้วยกฎหมาย ผู้นั้นไม่มีความผิด
Criminal Code, ss. 68-69 (unofficial English translation)
Section 68 Any person is to commit any act for defending his own right or other person's right in order to except from a danger arising out of violence tortuous to the law and such danger to be imminent, if reasonably having committed under the circumstance, such act is a lawful defense, and such person shall not have a quilt. Section 69 In the cases as provided in Sections 67 and 68, if the act committed is in excess of what is reasonable under the circumstances or in excess of what is necessary, or in excess of what is necessary for the defense, the Court may inflict less punishment to any extent than that provided by the law for such offence. But, if such act occurs out of excitement, fright or fear, the Court may not inflict any punishment at all.

a64f2cca292fcadb.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Colombia

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 32.6 of the Penal Code (Ley 599 of 2000) removes criminal liability for a person who acts out of the need to defend their own or another's right against an unjust, current or imminent aggression. Before 2022 the text required that the defence be "proportionate to the aggression"; the 2022 amendment (Ley 2197) left the sentence ending "siempre que la defensa sea:" and added a presumption for home and vehicle intrusions. The Supreme Court, as cited in a 2023 law-review study, describes the necessity requirement as an aggression "not rationally avertable by another route", so the chance to avoid the attack is weighed, though no code text expressly requires retreat. A person who exceeds the limits of self-defence is not acquitted but receives a reduced penalty: no less than one sixth of the minimum and no more than half of the maximum for the offence.

At home

Since 2022 (Ley 2197) art. 32.6.1 presumes self-defence ("legítima defensa privilegiada") against a stranger who uses tricks or violence to enter or remain without right in a dwelling, its immediate outbuildings, or an occupied vehicle, and states that lethal force may be used "exceptionally". A paragraph adds that in these cases the defence is still assessed under a standard of proportionality.

What the law says
Código Penal (Ley 599 de 2000), art. 32 num. 6 (as amended by Ley 2197 de 2022)
6. Se obre por la necesidad de defender un derecho propio o ajeno contra injusta agresión actual o inminente, siempre que la defensa sea: 6.1. Legítima defensa privilegiada. Se presume también como legítima la defensa que se ejerza para rechazar al extraño que usando maniobras o mediante violencia penetre o permanezca arbitrariamente en habitación o dependencias inmediatas, o vehículo ocupado. La fuerza letal se podrá ejercer de forma excepcional para repeler la agresión al derecho propio o ajeno. PARÁGRAFO. En los casos del ejercicio de la legítima defensa privilegiada, la valoración de la defensa se deberá aplicar un estándar de proporcionalidad en el elemento de racionalidad de la conducta.
Código Penal, art. 32 (excess)
El que exceda los límites propios de las causales consagradas en los numerales 3, 4, 5, 6 y 7 precedentes, incurrirá en una pena no menor de la sexta parte del mínimo ni mayor de la mitad del máximo de la señalada para la respectiva conducta punible.

3876bd4a46bb23cd.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Turkey

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Turkey's Penal Code (Law 5237 of 2004), article 25(1), excuses acts done out of the necessity to repel, at that moment and in proportion to the attack, an unjust attack on one's own or another's rights that is happening, about to happen, or certain to be repeated. The article on self-defence has no 'no other way out' wording; that wording appears only in the separate necessity rule in article 25(2). A law-firm guide (Harbiye Hukuk) says Turkish law does not impose a duty to flee and that the Court of Cassation's General Criminal Assembly has stressed that 'in no case can a duty to flee be imposed on the accused'; the defence must still be necessary and proportionate. A Court of Cassation General Assembly ruling of 18 September 2018 (E.2015/1-424, K.2018/399), as summarised on Hukuki Haber, held that a woman who killed her abusive husband while he lay asleep from drink was not acting under necessity because she could have left or taken other measures. If the limits of a defence are exceeded without intent, the penalty for the negligent offence is reduced by one sixth to one third (art. 27(1)); if excess in self-defence came from excusable excitement, fear or panic, there is no punishment at all (art. 27(2)).

What the law says
Türk Ceza Kanunu (Law 5237), art. 25(1) – Meşru savunma
Gerek kendisine ve gerek başkasına ait bir hakka yönelmiş, gerçekleşen, gerçekleşmesi veya tekrarı muhakkak olan haksız bir saldırıyı o anda hal ve koşullara göre saldırı ile orantılı biçimde defetmek zorunluluğu ile işlenen fiillerden dolayı faile ceza verilmez.
Turkish Criminal Code, art. 25(1) (English translation)
No punishment is given to an offender who acts with immediate necessity, according to the prevailing conditions, to repulse or eliminate an unjust assault against his or another person's rights, of which the recurrence is highly expected.
Türk Ceza Kanunu, art. 27 – Sınırın aşılması
(1) Ceza sorumluluğunu kaldıran nedenlerde sınırın kast olmaksızın aşılması halinde, fiil taksirle işlendiğinde de cezalandırılıyorsa, taksirli suç için kanunda yazılı cezanın altıda birinden üçte birine kadarı indirilerek hükmolunur. (2) Meşru savunmada sınırın aşılması mazur görülebilecek bir heyecan, korku veya telaştan ileri gelmiş ise faile ceza verilmez.
Law-firm explainer citing Yargıtay Ceza Genel Kurulu
hukuk sistemimiz saldırıya uğrayan kişiye kaçma yükümlülüğü yüklememiştir. Saldırı altındaki kimse, kaçma imkanı olsa bile kaçmak zorunda değildir – direnip kendini savunabilir. Yargıtay Ceza Genel Kurulu da "hiçbir halde sanığa kaçma mükellefiyeti yüklenemeyeceğini" vurgulamıştır.

e9e49bbe224fddc8.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Germany

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Under section 32 of the Criminal Code, a person may use whatever defensive force is necessary to stop a present unlawful attack on themselves or someone else, and such an act is lawful. The statute does not mention retreat, and German courts and commentary read it as imposing no general duty to flee: running away is not treated as a 'milder means' the defender must choose. There is also no strict proportionality test in the statute; instead, courts use the word 'called for' (geboten) to limit self-defence in a few recognised situations, such as a gross imbalance between what is attacked and the harm done, attacks by children or people plainly not responsible, close personal relationships, and cases where the defender provoked the attack; in those situations the defender may be expected to avoid the attack. If a person goes beyond the limits of self-defence out of confusion, fear or fright, section 33 says they incur no penalty.

At home

No separate home-defence rule; defence of the home is covered by the general self-defence provision (s. 32 StGB), which protects any legal interest, including property and the home.

What the law says
Strafgesetzbuch (Criminal Code), section 32 (official English translation)
(1) Whoever commits an act in self-defence does not act unlawfully. (2) 'Self-defence' means any defensive action which is necessary to avert a present unlawful attack on oneself or another.
Strafgesetzbuch (Criminal Code), section 33 (official English translation)
Whoever exceeds the limits of self-defence due to confusion, fear or fright incurs no penalty.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
