4b342d36e5a82063.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Spain

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Spanish law excuses a person who acts in defence of themselves or others if three conditions are met: an unlawful aggression, rational necessity of the means used to stop or repel it, and no sufficient provocation by the defender (Penal Code art. 20.4). The code says nothing about retreat. The Supreme Court has held that a person attacked is not required to flee: STS 399/2003 rejected the idea that the victim must take an available escape because that would mean 'the triumph of the aggressor', and STS 544/2007 said flight is not required, as summarised in a University of Zaragoza thesis. Whether escape was possible can still be weighed when judging whether the means used were rationally necessary. If not all conditions are met (for example the force was more than necessary), the defence becomes a mitigating circumstance (art. 21.1) and the court must lower the penalty by one or two degrees (art. 68), often called 'incomplete self-defence' (eximente incompleta).

At home

Article 20.4 of the Penal Code says that, when defending a dwelling or its outbuildings, unlawful entry into them counts as an 'unlawful aggression'. The means used must still be rationally necessary; there is no automatic right to use deadly force against an intruder.

What the law says
Código Penal (Ley Orgánica 10/1995), art. 20.4
Están exentos de responsabilidad criminal: ... 4.º El que obre en defensa de la persona o derechos propios o ajenos, siempre que concurran los requisitos siguientes: Primero. Agresión ilegítima. En caso de defensa de los bienes se reputará agresión ilegítima el ataque a los mismos que constituya delito y los ponga en grave peligro de deterioro o pérdida inminentes. En caso de defensa de la morada o sus dependencias, se reputará agresión ilegítima la entrada indebida en aquélla o éstas. Segundo. Necesidad racional del medio empleado para impedirla o repelerla. Tercero. Falta de provocación suficiente por parte del defensor.
Código Penal, art. 21.1
Son circunstancias atenuantes: 1.ª Las causas expresadas en el capítulo anterior, cuando no concurrieren todos los requisitos necesarios para eximir de responsabilidad en sus respectivos casos.
Código Penal, art. 68
En los casos previstos en la circunstancia primera del artículo 21, los jueces o tribunales impondrán la pena inferior en uno o dos grados a la señalada por la ley, atendidos el número y la entidad de los requisitos que falten o concurran, y las circunstancias personales de su autor...
Tribunal Supremo, STS 399/2003 (13 March 2003), as quoted in Univ. of Zaragoza TFG 2016-1024
[considera tesis no aceptable] la consistente en afirmar que siendo posible la huida, a ella debe acogerse el agredido porque, de hacerlo, significaría el éxito de la sinrazón y el triunfo del agresor, lo que vendría a constituir un factor criminógeno
Tribunal Supremo, STS 544/2007 (21 June 2007), as quoted in the same thesis
la fuga no es exigible, refiriéndose esta Sala Segunda a que fuese posible por inexistencia de riesgo y no vergonzante

fcf7637c4afdf42b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Cuba

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Cuba's former Penal Code (Ley 62 of 1987, art. 21) exempted from liability a person who prevents or repels an unlawful, imminent or current and unprovoked aggression, if the defence was objectively necessary and proportionate, judged "with reasonable criteria, according to the circumstances of persons, means, time and place". It did not mention retreat. If the defender exceeded the limits, especially by using disproportionate means, the court could cut the sentence by up to two thirds of its minimum, and could impose no sanction at all if the excess was caused by excitement or violent emotion provoked by the attack. That code was replaced by a new Penal Code, Ley 151 of 2022; a 2026 Cuban explainer cites its article 23 as exempting a person who acts "in defence of themselves, another person or legal interests" subject to necessity, reasonableness and no sufficient provocation, but the full current text could not be opened. The 1987 code also allowed defence of the "public peace" and state interests.

What the law says
Código Penal, Ley No. 62 de 1987 (repealed), art. 21
1. Está exento de responsabilidad penal el que obra en legítima defensa de su persona o derechos. 2. Obra en legítima defensa el que impide o repele una agresión ilegítima, inminente o actual y no provocada, si concurren, además, los requisitos siguientes: a) necesidad objetiva de la defensa; b) proporcionalidad entre la agresión y la defensa, determinada en cada caso con criterios razonables, según las circunstancias de personas, medios, tiempo y lugar. ... 5. Si el que repele la agresión se excede en los límites de la legítima defensa, y, especialmente, si usa un medio de defensa desproporcionado en relación con el peligro suscitado por el ataque, el tribunal puede rebajar la sanción hasta en dos tercios de su límite mínimo, y si se ha cometido este exceso a causa de la excitación o la emoción violenta provocada por la agresión, puede aún prescindir de imponerle sanción alguna.
Código Penal, Ley No. 151 de 2022, art. 23 (as quoted in a secondary source)
No es responsable penal quien actúe en defensa de sí mismo, de otra persona o de bienes jurídicos

81ba1b9618f3361e.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ukraine

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Article 36 of Ukraine's Criminal Code allows 'necessary defence' of one's own or another's rights, or public or state interests, by causing the harm that is necessary and sufficient to avert or stop an attack. The code states that every person has this right 'notwithstanding any possibility to avoid' the attack or to ask others or the authorities for help, so there is no duty to retreat. Excess of necessary defence means intentionally causing grave harm that is not adequate to the danger, and it is punishable only under two specific lighter offences (Articles 118 and 124, killing or grave injury in excess of defence); there is no liability if high excitement prevented the person judging proportionality. Using weapons against an armed attacker, a group, or a violent intrusion into a home is never treated as excess. The English text quoted is the 2010 version held in a university database; the official Ukrainian site could not be reached to check later amendments.

At home

Article 36(5): using weapons or other means to avert an unlawful violent intrusion into a dwelling or other premises is not treated as excess of necessary defence and carries no criminal liability, whatever the harm caused to the intruder.

What the law says
Criminal Code of Ukraine, Article 36 (English translation, 2010 version)
1. The necessary defense shall mean actions taken to defend the legally protected rights and interests of the defending person or another person, and also public interests and interests of the state, against a socially dangerous trespass, by inflicting such harm upon the trespasser as is necessary and sufficient in a given situation to immediately avert or stop the trespass, provided the limits of the necessary defense are not exceeded. 2. Every person shall have the right to necessary defense notwithstanding any possibility to avoid a socially dangerous trespass or request assistance of other persons or authorities. 3. The excess of necessary defense shall mean an intended causing of a grievous harm to the trespasser, which is not adequate to the danger of the trespass or circumstances of the defense. The excess of necessary defense shall entail criminal liability only in cases specifically prescribed in Articles 118 and 124 of this Code. 4. A person shall not be subject to criminal liability where that person was not able, due to high excitement, to evaluate if the harm caused by that person was proportionate to the danger of the trespass or circumstances of defense. 5. The use of weapons or other means or things for protection against an attack of an armed person or an attack of a group of persons, and also to avert an unlawful violent intrusion upon a dwelling place or other premises, shall not be treated as the excess of necessary defense and shall not entail criminal liability irrespective of the gravity of harm caused to the trespasser.

c671da6ce22f7efd.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Malaysia

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Malaysia's Penal Code (Act 574) was adopted from the Indian Penal Code (Yeo, 2011) and contains a 'right of private defence'; its exact text could not be opened from here. According to Prof. Stanley Yeo (NUJS Law Review, 2011), Malaysian courts have held that private defence carries no duty to retreat, citing Musa bin Yusof v Public Prosecutor [1953] MLJ 70 and Public Prosecutor v Balwant Singh (No. 2) [2003] 3 MLJ 395, and Malaysian and Singaporean cases read 'necessary' force as 'reasonably necessary'. The judgments themselves were not opened.

What the law says
S. Yeo, 'Staying True to the Indian Penal Code' (2011) 4 NUJS L Rev 163, text and n 14
As for references to non-Indian case authorities, the Court could have usefully referred to judicial decisions from jurisdictions like Malaysia and Singapore which have adopted the IPC ... The Court in Darshan Singh could also have referred to cases from these jurisdictions possessing the IPC to further support its ruling that our law of private defence does not impose a duty to retreat. [n 14:] Musa bin Yusof v. Public Prosecutor, [1953] MLJ 70; Public Prosecutor v. Balwant Singh (No. 2), [2003] 3 MLJ 395.

6b27543e0db809ac.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Iran

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Iran's Islamic Penal Code of 2013 (art. 156, in the IHRDC English translation) exempts from punishment conduct needed to defend one's own or another's life, honour, chastity, property or physical freedom against actual or imminent aggression or danger, if: the conduct is necessary; the defence rests on reasonable grounds or rational fear; the danger was not caused by the defender's own voluntary act or aggression; and turning to government forces in a reasonable time is not practicable or would not stop the aggression. Note 2 places on the aggressor the burden of proving the conditions were not met once the defence is established, and Note 3 says no diya (blood money) is owed for lawful defence, except against an insane person, when it is paid from the public treasury. The translated article does not mention retreat or escape, so the retreat question is not settled by the sources opened. The Persian original on official sites could not be reached; only short quotations were available from the translation.

At home

Art. 156 covers defence of property and 'physical freedom' as well as life, honour and chastity; no separate home-defence rule was read.

What the law says

Resorting to governmental forces is not practicable in a reasonable time

it is up to the aggressor to prove that the conditions for defense are not met

4e3945e279e10368.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Democratic Republic of the Congo

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

No article defining legitimate defence was found in the DRC Penal Code (decree of 30 January 1940, as amended); the only source found is a 2015 undergraduate thesis from the Université Officielle de Bukavu, which presents legitimate defence through doctrine and unnamed case law. That thesis says the attack must be current or imminent and unjust, force must be the only means of protection, and the response must be proportionate; it states the general view that a threatened person is not obliged to flee, with exceptions. It also cites article 66 ter of the Penal Code (from Ordinance-Law 78-015 of 4 July 1978) as making it a duty to defend others when this involves no risk to oneself or third parties. Because these points come from a student thesis without cited rulings, the retreat question is marked unclear.

021ff940a5ab1e1b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bangladesh

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Bangladesh still uses the Penal Code of 1860 (ss 96–106, 'right of private defence'). Deadly force in defence of the body is allowed against an assault that reasonably causes fear of death or grievous hurt, and against assaults intended to rape, abduct, kidnap or wrongfully confine (s 100). The Code does not require retreat, but there is no right of private defence 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities' (s 99). No Bangladeshi court decision on retreat was found in the sources opened.

At home

s 103: the right of private defence of property extends to causing death against robbery, house-breaking by night, arson of a building used as a dwelling, and theft, mischief or house-trespass that reasonably causes fear of death or grievous hurt.

What the law says
Penal Code, 1860 (Act XLV of 1860), s 99
There is no right of private defence against an act which does not reasonably cause the apprehension of death or of grievous hurt, if done, or attempted to be done by a public servant acting in good faith under colour of his office, though that act may not be strictly justifiable by law. ... There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities.
Penal Code, 1860, s 100
The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in the last preceding section, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the assailant, if the offence which occasions the exercise of the right be of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely:- Firstly.-Such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that death will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; Secondly.-Such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; Thirdly.-An assault with the intention of committing rape; ...
Penal Code, 1860, s 103
The right of private defence of property extends, under the restrictions mentioned in section 99, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the wrong-doer, if the offence ... be an offence of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely:- Firstly.-Robbery; Secondly.-House-breaking by night; Thirdly.-Mischief by fire committed on any building, tent or vessel, which building, tent or vessel is used as a human dwelling ...; Fourthly.-Theft, mischief or house-trespass, under such circumstances as may reasonably cause apprehension that death or grievous hurt will be the consequence, if such right of private defence is not exercised;

ed9646a8e31b7154.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Peru

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 20(3) of the Penal Code exempts from criminal liability a person who defends their own or another's legal interests, and since a 2024 amendment (Law 32026, promulgated by the President of Congress on 15 May 2024) the text expressly says this may include the use of lethal force. The defence must be against a current, unlawful and real attack, the means must be rationally necessary, and the defender must not have sufficiently provoked it. The code expressly excludes a 'proportionality of means' test and instead weighs the intensity and danger of the attack, how the attacker acted and the means available for defence. The 2024 law also bars pre-trial detention where self-defence clearly applies, unless there is firm evidence of a crime. Article 21 ('responsabilidad restringida') covers cases where not all requirements are met; its full text was not opened. No source was found that addresses whether a person must retreat, and there is no special home-defence rule in the text found.

What the law says
Código Penal (D. Leg. 635), art. 20(3), as amended in 2024 (text quoted by the Congress of Peru)
El que obra en defensa de bienes jurídicos propios o de terceros, con uso de la fuerza, incluido el uso de la fuerza letal, siempre que concurran las circunstancias siguientes: [...] Necesidad racional del medio empleado para impedirla o repelerla. Se excluye para la valoración de este requisito el criterio de proporcionalidad de medios, considerándose en su lugar, entre otras circunstancias, la intensidad y peligrosidad de la agresión, la forma de proceder del agresor y los medios de que se disponga para la defensa. Falta de provocación suficiente de quien hace la defensa.
Código Procesal Penal (D. Leg. 957), art. 268(d), added 2024
No precede la prisión preventiva en los casos de inminente aplicación de la legitima defensa propia o de tercero conforme a ley; salvo la presencia de antecedentes y/o pruebas fehacientes que justifiquen la existencia del delito o que recaiga sobre la persona sentencia firme condenatoria
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • Congreso de Perú promulga ley que excluye prisión preventiva en casos de legítima defensa (El Heraldo (Colombia))

2d1d4a2dd8939467.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Denmark

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Section 13 of the Danish Criminal Code makes acts of self-defence unpunishable if they were necessary to resist or avert a begun or imminent unlawful attack and do not 'obviously go beyond' what is justifiable given the danger of the attack, the attacker and the importance of what is attacked. Danish legal commentary (the national encyclopedia, written by law professors) states that killing can be lawful self-defence against someone who is himself trying to kill, but only 'unless the attack can be averted by flight, calling the police or the like', so escape is expected before lethal force where it is possible. If a person exceeds the limits of self-defence, they are still not punished when the excess is reasonably explained by fright or agitation caused by the attack (section 13(2)). Under civil (damages) law, an act that does not obviously exceed what is justifiable generally gives no liability for the harm caused. The wording of section 13 is the same in the 2022, 2024 and November 2025 consolidated texts.

At home

No separate home-defence rule in the Criminal Code; section 13 covers attacks on 'life, body, property etc.' generally.

What the law says
Straffeloven (Criminal Code), § 13, stk. 1
Handlinger foretagne i nødværge er straffri, for så vidt de har været nødvendige for at modstå eller afværge et påbegyndt eller overhængende uretmæssigt angreb og ikke åbenbart går ud over, hvad der under hensyn til angrebets farlighed, angriberens person og det angrebne retsgodes betydning er forsvarligt.
Straffeloven (Criminal Code), § 13, stk. 2
Overskrider nogen grænserne for lovligt nødværge, bliver han dog straffri, hvis overskridelsen er rimeligt begrundet i den ved angrebet fremkaldte skræk eller ophidselse.

  • nødværge (B. Grothe Nielsen & H. H. Vagner) (Lex.dk (Den Store Danske)), begrænset genbrug (limited reuse)

c7a2127e2a154d9e.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ireland

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Outside the home, Ireland's Non-Fatal Offences against the Person Act 1997 allows reasonable force in self-defence, and section 20(4) says the fact that a person had an opportunity to retreat 'shall be taken into account, in conjunction with other relevant evidence' when deciding whether the force was reasonable, so retreat is a factor rather than an absolute duty. Inside one's own dwelling, the 2011 Defence and the Dwelling Act removes any retreat requirement: force that is reasonable in the circumstances as the occupier believes them to be is not an offence, the force may include lethal force, and the chance to retreat is immaterial. The 2011 Act also gives the occupier immunity from civil (tort) claims for force it permits. The common-law rules on lethal self-defence outside the home were not covered by a source opened here.

At home

Criminal Law (Defence and the Dwelling) Act 2011: a person in their dwelling may use reasonable force, which can include force causing death, against someone they believe entered as a trespasser to commit a criminal act; it is 'immaterial' whether they had a safe and practicable chance to retreat, nothing in the Act requires them to retreat from their dwelling, and a person using force permitted by the Act is not liable in tort for resulting injury, loss or damage.

What the law says
Non-Fatal Offences against the Person Act 1997, s. 20(4)
The fact that a person had an opportunity to retreat before using force shall be taken into account, in conjunction with other relevant evidence, in determining whether the use of force was reasonable.
Criminal Law (Defence and the Dwelling) Act 2011, s. 2(5), 2(7), 3 and 5
2(5) It is immaterial whether the person using the force had a safe and practicable opportunity to retreat from the dwelling before using the force concerned. ... 2(7) The use of force shall not exclude the use of force causing death. ... 3.— Nothing in this Act shall operate to require— (a) a person to retreat from his or her dwelling, or (b) a lawful occupant in a dwelling to retreat from the dwelling. ... 5.— Notwithstanding the generality of any other enactment or rule of law concerning the civil liability of persons in relation to trespassers, a person who uses such force as is permitted by section 2 in the circumstances referred to in that section shall not be liable in tort in respect of any injury, loss or damage arising from the use of such force.

  • Non-Fatal Offences against the Person Act 1997, section 20 (Irish Statute Book (Office of the Attorney General))

5f0deb39363bd570.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Pakistan

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

The Pakistan Penal Code (1860, as amended) says nothing done in the exercise of the right of private defence is an offence (section 96). Deadly force is allowed against assaults that reasonably cause fear of death or grievous hurt, assaults intended to commit rape, unnatural lust, kidnapping or abduction, and certain wrongful confinements (section 100). The right does not exist 'in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities', and never extends to more harm than necessary (section 99). The code does not mention retreat, and no Pakistani court ruling on retreat was found, so whether the 'recourse to the authorities' limit requires running away is not settled by the sources checked.

At home

Section 103 of the Pakistan Penal Code allows causing death in defence of property against, among other things, robbery, 'house-breaking by night', and arson of a building used as a human dwelling, subject to the limits in section 99.

What the law says
Pakistan Penal Code (Act XLV of 1860), s. 96
Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence.
Pakistan Penal Code, s. 99 (extract)
There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities. Extent to which the right may be exercised: The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence.
Pakistan Penal Code, s. 100
The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in the last preceding section, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the assailant, if the offence which occasions the exercise of the right be of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely:-- First: Such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that death will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; Secondly: Such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; Thirdly: An assault with the intention of committing rape; Fourthly: An assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust. Fifthly: An assault with the intention of kidnapping or abduction. Sixthly: An assault with the intention of wrongfully confining a person, under circumstances which may reasonably cause him to apprehend that he will be unable to have recourse to the public authorities for his release.
Pakistan Penal Code, s. 103 (extract)
The right of private defence of property extends, under the restrictions mentioned in Section 99, to the voluntary Causing of death or of any other harm to the wrong-doer, if the offence ... be an offence of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely:- First: Robbery; Secondly: House-breaking by night; Thirdly: Mischief by fire committed on any building, tent or vessel, which building, tent or vessel is used as a human dwelling or as a place for the custody of property; Fourthly: Theft, mischief or house-trespass, under such circumstances as may reasonably cause apprehension that death or grievous hurt will be the consequence...

73a5f48882ea2877.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Croatia

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 21 of the Criminal Code (2011) says an act done in necessary defence is not unlawful, and defines necessary defence as the defence that is 'strictly necessary' (prijeko potrebna) to repel a simultaneous or directly imminent unlawful attack on oneself or another. The code does not mention retreat; by contrast, the necessity defence in article 22 applies only to a danger that 'could not be removed in another way'. No court ruling on retreat was found. A person who exceeds the limits of necessary defence may receive a lighter sentence, and is not guilty at all if the excess came from excusable severe fright caused by the attack; this fright rule was introduced by the 2011 code, according to a commentary in Informator, because courts had tended to impose high sentences for excess regardless of the defender's state of mind.

What the law says
Kazneni zakon (NN 125/11 and amendments), čl. 21
(1) Isključena je protupravnost djela počinjenog u nužnoj obrani. (2) Nužna je ona obrana koja je prijeko potrebna da se od sebe ili drugoga odbije istodobni ili izravno predstojeći protupravni napad. (3) Počinitelj koji prekorači granice nužne obrane može se blaže kazniti. (4) Nije kriv tko prekorači granice nužne obrane zbog ispričive jake prepasti prouzročene napadom.
Kazneni zakon, čl. 22(1) (necessity, for contrast)
Isključena je protupravnost djela počinjenog radi toga da se od sebe ili drugoga otkloni istodobna opasnost koja se na drugi način nije mogla otkloniti ako je učinjeno zlo manje od onoga koje je prijetilo.
Supreme Court of Croatia, I Kž-210/2019 (24 Apr 2019), as summarised in the court's 2019 bulletin
Kazneno djelo u prekoračenju nužne obrane može se počiniti i sa izravnom i sa neizravnom namjerom.

78b2be62edefa3bf.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

French Polynesia

Part of France, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

French Polynesia shares the French Penal Code: art. 711-1 makes Books I to V of the Code applicable there, subject to listed adaptations, so the self-defence rules are those of France. Under art. 122-5 a person is not criminally responsible for an act required by the necessity of defending themselves or another against an unjustified attack, done at the same time as the attack, unless the means used are disproportionate to the seriousness of the attack; intentional killing is never justified to protect property. Art. 122-6 presumes self-defence against night-time break-ins of inhabited places and violent theft. The code says nothing about retreat, and no French court decision on retreat was opened for this entry, so the question is left unsettled here (see the France entry).

At home

Under art. 122-6 a person is presumed to have acted in self-defence when repelling, at night, entry into an inhabited place by break-in, violence or trickery, or when defending against violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Code pénal (France), art. 122-5
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal (France), art. 122-6
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Code pénal (France), art. 711-1
Sous réserve des adaptations prévues au présent titre, les livres Ier à V du présent code sont applicables, dans leur rédaction résultant de la loi n° 2026-813 du 24 août 2026 ..., en Nouvelle-Calédonie, en Polynésie française et dans les îles Wallis et Futuna.

f609be22034bc3c8.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

The Bahamas

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

The Bahamas has a written Penal Code (Ch. 84) that grades how much force is allowed by the crime being resisted. Against any crime only necessary force short of a blow may be used; against criminal force short of a wound; against a felony short of 'dangerous harm'; and only against listed grave crimes (such as murder, robbery, burglary, house-breaking, rape and grievous harm) may necessary force extend, 'in the case of extreme necessity, even to killing'. Force beyond what is reasonably necessary is never justified (s. 99), and force used in an unlawful fight cannot be justified. A person who kills using more harm than was justified, while so terrified of immediate death or grievous harm that they lost self-control, is guilty of manslaughter rather than murder (s. 299(2)). The code does not mention retreat, and no Bahamian court decision on a duty to retreat was found.

At home

Penal Code s. 108(1) lets a person in actual possession of a house, land or vessel use force 'not extending to a wound or grievous harm' to repel someone trying forcibly and unlawfully to enter. Separately, s. 107(4) allows necessary force, in extreme necessity even killing, to prevent or defend against burglary, house-breaking or arson of a dwelling-house, among other listed crimes.

What the law says
Penal Code (Ch. 84), s. 99
Notwithstanding the existence of any matter of justification for force, force cannot be justified as having been used in pursuance of that matter — (1) which is in excess of the limits hereinafter prescribed in the section of this Title relating to that matter; (2) which in any case extends beyond the amount and kind of force reasonably necessary for the purpose for which force is permitted to be used.
Penal Code (Ch. 84), s. 107
(1) For the prevention of, or for the defence of himself or any other person against, any crime, a person may justify the use of necessary force, not extending to a blow, wound or grievous harm. (2) For the prevention of, or for the defence of himself or any other person against, any criminal force or harm, a person may justify the use of necessary force, not extending to a wound or grievous harm. (3) For the prevention of, or for the defence of himself or any other person against, any felony, a person may justify the use of necessary force not extending to dangerous harm. (4) For the prevention of, or for the defence of himself or any other person against, any of the following crimes, a person may justify any necessary force or harm, extending, in the case of extreme necessity, even to killing, namely — (a) treason; (b) piracy; (c) murder; (d) manslaughter, except manslaughter by negligence; (e) robbery; (f) burglary; (g) house-breaking; (h) arson of a dwelling-house or vessel; (i) rape; (j) forcible unnatural crime; (k) dangerous or grievous harm. [...] (6) No force used in an unlawful fight can be justified under any provision of this Code [...]
Penal Code (Ch. 84), s. 299(2)
A person who intentionally causes the death of another person by unlawful harm shall be deemed to be guilty only of manslaughter, and not of murder, if any of the following matters of extenuation are proved on his behalf, namely — [...] (2) that he was justified in causing some harm to the other person, and that, in causing harm in excess of the harm which he was justified in causing, he acted from such terror of immediate death or grievous harm as in fact deprived him for the time being of the power of self control

741fe569f8363b02.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

United Kingdom

No duty to retreat, written in the law

In England and Wales, self-defence is a common-law defence, and section 76 of the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008 says force is judged on the circumstances as the defender honestly believed them to be, and is not reasonable if it was disproportionate (or 'grossly disproportionate' in a householder case). Since 2013, section 76(6A) has stated that the possibility of retreat is only a factor to weigh, 'rather than as giving rise to a duty to retreat'; that subsection and the householder rule apply in England and Wales only, while the rest of section 76 also covers Northern Ireland. Self-defence is a complete defence: there is no partial 'excessive self-defence' verdict in these provisions, though the jury must consider that a person under attack cannot 'weigh to a nicety' the exact force needed. In civil law, an offender convicted of an imprisonable offence on the same occasion needs the court's permission to sue the defender for trespass to the person, and the defender has a defence unless their act was grossly disproportionate (Criminal Justice Act 2003, s. 329, England and Wales). Scotland has separate common-law rules that were not covered by the sources opened here.

At home

England and Wales: in a 'householder case' (force used by a non-trespasser inside a dwelling against someone believed to be a trespasser), force is unreasonable only if it was 'grossly disproportionate' in the circumstances as the defender believed them to be, instead of merely 'disproportionate' (s. 76(5A), inserted 2013). This householder rule does not apply in Northern Ireland or Scotland.

What the law says
Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, s. 76(5A), (6), (6A), (7)
(5A) In a householder case, the degree of force used by D is not to be regarded as having been reasonable in the circumstances as D believed them to be if it was grossly disproportionate in those circumstances. (6) In a case other than a householder case, the degree of force used by D is not to be regarded as having been reasonable in the circumstances as D believed them to be if it was disproportionate in those circumstances. (6A) In deciding the question mentioned in subsection (3), a possibility that D could have retreated is to be considered (so far as relevant) as a factor to be taken into account, rather than as giving rise to a duty to retreat. (7) In deciding the question mentioned in subsection (3) the following considerations are to be taken into account (so far as relevant in the circumstances of the case)— (a) that a person acting for a legitimate purpose may not be able to weigh to a nicety the exact measure of any necessary action; and (b) that evidence of a person's having only done what the person honestly and instinctively thought was necessary for a legitimate purpose constitutes strong evidence that only reasonable action was taken by that person for that purpose.
Criminal Justice Act 2003, s. 329(3)-(4)
(3) The court may give permission for the proceedings to be brought only if there is evidence that either— (a) the condition in subsection (5) is not met, or (b) in all the circumstances, the defendant's act was grossly disproportionate. (4) If the court gives permission and the proceedings are brought, it is a defence for the defendant to prove both— (a) that the condition in subsection (5) is met, and (b) that, in all the circumstances, his act was not grossly disproportionate.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

fefb1f54c9e43d26.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Panama

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 32 of Panama's Penal Code (Law 14 of 2007), there is no crime when a person acts in legitimate defence of themselves, their rights, or another person or their property, if the circumstances require it. Three conditions must be met: an unjust, current or imminent attack; use of a rational means to prevent or repel it; and no sufficient provocation by the defender. A person who reasonably repels someone who entered their home without consent is presumed to act in self-defence. The code does not mention retreat, and no Panamanian court decision on retreat or rule on excessive self-defence was found. The text used is the 2007 code as amended in 2008 (WIPO Lex copy); later amendments were not checked.

At home

Penal Code art. 32 presumes legitimate defence for anyone who reasonably repels a person who has entered their residence, dwelling, house or room without consent.

What the law says
Código Penal (Ley N° 14 de 18 de mayo de 2007, con modificaciones de la Ley N° 26 de 2008), art. 32
No comete delito quien actúe en legítima defensa de su persona, de sus derechos o de un tercero o sus bienes, siempre que las circunstancias así lo requieran. La defensa es legítima cuando concurran las siguientes condiciones: Existencia de una agresión injusta, actual o inminente de la que resulte o pudiera resultar afectado por el hecho; Utilización de un medio racional para impedir o repeler la agresión; y Falta de provocación suficiente por parte de quien se defiende o es defendido. Se presume que actúa en legítima defensa quien razonablemente repele al que, sin su consentimiento, ha ingresado a su residencia, morada, casa o habitación.

7e219012d28b5a70.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Nigeria

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Nigeria has two criminal codes: the Criminal Code (southern states) and the Penal Code (northern states); both allow self-defence as a complete defence. Under the Criminal Code, a person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force that kills or causes grievous harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous harm and they believe on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise save the person defended. Neither code text found says the person must run away, and the Supreme Court in Laoye v The State (1985) adopted the English rule that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run', though they should show they do not want to fight and are willing to disengage. Under the northern Penal Code, private defence does not arise when there is time to seek protection from public authorities (s. 63), and someone who in good faith goes beyond what private defence allows and kills, without premeditation, is guilty of culpable homicide not punishable with death (s. 222(2)) instead of murder. The 1999 Constitution, s. 33(2)(a), says a death from force reasonably necessary to defend a person from unlawful violence or to defend property does not breach the right to life.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act (Cap. C38), s. 286 (as quoted by Omaplex Law Firm)
When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault: Provided that the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely to cause death or grievous harm. If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable ground, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous harm.
Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999, s. 33(2)(a)
A person shall not be regarded as having been deprived of his life in contravention of this section, if he dies as a result of the use, to such extent and in such circumstances as are permitted by the law, of such force as is reasonably necessary- (a) for the defence of any person from unlawful violence or for the defence of property;
Penal Code (Northern Nigeria), ss. 59, 60 and 222(2), as quoted in Ali Abadallabe v Bornu Native Authority (FSC, 1963)
59. Nothing is an offence which is done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence ... 60. Every person has a right, subject to the restrictions hereinafter contained, to defend:- (a) His own body and the body of any other person against any offence affecting the human body ... 222.-(2) Culpable homicide is not punishable with death if the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private [defence] of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.
Laoye v The State [1985] 2 NSCC 1250 (Supreme Court), holding 4, quoting R v McInnes with approval
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal

c1c902273a07bb75.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

South Africa

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

South Africa has no criminal code on self-defence; 'private defence' is a common-law defence developed by the courts, and force must be necessary and reasonable against an unlawful attack. Whether a person must flee is not settled. In R v Zikalala (1953) the Appellate Division endorsed the proposition that a person who can save themselves by flight should flee rather than kill, but added that no one has to flee if flight is not a safe way out or risks 'a stab in the back'. Later courts have called it 'a somewhat vexed question', and in Grigor v S (Supreme Court of Appeal, 2012) the court noted the accused could simply have driven off; a Legal Aid South Africa lawyer concluded in 2015 that the courts 'have not definitively decided' whether there is a duty to flee. The leading criminal-law author Snyman argues there is no absolute duty to retreat and that the possibility of retreat should be one factor among others.

At home

In S v Engelbrecht (2005), as described by Goosen (PER 2013), Satchwell J was cautious about requiring an abused woman and her children to leave their home and leave the abusive spouse in occupation, and held that 'flight' may also include going to the police, courts, shelters or family. Goosen disagrees and argues the abuser's life takes precedence over the right to remain in the home. No statute on defending the home was found.

What the law says
R v Zikalala 1953 (2) SA 568 (A), endorsing Gardiner and Lansdown (as summarised on Wikipedia, used only as a pointer)
Where a man can save himself by flight, he should flee rather than kill his assailant [...]. But no one can be expected to take to flight to avoid an attack, if flight does not afford him a safe way of escape. A man is not bound to expose himself to the risk of a stab in the back, when by killing his assailant he can secure his own safety
Grigor v S (SCA, case no. 607/11, 1 June 2012), Tshiqi JA, as quoted by Sherika Maharaj (East London Justice Centre)
[t]he facts of this matter, even on the appellants version, show that he had several other harmless means he could have adopted to avoid a physical confrontation. He could have driven off and ignored the complainant
Commentary: Maharaj (2015)
It would appear that our courts have not definitively decided whether a person has a duty to flee an attack or whether the individual can stand his or her ground and take steps to ward off an impending attack.
Commentary: Goosen, PER 2013, quoting Snyman
Snyman argues that there is no duty upon the attacked person to flee, because "this is a negation of the whole essence of private defence [which deals] … with the upholding of justice … not a capitulation to injustice". However, he submits that "there is no absolute duty to retreat and that the approach of our law ought to be that the question of whether or not the battered woman could or should have retreated is merely one of the issues to be taken into account"
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • Battered Women and the Requirement of Imminence in Self-Defence (S Goosen), PER/PELJ 2013 vol. 16 no. 1, doi:10.4314/pelj.v16i1.4 (Potchefstroom Electronic Law Journal)

97e337c652521f4a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Mongolia

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Mongolia's Criminal Code of 2015 (art. 4.1, 'necessary defence') provides that an act having the features of a crime done against an unlawful and imminent attack on one's own or another person's life or health is not a crime (wording amended on 10 January 2020). Part 2 states that anyone has the right of necessary defence regardless of profession, special training or official position, and regardless of whether it was possible to avoid the dangerous attack or to ask others for help — so there is no duty to retreat. Defence may be used once an unlawful attack has started or is clearly about to start, but not after the attack has ended. The current text of art. 4.1 contains no separate clause on excessive defence; other consequences of excess were not examined. English summary is an unofficial translation.

At home

No separate home-defence rule found in art. 4.1.

What the law says
Criminal Code of Mongolia (2015), art. 4.1(1)–(3) (Mongolian, as displayed on the official portal)
4.1 ДҮГЭЭР ЗҮЙЛ.АРГАГҮЙ ХАМГААЛАЛТ 1.ӨӨРИЙН, ЭСХҮЛ БУСДЫН АМЬ НАС, ЭРҮҮЛ МЭНДИЙН ЭСРЭГ ХУУЛЬ БУС БА ТУЛГАРСАН ДОВТОЛГООНЫ ЭСРЭГ ХИЙСЭН ГЭМТ ХЭРГИЙН ШИНЖТЭЙ ҮЙЛДЛИЙГ ГЭМТ ХЭРЭГТ ТООЦОХГҮЙ. /ЭНЭ ХЭСЭГТ 2020 ОНЫ 01 ДҮГЭЭР САРЫН 10-НЫ ӨДРИЙН ХУУЛИАР ӨӨРЧЛӨЛТ ОРУУЛСАН./ 2.АЛИВАА ХҮН МЭРГЭЖИЛ, ТУСГАЙ БЭЛТГЭЛ, АЛБАН АЖЛЫН БАЙДАЛ, АЮУЛТАЙ ДОВТОЛГООНООС ЗАЙЛСХИЙХ, БУСДААС ТУСЛАМЖ АВАХААР ХАНДАХ БОЛОМЖТОЙ БАЙСАН ЭСЭХЭЭС ҮЛ ХАМААРАН АРГАГҮЙ ХАМГААЛАЛТ ХИЙХ ЭРХТЭЙ. 3.АРГАГҮЙ ХАМГААЛАЛТЫГ БУСДЫН ХУУЛЬ БУС ХАЛДЛАГА ЭХЭЛСЭН, ЭХЛЭХ ГЭЖ БАЙГАА НЬ ТОДОРХОЙ БОЛСОН ҮЕД ХИЙНЭ. 7ad5c6aaa95fe2db.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Turkmenistan

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Article 34 of the Turkmen Criminal Code says defending oneself, another person, society or the state by causing any harm to the attacker is lawful when the attack involved violence dangerous to life or an immediate threat of such violence. Against attacks not dangerous to life, defence is lawful only if the limits of necessary defence were not exceeded, meaning no deliberate acts clearly out of line with the nature and danger of the attack. The article states that the right of defence exists regardless of any possibility of avoiding the attack or turning to others or the authorities for help, so there is no duty to retreat. The text used is the Criminal Code of 12 June 1997 No. 222-I as amended to 12 April 2025, published on a Kazakh legal database (prg.kz); the penalty for excessive defence was not checked.

What the law says
Criminal Code of Turkmenistan, art. 34
1. Не является преступлением и признаётся правомерной защита личности, прав и законных интересов обороняющегося, другого лица, общества и государства путём причинения любого вреда посягающему, если нападение было совершено с насилием, опасным для жизни обороняющегося или другого лица, либо с непосредственной угрозой применения такого насилия. 2. Защита от нападения, не сопряжённого с насилием, опасным для жизни обороняющегося или другого лица, либо с угрозой применения такого насилия, является правомерной, если при этом не было допущено превышение пределов необходимой обороны, то есть умышленных действий, явно не соответствующих характеру и опасности посягательства. 3. Право на необходимую оборону принадлежит лицу независимо от возможности избежать посягательства либо обратиться за помощью к другим лицам или органам власти.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

a89d366de8068799.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Madagascar

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Madagascar's Penal Code (text consolidated to 31 March 2005 in the copy found) follows the old French model: there is no crime when homicide, wounds or blows were 'commanded by the current necessity of legitimate defence of oneself or another' (art. 328). Article 329, as amended in 1978 and 1996, lists four situations automatically counted as self-defence, including repelling night-time break-ins of homes and many other buildings, repelling violent, armed or gang robbery by day, and killing or wounding criminals during or while pursuing them, by members of the Fokonolona (local community) or the security forces, in cases of violent or armed banditry or tomb violation. The code says nothing about retreat, and no court decisions on retreat or on the proportionality test were found. The 2010 Constitution (art. 8) says death is not a violation of the right to life when it results from force 'absolutely necessary' to defend any person against illegal violence.

At home

Article 329(1) counts as 'current necessity of legitimate defence' any blows, wounds or homicide committed while repelling, at night, the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or the entrance of a house or flat or their outbuildings, and also of shops, warehouses, religious buildings, schools, hospitals, offices, factories, banks, cattle pens, stables, pigsties and poultry yards, or while preventing theft of harvested crops in the fields.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 328
Il n’y a ni crime ni délit, lorsque l’homicide, les blessures et les coups étaient commandés par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi-même ou d’autrui.
Code pénal, art. 329 (Loi n°78-039 du 13.07.78; Loi n°96-001 du 06.02.96), extract
Sont compris dans les cas de nécessité actuelle de légitime défense, les quatre cas suivants : 1° Si les coups ont été portés, si les blessures ont été faites, si l’homicide a été commis en repoussant pendant la nuit l’escalade ou l’effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d’une maison ou d’un appartement ou de leurs dépendances ... 2° Si les coups ont été portés, si les blessures ont été faites, si l’homicide a été commis en repoussant pendant le jour tout vol avec effraction, tout vol avec violence, toute attaque ou vol en bande ou tout vol avec port d’armes apparentes par nature ; 3° si les coups ont été portés, si les blessures ont été faites, si l’homicide a été commis sur les malfaiteurs au moment des faits ou au cours de leur poursuite par les membres du Fokonolona ou des agents de la force publique, en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillage ou de tout autre acte de banditisme, exécutés avec violence, ou en bande ou avec port d’armes apparentes ou cachées ...
Constitution 2010, art. 8 (English translation)
Death is not considered as inflicted in violation of this Article in the cases where it would result from recourse to the force rendered absolutely necessary, in view of assuring the defense of all persons against illegal violence.

3d4f9cc331b2f23d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

United Republic of Tanzania

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Tanzania's Penal Code (sections 18 to 18C, added in 1980) gives every person the right to defend themselves, another person, or property, but only with "such reasonable force as may be necessary for that defence". Deadly force or grievous harm is allowed where the defender acts in good faith with an honest belief, on reasonable grounds, that it is needed to preserve life or limb, including against acts reasonably feared to cause death or grievous harm, rape, kidnapping, burglary, robbery or arson. The Code does not mention retreat, and the sources opened here did not settle whether a chance to escape counts against the defender. A person who uses excessive force is criminally liable, and causing death through excessive defensive force is manslaughter rather than murder.

What the law says
Penal Code [Cap. 16], ss. 18B and 18C(1)
18B. (1) In exercising the right of self defence or in defence of another or in defence of property, a person shall be entitled to use only such reasonable force as may be necessary for that defence. (2) A person shall be criminally liable for any offence resulting from excessive force used in self defence or in defence of another or in defence of property. (3) Any person who causes the death of another as the result of excessive force used in defence, commits an offence of manslaughter. 18C. (1) The right of self defence or the defence of another or defence of property shall extend to a person who, in exercising that right, causes death or grievous harm to another and the person so acting, acts in good faith and with an honest belief based on reasonable grounds that his act is necessary for the preservation of his own life or limb or the life or limb of another or of property, in the circumstances where— (a) the lawful act is of such a nature as may reasonably cause the apprehension that his own death or the death of another person could be the consequence of that act; ... (c) the unlawful act is with the intention of committing rape or defilement or an unnatural offence; (d) the unlawful act is with the intention of kidnapping or abducting; or (e) the unlawful act is burglary or robbery or arson or any offence which endangers life or property.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

eb96e3af07eff8a4.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Fiji

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Fiji's Crimes Act 2009, which repealed the old Penal Code, defines self-defence in s 42 on the same model as the Australian Commonwealth Criminal Code: conduct is self-defence only if the person believes it is necessary to defend themselves or another (or for listed property and trespass purposes) and it is a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceive them. The section does not mention retreat and no duty to retreat is stated; no Fijian court decision on retreat was opened. Deadly force solely to protect property or deal with trespassers is excluded.

At home

No home-specific rule; force intentionally inflicting death or grievous harm may not be used only to protect property or to prevent or remove a criminal trespasser (s 42(3)).

What the law says
Crimes Act 2009, s 42 Self defence
(1) A person is not criminally responsible for an offence if he or she carries out the conduct constituting the offence in self defence. (2) A person carries out conduct in self defence if and only if he or she believes the conduct is necessary— (a) to defend himself or herself or another person; or (b) to prevent or terminate the unlawful imprisonment of himself or herself or another person; or (c) to protect property from unlawful appropriation, destruction, damage or interference; or (d) to prevent criminal trespass to any land or premises; or (e) to remove from any land or premises a person who is committing criminal trespass, and the conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as he or she perceives them. (3) This section does not apply if the person uses force that involves the intentional infliction of death or grievous harm— (a) to protect property; or (b) to prevent criminal trespass; or (c) to remove a person who is committing criminal trespass.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

a4d0ed3958dd65dd.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Egypt

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Egypt's Penal Code (Law 58 of 1937, as amended) exempts from punishment a person who kills or injures while lawfully defending their own or another's life or property, using the force 'necessary' to ward off a criminal act (arts. 245–246). The right does not exist when it is possible to rely in good time on the protection of the public authorities (art. 247); the code says nothing explicit about retreating. Intentional killing in self-defence is allowed only against an act feared on plausible grounds to cause death or serious wounds, rape or indecent assault by force, or kidnapping (art. 249). Someone who in good faith exceeds the limits of defence, without intending more harm than needed, is not fully exempt, but a judge may treat the act as excusable and impose detention instead of the normal felony penalty (art. 251).

At home

Article 250 allows intentional killing in defence of property when warding off, among other things, 'entering at night into a tenanted house or one of its appurtenances'.

What the law says
Penal Code (Law 58/1937), arts. 246–247 (English translation)
Article 246: The right of lawful self-defense allows a person, in other than the exceptional cases defined hereinafter, to use the power necessary to obviate any act considered as a crime on one's life prescribed as prescribed in this law. ... Article 247: Such right shall have no existence once it is possible to rely in due course on seeking the protection of the public authority men.
Penal Code, arts. 249–250
Article 249: The right of lawful self-defense shall not allow premeditated killing unless it is meant to ward off one of the matters: First: An act feared to cause death or deep wounds, if such fear is based on plausible reasons. Second: Lying with a woman or assaulting a person indecently by force. Third: Kidnapping a person. Article 250: The lawful right of defending the property and funds shall not allow premeditated killing unless it is meant to ward off one of the following matters: ... Third: Entering at night into a tenanted house or one of its appurtenances;
Penal Code, art. 251
Whoever exceeds in good faith the limits of the right of lawful defense, while using this right, without having the intent to cause a bigger harm than the demands of this defense shall not be fully exempted from punishment. However, the judge, in case the act constitutes a felony, may consider it excusable if there is place for that, and pass a ruling sentencing him/her to detention instead of the penalty prescribed in the law.

b62ddd403072155e.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Uzbekistan

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Article 37 of the Uzbek Criminal Code says an act done in necessary defence of oneself, another person, or public or state interests against an unlawful attack is not a crime, provided the limits of necessary defence were not exceeded. Exceeding the limits means a clear mismatch between the defence and the nature and danger of the attack. The code states that the right of defence belongs to a person regardless of any chance to seek help from others or the authorities or to avoid the attack in another way, so there is no duty to retreat. Deliberately provoking an attack in order to harm the attacker is not defence. Intentionally killing while exceeding the limits is a separate, lighter offence (article 100) punished by up to three years.

What the law says
Criminal Code of the Republic of Uzbekistan, art. 37 (Russian text)
Не является преступлением действие, совершенное в состоянии необходимой обороны, то есть при защите личности или прав обороняющегося либо другого лица, интересов общества или государства от противоправного посягательства путем причинения посягающему вреда, если при этом не было допущено превышение пределов необходимой обороны. Превышением пределов необходимой обороны признается явное несоответствие защиты характеру и опасности посягательства. Право на необходимую оборону принадлежит лицу независимо от имевшейся возможности обратиться за помощью к другим лицам или органам власти либо избежать посягательства иным способом. Не является необходимой обороной умышленная провокация посягательства с целью нанесения вреда.
Criminal Code, art. 100
Умышленное причинение смерти, совершенное при превышении пределов необходимой обороны, — наказывается исправительными работами до трех лет или ограничением свободы от одного года до трех лет либо лишением свободы до трех лет.

7db3274502d33a44.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ecuador

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 33 of the Comprehensive Organic Criminal Code (COIP, 2014) says self-defence exists when a person acts in defence of any right, their own or another's, if three conditions are met: a current and unlawful aggression, "rational necessity of the defence", and no sufficient provocation by the defender. The Code does not mention retreat. A 2024 article by an Azuay provincial prosecutor in the University of Cuenca law review expresses the scholarly view that the person attacked should prefer strictly defensive means or, "if possible, opt for a prudent retreat", as long as this does not put them at risk or dishonour; this is legal writing, not a code rule or court ruling. According to El Comercio (2023), the COIP (art. 31) punishes excessive self-defence with a penalty reduced to one third of the minimum for the offence. The sources opened here did not show a special rule for the home.

What the law says
Código Orgánico Integral Penal (COIP), art. 33
Artículo 33.- Legítima defensa.- Existe legítima defensa cuando la persona actúa en defensa de cualquier derecho, propio o ajeno, siempre y cuando concurran los siguientes requisitos: a) Agresión actual e ilegítima; b) Necesidad racional de la defensa; c) Falta de provocación suficiente por parte de quien actúa en defensa del derecho.
COIP, art. 31 (exceso), as quoted by El Comercio
una pena reducida en un tercio de la mínima prevista en el respectivo tipo penal
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • La legítima defensa: comparación entre los códigos penales cubano y ecuatoriano (Revista Mikarimin, Universidad Regional Autónoma de los Andes (Alfaro Matos & Balda Zambrano, 2015))
  • Legítima defensa: necesidad racional de la defensa (Revista IURIS, Universidad de Cuenca (Alberto Machuca Carpio, 2024))

486bd0798093f253.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ivory Coast

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Côte d'Ivoire's 1981 Penal Code (art. 100) allowed defence of oneself, another person or legally protected property against an unjust attack only if the attack 'could not be otherwise averted' and the defence was simultaneous with and proportionate to the circumstances, including the danger and gravity of the attack and the value of the property. That wording made defence conditional on there being no other way to avert the attack. The 1981 code was replaced by a new Penal Code (Law No. 2019-574, consolidated to 23 June 2024), whose table of contents places legitimate defence in Articles 97 and 98; their text could not be opened for this entry, so the current position on avoiding the attack is marked unclear.

At home

Under the 1981 Penal Code (art. 101), killing or wounding was presumed to be legitimate defence when repelling at night the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or entrances of a house or inhabited flat, or when defending against violent theft or looting. The wording of the corresponding rule in the 2019 Code could not be opened.

What the law says
Code pénal (1981), art. 100 — superseded by Loi n° 2019-574
Il n'y a pas d'infraction lorsque les faits sont commandés par la nécessité actuelle de défense de soi-même ou d'autrui ou d'un bien juridiquement protégé contre une attaque injuste, à condition que cette dernière ne puisse être écartée autrement et que la défense soit concomitante et proportionnée aux circonstances, notamment au danger et à la gravité de l'attaque, à l'importance et à la valeur du bien attaqué.
Code pénal (1981), art. 101 — superseded
Est présumé agir en état de légitime défense, celui qui commet un homicide, porte volontairement des coups ou fait des blessures soit en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrées d'une maison, d'un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances, soit en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

b2a67fabc19e8cb4.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Guinea

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

In the new Penal Code of Guinea (Ministry of Justice text dated February 2016; the law was enacted later in 2016, and article numbers in the final version could not be checked), there is no crime or offence when the act was required by the necessity of legitimate defence of oneself or another (art. 21(4)). The code text found does not mention retreat, and this article also does not spell out a proportionality test. Defence at night against forced or tricked entry into an inhabited place, and defence against violent robbery, are presumed to be legitimate defence. No specific rule on excessive self-defence was found.

At home

Article 22 presumes legitimate defence for a person who acts to repel at night entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place, or to defend against violent theft or looting; article 292 applies the same presumption to killing or wounding while repelling night-time climbing or break-in into a house or inhabited flat.

What the law says
Nouveau Code pénal (Ministère de la Justice, février 2016), art. 21(4)
Il n'y a ni crime ni délit, lorsque : ... 4. l'action du prévenu est commandée par la nécessité de sa légitime défense ou de celle d'autrui.
Nouveau Code pénal (2016), art. 22
Est présumé agir en état de légitime défense, celui qui accomplit l’acte : 1. pour repousser de nuit l’entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2. pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vol ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Nouveau Code pénal (2016), art. 292
Est présumé agir en état de légitime défense, celui qui commet un homicide, porte volontairement des coups ou fait des blessures soit en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l’escalade ou l’effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrées d’une maison, d’un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances, soit en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exercés avec violence.

30bdb361ec12be70.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Central African Republic

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

The Central African Republic's Penal Code (Law No. 10.001 of 2010) says killing, wounding and blows are justified when they were required by the 'present necessity of legitimate defence' of oneself or others, or of one's own or others' property. The article does not mention proportionality or retreat; its test is present necessity. It names two situations that count as such necessity: repelling night-time climbing or break-in into a home, and defending against violent theft or looting. No provision on excessive self-defence was found in the article.

At home

Article 49 counts as legitimate defence killing, wounding or striking while repelling at night the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or entrances of a house, inhabited flat or their outbuildings, and defence against violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Code pénal centrafricain (Loi n° 10.001), art. 49
L’homicide, les blessures et les coups sont justifiés et n’entraînent pas condamnation lorsqu’ils étaient commandés par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi ou d’autrui, de ses biens ou de ceux d’autrui. Sont compris dans les cas de nécessité actuelle de défense, les deux cas suivants : 1. Si l’homicide a été commis, si les blessures ont été faites ou si les coups ont été portés en repoussant pendant la nuit l’escalade ou l’effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrées d’une maison, d’un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances ; 2. Si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vol ou de pillage exécutés avec violence.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

6f0103560e86e49d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Angola

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Angola's Penal Code (Law No. 38/20 of 11 November 2020) defines legitimate defence as an act carried out 'as a necessary means' to repel a current and unlawful attack on legally protected interests of the defender or a third party. The code does not mention retreat or a duty to flee; the test is whether the means used were necessary. If the means used were excessive, the act is unlawful but the penalty may be specially reduced (art. 31). A person who exceeded the means because of non-blameworthy disturbance, fear or fright acts without guilt (art. 36). No separate home-defence rule was found.

What the law says
Código Penal (Lei n.º 38/20, de 11 de Novembro), art. 31.º (Legítima Defesa)
Constitui legítima defesa o facto praticado como meio necessário para repelir a agressão actual e ilícita de interesses juridicamente protegidos do agente ou de terceiro. Se houver excesso dos meios empregados em legítima defesa o facto é ilícito, mas a pena pode ser especialmente atenuada.
Código Penal (Lei n.º 38/20), art. 36.º (Excesso de Legítima Defesa Desculpante)
Age sem culpa quem exceder os meios empregues em legítima defesa, sempre que o excesso resultar de perturbação, medo ou susto não censuráveis.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Lei n.º 38/20, de 11 de Novembro — Código Penal Angolano (lex.ao)

bbff172a3cd5dcb7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Mali

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Mali adopted a new Penal Code in December 2024 (Law No. 2024-027). Under article 122-4, a person is not criminally responsible for an act required, at the same moment, by the need to defend themselves or another against an unjustified attack, unless the means of defence are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack. Defence of property may never extend to intentional homicide and must be strictly necessary and proportionate. The code says nothing about retreat or flight, and no Malian court decision on the point was found. No provision on excessive self-defence was found in the sections searched.

At home

A person is presumed to have acted in self-defence when repelling, at night, entry into an inhabited place by break-in, violence or trickery, or when defending against violent theft or looting (art. 122-5). Article 321-56 likewise counts as 'current necessity of defence' a homicide or injury committed while repelling, at night, an intrusion into a dwelling or its outbuildings, notably by climbing or breaking through fences, walls or enclosures.

What the law says
Code pénal (Loi n°2024-027 du 13 décembre 2024), art. 122-4
N’est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d’elle-même ou d’autrui, sauf s’il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l’atteinte. N’est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l’exécution d’un crime ou d’un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu’un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l’infraction.
Code pénal 2024, art. 122-5
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l’acte : 1°) pour repousser, de nuit, l’entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2°) pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Code pénal 2024, arts. 321-55 and 321-56
Article 321-55 : N’est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui commet un homicide, fait des blessures, porte des coups ou exerce des violences lorsque ceux-ci étaient commandés par la nécessité actuelle ou la légitime défense de soi-même ou d’autrui. Article 321-56 : Sont compris dans le cas de nécessité actuelle de défense, les deux cas suivants : 1°) si l’homicide a été commis, si les blessures ont été faites et les coups ont été portés ou si les violences ont été exercées en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l’intrusion dans une habitation ou ses dépendances, notamment par escalade ou effraction des clôtures, murs ou enclos. 2°) si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

cf4ed00d6c3b5d6b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Cameroon

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Cameroon's Penal Code (Law No. 2016/007 of 12 July 2016) says criminal liability cannot arise from an act required by the immediate necessity of defending oneself, another person, or one's own or another's right against an unlawful attack, provided the defence is proportionate to the seriousness of the attack (s. 84(1)). Killing or serious injury is always treated as proportionate to an attack that gives reason to fear death, serious injury, rape or sodomy (s. 84(2)). The code does not mention retreat. No separate provision on excessive self-defence or on home defence was found; section 85 gives a mitigating excuse for offences provoked by an unlawful act against the offender or close persons.

What the law says
Loi n° 2016/007 du 12 juillet 2016 portant Code pénal, art. 84 (Légitime défense) — text from an OCR-scanned copy, accents missing; 'centre' in the scan corrected to 'contre'
(1) La responsabilite penale ne peut resulter d'un acte commande par la necessite immediate de la defense de soi-meme ou d'autrui, ou d'un droit appartenant a soi-meme ou a autrui contre une atteinte illegitime a condition que la defense soit proportionnee a la gravite de l'atteinte. (2) Il y a toujours juste proportion entre l'homicide et l'atteinte qui donne lieu de craindre soit la mort soit les blessures graves telles que prevues au present Code, soit le viol ou la sodomie.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

dee0813a0bf01107.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Portugal

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Article 32 of the Portuguese Penal Code defines legitimate defence as an act carried out as the 'necessary means' to repel a present and unlawful aggression against legally protected interests of the person or of a third party. The code does not mention retreat or the home, and no Portuguese court decision or commentary on a duty to retreat could be found within this search (the search budget ran out). If the means used in legitimate defence are excessive, the act is unlawful but the penalty may be specially mitigated; the person is not punished if the excess results from disturbance, fear or fright that is not blameworthy (Article 33).

What the law says
Código Penal, artigo 32.º (Legítima defesa)
Constitui legítima defesa o facto praticado como meio necessário para repelir a agressão actual e ilícita de interesses juridicamente protegidos do agente ou de terceiro.
Código Penal, artigo 33.º (Excesso de legítima defesa)
1 - Se houver excesso dos meios empregados em legítima defesa, o facto é ilícito mas a pena pode ser especialmente atenuada. 2 - O agente não é punido se o excesso resultar de perturbação, medo ou susto, não censuráveis.
Penal Code, Articles 32-33 (English translation)
Article 32 Legitimate defence: An act constitutes legitimate defence when committed as the necessary means to repel a present and unlawful aggression on legally protected interests of the agent or of a third person. Article 33 Excess of legitimate defence: 1- If there is excess of the means employed in legitimate defence, the act is unlawful but punishment may be especially mitigated. 2- The agent is not punished if the excess results from non-censurable disturbance, fear or shock.
