92e941cccc1642ff.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Eritrea

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Eritrea's Penal Code (2015) excuses an act of self-defence or defence of another against an imminent and unlawful assault only 'where the assault or threat could not have been otherwise averted' and the defence was proportionate to the danger and gravity of the assault. The code does not use the word 'retreat', but this wording makes defence conditional on there being no other way to avert the assault; no court ruling interpreting it was found. Defence of property can never justify intentional killing or serious injury. A person who used disproportionate means gets a reduced sentence, may receive no punishment if the excess came from excusable fear, surprise or excitement, and remains civilly liable for injury caused by the excess.

At home

Article 30 allows a person in peaceable possession of property to use force to prevent unlawful taking or trespass, to retake just-taken property, or to remove a trespasser from land, but not to intentionally kill or seriously injure, and not with more force than is reasonable.

What the law says
Penal Code of Eritrea (2015), art. 29 (Self-Defense and Defense of Another)
An act done under the necessity of self-defense or the defense of another person against an imminent and unlawful assault or a threat of an assault directed against a legally protected belonging shall not be punishable where the assault or threat could not have been otherwise averted and where the defense was proportionate to the needs of the case, in particular to the danger and gravity of the assault and the importance of the belonging to be defended.
Penal Code of Eritrea (2015), art. 30(2)
Sub-Article (1) does not apply where the person: (a) intentionally kills or inflicts serious bodily injury on another person; or (b) uses more force than is reasonable for the purposes described in that subsection.
Penal Code of Eritrea (2015), art. 31 (Excess in Self-Defense)
(1) Where a person, in fending off an unlawful assault, exceeds the limits of self-defense by using disproportionate means or by going beyond the acts necessary for averting the danger, the Court shall without restriction reduce the penalty. (2) The Court may impose no punishment where the excess committed was due to excusable fear, surprise or excitement caused by the assault. (3) Where a person has exceeded strict self-defense, he shall remain civilly liable for the injury caused by his excess.

f2dbe1a823e3eaf7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Austria

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Section 3 of the Criminal Code (StGB) makes defence lawful when it is the defence 'that is necessary' to repel a present or imminent unlawful attack on life, health, bodily integrity, sexual integrity, freedom or property; it is not justified if the person attacked obviously faced only a minor harm and the defence is inappropriate. There is no general duty to retreat: the Supreme Court (OGH) has held that the right of self-defence is not lost because one could perhaps escape further attacks by moving away (RS0088885, 1962). But the OGH has also said defence must be the last resort, and that a person should give way to attacks by children, the mentally ill or drunk people (RS0089005, 1972), and that someone who culpably provoked the attack must try to avoid it (RS0088713, 1977). Under section 3(2), a person who goes beyond the justified limit only out of confusion, fear or fright is punished only if the excess was negligent and negligence is a crime for that act.

What the law says
Strafgesetzbuch (StGB), § 3
(1) Nicht rechtswidrig handelt, wer sich nur der Verteidigung bedient, die notwendig ist, um einen gegenwärtigen oder unmittelbar drohenden rechtswidrigen Angriff auf Leben, Gesundheit, körperliche Unversehrtheit, sexuelle Integrität und Selbstbestimmung, Freiheit oder Vermögen von sich oder einem anderen abzuwehren. Die Handlung ist jedoch nicht gerechtfertigt, wenn es offensichtlich ist, daß dem Angegriffenen bloß ein geringer Nachteil droht und die Verteidigung, insbesondere wegen der Schwere der zur Abwehr nötigen Beeinträchtigung des Angreifers, unangemessen ist. (2) Wer das gerechtfertigte Maß der Verteidigung überschreitet oder sich einer offensichtlich unangemessenen Verteidigung (Abs. 1) bedient, ist, wenn dies lediglich aus Bestürzung, Furcht oder Schrecken geschieht, nur strafbar, wenn die Überschreitung auf Fahrlässigkeit beruht und die fahrlässige Handlung mit Strafe bedroht ist.
OGH Rechtssatz RS0088885 (9 Os 50/62, 17 Jan 1962)
Weder durch das Vorhersehen eines tätlichen Angriffes noch durch die Möglichkeit, sich unter Umständen durch Ausweichen weiterer Angriffe zu entziehen, wird das Recht auf Notwehr verwirkt.
OGH Rechtssatz RS0089005 (13 Os 83/72, 23 Nov 1972)
Aus dem Hinweis des Gesetzes auf die "nötige" Verteidigung (nunmehr : "Verteidigung, die notwendig ist") ist abzuleiten, daß die Notwehrhandlung das letzte Mittel zur Verteidigung der genannten Rechtsgüter sein müsse. Stehen andere Möglichkeiten zu deren Erhaltung zur Verfügung, so liegt grundsätzlich eine Notwehrsituation nicht vor. ... Ein Ausweichen vor einem rechtswidrigen Angriff ist insbesondere gegenüber Unreifen, Geisteskranken, Betrunkenen (ohne Rücksicht auf verschuldete Trunkenheit) geboten, da es hier einer Bewährung der Rechtsordnung nicht bedarf.
OGH Rechtssatz RS0088713 (13 Os 158/77, 10 Nov 1977)
Eine schuldhafte Provokation verpflichtet zwar zum Ausweichen vor dem provozierten Angriff, schließt aber (anders als Absichtsprovokation) Notwehr als letztes Mittel ... nicht grundsätzlich aus.

ecb66549ce649c7a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Kenya

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Kenya's Penal Code does not set out its own self-defence rules: section 17 says criminal responsibility for force used in defence of person or property is decided by the principles of English common law. Kenyan courts apply the Privy Council case Palmer v R (1971): a person who is attacked may do what is reasonably necessary to defend themselves, judged on the facts, and force wholly out of proportion is not covered. The High Court in Republic v Faris Wakhungu (2020) stated that Palmer was approved and followed in the English case R v McInnes; McInnes, as quoted with approval by Nigeria's Supreme Court, holds that a threatened person need not 'take to his heels and run' but should show they do not want to fight. No Kenyan judgment ruling directly on retreat could be opened (the Kenya Law website refused access), so the retreat position here rests on the English authorities Kenyan courts say they follow. Where the force was excessive, Kenyan courts have convicted of manslaughter instead of murder (Wakhungu: 10 years' imprisonment), and Mungai v Republic (1984) treats acts done in excess of self-defence or under provocation as rebutting malice.

What the law says
Penal Code (Cap. 63), s. 17 – Defence of person or property
Subject to any express provisions in this Code or any other law in operation in Kenya, criminal responsibility for the use of force in the defence of person or property shall be determined according to the principles of English Common Law.
Republic v Faris Wakhungu [2020] eKLR (High Court, Bungoma), quoting Palmer v R [1971] AC 814
It is both good law and good sense that a man who is attacked may defend himself. It is both good law and common sense that he may do, but may only do, what is reasonably necessary. But everything will depend upon the particular facts and circumstances.
Republic v Faris Wakhungu [2020] eKLR, quoting Mungai v Republic (1984) KLR 85
it matters little whether the circumstances relied on are regarded as acts done in excess of the right of self-defence of person or property or as acts done under the stress of provocation. The essence of crime of murder is malice aforethought and if the circumstances show that the fatal blow was given in the heat of passion on a sudden attack or threat of attack which is near enough and serious enough to cause loss of control, then the inference of malice is rebutted and the offence will be manslaughter.
R v McInnes [1971] 3 All ER 295 (England), as quoted in Laoye v The State (Nigeria SC, 1985)
It is not as we understand it the law that a person threatened must take to his heels and run in the dramatic way suggested by counsel for the appellant but what is necessary is that he should demonstrate by his action that he does not want to fight. He must demonstrate that he is prepared to temporise and disengage and perhaps to make some physical withdrawal

d644949db04b2762.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Nicaragua

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 34(4) of Nicaragua's Penal Code (Law 641), a person is exempt from criminal liability when acting in legitimate defence of their own or another's person or rights, if there is an unlawful attack, the means used are rationally necessary to prevent or repel it, and the defender did not sufficiently provoke it. For property, only an attack that is a crime and puts the property in serious danger of imminent loss counts; for a home, improper entry counts as the attack. The code does not mention retreat, and no Nicaraguan court decision on retreat was found. If not all requirements are met, the defence becomes an 'incomplete exemption' that mitigates the penalty (art. 35(1)).

At home

Penal Code art. 34(4)(a) says that, for an unlawful attack on a dwelling and its outbuildings, improper entry into them counts as the unlawful attack, so a resident may defend against an intruder subject to the rational-necessity and no-provocation requirements.

What the law says
Código Penal (Ley N° 641), art. 34(4)
Está exento de responsabilidad penal quien: [...] 4. Actúe en legítima defensa de la persona o derechos propios o ajenos, siempre que concurran los requisitos siguientes. a) Agresión ilegítima; en caso de defensa de los bienes se considerará agresión ilegítima, el ataque a los mismos que constituya delito y los ponga en grave peligro de deterioro o pérdida inminentes. En caso de agresión ilegítima a la morada y sus dependencias, se considerará la entrada indebida en una u otras; b) Necesidad racional del medio empleado para impedir o repeler la agresión; c) Falta de provocación suficiente por parte del defensor.
Código Penal (Ley N° 641), art. 35(1)
Son circunstancias atenuantes: 1. Eximentes incompletas. Las causas expresadas en el capítulo anterior, cuando no concurran todos los requisitos necesarios para eximir de responsabilidad penal en sus respectivos casos.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

c7ee51adc341581b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Botswana

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Botswana's Penal Code (1964, as amended) says a person is not criminally responsible for using force to repel an unlawful attack on their own person or property, or that of someone they have a moral or legal duty to protect, if the means and degree of force are 'no more than is reasonably necessary in the circumstances' (s. 16). The Constitution (s. 4(2)) likewise does not treat a death as a breach of the right to life if it results from reasonably justifiable force used to defend any person from violence or to defend property. The statute does not mention retreat; a 2024 High Court acquittal reported by the government Daily News applied section 16 and found the response proportionate, but no ruling on a duty to retreat was found.

At home

Section 16 of the Penal Code covers repelling an unlawful attack on one's 'person or property', with the same 'reasonably necessary' limit; no separate dwelling rule was found.

What the law says
Penal Code (Cap. 08:01), s. 16 (Defence of person or property)
Subject to the express provisions of this Code or any other law for the time being in force, a person shall not be criminally responsible for the use of force in repelling an unlawful attack upon his person or property or the person or property of anyone whom it is his moral or legal duty to protect if the means he uses and the degree of force he employs in so doing are no more than is reasonably necessary in the circumstances.
Constitution of Botswana, s. 4(2)(a)
A person shall not be regarded as having been deprived of his or her life in contravention of subsection (1) of this section if he or she dies as the result of the use, to such extent and in such circumstances as are permitted by law, of such force as is reasonably justifiable- (a) for the defence of any person from violence or for the defence of property;
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

774ce2fb8ff962ce.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ghana

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Ghana's Criminal Offences Act, 1960 (Act 29) allows force or harm 'reasonably necessary' to prevent or defend against a crime, 'extending in case of extreme necessity, even to killing' (s. 37), and no force can be justified beyond what is reasonably necessary (s. 32). The statute does not mention retreat, but the Court of Appeal in Yeboah v The State (1967) held that killing is justified only if there was no other means of saving one's life, and that a person who 'could have avoided the act, say by easily escaping from his assailant' cannot justify killing the assailant. Force used in an unlawful fight cannot be justified (s. 38). No statutory 'excessive self-defence' reduction was found.

At home

Section 39 lets a person in actual possession of a house, land, vessel or goods use 'such force as is reasonably necessary' to repel someone trying to enter forcibly and unlawfully, or to remove someone who refuses to leave; it does not separately authorise killing.

What the law says
Criminal Offences Act, 1960 (Act 29), s. 37
For the prevention of, or for the defence of himself or any other person against any crime, or for the suppression or dispersion of a riotous or unlawful assembly, a person may justify any force or harm which is reasonably necessary extending in case of extreme necessity, even to killing.
Criminal Offences Act, 1960 (Act 29), s. 32
Notwithstanding the existence of any matter of justification for force, force cannot be justified as having been used in pursuance of that matter— (a) which is in excess of the limits hereinafter prescribed in the section of this Chapter relating to that matter; or (b) which in any case extends beyond the amount and kind of force reasonably necessary for the purpose for which force is permitted to be used.
Criminal Offences Act, 1960 (Act 29), s. 39(a)
a person in actual possession of a house, land, or vessel, or goods, or his servant or any other person authorised by him, may use such force as is reasonably necessary for repelling a person who attempts forcibly and unlawfully to enter the house, land, or vessel, or to take possession of the goods;
Yeboah v The State [1967] GLR 512 (Court of Appeal, 10 July 1967)
... that short of killing the deceased, there was no other means of saving his own life. ... could have avoided the act, say by easily escaping from his assailant ... he cannot justify the killing of his assailant.

  • Yeboah v. The State [1967] GLR 512 (SuperLaw Ghana)

b23e75555ac9c186.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Republic of Serbia

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 19 of the Serbian Criminal Code says an act done in necessary defence is not a crime, where the defence is 'absolutely necessary' to repel a simultaneous unlawful attack on one's own or another's interests. The code does not mention retreat, and a 2017 article by Igor Vuković (University of Belgrade Faculty of Law) reports that Serbian courts do not impose a duty to retreat: one court called it 'unacceptable' to say the accused should have called neighbours for help or escaped through a window. Courts do expect the defender to avoid or give way to attacks by children, mentally ill or drunk people, and a person who willingly joins a fight cannot claim self-defence; the same article says courts accept self-defence 'very restrictively', especially when the attacker died. A person who exceeds the limits of necessary defence may receive a reduced sentence, or no sentence if the excess came from strong agitation or fright caused by the attack. In 2022 the Interior Ministry proposed widening the definition to cover attacks that are about to happen; the code text checked here still has the old wording.

At home

The Criminal Code has no special home-defence rule: the same test (defence 'absolutely necessary' to repel a simultaneous unlawful attack) applies inside and outside the home. A Belgrade law professor argues the home should be treated separately and criticises courts for applying the test very restrictively in home-defence cases.

What the law says
Krivični zakonik (Criminal Code), član 19
(1) Nije krivično delo ono delo koje je učinjeno u nužnoj odbrani. (2) Nužna je ona odbrana koja je neophodno potrebna da učinilac od svog dobra ili dobra drugoga odbije istovremen protivpravan napad. (3) Učiniocu koji je prekoračio granice nužne odbrane može se kazna ublažiti. Ako je učinilac prekoračio granice nužne odbrane usled jake razdraženosti ili prepasti izazvane napadom može se i osloboditi od kazne.

  • Samoodbrana i pre napada: U Krivičnom zakoniku biće proširena definicija pojma "nužna odbrana" (24 Sept 2022) (Večernje novosti)

8db6d12de610ec16.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Czechia

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Section 29 of the Criminal Code (Act No. 40/2009) says an act that repels a directly threatening or continuing attack on an interest protected by criminal law is not a crime, unless the defence was 'quite obviously disproportionate' to the manner of the attack. The code says nothing about retreat, but the Supreme Court has held that, unlike necessity, self-defence does not require that the defender could not have avoided the attack in another way (6 Tdo 339/2008), and that failing to use a chance to flee cannot by itself be the basis for finding the defence excessive (5 Tdo 162/2007). The court also says the defence may be stronger than the attack, since otherwise it would have no chance of success, and that it is judged partly by how the attack appeared to the defender. Defence that was quite obviously disproportionate ('intensive excess') is not justified and can be punished.

What the law says
Trestní zákoník (Act No. 40/2009 Coll.), § 29
(1) Čin jinak trestný, kterým někdo odvrací přímo hrozící nebo trvající útok na zájem chráněný trestním zákonem, není trestným činem. (2) Nejde o nutnou obranu, byla-li obrana zcela zjevně nepřiměřená způsobu útoku.
Supreme Court, resolution 6 Tdo 339/2008 (26 Mar 2008), headnote as published by epravo.cz
Podmínkou nutné obrany není, že se bránící nemohl vyhnout útoku jinak. Obrana ale nesmí být zcela zjevně nepřiměřená způsobu útoku. ... obrana musí být, má-li být způsobilá k jistému odvrácení útoku bez rizika pro napadeného, silnější než útok.
Supreme Court, resolution 5 Tdo 162/2007 (28 Feb 2007), as summarised in epravo.cz article
sama skutečnost, že napadený nevyužil možnost útěku, ale aktivně se útoku bránil, nemůže být podkladem pro závěr, že spáchal trestný čin v důsledku překročení mezí nutné obrany. Podle Nejvyššího soudu ČR tak nikdo není povinen snášet útok vůči své osobě a vůči zájmům chráněným trestním zákoníkem, ale má právo se bránit i v případě, že je možné se teoreticky útoku vyhnout jinak.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

f4b98e1aa541a934.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Tunisia

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Tunisia's Penal Code (1913, official 2012 edition) has a short general rule in article 39: there is no offence when the person was forced to act by a circumstance that exposed their own life, or that of a close relative (ascendants, descendants, siblings, spouse), to imminent danger, 'and when this danger could not otherwise be averted'. If the person threatened is not a close relative, the judge assesses the degree of responsibility. The wording therefore makes the defence depend on there being no other way to avoid the danger, and on a threat to life. Article 40 separately says there is no offence when a killing or injury happens while repelling a night-time break-in to a dwelling or defending against violent theft or looting. No Tunisian court decisions on how the 'no other way' condition applies to flight, and no provision on excessive defence, were found.

At home

There is no offence where homicide, wounds or blows occur while repelling, at night, the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or entrances of a dwelling or its outbuildings, or while defending against violent theft or looting (art. 40).

What the law says
Code pénal (Décret du 9 juillet 1913, édition officielle 2012), art. 39
Il n'y a pas d'infraction lorsque l'auteur y a été contraint par une circonstance qui exposait sa vie ou celle de l’un de ses proches à un danger imminent, et lorsque ce danger ne pouvait être autrement détourné. Sont considérés comme proches : 1°- les ascendants et descendants, 2°- les frères et sœurs, 3°- les époux. Si la personne menacée n’est pas un proche, le juge appréciera le degré de responsabilité.
Code pénal, art. 40
Il n'y a pas d'infraction : 1) si l'homicide a été commis, si les blessures ont été faites ou les coups portés en repoussant, la nuit, l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrées d'une habitation ou de ses dépendances. 2) si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Le Code pénal (Publications de l’Imprimerie Officielle de la République Tunisienne, 2012) (Policinglaw.info (copy of the Imprimerie Officielle edition))
f4b98e1aa541a934.t: Tunisia · A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

6afef7a4694b0929.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Mauritania

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Mauritania's Penal Code (Ordinance 83-162 of 9 July 1983) keeps the old French self-defence wording alongside Islamic-law offences: there is no crime when homicide, wounds or blows were 'commanded by the current necessity of legitimate defence of oneself or another' (art. 304). Article 305 lists two situations that automatically count as such necessity: repelling a night-time break-in into an inhabited home, and defending against violent theft or looting. The code says nothing about retreat or proportionality, and no Mauritanian court decisions on whether a person must avoid the attack were found. A killing provoked by serious blows or violence, or done while repelling a daytime break-in, is 'excusable' (arts. 297–298); when the excuse is proven, a crime carrying death or life hard labour is reduced to one to five years' imprisonment (art. 302).

At home

Article 305 counts as 'current necessity of defence' a homicide, wounding or blows committed while repelling, at night, the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or the entrance of an inhabited house or flat or its outbuildings. Repelling such a break-in by day is not justified but 'excusable' (art. 298), which lowers the penalty.

What the law says
Code pénal (Ordonnance n° 83-162 du 9 juillet 1983), art. 304
Il n'y [a] ni crime ni délit lorsque l'homicide, les blessures et les coups étaient commandés par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi-même ou d'autrui.
Code pénal, art. 305
Sont compris dans les cas de nécessité actuelle de défense, les deux cas suivants : 1. Si l'homicide a été commis, si les blessures ont été faites, ou si les coups ont été portés en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d'une maison ou d'un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances; 2. Si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou pillages exécutés avec violence.
Code pénal, arts. 297, 298 and 302
ART. 297. - Le meurtre ainsi que les blessures et les coups sont excusables, s'ils ont été provoqués par des coups ou violences graves envers les personnes. ART. 298. - Les crimes ou délits mentionnés au précédent article sont également excusables, s'ils ont été commis en repoussant pendant le jour l'escalade ou l'effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d'une maison ou d'un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances. Si le fait est arrivé pendant la nuit, ce cas est réglé par l'article 305. ... ART. 302. - Lorsque le fait d'excuse sera prouvé, s'il s'agit d'un crime emportant la peine de mort, ou celle des travaux forcés à perpétuité, la peine sera réduite à un emprisonnement d'un an à cinq ans.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

b0fc460b1ce09fa9.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Malawi

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Malawi's Penal Code section 17 says criminal responsibility for force used in defence of person or property is decided by the principles of common law. Malawian courts apply the Privy Council case Palmer v R: a person who is attacked may do what is reasonably necessary, a person cannot be expected to weigh the exact measure of defensive force, and force used after the danger has passed is revenge, not self-defence. The Supreme Court of Appeal in Paison v Republic (1998) added that a person needing to defend themselves cannot be expected to choose the right weapon or target. No Malawian statute or judgment found says whether a person must retreat, so the retreat question is not settled by the sources found. Where self-defence fails only because the force was more than reasonably necessary, Malawian courts convict of manslaughter instead of murder (Jackson v Reginam; Paison; Republic v Smart John Phiri, 2021).

At home

In Ngozo v Republic (High Court, 1997) the trial court had thought self-defence was unavailable because the complainant was injured at his own house; the High Court said that was wrong, because the necessity to protect one's body 'can arise anywhere even in the victim's house'. No specific home or castle rule was found.

What the law says
Penal Code (Cap. 7:01), s. 17 – Defence of person or property
Subject to any express provisions in this Code or any other law in operation in Mala[w]i, criminal responsibility for the use of force in the defence of person or property shall be determined according to the principles of common law.
Republic v Smart John Phiri, Homicide Case No. 28 of 2020 (High Court, 17 Feb 2021), citing Jackson v Reginam, Paison v Rep [1998] MLR 302 (SCA) and Nyirenda v Rep
where the defence of self-defence fails merely because the person used excessive force than was reasonably necessary ... that person would normally be entitled to be convicted for the lesser offence of manslaughter.
Republic v Smart John Phiri (2021), citing Paison v Rep [1998] MLR 302 (SCA)
the law also recognizes that when a person finds himself in a situation which demands self-defence ... he cannot be expected to have time to select the right weapon and to target the correct part of the body.
Francisco Macloud Ngozo v Republic, Criminal Appeal No. 106 of 1996 (High Court, 31 Jan 1997)
The defence is based on necessity to protect ones limb or body or that of another. Such necessity can arise anywhere even in the victim's house.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • Republic v Smart John Phiri (Homicide Case 28 of 2020) [2021] MWHC (MalawiLII)
  • Ngozo v Republic (Criminal Appeal 106 of 1996) [1997] MWHC 1 (MalawiLII)
  • Republic v Joseph Muliya (Criminal Case 364 of 2010) [2016] MWHC 645 (MalawiLII)

891f6b3b7a1eee8c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

United Arab Emirates

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The UAE's federal Crimes and Penalties Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021, in force 2 January 2022) says there is no crime when an act is done in the use of the right of legitimate defence (art. 58). According to the official English text, as summarised when it was opened, the right applies when the defender faces an immediate threat of a forcible crime against themselves, their property or another person or their property (or reasonably believes so), cannot get timely help from the authorities, and has no other way to stop the danger; the defence must also be necessary and proportionate. Intentional killing is justified only to repel a reasonably feared act causing death or serious injury, forced intercourse or 'disgracing' a person, kidnapping, arson, destruction or theft felonies, or a night-time entry into an inhabited house (art. 59). Exceeding the limits in good faith is treated as an extenuating excuse, and the judge may pardon the person (art. 61). The full article texts could only be read in short excerpts, so the wording of the 'no other way' condition is paraphrased here, not quoted.

At home

Article 59 lists 'entering at night an inhabited house or any of its annexes' among the five situations in which legitimate defence may extend to intentional killing.

What the law says
Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021 (Crimes and Penalties Law), art. 58 (official English translation; excerpts)
There is no crime if the act is committed in the use of the right of legitimate defence. ... If the defence is necessary in order to repel the attack and is proportionate thereto.
Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021, art. 59 (excerpts)
The right of legitimate defence does not justify premeditated murder, unless ... Entering at night an inhabited house or any of its annexes.
Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021, art. 61 (excerpt)
Exceeding the limits of justification in good faith is considered an extenuating excuse
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Federal Decree-Law No. (31) of 2021 Promulgating the Crimes and Penalties Law (UAE Legislation portal (federal government))
891f6b3b7a1eee8c.t: United Arab Emirates · A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

54dc4588eafde79e.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Washington

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Washington has no stand-your-ground statute. Homicide is justifiable in lawful defence of oneself, a relative or anyone in one's presence when there is reasonable ground to fear a design to commit a felony or do great personal injury and the danger is imminent, or in actually resisting an attempted felony on the person or in a dwelling where they are (RCW 9A.16.050, from 1975). The statutes say nothing about retreat; according to the Giffords Law Center, the Washington Supreme Court has held there is no duty to retreat before using force where a person has a right to be (State v. Hiatt, 1936; State v. Allery, 1984; State v. Redmond, 2003), and the pattern instruction WPIC 16.08 tells juries so. Instead of immunity, Washington has a rule that no one 'shall be placed in legal jeopardy of any kind whatsoever' for protecting themselves, their family or property by any reasonable means necessary, and that a defendant acquitted on self-defence (proved by a preponderance of the evidence) must be reimbursed by the state for legal fees, lost time and other costs (RCW 9A.16.110). The judge may deny or reduce the award if the defendant was engaged in criminal conduct substantially related to the events. No statutory presumption of reasonable fear or pretrial immunity hearing was found. The texts of the cases and WPIC 16.08 could not be opened for this entry, so limits such as the initial-aggressor rule are not quoted here.

At home

RCW 9A.16.050(2) makes homicide justifiable 'in the actual resistance of an attempt to commit a felony upon the slayer, in his or her presence, or upon or in a dwelling, or other place of abode, in which he or she is'. No separate castle presumption was found.

No-retreat rule taken from a secondary source citing the cases and WPIC 16.08; those were not opened.

What the law says
RCW 9A.16.050 (1975 1st ex.s. c 260; 2011 c 336)
Homicide is also justifiable when committed either: (1) In the lawful defense of the slayer, or his or her husband, wife, parent, child, brother, or sister, or of any other person in his or her presence or company, when there is reasonable ground to apprehend a design on the part of the person slain to commit a felony or to do some great personal injury to the slayer or to any such person, and there is imminent danger of such design being accomplished; or (2) In the actual resistance of an attempt to commit a felony upon the slayer, in his or her presence, or upon or in a dwelling, or other place of abode, in which he or she is.
RCW 9A.16.110(1)-(2) (legal jeopardy; reimbursement)
No person in the state shall be placed in legal jeopardy of any kind whatsoever for protecting by any reasonable means necessary, himself or herself, his or her family, or his or her real or personal property ... When a person charged with a crime listed in subsection (1) of this section is found not guilty by reason of self-defense, the state of Washington shall reimburse the defendant for all reasonable costs ...
State v. Redmond, 150 Wn.2d 489 (2003); State v. Allery, 101 Wn.2d 591 (1984); State v. Hiatt, 187 Wash. 226, 237 (1936); WPIC 16.08 (as cited by Giffords)
Though Washington does not have a stand your ground statute, the state supreme court has held that there is no duty to retreat before using force in public. [Giffords summary]
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • RCW 9A.16.050 and 9A.16.110 (Washington State Legislature)
  • Stand Your Ground in Washington (Giffords Law Center)

de331268ba451c47.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Niger

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Niger's Penal Code (Law 61-27 of 1961 as amended by Law 2003-025 of 13 June 2003) follows the old French model: there is no offence when the act was 'commanded by the current necessity of legitimate defence of oneself or another' (art. 43). Article 44 lists two situations that automatically count as such necessity: repelling a night-time break-in into an inhabited home, and defending against violent theft or looting. The code does not mention retreat or proportionality, and no Nigerien court decisions on whether a person must avoid the attack were found. Killing or injuring after being provoked by serious blows or violence, or while repelling a daytime break-in, is 'excusable' (art. 245), which reduces the penalty; a spouse who kills the other spouse or their partner on catching them in adultery in the marital home is also excused (art. 246).

At home

Article 44 counts as 'current necessity of defence' a homicide, wounding or blows committed while repelling, at night, the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or the entrance of an inhabited house or flat or its outbuildings. If the same thing happens by day, the killing or injury is not justified but is 'excusable', which lowers the penalty (art. 245(2)).

What the law says
Code pénal (Loi n° 61-27, modifiée par Loi n° 2003-025), art. 43
Il n’y a pas d’infraction lorsque le fait a été commandé par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi-même ou d’autrui.
Code pénal, art. 44
Sont compris dans les cas de nécessité actuelle de défense les deux cas suivants : 1) si l’homicide a été commis, si les blessures ont été faites ou si les coups ont été portés en repoussant, pendant la nuit, l’escalade ou l’effraction des clôtures, murs, ou entrée d’une maison, ou d’un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances ; 2) si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols, ou pillages exécutés avec violence.
Code pénal, art. 245
Le meurtre ainsi que les blessures et les coups sont excusables : 1) s’ils ont été provoqués par des coups et violences graves envers les personnes ; 2) s’ils ont été commis en repoussant, pendant le jour, l’escalade ou l’effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d’une maison ou d’un appartement habité, ou de leurs dépendances. Toutefois le parricide, le génocide et les crimes contre l’humanité ne sont jamais excusables
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Code pénal du Niger (Loi n° 2003-025 du 13 juin 2003 modifiant la loi n° 61-27) (Policinglaw.info (copy of Ministry of Justice edition))

b0fbcf1c3789165a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Costa Rica

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 28 of the Penal Code (Ley 4573 of 1970), a person does not commit a crime when defending their own or another's person or rights, if there is an unlawful aggression and a "reasonable necessity of the defence used" to repel or prevent it. The Code does not mention retreat, and the sources opened here did not settle whether flight is expected. A separate article (art. 29, headed "Excess in defence") deals with defenders who go beyond these limits; its text could not be read in the source opened. The home rule added in 1975 covers intruders inside a building who endanger the occupants.

At home

Since Ley 5743 of 1975, art. 28 states that self-defence applies to anyone who commits violent acts against a stranger who, without any right and endangering the inhabitants or occupants, is inside a building or its outbuildings, "whatever the harm caused to the intruder".

What the law says
Código Penal (Ley 4573), art. 28, as amended by Ley 5743 of 4 August 1975
No comete delito el que obra en defensa de la persona o derechos, propios o ajenos, siempre que concurran las siguientes circunstancias: a) Agresión ilegítima; y b) Necesidad razonable de la defensa empleada para repeler o impedir la agresión. Se entenderá que concurre esta causal de justificación para aquel que ejecutare actos violentos contra el individuo extraño que, sin derecho alguno y con peligro para los habitantes u ocupantes de la edificación o sus dependencias, se hallare dentro de ellas, cualquiera que sea el daño causado al intruso.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Código Penal de Costa Rica (Ley 4573), consolidated (Bufete de Costa Rica (legal library))
  • Reforma del Artículo 28 del Código Penal de Costa Rica (Ley N° 5743) (Bufete de Costa Rica)

0920d7b331d83aad.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

California

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

California's statute (Penal Code § 197) makes a homicide justifiable when resisting an attempt to murder, to commit a felony, or to do great bodily injury, and in defence of a person or home against someone who manifestly intends a violent felony. The statute is silent on retreat outside the cases of an assailant or mutual combatant, but the courts have long held there is no duty to retreat, and the official jury instruction tells jurors that a defendant 'is not required to retreat' and may stand their ground 'even if safety could have been achieved by retreating' (CALCRIM No. 505, citing People v. Hughes (1951) 107 Cal.App.2d 487 and People v. Hatchett (1942) 56 Cal.App.2d 20). Deadly force is lawful only if the defendant reasonably believed they or someone else faced imminent danger of death or great bodily injury, reasonably believed immediate deadly force was necessary, and used no more force than was reasonably necessary; the prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the killing was not justified. An initial aggressor or mutual combatant must really and in good faith try to decline further fighting before the right of self-defence returns (§ 197(3)). Inside the home, a 1984 statute presumes reasonable fear when the person killed or injured had unlawfully and forcibly entered (§ 198.5). If the defendant actually but unreasonably believed deadly force was needed, the killing is 'imperfect self-defense' and is reduced from murder to voluntary manslaughter (CALCRIM No. 571; People v. Flannel (1979) 25 Cal.3d 668; In re Christian S. (1994) 7 Cal.4th 768), though not if the belief was entirely delusional (People v. Elmore (2014)). California has no statutory immunity from prosecution or pretrial immunity hearing for self-defence.

At home

Cal. Penal Code § 198.5 (added 1984, Stats. 1984 ch. 1666): a person who uses deadly force inside their own residence is presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent death or great bodily injury to themselves, family or household when the force is used against someone (not a family or household member) who unlawfully and forcibly entered, and the person knew or had reason to believe that a forcible entry occurred. Penal Code § 197(2) also makes homicide justifiable in defence of habitation against someone who violently or riotously tries to enter to offer violence to a person inside.

What the law says
CALCRIM No. 505 (Justifiable Homicide: Self-Defense or Defense of Another)
A defendant is not required to retreat. He or she is entitled to stand his or her ground and defend himself or herself ... This is so even if safety could have been achieved by retreating.
Cal. Penal Code § 197(1), (3)
Homicide is also justifiable when committed by any person in any of the following cases: (1) When resisting any attempt to murder any person, or to commit a felony, or to do some great bodily injury upon any person. ... (3) ... but such person, or the person in whose behalf the defense was made, if he or she was the assailant or engaged in mutual combat, must really and in good faith have endeavored to decline any further struggle before the homicide was committed.
Cal. Penal Code § 198.5
Any person using force intended or likely to cause death or great bodily injury within his or her residence shall be presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or great bodily injury to self, family, or a member of the household when that force is used against another person, not a member of the family or household, who unlawfully and forcibly enters or has unlawfully and forcibly entered the residence ...
CALCRIM No. 571 (Voluntary Manslaughter: Imperfect Self-Defense)
A killing that would otherwise be murder is reduced to voluntary manslaughter ... At least one of those beliefs was unreasonable.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • CALCRIM No. 571, Voluntary Manslaughter: Imperfect Self-Defense (Judicial Council of California (via Justia))
  • California Penal Code § 197 (Public.Law (text from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov))
  • California Penal Code § 198.5 (Added by Stats. 1984, Ch. 1666, Sec. 1) (Onecle (text from California Legislature))

f7a49e3fab722b28.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Tasmania

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Tasmania's Criminal Code (s 46, substituted in 1987) justifies the force that, in the circumstances as the person believes them to be, it is reasonable to use in defence of themselves or another. The section says nothing about retreat and no duty to retreat is stated in the Code. No Tasmanian provision on excessive self-defence was found in the Code text consulted.

At home

s 40: a person in peaceable possession of a dwelling-house may use the force they believe on reasonable grounds is necessary to prevent forcible breaking and entering by someone they believe intends to commit a crime there, or to eject such a person.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act 1924 (Tas), Schedule 1, s 46 Self-defence and defence of another person
A person is justified in using, in the defence of himself or another person, such force as, in the circumstances as he believes them to be, it is reasonable to use.
Criminal Code Act 1924 (Tas), s 40 Defence of dwelling-house
It is lawful for any person who is in peaceable possession of a dwelling-house, and for any person lawfully assisting him or acting by his authority, to use such force as the person using the same believes on reasonable grounds to be necessary to prevent the forcible breaking and entering of the dwelling-house by any person whom he believes on reasonable grounds to be attempting to break or enter the dwelling-house with intent to commit any crime therein, or to eject therefrom any person who has unlawfully entered the dwelling-house, and whom he believes on reasonable grounds to intend to commit a crime therein.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Criminal Code Act 1924 (current version) (Tasmanian Legislation, Office of Parliamentary Counsel)
Australia as a whole

Most criminal law in Australia is made by the six states and two territories, each with its own self-defence rule; this national entry describes the Commonwealth Criminal Code, which covers federal offences. Under s 10.4 a person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them. No Australian statute found imposes a duty to retreat; in jury directions (NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book) the availability of retreat is listed as one matter the jury may weigh in deciding whether the response was reasonable. Deadly or really serious force cannot be justified solely to protect property or deal with trespassers. Whether excessive force reduces murder to manslaughter depends on the state or territory (e.g. NSW s 421, WA s 248(3), SA s 15(2)).

Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book — Self-defence (Judicial Commission of New South Wales)

d98a79824daefcc3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Iraq

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Iraq's Penal Code (No. 111 of 1969) says there is no crime when an act is committed in legal defence, but only if the person could not take refuge with the public authorities in time and 'has no other means with which to ward off such threat' (art. 42). The code does not use the word 'retreat'; these conditions make defence available only when there is no other way out, and no court ruling interpreting them was found. Killing in self-defence is allowed only against a reasonably feared risk of death or serious injury, rape or sodomy by force, or kidnapping (art. 43), and in defence of property only against arson, theft, night-time entry into a home, or a feared risk of death or injury (art. 44). A person who deliberately or negligently goes beyond the limits of the right is responsible for the offence, but the court must impose the lower penalty class (misdemeanour instead of felony) (art. 45).

At home

Paragraph (article) 44 allows killing in defence of property when warding off, among other things, 'entering at night a residential building or part thereof'.

What the law says
Penal Code No. 111 of 1969, para. 42 (Ministry of Justice English translation)
There is no crime if the act is committed while exercising a right of legal defense. This right exists if the following conditions apply: (1) If a person defends himself and his property against the threat of a criminal act or reasonably believes that such threat exists. (2) If he is unable to take refuge with the public authorities in order to protect himself from such threat at the appropriate time. (3) If he has no other means with which to ward off such threat.
Penal Code No. 111 of 1969, paras. 43–45
Paragraph 43 - The right of legal self-defense does not permit murder unless it is intended that one of the following situations is to be avoided: (1) An act as a result of which it is reasonably feared that death or serious injury may occur. (2) Rape or buggery of a man or woman against his or her will. (3) Kidnapping. ... Paragraph 45 - The right of legal defense does not permit the infliction of greater harm than is necessary and if the person concerned oversteps the limits of that right either deliberately or negligently or if he mistakenly thinks that he is in a situation of legal defense, then he will be responsible for the offence he commits. In this case, the court is only permitted to impose the penalty for a misdemeanor rather than that prescribed for a felony and the penalty for an infraction rather than that prescribed for a misdemeanor.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

41a6cad06047fc02.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Hungary

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Hungary's Criminal Code (Act C of 2012) says an act necessary to fend off an unlawful attack, or a direct threat of one, against one's own or another's person or property or the public interest is not punishable. The statute states directly that the person attacked is not obliged to step aside from the unlawful attack, so there is no duty to retreat. Certain attacks (at night, armed, by a group, or home intrusions of those kinds) must be treated as if they were aimed at killing the defender, which widens what force counts as necessary. A person who goes beyond the necessary degree of defence out of fright or excusable agitation is not punishable.

At home

Section 22(2) of the Criminal Code treats an unlawful intrusion into a home at night, with a weapon displayed or carried, or by a group, and an armed unlawful intrusion into the fenced area belonging to a home, as if it were also aimed at killing the defender. Section 21 also allows non-lethal protective devices installed in advance, if the owner did everything reasonable to prevent them causing harm.

What the law says
Büntető Törvénykönyv (Act C of 2012), 22. § (1)-(4)
(1) Nem büntetendő az a cselekmény, amely a saját, illetve más vagy mások személye, javai vagy a közérdek ellen intézett, illetve ezeket közvetlenül fenyegető jogtalan támadás elhárításához szükséges. (2) A jogtalan támadást úgy kell tekinteni, mintha az a védekező életének kioltására is irányult volna, ha a) azt személy ellen aa) éjjel, ab) fegyveresen, ac) felfegyverkezve vagy ad) csoportosan követik el, b) az a lakásba ba) éjjel, bb) fegyveresen, bc) felfegyverkezve vagy bd) csoportosan történő jogtalan behatolás, vagy c) az a lakáshoz tartozó bekerített helyre fegyveresen történő jogtalan behatolás. (3) Nem büntethető, aki az elhárítás szükséges mértékét ijedtségből vagy menthető felindulásból lépi túl. (4) A megtámadott nem köteles kitérni a jogtalan támadás elől.
Criminal Code, section 22(3)-(4) (English translation in CJAD database)
(3) Any person who exceeds the reasonable force of self-defense due to shock or justifiable aggravation shall not be prosecuted. (4) The person assaulted shall not be liable to take evasive action so as to avoid the unlawful attack.
Büntető Törvénykönyv (Act C of 2012), 21. §
Nem büntetendő annak a cselekménye, aki a saját, illetve a mások személye vagy javai elleni jogtalan támadás megelőzése céljából telepített, az élet kioltására nem alkalmas védelmi eszközzel a jogtalan támadónak sérelmet okoz, feltéve, hogy a védekező mindent megtett, ami az adott helyzetben elvárható annak érdekében, hogy az általa telepített védelmi eszköz ne okozzon sérelmet.

a0b82867bdb3f238.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Sri Lanka

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Sri Lanka's Penal Code gives a right of private defence of body and property, limited by section 92(3), which removes the right where 'there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities'. In The Queen v. A. O. Rodrigo (Court of Criminal Appeal, 31 October 1962), the court held that this limit does not apply when a person is set upon by an assailant and there is imminent danger of death or grievous hurt; it applies only where the attack is known beforehand and there is enough time to seek the authorities' protection. On the accused's version of events, there was 'no legal obligation on him to have run away' and he was 'justified in law in holding his ground and defending his body'. A trial direction suggesting he should have run away was held wrong in law and his conviction was quashed. The Penal Code's text itself, and rules on excessive defence, were not directly checked because the official and CommonLII copies could not be reached.

What the law says
Penal Code, s. 92(3), as quoted in The Queen v. A. O. Rodrigo (1962)
there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities
The Queen v. A. O. Rodrigo, Court of Criminal Appeal, Appeal No. 95 of 1962 (66 NLR), Basnayake C.J., Herat J., G. P. A. Silva J.
According to appellant's version, there was no legal obligation on him to have run away. ... He was justified in law in holding his ground and defending his body.

0f2c10ff8ae7794a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Louisiana

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Louisiana makes a homicide justifiable when committed in self-defence by someone who reasonably believes they are in imminent danger of losing their life or receiving great bodily harm and that the killing is necessary to save themselves, or to prevent a violent or forcible felony involving danger to life or great bodily harm (La. R.S. 14:20(A)). A person who is not engaged in unlawful activity and is in a place where they have a right to be has no duty to retreat before using deadly force and may stand their ground and meet force with force (§ 14:20(C)). Louisiana goes further than most states: the judge or jury is not allowed to consider the possibility of retreat at all when deciding whether the person's belief that deadly force was necessary was reasonable (§ 14:20(D)). These retreat provisions and the home presumption were added by Acts 2006, No. 141, and amended by Acts 2014, No. 163; the parallel non-deadly force section (§ 14:19) was extended to churches and places of worship and last amended in 2026 (Acts 2026, No. 148). A person who is the aggressor or 'who brings on a difficulty' cannot claim self-defence unless they withdraw in good faith in a way the adversary knows or should know (§ 14:21). The sources consulted for this entry show no statutory immunity from criminal prosecution or pretrial immunity hearing; civil immunity was not checked.

At home

La. R.S. 14:20(A)(4) and (B): a homicide is justifiable when committed by a person lawfully inside a dwelling, place of business or motor vehicle when the conflict began, against someone trying to enter unlawfully or who has entered unlawfully, if the person reasonably believes deadly force is necessary to prevent the entry or make the intruder leave; the law presumes that belief was reasonable if the intruder was unlawfully and forcibly entering and the person knew or had reason to believe it. This home/business/vehicle rule does not apply to someone who is at that time engaged in acquiring or distributing illegal drugs or possessing them with intent to distribute. § 14:20(A)(3) also allows deadly force against someone reasonably believed likely to use unlawful force against a person in a dwelling, business or vehicle while committing burglary or robbery there.

What the law says
La. R.S. 14:20(C)–(D)
C. A person who is not engaged in unlawful activity and who is in a place where he or she has a right to be shall have no duty to retreat before using deadly force as provided for in this Section, and may stand his or her ground and meet force with force. D. No finder of fact shall be permitted to consider the possibility of retreat as a factor in determining whether or not the person who used deadly force had a reasonable belief that deadly force was reasonable and apparently necessary to prevent a violent or forcible felony involving life or great bodily harm or to prevent the unlawful entry.
La. R.S. 14:20(A)(1)–(2)
A homicide is justifiable: (1) When committed in self-defense by one who reasonably believes that he is in imminent danger of losing his life or receiving great bodily harm and that the killing is necessary to save himself from that danger. (2) When committed for the purpose of preventing a violent or forcible felony involving danger to life or of great bodily harm by one who reasonably believes that such an offense is about to be committed and that such action is necessary for its prevention.
La. R.S. 14:20(B)
there shall be a presumption that a person lawfully inside a dwelling, place of business, or motor vehicle held a reasonable belief that the use of deadly force was necessary to prevent unlawful entry thereto, or to compel an unlawful intruder to leave the dwelling, place of business, or motor vehicle when the conflict began, if both of the following occur: (1) The person against whom deadly force was used was in the process of unlawfully and forcibly entering or had unlawfully and forcibly entered ...
La. R.S. 14:21
A person who is the aggressor or who brings on a difficulty cannot claim the right of self-defense unless he withdraws from the conflict in good faith and in such a manner that his adversary knows or should know that he desires to withdraw and discontinue the conflict.

5f580ab6e9a29373.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Zimbabwe

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Zimbabwe's Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act 2004 makes defence of a person a complete defence only if the attack had begun or was imminent, the defender's conduct was necessary to avert it "and he or she could not otherwise escape from or avert the attack" (or reasonably believed so), the means used were reasonable, and the harm was not grossly disproportionate and fell on the attacker rather than an innocent third party. So the law expressly builds in a duty to escape or avoid the attack where that is possible. Courts must take account of the defender's circumstances, including stress or fear. If everything else is met but the means used were unreasonable, a person charged with murder is instead guilty of culpable homicide (s. 254). A genuine and reasonable mistaken belief in an attack counts as if it were true (s. 255). The sources opened here did not show a separate home rule.

What the law says
Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act [Chapter 9:23], s. 253(1)
the fact that a person accused of a crime was defending himself or herself or another person against an unlawful attack ... shall be a complete defence to the charge if— (a) when he or she did or omitted to do the thing, the unlawful attack had commenced or was imminent or he or she believed on reasonable grounds that the unlawful attack had commenced or was imminent, and (b) his or her conduct was necessary to avert the unlawful attack and he or she could not otherwise escape from or avert the attack or he or she, believed on reasonable grounds that his or her conduct was necessary to avert the unlawful attack and that he or she could not otherwise escape from or avert the attack, and (c) the means he or she used to avert the unlawful attack were reasonable in all the circumstances; and (d) any harm or injury caused by his or her conduct— (i) was caused to the attacker and not to any innocent third party; and (ii) was not grossly disproportionate to that liable to be caused by the unlawful attack.
Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act, s. 254
If a person accused of murder was defending himself or herself or another person against an unlawful attack ... he or she shall be guilty of culpable homicide if all the requirements for defence of person specified in section two hundred andfifty-three are satisfied in the case except that the means he or she used to avert the unlawful attack were not reasonable in all the circumstances.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Self-defence - national proceedings: Zimbabwe (Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act 2004) (Case Matrix Network / University of Nottingham, Criminal Justice and Armed Defence (CJAD) legislation database)

847cf2b08efc2c31.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

South Georgia and the Islands

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands is a British Overseas Territory with no permanent population. Its government's official laws website explains that English common law and some English statutes apply there, through direct UK legislation, reception of common law and pre-1900 statutes of general application, local Ordinances and the Interpretation and General Clauses Ordinance 1977, and that working out exactly which English laws apply is 'ultimately a matter of judgement for the courts'. No local Ordinance or court decision on self-defence, retreat or home defence was found, and no source confirms whether modern English self-defence statutes apply, so the retreat rule here is not settled by the sources found.

What the law says
SGSSI Laws website, 'English Statutory Law' (Government of South Georgia & the South Sandwich Islands)
There are several ways in which English statute law either applied or continues to apply in South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands. These include: direct legislation by the Crown and Parliament; reception of English common law and statutes of general application by virtue of South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands having being claimed for the Crown by settlement; the application of English statute law by a local Ordinance; the operation of the Interpretation and General Clauses Ordinance (1977) with regard to what is termed 'Imperial Enactments'; and by implication.

cb6b1f328e3b143a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Switzerland

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 15 of the Swiss Criminal Code entitles the person attacked, and anyone else, to ward off an unlawful attack or imminent threat of attack 'by means that are reasonable in the circumstances'. According to a 2023 article by Prof. Felix Bommer (University of Zurich) reviewing Swiss doctrine and Federal Supreme Court case law, there is no duty to flee or step aside in a self-defence situation, but Swiss practice requires that there be no obvious imbalance between the value of what is attacked and the harm done to the attacker; a person who negligently provoked the attack may, in some decisions, be required to step aside. If a defender exceeds the limits of self-defence, the court must reduce the sentence (Art. 16(1)); if the excess came from excusable excitement or panic caused by the attack, the defender is not guilty (Art. 16(2)), though courts rarely find an excess excusable.

At home

No separate home-defence rule. The right to exclude others from one's home (Hausrecht) can be defended, but Swiss practice still requires that the harm caused not be grossly out of proportion; Prof. Bommer gives the example that a homeowner may not fire a warning shot to chase an uninvited guest out of an office.

What the law says
Schweizerisches Strafgesetzbuch, Art. 15 (German text)
Wird jemand ohne Recht angegriffen oder unmittelbar mit einem Angriff bedroht, so ist der Angegriffene und jeder andere berechtigt, den Angriff in einer den Umständen angemessenen Weise abzuwehren.
Swiss Criminal Code, Art. 15-16 (English translation)
Art. 15 If any person is unlawfully attacked or threatened with imminent attack, the person attacked and any other person are entitled to ward off the attack by means that are reasonable in the circumstances. Art. 16 1 If a person in defending himself exceeds the limits of self-defence as defined in Article 15 and in doing so commits an offence, the court shall reduce the sentence. 2 If a person in defending himself exceeds the limits of self-defence as a result of excusable excitement or panic in reaction to the attack, he does not commit an offence.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Das deutsche Notwehrrecht – Ein knapper Blick von außen (Felix Bommer), KriPoZ 6/2023 (Kriminalpolitische Zeitschrift (KriPoZ))
  • Self-defence - national proceedings: Switzerland (Criminal Code 1937 (2017) EN) (University of Nottingham, CJAD database)

563a7393793d9adf.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Libya

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under Libya's Penal Code (1953, as amended by Law No. 48 of 1956), there is no punishment for an act committed in exercise of the right of lawful defence, which covers 'any act that is necessary in order to avert a crime' that would harm oneself or others (art. 70). The right does not exist when it would have been possible to seek the protection of the public authorities in time. The code text found does not mention retreat or escape, and no Libyan court decisions on the point were found. Wilful killing is justified only to avert a reasonably feared act causing death or severe injury, forcible sexual intercourse or violation, kidnapping, felony theft, or night-time entry into an inhabited residence (art. 70 bis (b)). If the limits imposed by necessity are negligently exceeded, the person is punished under the rules for negligent offences where they exist (art. 73).

At home

Article 70 bis (b) lists 'entry by night of an inhabited residence or any of its appurtenances' among the situations in which lawful defence may extend to wilful killing.

What the law says
Penal Code (as amended by Law No. 48 of 1956), art. 70 – Lawful Defence (DCAF English translation)
There is no punishment if the act is committed during exercise of the right to lawful defence. This right exculpates a person for commission of any act that is necessary in order to avert a crime that would cause damage to himself or others. This right does not exist when it would have been possible to seek the protection of the public authorities in a timely manner.
Penal Code, art. 70 bis (b)
The right to lawful defence does not exculpate wilful murder unless it was intended in order to avert the following situations: An act that it is feared would cause death or severe injury, when this fear rests on reasonable grounds. Sexual intercourse or violation by force or under threat. Kidnapping. Felony theft. Entry by night of an inhabited residence or any of its appurtenances.
Penal Code, art. 73 – Transgression of the Limits of Lawful Defence
If in the commission of any of the acts set forth in the preceding articles, the limits prescribed by law, by the order of an authority, or imposed by necessity are negligently exceeded, the perpetrator shall be punished by the penalties for negligent offences, if the law provides that the commission of such offences may constitute negligence.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

404f1753ef66bcc0.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bulgaria

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 12 of the Criminal Code says an act done in 'necessary defence' to protect state or public interests, oneself or another from an immediate unlawful attack, by harming the attacker within the necessary limits, is not socially dangerous (not a crime). The limits are exceeded when the defence is clearly out of line with the nature and danger of the attack. The code does not mention retreat, unlike the necessity defence in article 13, which requires a danger that 'could not be avoided in another way'; no court ruling on retreat was found. A person who exceeds the limits is not punished if the excess was due to fright or confusion (article 12(4)).

At home

Article 12(3): there is no excess of self-defence if the attack was made by forcibly entering, or breaking into, a dwelling. This survives from a 1997 amendment; the Constitutional Court (Decision No. 19 of 21 Nov 1997) struck down other parts of that amendment (for example those covering holiday homes and business premises) as allowing killing regardless of the real danger, but upheld the dwelling clause. The current wording dates from a 2006 amendment.

What the law says
Наказателен кодекс (Criminal Code), чл. 12
(1) Не е общественоопасно деянието, което е извършено при неизбежна отбрана - за да се защитят от непосредствено противоправно нападение държавни или обществени интереси, личността или правата на отбраняващия се или на другиго чрез причиняване вреди на нападателя в рамките на необходимите предели. (2) Превишаване пределите на неизбежната отбрана има, когато защитата явно не съответствува на характера и опасността на нападението. (3) (Изм. - ДВ, бр. 62 от 1997 г., изм. - ДВ, бр. 75 от 2006 г., в сила от 13.10.2006 г.) Няма превишаване пределите на неизбежната отбрана, ако нападението е извършено чрез проникване с насилие или с взлом в жилище. (4) ... Деецът не се наказва, когато извърши деянието при превишаване пределите на неизбежната отбрана, ако това се дължи на уплаха или смущение.
Наказателен кодекс, чл. 13(1) (necessity, for contrast)
Не е общественоопасно деянието, което е извършено от някого при крайна необходимост - за да спаси държавни или обществени интереси, както и свои или на другиго лични или имотни блага от непосредствена опасност, която деецът не е могъл да избегне по друг начин, ако причинените от деянието вреди са по-малко значителни от предотвратените.
Constitutional Court, Decision No. 19 of 21 November 1997 (case 13/1997), operative part
Обявява за противоконституционни разпоредбите на т. 1, т. 2, т. 3 относно думите "вилен имот или стопански обект", т. 4 и т. 5 от ал. 3 на чл. 12 от Наказателния кодекс ... Отхвърля искането за установяване на несъответствие с чл. 6, ал. 1 от Международния пакт за гражданските и политическите права на разпоредбите на т. 3 относно израза "нападението е извършено чрез проникване с насилие или с взлом в жилище" и на т. 6 от ал. 3 на чл. 12

4abba1d8f2a97693.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Suriname

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Suriname's Penal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht, 1910, Dutch-based) says a person is not punishable for an act required by the necessary defence of their own or another's body, sexual integrity or property against an immediate, unlawful attack (art. 66). Going beyond the limits of necessary defence is also not punishable if it was the direct result of a violent emotion caused by the attack ('noodweerexces'). The code does not mention retreat or contain a special home-defence rule, and no Surinamese court decision on retreat was found. The text used is the National Assembly's consolidated version amended up to 2004 (listed under laws in force to 2005); later amendments were not checked.

What the law says
Wetboek van Strafrecht (Suriname), art. 66
Niet strafbaar is hij die een feit begaat, geboden door de noodzakelijke verdediging van eigen of eens anders lijf, eerbaarheid of goed tegen ogenblikkelijke, wederrechtelijke aanranding. Niet strafbaar is de overschrijding van de grenzen van noodzakelijke verdediging, indien zij het onmiddellijk gevolg is geweest van een hevige gemoedsbeweging, door de aanranding veroorzaakt.

146eecc01fe62537.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Liberia

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Liberia's Penal Law (Title 26, approved 1976, published 1978) follows the American Model Penal Code. Force is justified when the person believes it is immediately necessary to protect themselves against unlawful force on the present occasion (§ 5.3(1)). Deadly force is justified only against death, serious bodily harm, kidnapping, or rape or sodomy compelled by force or threat, and is not justified if the person knows they can avoid the need for it 'with complete safety by retreating' or by handing over property or complying with a demand (§ 5.3(3)). The retreat duty does not apply in one's own dwelling or place of work (with exceptions for initial aggressors and co-workers). Using more force than the person believes necessary and appropriate is not justified (§ 5.1(5)), and justification under the criminal law does not bar a civil action (§ 5.1(4)).

At home

A person 'is not obliged to retreat from his dwelling or place of work', unless they are the initial aggressor, or are attacked at work by someone whose place of work they know it also is (§ 5.3(3)(a)).

What the law says
Penal Law (Liberian Codes Revised, Title 26), § 5.3(1) and (3) – Self-defense
1. Use of force justifiable in self-defense. Subject to the provisions of this section and of section 5.9 the use of force upon or toward another person is justifiable when the actor believes that such force is immediately necessary for the purpose of protecting himself against the use of unlawful force by such other person on the present occasion. ... 3. Deadly force. The use of deadly force is not justifiable under this section unless the person using force believes that such force is necessary to defend himself against death, serious bodily harm, kidnapping, rape or sodomy compelled by force or threat; nor is it justifiable if the person using force knows that he can avoid the necessity of using such force with complete safety by retreating or by surrendering possession of a thing to a person asserting a claim of right thereto or by complying with a demand that he abstain from any action which he has no duty to take, except that: (a) The person using force is not obliged to retreat from his dwelling or place of work, unless he is the initial aggressor or is assailed in his place of work by another person whose place of work the person using force knows it to be
Penal Law, § 5.1(4)–(5) – General provisions
4. Civil remedy unimpaired. That conduct may be justified within the meaning of this subchapter does not abolish or impair any remedy for such conduct which is available in any civil action. 5. Excessive force. A person is not justified in using more force than he believes to be necessary and appropriate under the circumstances.

008475b42f2b133b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Moldova

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Article 36 of Moldova's Criminal Code says an act committed in legitimate defence is not a crime, where it repels a direct, immediate, material and real attack on oneself, another person or a public interest that seriously endangers them. Preventing a violent entry into a house or other space that endangers life or health also counts as legitimate defence. The code text found does not say whether the defender must avoid the attack if they can; a student article from Moldova State University notes this gap and proposes adding a paragraph that would allow defence 'regardless of the possibility' of avoiding the attack, which indicates the statute does not now say so. No court ruling settling the retreat question was found.

At home

Article 36(3) treats as legitimate defence an act done to prevent someone from violently entering a house or other space, where this endangers a person's life or health, or under threat of such violence.

What the law says
Criminal Code of the Republic of Moldova (2002), Article 36(1)-(3) (English translation, 2009 version)
(1) An act provided by criminal law and committed in legitimate defense is not a crime. (2) A person who commits an act in order to repel a direct, immediate, material, and real attack against him/herself, against another person, or against a public interest and which seriously endangers the person or the rights of the attacked person or the public interest shall be in a state of legitimate defense. (3) A person who commits an act set forth in paragraph (2) in order to prevent someone violently entering into a house or other space thus endangering a person's life or health or by a threat of such violence shall be in a state of legitimate defense.

076bd680b052f470.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Sierra Leone

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

The only Sierra Leonean text on self-defence found was the 1991 Constitution: a death does not breach the right to life if it results from force 'reasonably justifiable in the circumstances of the case' for the defence of any person from unlawful violence or for the defence of property, without affecting liability under any other law (s. 16(2)(a)). No criminal statute or court decision setting the rules of self-defence, the retreat question, defence of the home, or the result of excessive force was found in this research pass. The retreat question is therefore not settled by the sources found.

What the law says
Constitution of Sierra Leone 1991, s. 16(2)(a)
Without prejudice to any liability for a contravention of any other law with respect to the use of force in such cases as are hereinafter mentioned, a person shall not be regarded as having been deprived of his life in contravention of this section if he dies as a result of the use of force to such extent as is reasonably justifiable in the circumstances of the case, that is to say — a. for the defence of any person from unlawful violence or for the defence of property ;

52ecd466c06940c3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Aland

Part of Finland, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Åland is a self-governing region of Finland, but under section 27 of the Act on the Autonomy of Åland (1144/1991) criminal law is a matter for Finland's national legislature, except that Åland may set penalties within its own fields of law (section 18, point 25). So the Finnish Criminal Code's self-defence rule applies in Åland. Chapter 4, section 4 of that code allows a defensive act that is necessary to repel a begun or directly threatening unlawful attack, unless it obviously exceeds what is justifiable overall, considering the nature and strength of the attack, the persons of defender and attacker, and other circumstances. The code does not mention retreat, and no Finnish court ruling on retreat was checked. If the limits were exceeded, the defender is still free from criminal liability if, given the danger and surprise of the attack and the situation as a whole, no other reaction could reasonably have been required.

What the law says
Rikoslaki (Criminal Code of Finland, 39/1889), 4 luku 4 § Hätävarjelu
Aloitetun tai välittömästi uhkaavan oikeudettoman hyökkäyksen torjumiseksi tarpeellinen puolustusteko on hätävarjeluna sallittu, jollei teko ilmeisesti ylitä sitä, mitä on pidettävä kokonaisuutena arvioiden puolustettavana, kun otetaan huomioon hyökkäyksen laatu ja voimakkuus, puolustautujan ja hyökkääjän henkilö sekä muut olosuhteet. Jos puolustuksessa on ylitetty hätävarjelun rajat (hätävarjelun liioittelu), tekijä on kuitenkin rangaistusvastuusta vapaa, jos olosuhteet olivat sellaiset, ettei tekijältä kohtuudella olisi voinut vaatia muunlaista suhtautumista, kun otetaan huomioon hyökkäyksen vaarallisuus ja yllätyksellisyys sekä tilanne muutenkin.
Ahvenanmaan itsehallintolaki (Act on the Autonomy of Åland, 1144/1991), 27 § (extract)
Valtakunnalla on lainsäädäntövalta asioissa, jotka koskevat: ... rikosoikeutta 18 §:n 25 kohdassa säädetyin poikkeuksin;
Självstyrelselag för Åland (1144/1991), 27 § (Swedish, extract)
straffrätt med undantag av vad som stadgas i 18 § 25 punkten,
