be8ef1ef9a800ed2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

New South Wales

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Self-defence in NSW is set out in Part 11 (ss 418–423) of the Crimes Act 1900, inserted by the Crimes Amendment (Self-defence) Act 2001. A person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them; the prosecution must disprove self-defence beyond reasonable doubt (s 419). There is no stated duty to retreat: the judges' Bench Book tells juries that the availability of retreat is one matter they may consider when judging whether the response was reasonable. If a person who believed deadly force was necessary used force that was not a reasonable response, the result is manslaughter rather than murder ('excessive self-defence', s 421).

At home

The Bench Book notes that the 2001 amending Act repealed the Home Invasion (Occupants Protection) Act 1998; home defence now falls under the general self-defence test in Part 11 of the Crimes Act 1900 (the official statute site could not be opened from here).

What the law says
NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book, Self-defence [6-460] (suggested jury direction)
[It may be necessary to give directions on such matters as arise on the evidence relating to, for example, the imminence of a threatened attack or the availability of other remedies to the accused, such as retreat. It should, however, be made emphatically clear to the jury that it is the accused’s perception of the circumstances which must be considered.]
NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book, Self-defence [6-455] (summary of Crimes Act ss 418, 421)
A direction for self-defence in cases of murder must contain all the above numbers 1–5 essential components. The difference is that they are applied to the facts in a sequential way to accommodate the offence of manslaughter by excessive self-defence.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book — Self-defence (Judicial Commission of New South Wales)
  • Self-defence (Australia) — used only as a pointer to Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) ss 418–423 (Wikipedia), CC BY-SA 4.0
Australia as a whole

Most criminal law in Australia is made by the six states and two territories, each with its own self-defence rule; this national entry describes the Commonwealth Criminal Code, which covers federal offences. Under s 10.4 a person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them. No Australian statute found imposes a duty to retreat; in jury directions (NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book) the availability of retreat is listed as one matter the jury may weigh in deciding whether the response was reasonable. Deadly or really serious force cannot be justified solely to protect property or deal with trespassers. Whether excessive force reduces murder to manslaughter depends on the state or territory (e.g. NSW s 421, WA s 248(3), SA s 15(2)).

36c1d7c8a83c4be4.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

North Carolina

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

North Carolina's 2011 law (Session Law 2011-268) put self-defence into statute. A person may use deadly force, and has no duty to retreat in any place they have a lawful right to be, if they reasonably believe it is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to themselves or another (G.S. 14-51.3). In a home (including its curtilage), motor vehicle or workplace, a lawful occupant who uses deadly force against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering, or trying to remove a person against their will, is presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent death or serious bodily harm (G.S. 14-51.2). That presumption can be rebutted and does not apply against another lawful resident (unless there is a protective or no-contact order), a parent or guardian retrieving their own child, a law officer or bail bondsman lawfully entering, an intruder who has stopped and left, or an occupant who is using the place for a violent crime. A person who uses force as these sections permit is justified and 'immune from civil or criminal liability', except against an identified officer or bondsman acting lawfully. The justification is unavailable to someone committing or escaping from a felony, or to someone who provoked the force, unless they then faced deadly force with no reasonable means to retreat, or withdrew in good faith and clearly signalled it (G.S. 14-51.4). The statute does not set up a separate pretrial immunity hearing, and it preserves any other common-law defence.

At home

G.S. 14-51.2 (2011) covers the home (including curtilage, tents and mobile homes), motor vehicles and workplaces: a lawful occupant who uses deadly force against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering, or trying to drag someone out, is presumed to have had reasonable fear of death or serious harm, the intruder is presumed to intend violence, the occupant has no duty to retreat, and is immune from civil and criminal liability.

What the law says
G.S. 14-51.3(a) (S.L. 2011-268)
However, a person is justified in the use of deadly force and does not have a duty to retreat in any place he or she has the lawful right to be if either of the following applies: (1) He or she reasonably believes that such force is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to himself or herself or another. (2) Under the circumstances permitted pursuant to G.S. 14-51.2.
G.S. 14-51.2(b) (presumption)
The lawful occupant of a home, motor vehicle, or workplace is presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent death or serious bodily harm to himself or herself or another when using defensive force that is intended or likely to cause death or serious bodily harm to another if both of the following apply: ...
G.S. 14-51.2(f)
A lawful occupant within his or her home, motor vehicle, or workplace does not have a duty to retreat from an intruder in the circumstances described in this section.
G.S. 14-51.3(b) (immunity)
A person who uses force as permitted by this section is justified in using such force and is immune from civil or criminal liability for the use of such force, unless the person against whom force was used is a law enforcement officer or bail bondsman who was lawfully acting in the performance of his or her official duties ...
G.S. 14-51.4 (limits)
The justification described in G.S. 14-51.2 and G.S. 14-51.3 is not available to a person who used defensive force and who: (1) Was attempting to commit, committing, or escaping after the commission of a felony. (2) Initially provokes the use of force against himself or herself.

4ab32f5dfe754ba3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Uruguay

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 26 of the Penal Code exempts from liability anyone who defends their own or another's person or rights against an unlawful attack, if the means used are rationally necessary and the defender did not sufficiently provoke it. The 2020 Law of Urgent Consideration (Law 19.889) defined a 'rational' means as a sufficient and adequate response to the danger, said that defence of property is judged even if there was no physical attack, and added presumptions for defence of homes, business and farm premises, and for police and military officers. A 2020 law-review article describes these as presumptions that can be rebutted by evidence ('presunción simple'). The code text found says nothing about retreat, and no court decision or commentary on a duty to retreat was found. The rule for excessive self-defence could not be checked because the official code database (IMPO) returned errors.

At home

Penal Code art. 26 (as replaced by Law 19.889 of 2020) deems all three requirements of self-defence met for a person who defends the entrance of an inhabited house or its outbuildings, or uses violence against an outsider surprised inside; outbuildings are defined (balconies, gardens, garages; in rural areas sheds near the dwelling). A similar presumption covers repelling violent intruders from commercial, industrial or farm premises. The 2020 law removed the earlier 'at night' limit, according to Montevideo Portal.

What the law says
Código Penal, art. 26 (texto dado por Ley 19.889, art. 1, 2020)
ARTÍCULO 26. (Legítima defensa).- Se halla exento de responsabilidad el que obra en defensa de su persona o derechos, o de la persona o derechos de otro, siempre que concurran las circunstancias siguientes: A) Agresión ilegítima. B) Necesidad racional del medio empleado para repelerla o impedir el daño. El medio se considerará racional cuando resulte ser una respuesta suficiente y adecuada a fin de conjurar el peligro derivado de la agresión sufrida. Cuando la defensa deba ser ejercida respecto de cualquier derecho de contenido patrimonial, la racionalidad deberá ser apreciada con prescindencia de que no haya existido o ya hubiera cesado una agresión física a la persona que se defiende. C) Falta de provocación suficiente por parte del que se defiende. [...] Se entenderá que concurren estas tres circunstancias respecto de: I) Aquel que defiende la entrada de una casa habitada o de sus dependencias, o emplea violencia contra el individuo extraño a ella que es sorprendido dentro de la casa o de las dependencias. [...] III) Aquel que repele el ingreso de personas extrañas, con violencia o amenazas en las cosas o personas o con la generación de una situación de peligro para la vida o demás derechos, en un establecimiento que desarrolle actividad comercial, industrial o agraria [...]

d79f5832ff302368.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

South Australia

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Self-defence in South Australia is in s 15 of the Criminal Law Consolidation Act 1935: a person may use conduct they genuinely believe is reasonable and necessary for a defensive purpose, and it is a full defence, including to murder, if the force was reasonably proportionate to the threat they genuinely believed existed. If the force was not reasonably proportionate, the person who genuinely believed it necessary is guilty of manslaughter rather than murder (s 15(2)); since 1 September 2025 this partial defence is not available where the belief was substantially affected by voluntary intoxication (s 15(2a)). No source found states a duty to retreat. The official statute site could not be opened from here, so the description relies on the Legal Services Commission's Law Handbook.

At home

s 15C (as described by the Legal Services Commission): a defendant who genuinely believed the victim was committing or had just committed a home invasion keeps the defence even if the force was not objectively reasonably proportionate; not available against an on-duty police officer, if the defendant was engaged in related criminal activity, or if substantially affected by voluntary drug or alcohol use.

Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Law Handbook — Self defence (Legal Services Commission of South Australia)
  • Law Handbook — Home invasion (Legal Services Commission of South Australia)
Australia as a whole

Most criminal law in Australia is made by the six states and two territories, each with its own self-defence rule; this national entry describes the Commonwealth Criminal Code, which covers federal offences. Under s 10.4 a person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them. No Australian statute found imposes a duty to retreat; in jury directions (NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book) the availability of retreat is listed as one matter the jury may weigh in deciding whether the response was reasonable. Deadly or really serious force cannot be justified solely to protect property or deal with trespassers. Whether excessive force reduces murder to manslaughter depends on the state or territory (e.g. NSW s 421, WA s 248(3), SA s 15(2)).

  • Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book — Self-defence (Judicial Commission of New South Wales)

a330259756dbf626.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Belgium

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Belgium's new Criminal Code, adopted by Parliament on 22 February 2024, entered into force on 1 September 2026 according to the Federal Justice Service. Its article 14 allows self-defence only for a person who 'has no possibility of avoiding' a serious, current, unlawful attack on himself or another 'other than by committing' the offence, and who defends in a proportionate way with the intention of repelling the attack; so the law expressly requires avoiding the attack when that is possible. Article 14 covers attacks on persons; it opens with the rule that no one may take justice into their own hands by committing an offence. Under article 34, a new 'excess of self-defence' excuse applies where the reaction was disproportionate or unnecessary but directly caused by the intense emotion the attack provoked; the penalty is then replaced by a much lower penalty level (for example level 3 instead of level 8 or 7).

At home

No dwelling-specific rule (such as a presumption for night-time break-ins) was found in the text of Book I of the new Criminal Code adopted in 2024; amendments made after February 2024 were not checked.

What the law says
Code pénal, Livre Ier (loi du 29 février 2024), art. 14 – La légitime défense (text adopted in plenary, DOC 55 3374/012 = 3374/010)
Nul ne peut se faire justice à lui-même en commettant une infraction. Il y a toutefois légitime défense et donc absence d'infraction lorsque la personne, qui n'a pas la possibilité d'éviter une agression illégitime, grave et actuelle contre sa personne ou la personne d'un tiers autrement qu'en commettant le fait qualifié infraction, se défend de façon proportionnée dans l'intention de repousser cette agression.
Strafwetboek, Boek I, art. 14 – Wettige verdediging (Dutch text, same document)
Eigenrichting waarbij een misdrijf wordt gepleegd, is niet geoorloofd. Er is evenwel wettige verdediging en dus geen misdrijf wanneer iemand, die niet in de mogelijkheid verkeert om een onrechtmatige, ernstige en ogenblikkelijke aanval tegen zijn persoon of tegen de persoon van een derde te ontwijken, anders dan door het als misdrijf omschreven feit te plegen, zich met de wil om deze aanval af te weren op een evenredige manier verweert.
Code pénal, Livre Ier, art. 34 – L'excès de légitime défense
Il y a excès de légitime défense lorsque la personne réagit de manière disproportionnée ou non nécessaire à une agression illégitime, grave et actuelle contre sa personne ou la personne d'un tiers et que cette réaction a été en relation causale directe avec l'intense émotion causée par l'agression. Lorsque l'infraction est commise avec excès de légitime défense, la peine est remplacée par une peine de niveau 3 si une peine de niveau 8 ou 7 est prévue pour l'infraction commise, par une peine de niveau 2 si une peine de niveau 6, 5 ou 4 est prévue pour l'infraction commise et par une peine de niveau 1 si une peine de niveau 3 ou 2 est prévue pour l'infraction commise.

ff468723eaca7d5c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Wisconsin

Part of United States, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Wisconsin lets a person use force they reasonably believe necessary to stop an unlawful interference with their person, and deadly force only if they reasonably believe it necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm (Wis. Stat. § 939.48(1)). The statute imposes no duty to retreat, but courts allow the chance to retreat to be weighed: in State v. Wenger (1999) the Court of Appeals approved a jury instruction that whether an opportunity to retreat was available goes to whether the defendant reasonably believed the force was necessary. 2011 Wisconsin Act 94 created a castle exception: in one's dwelling, motor vehicle or place of business, against a forcible unlawful intruder, retreat may not be considered and the belief in necessity is presumed reasonable, and the actor is immune from civil liability (§ 895.62). A person who provokes an attack by unlawful conduct loses the privilege unless the attack puts them in imminent danger of death, and even then may use deadly force only after exhausting every other reasonable means of escape; someone who provokes an attack in order to have an excuse to kill or injure has no privilege at all; a provoker can regain the privilege by withdrawing in good faith and giving notice (§ 939.48(2)). If a person kills believing deadly force was necessary but that belief was unreasonable ('unnecessary defensive force'), first-degree intentional homicide is reduced to second-degree intentional homicide (§ 940.01(2)(b)). There is no stand-your-ground statute for public places and no pretrial immunity hearing was found.

At home

Since 2011 Wisconsin Act 94, when a person present in their dwelling, motor vehicle, or a business they own or operate uses deadly force against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering (or who has forcibly entered), the court may not consider whether they could have fled or retreated, and they are presumed to have reasonably believed the force was necessary (Wis. Stat. § 939.48(1m)). The presumption does not apply if the actor was engaged in criminal activity there, or against an identified public safety worker on duty. The same 2011 Act gives civil immunity in those situations (§ 895.62).

What the law says
Wis. Stat. § 939.48(1)
The actor may not intentionally use force which is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm unless the actor reasonably believes that such force is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to himself or herself.
Wis. Stat. § 939.48(1m)(ar) (2011 Wis. Act 94)
If an actor intentionally used force that was intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm, the court may not consider whether the actor had an opportunity to flee or retreat before he or she used force and shall presume that the actor reasonably believed that the force was necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to himself or herself if the actor makes such a claim under sub. (1) and either of the following applies: 1. The person against whom the force was used was in the process of unlawfully and forcibly entering the actor’s dwelling, motor vehicle, or place of business ...
State v. Wenger, 225 Wis. 2d 495, 593 N.W.2d 467 (Ct. App. 1999) (annotation to § 939.48)
While there is no statutory duty to retreat, whether the opportunity to retreat was available goes to whether the defendant reasonably believed the force used was necessary to prevent an interference with the defendant’s person. A jury instruction to that effect was proper.
Wis. Stat. § 940.01(2)(b) (unnecessary defensive force)
Death was caused because the actor believed he or she or another was in imminent danger of death or great bodily harm and that the force used was necessary to defend the endangered person, if either belief was unreasonable.
Wis. Stat. § 895.62(2) (civil immunity)
... an actor is immune from civil liability arising out of his or her use of force that is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm if the actor reasonably believed that the force was necessary to prevent imminent death or bodily harm to himself or herself or to another person and either of the following applies: ...
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • Wis. Stat. § 940.01 (Wisconsin Legislature)
  • Wis. Stat. § 895.62 (Wisconsin Legislature)
  • Stand Your Ground in Wisconsin (Giffords Law Center)

49e1031ebe42c59d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Dominican Republic

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

The Dominican Republic replaced its 1884 Penal Code with a new Penal Code, Ley 74-25, promulgated in August 2025 and, according to the law firm Pellerano & Herrera, entering into force in August 2026 after a one-year waiting period. As reported by the newspaper El Caribe, article 19 of the new code makes an act not punishable when a person, defending themselves or a third party, repels "a current, imminent and unjustified aggression", and the means used must be "necessary and proportionate" and used at the same moment as the attack. The sources opened here did not mention retreat, a home rule, or what happens when the defence is excessive. The full official text of article 19 could not be opened.

What the law says
Código Penal (Ley 74-25), art. 19, as paraphrased and partly quoted by El Caribe
rechace una agresión actual, inminente e injustificada ... necesario y proporcional
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

efa6c9b90280274e.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Lithuania

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Article 28 of the Lithuanian Criminal Code gives every person a right to self-defence and says it may be used 'regardless of whether he had the possibility of avoiding the attempt or applying for assistance to other persons or authorities', so there is no duty to retreat. Defence of oneself, another person, property, the inviolability of a dwelling and other rights against a begun or imminent dangerous attack is not punishable while within the permitted limits. The limits are exceeded only when a killing or serious injury is caused with specific intent and the defence was clearly disproportionate to the attack; they are not exceeded when the person acted out of extreme confusion or fright, or was defending against a break-in to a dwelling. A person who exceeds the limits is criminally liable, but the penalty may be reduced under Article 62. The English text quoted is the 2010 version held in a university database; later amendments were not checked against the official Lithuanian text.

At home

Article 28(3) says the limits of self-defence are not considered exceeded by an act committed in the course of defence against breaking into a dwelling; 'inviolability of a dwelling' is listed among the interests that may be defended.

What the law says
Criminal Code (Baudžiamasis kodeksas), Article 28 (English translation, 2010 version)
1. A person shall have the right to self-defence. He may exercise this right regardless of whether he had the possibility of avoiding the attempt or applying for assistance to other persons or authorities. 2. A person shall not be held liable under this Code where he, while acting within the limits permitted by self-defence, committed an act formally having the features of a crime or misdemeanour provided for in a criminal law when defending himself or another person, property, inviolability of a dwelling, other rights, interests of society or the State against an initiated or imminent dangerous attempt. 3. The limits of self-defence shall be exceeded when a murder is committed or a serious health impairment is caused with a specific intent, where defence has been clearly disproportionate to the nature and dangerousness of an attempt. The limits of self-defence shall not be considered to have been exceeded by reason of extreme confusion or fright caused by the dangerous attempt or an act committed in the course of defence against breaking into a dwelling. 4. A person who has exceeded the limits of self-defence shall be held criminally liable, however a penalty imposed upon him may be commuted under Article 62 of this Code.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Self-defence - national proceedings: Lithuania (Criminal Code 2000 (2010) EN) (University of Nottingham, CJAD database)

d4142eff93d414ba.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Seychelles

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

The Seychelles Criminal Code says criminal responsibility for force used in defence of person or property is decided by the principles of English common law. In Freminot v Republic (2015) the Court of Appeal applied Palmer v R: a person attacked may do what is reasonably necessary, cannot be expected to weigh the exact measure of defensive force, and force wholly out of proportion is not covered. The court quoted Archbold that 'the old rule of law that a man attacked must retreat as far as he can has disappeared', and that whether the accused retreated is only one element for the jury to consider. It also said a person about to be attacked does not have to wait for the first blow, and that the prosecution must disprove self-defence. No statute or ruling on defending the home, or on the result when force is excessive, was found.

What the law says
Penal Code (Cap. 158), general rules as to criminal responsibility (defence of person or property)
Subject to any express provisions in this Code or any other law in operation in Seychelles criminal responsibility for the use of force in the defence of person or property shall be determined according to the principles of English common law.
Steve Freminot v Republic, SCA 17/2012 (Court of Appeal, 17 April 2015), para. 9, quoting Archbold
The old rule of law that a man attacked must retreat as far as he can has disappeared. ... Whether the accused did retreat is only one element for the jury to consider
Freminot v Republic (2015), para. 7, quoting Palmer v R
It is both good law and common sense that he may do, but may only do, what is reasonably necessary. ... It may in some cases be only sensible and clearly possible to take some simple avoiding action.
Freminot v Republic (2015), para. 22
A person about to be attacked does not have to wait for the assailant to strike the first blow.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Steve Freminot v The Republic (SCA 17/2012) [2015] SCCA 14 (SeyLII)
  • Self-defence – national proceedings: Seychelles (Cooperation and Judicial Assistance Database (CJAD), University of Nottingham)

f3513afa3efe7426.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Uganda

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Uganda's Penal Code Act says criminal responsibility for force used in defence of person or property is decided by the principles of English law (s. 15 in the current revision; the Court of Appeal in 2002 referred to it as s. 17). In Wandera Fred & 2 Others v Uganda (Court of Appeal, 2002) the court set out a two-part rule: a person who is violently or feloniously attacked may kill the attacker if there is reasonable necessity or an honest belief on reasonable grounds that it was necessary, and in such cases 'there appears to be no duty in law to retreat'. In other cases, where no violent felony is attempted, a person may use reasonable force only provided they do all that is necessary 'to retreat or avoid a fight or disengage from the fight'. If the force used is excessive but other elements of self-defence are present, the result may be a manslaughter conviction instead of murder. In Wandera the court found there was no opportunity to retreat and acquitted the appellants on complete self-defence.

What the law says
Penal Code Act (Cap. 120), s. 15 – Defence of person or property and rash, reckless and negligent acts
Subject to any express provisions in this Code or any other law in force in Uganda, criminal responsibility— (a) for the use of force in the defence of person and property; and (b) in respect of rash, reckless or negligent acts, shall be determined according to the principles of English law.
Wandera Fred & 2 Others v Uganda, Criminal Appeal No. 113 of 1999 (Court of Appeal, reasons 23 Jan 2002)
A person who is violently or feloniously attacked can repel force by force and if in so doing he kills the attacker ... that killing is justifiable, provided there is reasonable necessity for killing ... an honest belief based on reasonable grounds that it was necessary ... the violence attempted by or apprehended from the attack is really serious. In such cases there appears to be no duty in law to retreat. In other cases of self defence where no violent felony is attempted a person is entitled to reasonable force against an assault, and if he is reasonably in apprehension of serious injury, ... provided he does all that is necessary in the circumstances to retreat or avoid a fight or disengage from the fight ... In either case if force used is excessive, but there are other elements of self defence present ... there may be conviction of manslaughter.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Wandera Fred & 2 Others v Uganda (Criminal Appeal No. 113 of 1999) [2002] UGCA 3 (Uganda Legal Information Institute (ULII))
  • Uganda Penal Code Act (International Center for Not-for-Profit Law (ICNL) library)

b227501fd8352d26.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Maryland

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Maryland has no self-defence statute for criminal cases; self-defence is a common-law doctrine set by the courts. According to the Department of Legislative Services' summary of the case law, a person claiming self-defence must not have been the aggressor or provoked the conflict, must have had reasonable grounds to believe they were in apparent imminent danger of death or serious bodily harm, must actually have believed it, and must not have used more force than the situation demanded (Marquardt v. State, 164 Md. App. 95 (2005); Sydnor v. State, 365 Md. 205 (2001)). Maryland keeps a duty to retreat: a person must retreat and escape the danger if it is in their power to do so consistently with their own safety (Sydnor, 365 Md. at 216). The main exception is the home, where under the castle doctrine a person attacked in their dwelling need not retreat and may kill the attacker if necessary (Burch v. State (1997)); the legislative note adds that courts nationally are divided on whether that exception applies against co-occupants and guests. Deadly force has traditionally not been allowed to defend property alone. Maryland has no criminal immunity statute or pretrial immunity hearing; the only statutory protection found is civil: a person who reasonably used force against someone who entered their home or business to repel an attack is not liable for damages, unless convicted of a violent crime, second-degree assault or reckless endangerment arising from the incident (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 5-808). A 2026 bill (HB 1406) concerned admitting evidence of the victim's prior acts and did not change the retreat rule.

At home

Maryland follows the common-law 'castle doctrine': according to the Maryland Court of Appeals, a person 'faced with the danger of an attack upon his/her dwelling need not retreat from his/her home to escape the danger, but instead may stand their ground and, if necessary to repel the attack, may kill the attacker' (Burch v. State, 346 Md. 253 (1997), quoting Crawford v. State, 231 Md. 354 (1963)). In civil law, Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 5-808 protects a person from damages for injuring or killing someone who enters their dwelling or place of business if they reasonably believed force or deadly force was necessary to repel an attack and the force was reasonable. There is no statutory presumption of reasonable fear.

What the law says
Sydnor v. State, 365 Md. 205, 216 (2001), as summarised by the Department of Legislative Services
Included in the doctrine of self-defense is a duty to retreat, that is, a duty by the individual claiming self-defense to retreat and escape the danger if it was in his/her power to do so and was consistent with maintaining his/her safety.
Burch v. State, 346 Md. 253, 283-4 (1997), quoting Crawford v. State, 231 Md. 354, 361 (1963)
a man faced with the danger of an attack upon his/her dwelling need not retreat from his/her home to escape the danger, but instead may stand their ground and, if necessary to repel the attack, may kill the attacker.
Md. Code, Courts and Judicial Proceedings § 5-808(b)
A person is not liable for damages for a personal injury or death of an individual who enters the person’s dwelling or place of business if: (1) The person reasonably believes that force or deadly force is necessary to repel an attack by the individual; and (2) The amount and nature of the force used by the person is reasonable under the circumstances.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Fiscal and Policy Note, House Bill 1406 (2026 Session), Criminal Law – Self-Defense – Prior Acts by Victim (Current Law: Self-Defense) (Maryland Department of Legislative Services)
  • Md. Code, Courts and Judicial Proceedings § 5-808 (Maryland General Assembly)
b227501fd8352d26.t: Maryland · A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

3f2a72e80c114b42.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bosnia and Herzegovina

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Bosnia and Herzegovina has four criminal codes: one for the state level and one each for the Federation of BiH, Republika Srpska and Brčko District; ordinary crimes such as homicide are mostly tried under the entity codes, which were not checked here. The state-level Criminal Code (article 24) says an act committed in necessary defence is not a crime, and defines necessary defence as one that is absolutely necessary to repel a simultaneous or directly imminent unlawful attack on oneself or another and that is proportionate to the attack. The code does not mention retreat, and no court ruling on retreat was found. A person who exceeds the limits may receive a lighter sentence, and may be spared punishment entirely if the excess was caused by strong irritation or fright caused by the attack.

What the law says
Krivični zakon Bosne i Hercegovine (state-level Criminal Code), član 24
(1) Nije krivično djelo ono djelo koje je učinjeno u nužnoj odbrani. (2) Nužna je ona odbrana koja je neophodno potrebna da učinitelj od sebe ili drugog odbije istovremeni ili direktno predstojeći protupravni napad, a koja je srazmjerna napadu. (3) Učinitelj koji prekorači granice nužne odbrane može se blaže kazniti, a ako je prekoračenje učinio zbog jake razdraženosti ili straha izazvanog napadom, može se i osloboditi od kazne.
Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Article 24 (parallel English translation in same document)
(1) An act committed in necessary defence is not considered a criminal offence. (2) A defence is considered to be necessary if it is absolutely necessary for the defender to avert a coinciding or direct and imminent illicit attack from himself or from another, and which is proportionate to the attack. (3) If the perpetrator exceeds the limits of necessary defence, the punishment can be reduced, and if the excess occurs due to strong irritation or fright caused by the attack, the punishment can be remitted.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Krivični zakon Bosne i Hercegovine / The Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina (bilingual edition) (BH novinari (hosted copy))
3f2a72e80c114b42.t: Bosnia and Herzegovina · No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

a064a10a86bc9044.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Victoria

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Since 2014 (Act No. 63/2014) self-defence in Victoria is defined by s 322K of the Crimes Act 1958, which replaced the common-law defence (s 322N). Conduct is self-defence if the person believes it is necessary and it is a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceive them; for murder, the person must believe the conduct is necessary to defend against death or really serious injury. The statute does not mention retreat and imposes no duty to retreat; whether escape was possible goes to whether the response was reasonable. Where family violence is involved, s 322M says the response can still be reasonable even if the harm was not immediate or the force used was greater than the force threatened.

At home

No separate home-defence provision found in Part IC of the Crimes Act 1958; the general test in s 322K applies.

What the law says
Crimes Act 1958 (Vic), s 322K Self-defence
(1) A person is not guilty of an offence if the person carries out the conduct constituting the offence in self-defence. (2) A person carries out conduct in self-defence if— (a) the person believes that the conduct is necessary in self-defence; and (b) the conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as the person perceives them. (3) This section only applies in the case of murder if the person believes that the conduct is necessary to defend the person or another person from the infliction of death or really serious injury.
Crimes Act 1958 (Vic), s 322M(1) Family violence and self-defence
(1) Without limiting section 322K, for the purposes of an offence in circumstances where self-defence in the context of family violence is in issue, a person may believe that the person's conduct is necessary in self-defence, and the conduct may be a reasonable response in the circumstances as the person perceives them, even if— (a) the person is responding to a harm that is not immediate; or (b) the response involves the use of force in excess of the force involved in the harm or threatened harm.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Crimes Act 1958, Authorised Version No. 323 (30 September 2026) (Victorian Legislation, Chief Parliamentary Counsel)
Australia as a whole

Most criminal law in Australia is made by the six states and two territories, each with its own self-defence rule; this national entry describes the Commonwealth Criminal Code, which covers federal offences. Under s 10.4 a person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them. No Australian statute found imposes a duty to retreat; in jury directions (NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book) the availability of retreat is listed as one matter the jury may weigh in deciding whether the response was reasonable. Deadly or really serious force cannot be justified solely to protect property or deal with trespassers. Whether excessive force reduces murder to manslaughter depends on the state or territory (e.g. NSW s 421, WA s 248(3), SA s 15(2)).

a483c553de6a9e1e.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Georgia

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Georgia's Criminal Code (1999, as amended to 2024) says injuring an attacker during an unlawful attack to protect one's own or another's legally protected interests is not unlawful. Article 28(2) states the right to self-defence exists whether or not the person could prevent the attack or seek help from someone else, so there is no duty to retreat. Force may also be used right after a theft to recover property while it can still be recovered immediately. Defence that is 'clearly disproportionate' to the character and threat of the assault is an 'excessive act of self-defence' and can still be punished. The article does not contain a separate home-defence rule.

What the law says
Criminal Code of Georgia (1999, version 2024), art. 28 (Self-defence)
2. A person shall have the right to self-defence regardless of whether or not he/she is able to prevent infringement or seek assistance from another person. ... 4. An excessive act of self-defence shall mean an act of the person acting in self-defence that is clearly disproportionate to the character and threat of the assault.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

a0fac4376deb0ff4.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Latvia

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Section 29 of the Latvian Criminal Law allows necessary self-defence of one's own or another person's rights, or of state or public interests, by harming the assailant, with liability only if the limits of necessary self-defence are exceeded. The statute says a person has this right 'irrespective of the possibilities of avoiding the assault or turning to other persons for help', so there is no duty to retreat. The limits are exceeded by protective acts that are obviously disproportionate to the nature and danger of the assault and were not necessary to prevent or repel it; causing harm to the assailant through negligence while repelling an assault is not punishable. Killing in excess of the limits of necessary self-defence is a separate, much lighter offence (section 121: up to two years' deprivation of liberty or lesser penalties), and section 128 covers serious or moderate injury inflicted in excess of those limits. No specific home-defence rule was found in the provisions opened.

What the law says
Criminal Law (Krimināllikums), Section 29 (official English translation)
(1) Necessary self-defence is an act which is committed in defence of the interests of the State or the public, or the rights of oneself or another person, as well as in defence of a person against assault, or threats of assault, in such a manner that harm is caused to the assailant. Criminal liability for this act applies if the limits of the necessary self-defence have been exceeded. (2) Protective acts obviously disproportionate to the nature and danger of the assault which were not necessary for prevention or repelling of the assault and as a result of which harm is caused to the assailant, shall be considered as exceeding the limits of the necessary self-defence. (3) Causing harm to the assailant through negligence, while repelling an assault, shall not be criminally punishable. (4) A person has the right to necessary self-defence, irrespective of the possibilities of avoiding the assault or turning to other persons for help.
Criminal Law, Section 121 (official English translation)
Murder Committed Exceeding the Limits of Necessary Self-defence. For a person who commits murder in the course of exceeding the limits of necessary self-defence, the applicable punishment is the deprivation of liberty for a period of up to two years or temporary deprivation of liberty, or probationary supervision, or community service, or fine.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

7cd9ad2737471ad1.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Taiwan

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 23 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of China says an act done to defend one's own or another's rights against a present unlawful attack is not punished. If the defence was excessive, the punishment may be reduced or waived. The code does not mention retreat, and unlike the necessity defence (article 24), it does not require the act to be 'unavoidable' (不得已). A 2021 article in the Hwa Kang Law Review explains that the defence need not be the last and only option, but the response must be necessary to stop the attack and not grossly out of balance with it, and the defender should use the mildest effective means, judged from the defender's position at the time.

What the law says
Criminal Code of the Republic of China, art. 23
對於現在不法之侵害，而出於防衛自己或他人權利之行為，不罰。但防衛行為過當者，得減輕或免除其刑。
Criminal Code, art. 24(1) (necessity, for contrast)
因避免自己或他人生命、身體、自由、財產之緊急危難而出於不得已之行為，不罰。但避難行為過當者，得減輕或免除其刑。
方文宗, 正當防衛界限判斷, 華岡法粹 (Dec 2021), p. 141
基本上，對於正當防衛行為的要求，雖非必須最後唯一手段，但仍須考慮防衛行為與侵害程度的均衡關係，防衛者盡可能使用最柔性的防衛手段

fa9d629181fd1068.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Virginia

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Virginia has no self-defence or stand-your-ground statute; the law of self-defence is common law made by its courts. According to the Giffords Law Center, Virginia courts have held that there is no duty to retreat before using force in public, citing Foote v. Commonwealth, 11 Va. App. 61, 67 (1990), which relies on McCoy v. Commonwealth, 125 Va. 771, 775 (1919). The rule therefore comes from case law rather than legislation. No statute on deadly force in the home, a presumption of reasonable fear, civil or criminal immunity, or a pretrial immunity hearing was found. The opinions themselves and Virginia's model jury instructions could not be opened for this entry, so the limits that Virginia courts attach to the rule (for example, for a person who was partly at fault in starting the fight) are not described here; a fuller entry needs those primary sources.

Thin entry: based on one secondary source; the cases and pattern jury instruction were not opened (web search budget exhausted during this run).

What the law says
Foote v. Commonwealth, 11 Va. App. 61, 67 (1990), citing McCoy v. Commonwealth, 125 Va. 771, 775 (1919) (leading cases, as cited by Giffords)
Though Virginia does not have a stand your ground statute, the state courts have held that there is no duty to retreat before using force in public. [Giffords summary]
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

fbb9b4b60587e697.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Benin

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Benin's Penal Code (Law No. 2018-16) says a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same moment out of the necessity of legitimate defence, unless the means of defence were disproportionate to the seriousness of the attack. The code says nothing about retreating or avoiding the attack. Defending property against a crime or offence can never justify an intentional killing and must be strictly necessary and proportionate. Defence at night against break-ins into a home and against violent robbery is presumed lawful. No specific 'excessive self-defence' reduction was found in the code text.

At home

Article 29 presumes legitimate defence for a person who acts to repel, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place, or to defend against violent theft or looting. Article 543 likewise counts as legitimate defence killing or wounding while repelling at night the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or entrances of an inhabited house or flat.

What the law says
Code pénal (Loi n° 2018-16), art. 28
N’est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d’elle-même ou d’autrui, sauf s’il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l’atteinte. N’est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l’exécution d’un crime ou d’un délit, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu’un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l’infraction.
Code pénal (Loi n° 2018-16), art. 29
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l’acte : 1- pour repousser de nuit, l’entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2- pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
Code pénal (Loi n° 2018-16), arts. 542–543
Article 542 : Il n’y a ni crime ni délit lorsque l’homicide, les blessures et les coups étaient commandés par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense de soi-même ou d’autrui. Article 543 : Sont compris dans les cas de nécessité actuelle de légitime défense, les deux cas suivants : 1- si l’homicide a été commis, si les blessures ont été faites ou si les coups ont été portés, en repoussant pendant la nuit, l’escalade ou l’effraction des clôtures, murs ou entrée d’une maison ou d’un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances ; 2- si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillage exécutés avec violence.

92b56c1ebb2ee190.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Belize

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Belize's Criminal Code (Cap. 101) allows a person to use "necessary force" to prevent or defend themselves or others against crime, with graded limits: force extending to killing is allowed only "in case of extreme necessity" against listed serious crimes such as murder, robbery, burglary, rape, and dangerous or grievous harm (s. 36). Force is never justified beyond "the amount and kind of force reasonably necessary" (s. 32), and force used in an unlawful fight cannot be justified. The Code does not mention retreat, and the Belize court judgments found could not be read, so the retreat question is not settled here. Since 1994, a person who kills while claiming defence against one of the listed crimes may be charged with murder only with the written leave of the Director of Public Prosecutions. Under s. 119, an intentional killing is reduced to manslaughter if there is reasonable doubt whether the accused, justified in causing some harm, went further out of terror of immediate death or grievous harm that deprived them of self-control.

At home

Killing may be justified in case of extreme necessity to prevent or defend against burglary, aggravated burglary, or arson of a dwelling-house, among other listed crimes (Criminal Code s. 36(4)).

What the law says
Criminal Code, Cap. 101 (Rev. Ed. 2020), s. 36
36.-(1) For the prevention of or for the defence of himself or of any other person against crime, a person may justify the use of necessary force not extending to a blow, wound or grievous harm. ... (4) For the prevention of or for the defence of himself or of any other person against any of the following crimes, a person may justify the use of necessary force or harm, extending in case of extreme necessity even to killing, namely– (a) treason; (b) piracy; (c) murder; (d) manslaughter, except manslaughter by negligence; (e) robbery; (f) burglary; (g) aggravated burglary; (h) arson of a dwelling-house or vessel; (i) rape; (j) forcible unnatural crime; (k) dangerous or grievous harm. ... (7) Where a person is alleged to have killed another person and the accused person claims that he did so for the prevention of or for the defence of himself or of any other person against any of the crimes specified in sub-section (4), no charge shall be laid or prosecution commenced against such person for the offence of murder except with the leave of the Director of Public Prosecutions given in writing.
Criminal Code, s. 32
Notwithstanding the existence of any matter of justification for force, force cannot be justified as having been used in pursuance of that matter– (a) which is in excess of the limits hereafter prescribed in the section of this Title relating to that matter; or (b) which in any case extends beyond the amount and kind of force reasonably necessary for the purpose for which force is permitted to be used.
Criminal Code, s. 119(b)
A person who intentionally causes the death of another person by unlawful harm shall be deemed to be guilty only of manslaughter, and not of murder, if there is such evidence as raises a reasonable doubt as to whether– ... (b) he was justified in causing some harm to the other person, and that in causing harm in excess of the harm which he was justified in causing he acted from such terror of immediate death or grievous harm as in fact deprived him, for the time being, of the power of self-control

fe280177edf24355.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Somalia

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Somalia's Penal Code (Legislative Decree No. 5 of 16 December 1962), based on the Italian Penal Code of 1930, is still applied in south and central Somalia, Puntland and Somaliland according to the publisher of the English text. A person who acts because they were 'compelled by the necessity of defending' their own or another's right against an actual danger of unlawful injury is not punishable, 'provided that the defence is proportionate to the injury' (art. 34). The code does not mention retreat, and no Somali court decisions on whether a person must avoid the attack were found. If the limits imposed by necessity are exceeded through negligence (culpa), the person is punished under the rules for negligent crimes where such a crime exists (art. 37).

What the law says
Penal Code (Legislative Decree No. 5 of 16 December 1962), art. 34 – Private Defence
Whoever has committed an act, having been compelled by the necessity of defending his own or another person's right against the actual danger of an unlawful injury, shall not be punishable provided that the defence is proportionate to the injury
Penal Code 1962, art. 37 – Excess Committed With Culpa
Where, in committing any of the acts referred to in articles 33, 34, 35 and 36, the limits imposed by necessity are exceeded with culpa, and where the act constitutes a crime committed with culpa, the provisions relating to crimes committed with culpa shall apply.

a515a502b122a930.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Togo

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Togo's Penal Code of 2015 (Law No. 2015-010 of 24 November 2015) lists self-defence as a justification (art. 18). A person is not criminally responsible for an act required, at the same moment, by the need to defend themselves or another against an unjustified attack, unless the means of defence are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack (art. 19). Defence of property can never extend to intentional homicide and must be strictly necessary and proportionate (art. 20). The code does not mention retreat or flight, and no Togolese court decisions on the point were found. No provision on excessive self-defence was found in the sections searched.

At home

A person is presumed to have acted in self-defence when repelling, at night, entry by climbing, break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place, a shop, a farm or business building or any other outbuilding of rented premises, or when defending against violent theft or looting (art. 21).

What the law says
Code pénal (Loi n° 2015-010 du 24 novembre 2015), art. 19
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, commet, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte.
Code pénal 2015, art. 20
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, commet un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal 2015, art. 21
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui commet l’infraction : 1) pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par escalade, effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité, dans un magasin, dans un bâtiment d’exploitation ou dans toute autre dépendance d’un lieu loué ; 2) pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

4d93061d609071c6.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Maine

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Maine allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes it is necessary and reasonably believes the other person is about to use unlawful deadly force against them or a third person, or is committing or about to commit a kidnapping, robbery or gross sexual assault by compulsion against them or a third person (Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 108(2)(A)). Maine keeps a duty to retreat: deadly force is not justified if the person knows that they or the third person can, with complete safety, retreat from the encounter, surrender property to someone with a colourable claim to it, or comply with a demand to stop doing something they are not obliged to do (§ 108(2)(C)(3)). The only place exception is the person's own dwelling place, and only if they were not the initial aggressor; Maine has no workplace exception. The retreat rule has been part of the code since 1975 (PL 1975, c. 499) and was restated in 2007 (PL 2007, c. 173). Deadly force is also not justified for someone who provoked the other, intending to cause harm, into using deadly force, or to defend someone the person knows intentionally and unlawfully provoked the attack; non-deadly force is barred for a provoker, an initial aggressor who has not withdrawn and clearly communicated it, or in a fight by agreement (§ 108(1)–(2)). Since 2019 (PL 2019, c. 462), force is not justified when based solely on discovering the victim's gender, gender identity or sexual orientation, including after an unwanted non-forcible advance. The sources consulted show no statutory immunity from prosecution or civil suit and no pretrial immunity hearing.

At home

Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 108(2)(B): deadly force is justified when a person reasonably believes another has entered or is trying to enter a dwelling place (or has secretly stayed inside) without licence or privilege, and that deadly force is necessary to prevent that person from inflicting bodily injury on someone present in the dwelling. The duty to retreat does not apply in one's own dwelling place if one was not the initial aggressor (§ 108(2)(C)(3)(a)). There is no statutory presumption of reasonable fear.

What the law says
Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 108(2)(C)(3)
However, a person is not justified in using deadly force as provided in paragraph A if: ... (3) The person knows that the person or a 3rd person can, with complete safety: (a) Retreat from the encounter, except that the person or the 3rd person is not required to retreat if the person or the 3rd person is in the person's dwelling place and was not the initial aggressor; (b) Surrender property to a person asserting a colorable claim of right thereto; or (c) Comply with a demand that the person abstain from performing an act that the person is not obliged to perform.
Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 108(2)(A)
A person is justified in using deadly force upon another person: A. When the person reasonably believes it necessary and reasonably believes such other person is: (1) About to use unlawful, deadly force against the person or a 3rd person; or (2) Committing or about to commit a kidnapping, robbery or a violation of section 253, subsection 1, paragraph A, against the person or a 3rd person ...
Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 108(2)(B)
When the person reasonably believes: (1) That such other person has entered or is attempting to enter a dwelling place or has surreptitiously remained within a dwelling place without a license or privilege to do so; and (2) That deadly force is necessary to prevent the infliction of bodily injury by such other person upon the person or a 3rd person present in the dwelling place ...
Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 17-A, § 108(3)
A person is not justified in using force against another based solely on the discovery of, knowledge about or potential disclosure of the victim's actual or perceived gender, gender identity, gender expression or sexual orientation ...
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

81ac7293a00f2f46.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Marshall Islands

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

The Marshall Islands Criminal Code 2011 (31 MIRC Ch. 1), modelled on the US Model Penal Code, allows force a person believes immediately necessary to protect themselves against unlawful force. Deadly force is allowed only against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping or forced sexual intercourse, and not if the person knows they can avoid the need for it with reasonable safety by retreating, handing over property, or complying with a demand to stop doing something they have no duty to do. There is no duty to retreat from one's own home or workplace, except for an initial aggressor or when attacked at work by a co-worker. Outside the deadly-force rule, a person may judge the need for force without retreating (§3.04(2)(c)).

At home

No duty to retreat from one's own dwelling or place of work, unless the person was the initial aggressor or is attacked at work by someone whose workplace it also is (§3.04(2)(b)(ii)(A)).

What the law says
Criminal Code 2011 (31 MIRC Ch. 1), §3.04(2)(b)
The use of deadly force is not justifiable under this Section unless the actor believes that such force is necessary to protect himself or herself against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping or sexual intercourse compelled by force or threat; nor is it justifiable if: (i) the actor, with the purpose of causing death or serious bodily injury, provoked the use of force against himself or herself in the same encounter, unless the actor completely withdraws from the conflict and successfully communicates that to the victim; or (ii) the actor knows that he or she can avoid the necessity of using such force with reasonable safety by retreating or by surrendering possession of a thing to a person asserting a claim or right thereto or by complying with a demand that the actor abstain from any action that he or she has no duty to take, except that: (A) the actor is not obliged to retreat from the actor’s dwelling or place of work, unless he or she was the initial aggressor or is assailed in his or her place of work by another person whose place of work the actor knows it to be; ...
Criminal Code 2011, §3.04(2)(c)
Except as required by paragraphs (a) and (b) of this Subsection, a person employing protective force may estimate the necessity of such force under the circumstances as the person believes them to be when the force is used, without retreating, surrendering possession, doing any other act that the person has no legal duty to do, or abstaining from any lawful action.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Criminal Code, 2011 (P.L. 2011-59) (Nitijela (Parliament) of the Republic of the Marshall Islands)

f7d6d5b7119ebcad.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

New York

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

New York's Penal Law (section 35.15) allows deadly physical force only when the person reasonably believes the other person is using or about to use deadly force, or is committing a kidnapping, forcible rape, forcible aggravated sexual abuse or robbery, or a burglary in the circumstances set out in section 35.20. Against deadly force, New York keeps a duty to retreat: the person may not use deadly force if they know they can avoid it with complete personal safety, to themselves and others, by retreating. The only exceptions are being in one's own dwelling and not the initial aggressor, or being a police or peace officer (or assisting one). There is no exception for vehicles, workplaces or public places, and the retreat rule does not apply to the separately listed cases of kidnapping, rape, robbery and burglary. Physical force is not justified when the person provoked the other with intent to cause injury, was the initial aggressor (unless they withdrew and communicated it), or the force came from an agreed fight. The occupant of a dwelling or occupied building may use deadly force they reasonably believe necessary to prevent or end a burglary (35.20(3)). No presumption of reasonable fear, civil immunity or pretrial immunity hearing exists in current law; bills such as S1473 (2025) would remove the retreat duty, bar jurors from considering retreat and grant criminal and civil immunity, but they had not been enacted in the compiled law checked (last modified 6 September 2024).

At home

No duty to retreat in one's dwelling if not the initial aggressor (Penal Law 35.15(2)(a)(i)). A person in possession or control of, or licensed or privileged to be in, a dwelling or occupied building may use deadly force when they reasonably believe it necessary to prevent or end a burglary of it (35.20(3)); deadly force against a burglar is also allowed by cross-reference in 35.15(2)(c).

What the law says
Penal Law § 35.15(2)(a)
The actor reasonably believes that such other person is using or about to use deadly physical force. Even in such case, however, the actor may not use deadly physical force if he or she knows that with complete personal safety, to oneself and others he or she may avoid the necessity of so doing by retreating; except that the actor is under no duty to retreat if he or she is: (i) in his or her dwelling and not the initial aggressor; or (ii) a police officer or peace officer ...
Penal Law § 35.15(2)(b)
He or she reasonably believes that such other person is committing or attempting to commit a kidnapping, forcible rape, forcible aggravated sexual abuse, a crime formerly defined in section 130.50 of this chapter by force, or robbery
Penal Law § 35.20(3)
A person in possession or control of, or licensed or privileged to be in, a dwelling or an occupied building, who reasonably believes that another person is committing or attempting to commit a burglary of such dwelling or building, may use deadly physical force upon such other person when he or she reasonably believes such to be necessary to prevent or terminate the commission or attempted commission of such burglary.
Senate Bill S1473 (2025) – proposed, not law
A person who is justified in threatening or using physical force against another person in defense of themself, another person, or property pursuant to this section is immune from criminal and civil liability ...

5f06416a8b31bd86.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Albania

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 19 of the Criminal Code (Law No. 7895 of 1995) says a person bears no criminal liability for an act done when 'compelled' to defend the life, health, rights or interests of himself or another against an unjust, real and immediate attack, provided the defence is proportionate to the danger of the attack; an obvious mismatch between them is an excess of the limits of necessary defence. The code does not mention retreat, and no court ruling on retreat was found; by contrast, the necessity defence (article 20) covers only harm that is unavoidable by other means. Killing while exceeding the limits of necessary defence is a separate offence (article 83) punished by up to seven years in prison.

What the law says
Kodi Penal i Republikës së Shqipërisë (Law No. 7895, 27.1.1995, as amended), neni 19
Nuk ka përgjegjësi penale personi që ka kryer veprën duke qenë i detyruar të mbrojë jetën, shëndetin, të drejtat dhe interesat e tij ose të një tjetri, nga një sulm i padrejtë, i vërtetë dhe i çastit me kusht që, karakteri i mbrojtjes të jetë në proporcion me rrezikshmërinë e sulmit. Mospërputhja haptazi ndërmjet tyre përbën kapërcim të kufijve të mbrojtjes së nevojshme.
Kodi Penal, neni 20 (necessity, for contrast)
Nuk ka përgjegjësi penale personi që ka kryer veprën nga nevoja për të përballuar një rrezik real dhe të çastit që e kërcënon atë, një person tjetër apo pasurinë nga një dëmtim i rëndë dhe i pashmangshëm me mënyra të tjera, me kusht që të mos jetë i provokuar prej tij dhe dëmi i shkaktuar të mos jetë më i madh së dëmi i zmbrapsur.
Kodi Penal, neni 83
Vrasja e kryer në kushtet e kapërcimit të kufijve të mbrojtjes së nevojshme dënohet me burgim gjer në shtatë vjet.

ff453ba84712e313.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Federated States of Micronesia

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

The national Revised Criminal Code (Title 11 FSMC, PL 11-72) contains no self-defence section in the chapters checked; self-defence comes from court decisions annotated in the Code. The FSM Supreme Court Appellate Division held that a person threatened with imminent serious bodily harm or death may use deadly force if necessary, while non-deadly threats allow only non-deadly force reasonable in light of the aggressor's force (Alik v. Kosrae, 1994). The annotations do not mention retreat, so the retreat question is not settled by the sources opened. The four states (Chuuk, Kosrae, Pohnpei, Yap) have their own codes, which were not reviewed.

At home

Courts allow reasonable force to protect oneself, one's family, home and property from an intruder and to expel the intruder, and this privilege may extend onto the road next to the home (FSM v. Ruben, 1981; Tosie v. FSM, 1991). In Ruben the court assumed that under customary law a homeowner should 'go lightly' with a forcibly entering in-law.

What the law says
Title 11 FSMC, Chapter 1, case annotations — Alik v. Kosrae, 6 FSM Intrm. 469, 473 (App. 1994)
There are two different standards used when reviewing a claim of self-defense. When one is threatened with imminent serious bodily harm or death by another he may justifiably use deadly force if necessary to protect himself from great bodily harm or death. When one is threatened with imminent unlawful bodily harm (but not serious bodily harm or death) he may justifiably use nondeadly force if force is necessary to prevent the unlawful bodily harm. ... The force employed must be reasonable in the light of the amount, degree and kind of force being used by the aggressor.
Title 11 FSMC, Chapter 1, case annotations — Tosie v. FSM, 5 FSM Intrm. 175 (App. 1991)
Privilege to use reasonable force in defense of family, home and property may under the circumstances extend onto the road adjacent to the home. ... A person can use no more force than is reasonably necessary to protect himself, his family, home and property from an intruder, and to expel the intruder.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • FSM Code, Title 11 Crimes, Chapter 1 (with case annotations) (Legal Information System of the Federated States of Micronesia)

1f5ae901cda80b50.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Slovakia

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Section 25 of the Slovak Criminal Code (Act 300/2005) says an act done to avert an impending or ongoing attack on an interest protected by the Code is not a crime. Self-defence is excluded only if the intensity of the defence 'clearly exceeds' the intensity of the attack, judged by the manner, place and time of the attack and the circumstances of attacker and defender. The statute says nothing about retreat; a Slovak legal article on necessity contrasts the two defences, explaining that under necessity (§ 24) the danger must not be avertable in another way, so the defender would first have to try to avoid it, whereas self-defence carries no such requirement. A person who exceeds the limits is not criminally liable if they acted in intense agitation caused by the attack, such as confusion, fear or fright. The English text quoted is the 2010 version in a university database; the current official text could not be opened to check later changes.

What the law says
Criminal Code (Trestný zákon, Act 300/2005), Section 25 (English translation, 2010 version)
(1) An act, which otherwise gives rise to criminal liability, shall not be considered as a criminal offence if it is performed in order to avert an impending or actual attack on an interest protected under this Act. (2) Necessary self-defence shall not be invoked if the intensity of defence clearly exceeds the intensity of an attack, in particular in view of the mode, place, time of an attack, the circumstances related to an assailant or a defender. (3) Any person who averts an attack in a manner referred to in paragraph 2 shall not be held criminally liable if he acted in a state of intense agitation caused by an attack, in particular as a consequence of confusion, fear or fright.

afc0540c85f1d926.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Armenia

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Armenia's 2003 Criminal Code (art. 42) said a person may use necessary defence 'regardless of the possibility to avoid encroachment' or to call on other people or the authorities, so there was no duty to retreat, and any harm including death could be caused when defending against violence dangerous to life. Intentional actions obviously out of proportion to the danger were 'excess of necessary defence'; murder in excess of necessary defence carried at most three years' imprisonment (art. 108). A new Criminal Code adopted 5 May 2021 took effect on 1 July 2022; its Article 32 is titled 'Necessary Defence' and Article 159 'Murder in Excess of Necessary Defence', but the full text of the 2021 articles could not be opened for this entry, so it is not confirmed whether the current law keeps the 2003 wording; the category is therefore marked unclear.

At home

Under the 2003 Criminal Code (art. 42(5)), using a weapon or other means to prevent illegal and forced intrusion into a residence or other premises was not an excess of defence, whatever harm was caused to the intruder. The wording of the corresponding rule in the 2021 Code could not be opened.

What the law says
Criminal Code of Armenia (2003, as amended 2004), art. 42 (Necessary defence) — superseded 1 July 2022
2. While being defended from violence dangerous to human life or from an encroachment accompanied by a real threat of such violence, any harm, including death, may be caused. 3. A person shall be entitled to the right of necessary defence, regardless of the possibility to avoid encroachment or apply to the support of other persons or state authorities and of professional and other special competences and official position. ... 5. Discharge of weapons or any other means or objects for the purpose of being defended from the attack of an armed person or an armed group of persons and for preventing illegal and forced intrusion into a residence or other premises, regardless of the gravity of harm caused to the encroacher, shall not be considered as an excess of necessary defence and shall not result in criminal liability.
Criminal Code of Armenia (2003), art. 108
Murder in excess of necessary defence — shall be punished by imprisonment for a term of maximum three years.

a762085a606e89c2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

French Guiana

An overseas region of France, part of France itself. Shown with the entry for France, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 122-5 of the Penal Code, a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same time in a way required by the necessity of self-defence, unless the means used are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack. The defence must be simultaneous with the attack; a blow struck after the attacker has left is treated as ordinary violence. Neither art. 122-5 nor art. 122-6 mentions retreat, and the sources opened here did not address whether flight is expected. Defence of property can never justify intentional homicide. Judges decide whether the defence was disproportionate; Encyclopaedia Universalis notes that an excessive response may lead to mitigating circumstances or a conviction for a lesser offence rather than full exoneration.

At home

Art. 122-6 of the Penal Code presumes self-defence for a person who acts "to repel, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place", and against perpetrators of violent theft or looting. The presumption is rebuttable and does not cover daytime intrusions, which fall under the general rule of art. 122-5.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 122-5
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal, art. 122-6
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
