d6d1d00271b39b09.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Kentucky

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Kentucky allows deadly force when the defendant believes it is necessary to protect against death, serious physical injury, kidnapping, sexual intercourse compelled by force or threat, a felony involving the use of force, or in the home-intrusion situations covered by § 503.055 (Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.050(2)). Since 2006 Ky. Acts ch. 192 (effective 12 July 2006), 'a person does not have a duty to retreat prior to the use of deadly physical force' (§ 503.050(4)), and a person not engaged in unlawful activity who is attacked in any place where they have a right to be may stand their ground and meet force with force, including deadly force, to prevent death, great bodily harm or a violent felony (§ 503.055(3)). The same 2006 Act created the home, residence and occupied-vehicle presumption of reasonable fear (§ 503.055). Force is not justified to resist a known arrest by an officer using reasonable force (even if the arrest is unlawful), by someone who provoked the other intending to kill or seriously injure, or by an initial aggressor, unless their first force was non-deadly and the response put them in imminent deadly danger, or they withdrew and clearly communicated it (§ 503.060). A person who used permitted force is immune from criminal prosecution (including arrest, detention and charging) and civil action, except against an identified or recognisable on-duty peace officer; police may not arrest without probable cause that the force was unlawful, and a court must award fees, costs and lost income to a civil defendant found immune (§ 503.085). If the defendant's belief in the need for force was wanton or reckless, the justification is unavailable for offences requiring only wantonness or recklessness, such as second-degree manslaughter or reckless homicide (§ 503.120(1)).

At home

Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.055(1) (2006): a person is presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent death or great bodily harm when using deadly force against someone who was unlawfully and forcibly entering (or had entered) a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle, or was removing someone from it, if the person knew or had reason to believe that was happening; and an unlawful forcible intruder is presumed to intend violence (§ 503.055(4)). The presumption does not apply against another lawful resident with no domestic-violence injunction or no-contact order, a parent or guardian taking their own child, an identified or recognisable peace officer on duty, or where the defender is engaged in unlawful activity.

What the law says
Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.050(4)
A person does not have a duty to retreat prior to the use of deadly physical force.
Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.055(3)
A person who is not engaged in an unlawful activity and who is attacked in any other place where he or she has a right to be has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his or her ground and meet force with force, including deadly force, if he or she reasonably believes it is necessary to do so to prevent death or great bodily harm to himself or herself or another or to prevent the commission of a felony involving the use of force.
Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.055(1)
A person is presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or great bodily harm to himself or herself or another when using defensive force that is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm to another if: (a) The person against whom the defensive force was used was in the process of unlawfully and forcibly entering or had unlawfully and forcibly entered a dwelling, residence, or occupied vehicle ...
Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.060(2)–(3)
the use of physical force by a defendant upon another person is not justifiable when: ... (2) The defendant, with the intention of causing death or serious physical injury to the other person, provokes the use of physical force by such other person; or (3) The defendant was the initial aggressor, except that ...
Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.085(1)
A person who uses force as permitted in KRS 503.050, 503.055, 503.070, and 503.080 is justified in using such force and is immune from criminal prosecution and civil action for the use of such force ... As used in this subsection, the term "criminal prosecution" includes arresting, detaining in custody, and charging or prosecuting the defendant.
Ky. Rev. Stat. § 503.120(1)
but the defendant is wanton or reckless in believing the use of any force, or the degree of force used, to be necessary ... the justification afforded by those sections is unavailable in a prosecution for an offense for which wantonness or recklessness, as the case may be, suffices to establish culpability.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

87bf943f5ef5d83d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Crimea

Part of Ukraine, occupied and annexed by Russia since 2014, which applies its own criminal code there (see Russia). Shown with the entry for Ukraine, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Article 36 of Ukraine's Criminal Code allows 'necessary defence' of one's own or another's rights, or public or state interests, by causing the harm that is necessary and sufficient to avert or stop an attack. The code states that every person has this right 'notwithstanding any possibility to avoid' the attack or to ask others or the authorities for help, so there is no duty to retreat. Excess of necessary defence means intentionally causing grave harm that is not adequate to the danger, and it is punishable only under two specific lighter offences (Articles 118 and 124, killing or grave injury in excess of defence); there is no liability if high excitement prevented the person judging proportionality. Using weapons against an armed attacker, a group, or a violent intrusion into a home is never treated as excess. The English text quoted is the 2010 version held in a university database; the official Ukrainian site could not be reached to check later amendments.

At home

Article 36(5): using weapons or other means to avert an unlawful violent intrusion into a dwelling or other premises is not treated as excess of necessary defence and carries no criminal liability, whatever the harm caused to the intruder.

What the law says
Criminal Code of Ukraine, Article 36 (English translation, 2010 version)
1. The necessary defense shall mean actions taken to defend the legally protected rights and interests of the defending person or another person, and also public interests and interests of the state, against a socially dangerous trespass, by inflicting such harm upon the trespasser as is necessary and sufficient in a given situation to immediately avert or stop the trespass, provided the limits of the necessary defense are not exceeded. 2. Every person shall have the right to necessary defense notwithstanding any possibility to avoid a socially dangerous trespass or request assistance of other persons or authorities. 3. The excess of necessary defense shall mean an intended causing of a grievous harm to the trespasser, which is not adequate to the danger of the trespass or circumstances of the defense. The excess of necessary defense shall entail criminal liability only in cases specifically prescribed in Articles 118 and 124 of this Code. 4. A person shall not be subject to criminal liability where that person was not able, due to high excitement, to evaluate if the harm caused by that person was proportionate to the danger of the trespass or circumstances of defense. 5. The use of weapons or other means or things for protection against an attack of an armed person or an attack of a group of persons, and also to avert an unlawful violent intrusion upon a dwelling place or other premises, shall not be treated as the excess of necessary defense and shall not entail criminal liability irrespective of the gravity of harm caused to the trespasser.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

843f80d73e8dc18c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Hawaii

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Hawaii's 1972 penal code (L 1972, c 9), which follows the Model Penal Code, allows deadly force when the actor believes it is necessary to protect themselves against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping, rape or forcible sodomy (Haw. Rev. Stat. § 703-304(2)). Hawaii keeps a duty to retreat: deadly force is not justified if the actor knows they can avoid the need for it with complete safety by retreating, by handing over property to someone claiming a right to it, or by complying with a demand to refrain from something they have no duty to do (§ 703-304(5)(b)). There is no duty to retreat from one's dwelling or place of work, except for an initial aggressor or a person attacked at work by a co-worker; police and people lawfully assisting them need not give up an arrest. For non-deadly force there is no retreat requirement (§ 703-304(3)). Deadly force is also not justified if the actor provoked the use of force in the same encounter intending to cause death or serious injury, and force may not be used to resist a known arrest by an officer even if the arrest is unlawful (§ 703-304(4)–(5)). The test is the actor's own belief, but if that belief was reckless or negligent, the justification is not available for offences that need only recklessness or negligence, such as manslaughter or negligent homicide (§ 703-310). The section was last amended in 2001 (L 2001, c 91); the sources consulted show no statutory immunity from prosecution or civil suit.

At home

Haw. Rev. Stat. § 703-304(5)(b)(i): the actor is not obliged to retreat from their dwelling or place of work, unless they were the initial aggressor or are attacked at work by a co-worker (someone whose place of work the actor knows it to be). There is no statutory presumption of reasonable fear for home intrusions.

What the law says
Haw. Rev. Stat. § 703-304(5)
The use of deadly force is not justifiable under this section if: (a) The actor, with the intent of causing death or serious bodily injury, provoked the use of force against himself in the same encounter; or (b) The actor knows that he can avoid the necessity of using such force with complete safety by retreating or by surrendering possession of a thing to a person asserting a claim of right thereto or by complying with a demand that he abstain from any action which he has no duty to take, except that: (i) The actor is not obliged to retreat from his dwelling or place of work, unless he was the initial aggressor or is assailed in his place of work by another person whose place of work the actor knows it to be ...
Haw. Rev. Stat. § 703-304(2)
The use of deadly force is justifiable under this section if the actor believes that deadly force is necessary to protect himself against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping, rape, or forcible sodomy.
Haw. Rev. Stat. § 703-310(1)
When the actor believes that the use of force ... is necessary ... but the actor is reckless or negligent in having such belief ..., the justification afforded by those sections is unavailable in a prosecution for an offense for which recklessness or negligence, as the case may be, suffices to establish culpability.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • Hawaii Revised Statutes § 703-310, Provisions generally applicable to justification (Hawaii State Legislature)

5d81889532a4df3a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Slovenia

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Article 22 of the Slovenian Criminal Code (KZ-1) says an act committed in self-defence (silobran) is not unlawful, where the defence is 'absolutely necessary' to repel a simultaneous unlawful attack on oneself or another. The code does not mention retreat. Court summaries collected by a Slovenian legal database show that the Supreme Court judges necessity and appropriateness of the defence on the whole situation the attacker created, that people who knowingly enter a mutual fight cannot normally claim self-defence, and that in at least one 1999 appellate case (Celje Higher Court, Kp 277/99) the court rejected self-defence because the defendant 'could have avoided the attack by withdrawing' instead of throwing a stone. No source was found stating a general rule for or against a duty to retreat. A person who exceeds the limits of self-defence may receive a lighter sentence, and the sentence may be waived if the excess came from strong agitation or fright caused by the attack.

What the law says
Kazenski zakonik (KZ-1), 22. člen
(1) Dejanje, ki je storjeno v silobranu, ni protipravno. (2) Silobran je obramba, ki je nujno potrebna, da storilec odvrne od sebe ali koga drugega istočasen protipraven napad. (3) Storilec, ki je prekoračil meje silobrana, se sme kaznovati mileje; če je prekoračil silobran zaradi močne razdraženosti ali prestrašenosti, povzročene z napadom, se mu sme kazen tudi odpustiti.
Criminal Code (KZ-1), Article 22 (English translation)
(1) An act committed in self-defence shall not constitute a criminal offence. (2) Self-defence shall be understood to mean such defence as is absolutely necessary for the perpetrator to avert an immediate and unlawful attack on himself or on any other person. (3) In the event that the perpetrator has acted beyond the limits of justifiable self defence, his sentence may be reduced; if he has so acted by reason of great excitement or fright provoked by the attack, the sentence may be withdrawn.

b118bc3c4159bef3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Cabo Verde

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Cabo Verde's Penal Code (2003) defines legitimate defence as an act carried out 'as a necessary means' to repel a current and unlawful attack on legally protected and relevant interests of the defender or another person. The code does not mention retreat or a duty to flee; the test is whether the means used were necessary. Its explanatory preamble says the 'relevant interests' wording was chosen so that very minor or insignificant attacks do not justify defensive harm. If the defender used excessive means the act stays unlawful but the penalty can be freely reduced (art. 37), and a person who exceeded the means because of non-blameworthy disturbance, fear or fright acts without guilt (art. 41). No specific home-defence rule was found.

What the law says
Código Penal (2003), art. 36 (Legítima defesa)
Constitui legítima defesa o facto praticado como meio necessário para afastar a agressão actual e ilícita de interesses juridicamente protegidos e relevantes do agente ou de terceiro.
Código Penal (2003), art. 37 (Excesso de legítima defesa)
Não é excluída a ilicitude do facto, se houver excesso dos meios utilizados pelo defendente, mas a pena pode ser livremente atenuada, nos termos e com os limites referidos no n.º 2 do artigo 22.º.
Código Penal (2003), art. 41 (Excesso de legítima defesa não censurável)
Age sem culpa quem se exceder nos meios empregados em legítima defesa, em virtude de perturbação, medo ou susto não censuráveis.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Código Penal de Cabo Verde (2003), with preamble (Government of Cabo Verde (hosted by policinglaw.info))

c846c371ff45cb77.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Guatemala

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 24(1) of the Penal Code, a person who defends their own or another's person, property or rights is justified if there is an unlawful aggression, "rational necessity of the means used" to prevent or repel it, and no sufficient provocation by the defender. The Code does not mention retreat, and the sources opened here did not address whether flight is expected. The no-provocation requirement is waived for defence of close relatives, a spouse or partner, parents or adopted children, if the defender took no part in the provocation. Rules on excessive defence were not found in the source opened.

At home

Art. 24(1) deems all three conditions of self-defence to be met for a person who repels someone trying to enter, or who has entered, another's dwelling or its outbuildings, if that person's conduct shows an imminent danger to the life, property or rights of the occupants.

What the law says
Código Penal (Decreto 17-73), art. 24(1)
Son causas de justificación: Legítima defensa 1º. Quien obra en defensa de su persona, bienes o derechos, o en defensa de la persona, bienes o derechos de otra, siempre que concurran las circunstancias siguientes: a) Agresión ilegítima; b) Necesidad racional del medio empleado para impedirla o repelerla; c) Falta de provocación suficiente por parte del defensor. Se entenderá que concurren estas tres circunstancias respecto de aquel que rechaza al que pretenda entrar o haya entrado en morada ajena o en sus dependencias, si su actitud denota la inminencia de un peligro para la vida, bienes o derechos de los moradores. El requisito previsto en el literal c) no es necesario cuando se trata de la defensa de sus parientes dentro de los grados de ley, de su cónyuge o concubinario, de sus padres o hijos adoptivos, siempre que el defensor no haya tomado parte en la provocación.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Artículo 24 del Código Penal (Guatemala) (Conceptos Jurídicos)

44e5c8f1a4f9bd99.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Illinois

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Illinois allows deadly force only when a person reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to themselves or another, or the commission of a forcible felony (720 ILCS 5/7-1(a)). The statute does not mention retreat, but Illinois courts hold that a person who did not provoke the fight has no duty to retreat, and the official pattern jury instruction tells jurors that such a person 'has no duty to attempt to escape the danger before using force against the aggressor' (IPI Criminal 24-25.09X, citing People v. Hughes, 46 Ill. App. 3d 490 (1977), and People v. Miller, 259 Ill. App. 3d 257 (1994)). The no-retreat rule therefore applies anywhere, by case law. An initial aggressor may use deadly force only if they face imminent danger of death or great bodily harm and have exhausted every reasonable means of escape, or if they withdrew in good faith and clearly said so and the other person kept attacking; a person committing or escaping from a forcible felony, or who provoked force as an excuse to hurt the other person, cannot claim self-defence (720 ILCS 5/7-4; IPI 24-25.09–24-25.11). If the defendant actually but unreasonably believed deadly force was justified, first-degree murder is reduced to second-degree murder (720 ILCS 5/9-2(a)(2); IPI 7.05). Since 2004 (P.A. 93-832), a person who used justified force cannot be sued by the aggressor or the aggressor's estate or family unless the force involved willful or wanton misconduct (720 ILCS 5/7-1(b)); there is no immunity from criminal prosecution or pretrial immunity hearing.

At home

720 ILCS 5/7-2 (as set out in Illinois Pattern Jury Instruction Criminal 24-25.07): force is justified to prevent or end another's unlawful entry into or attack on a dwelling, and deadly force is justified if the entry is made or attempted in a violent, riotous or tumultuous manner and the person reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent an assault on someone in the dwelling, or if they reasonably believe it is necessary to prevent a felony in the dwelling. The IPI committee note, citing People v. Yanez, 2022 IL App (3d) 200007, says a home dweller need not wait for the entry to be completed, and that unlike self-defence, defence of a dwelling does not require danger to life or great bodily harm. There is no statutory presumption of reasonable fear.

What the law says
Illinois Pattern Jury Instructions, Criminal, No. 24-25.09X (Non-Initial Aggressor—No Duty To Retreat)
A person who has not initially provoked the use of force against himself has no duty to attempt to escape the danger before using force against the aggressor.
720 ILCS 5/7-1(a)
However, he is justified in the use of force which is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm only if he reasonably believes that such force is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to himself or another, or the commission of a forcible felony.
720 ILCS 5/7-1(b)
In no case shall any act involving the use of force justified under this Section give rise to any claim or liability brought by or on behalf of any person acting within the definition of "aggressor" set forth in Section 7-4 of this Article, or the estate, spouse, or other family member of such a person, against the person or estate of the person using such justified force, unless the use of force involves willful or wanton misconduct.
IPI Criminal 24-25.09 (Initial Aggressor's Use of Force), from 720 ILCS 5/7-4(c)
A person who initially provokes the use of force against himself is justified in the use of force only if [1] the force used against him is so great that he reasonably believes he is in imminent danger of death or great bodily harm, and he has exhausted every reasonable means to escape the danger other than the use of force which is likely to cause death or great bodily harm to the other person. [or] [2] in good faith, he withdraws from physical contact with the other person and indicates clearly to the other person that he desires to withdraw ...
IPI Criminal 7.05 (Second Degree Murder—Belief in Justification), from 720 ILCS 5/9-2(a)(2)
A mitigating factor exists so as to reduce the offense of first degree murder to the lesser offense of second degree murder if at the time of the killing the defendant believes that circumstances exist which would justify the deadly force he uses, but his belief that such circumstances exist is unreasonable.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • 720 ILCS 5/7-1, Use of force in defense of person (Source: P.A. 93-832, eff. 7-28-04) (Illinois General Assembly)

Criminal Offences Bill, 2020 (The Gambia), s. 17 (as summarised from the National Assembly copy; full wording not captured)

6f90e36bf84441ba.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

West Virginia

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

West Virginia's stand-your-ground and castle rules are written in W. Va. Code § 55-7-22, a section placed in the civil-actions chapter (first enacted by HB 4658 in 2004 and amended by SB 145 in 2008). In the home or residence, a lawful occupant may use reasonable and proportionate force, including deadly force, against an intruder to prevent or end a forcible entry when they reasonably fear death or serious harm or reasonably believe the intruder means to commit a felony, and has no duty to retreat. Outside the home, a person not engaged in unlawful activity who is attacked anywhere they have a legal right to be may use deadly force 'without a duty to retreat' if they reasonably believe they or another are in imminent danger of death or serious bodily harm that only deadly force can prevent. The force must be 'reasonable and proportionate'. Justified force is a full and complete defence to any civil suit by the intruder or attacker, but that defence is not available to someone committing or escaping a felony, someone who provoked force as an excuse to injure, or an initial aggressor who did not clearly withdraw. The section does not authorise resisting a police officer or setting traps on property. Because the section sits in the civil code, its exact effect in criminal prosecutions (where West Virginia's common law also applies) was not confirmed from a criminal case or jury instruction for this entry. No statutory presumption of reasonable fear or pretrial criminal immunity hearing was found; the bill history page lists a 2024 bill (HB 5621) touching the section, whose outcome was not checked.

At home

A lawful occupant of a home or other residence may use reasonable and proportionate force, including deadly force, to prevent or end a forcible unlawful entry if they reasonably fear death or serious harm to anyone inside, or reasonably believe the intruder intends a felony there and that deadly force is necessary; there is no duty to retreat from the intruder (W. Va. Code § 55-7-22(a)-(b), enacted 2004, amended 2008).

What the law says
W. Va. Code § 55-7-22(c)
A person not engaged in unlawful activity who is attacked in any place he or she has a legal right to be outside of his or her home or residence may use reasonable and proportionate force against an intruder or attacker: Provided, That such person may use deadly force against an intruder or attacker in a place that is not his or her residence without a duty to retreat if the person reasonably believes that he or she or another is in imminent danger of death or serious bodily harm from which he or she or another can only be saved by the use of deadly force against the intruder or attacker.
W. Va. Code § 55-7-22(a)-(b) (home)
(b) A lawful occupant within a home or other place of residence does not have a duty to retreat from an intruder or attacker in the circumstances described in subsection (a) of this section.
W. Va. Code § 55-7-22(d)-(e) (civil defence and limits)
(d) The justified use of reasonable and proportionate force under this section shall constitute a full and complete defense to any civil action brought by an intruder or attacker against a person using such force. (e) The full and complete civil defense created by the provisions of this section is not available to a person who: (1) Is attempting to commit, committing or escaping from the commission of a felony; (2) Initially provokes the use of force against himself herself or another with the intent to use such force as an excuse to inflict bodily harm upon the assailant ...
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • Stand Your Ground in West Virginia (Giffords Law Center)

c88302c617165080.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Minnesota

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Minnesota allows an intentional killing only when necessary to resist or prevent an offence that the actor reasonably believes exposes them or another to great bodily harm or death, or to prevent a felony in the actor's home (Minn. Stat. § 609.065); reasonable non-deadly force may be used to resist an offence against the person (§ 609.06, subd. 1(3)). The statutes do not mention retreat, but the Minnesota Supreme Court holds that 'generally, the law mandates a duty to retreat if reasonably possible when acting in self-defense' (State v. Glowacki, 630 N.W.2d 392 (Minn. 2001)), and the pattern jury instruction (CRIMJIG 7.08) tells jurors that self-defence 'is available only to those who act honestly and in good faith', which 'includes the duty to retreat or avoid the danger if reasonably possible'. The exception is the home: Glowacki held there is no duty to retreat from one's own home, even when the attacker is someone who lives there too. To succeed, the defendant must also have reasonably believed force was necessary and used only the level of force reasonably necessary. Minnesota has not enacted a stand-your-ground statute (section 609.065 was last amended in 1986), and the sources consulted show no statutory immunity from prosecution or civil suit.

At home

State v. Glowacki, 630 N.W.2d 392 (Minn. 2001): there is no duty to retreat from one's own home when acting in self-defence in the home, regardless of whether the aggressor is a co-resident. Minn. Stat. § 609.065 also allows a killing when necessary to prevent the commission of a felony in the actor's place of abode. There is no statutory presumption of reasonable fear.

What the law says
State v. Glowacki, 630 N.W.2d 392 (Minn. 2001)
Generally, the law mandates a duty to retreat if reasonably possible when acting in self-defense. ... There is no duty to retreat from one's own home when acting in self-defense in the home, regardless of whether the aggressor is a co-resident.
CRIMJIG 7.08 (as quoted in State v. Glowacki)
The legal excuse of self-defense is available only to those who act honestly and in good faith and this includes the duly to [retreat or] avoid the danger if reasonably possible.
Minn. Stat. § 609.065
The intentional taking of the life of another is not authorized by section 609.06, except when necessary in resisting or preventing an offense which the actor reasonably believes exposes the actor or another to great bodily harm or death, or preventing the commission of a felony in the actor's place of abode.
Minn. Stat. § 609.06, subd. 1(3)
reasonable force may be used upon or toward the person of another without the other's consent when the following circumstances exist or the actor reasonably believes them to exist: ... (3) when used by any person in resisting or aiding another to resist an offense against the person ...
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • State v. Glowacki, 630 N.W.2d 392 (Minn. 2001) (CourtListener (Free Law Project))
  • Minnesota Statutes §§ 609.06, 609.065 (Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes)

52681488dbf4652d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bhutan

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Bhutan's Penal Code 2004 treats self-defence as a justification: force to protect oneself or a third person is allowed if it is the same or a lesser degree of force, the defendant believes it necessary, and it is no greater than necessary (s 95). Deadly force is justified only against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping or rape, and not if the defendant provoked it with intent to kill or seriously injure, or knew how to or could avoid the need for deadly force by retreating, handing over property or complying with a demand (s 98). There is no duty to retreat from one's home or workplace except for an initial trespasser or someone attacked at work by another person (s 102). This is the 2004 English text; the 2011 and 2021 amendment Acts were not checked for changes to these sections.

At home

s 102: a defendant is not obliged to retreat from an abode or place of work, except when the defendant is the initial trespasser or is attacked at their place of work by another person.

What the law says
Penal Code of Bhutan 2004, s 95
A defendant shall have the defence of justification, when the defendant uses force upon or towards another person to protect the defendant or a third person if: (a) The defendant uses the same or a lesser degree of force to protect oneself or the third person; (b) The defendant believes that the force is necessary for the protection of oneself or the third person; and (c) The force used is no greater than that which is necessary.
Penal Code of Bhutan 2004, s 98
A defendant shall not have the defence of justification, if the defendant uses deadly force unless the defendant believes that the use of deadly force was necessary to protect the defendant or a third person from death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping, or rape except, if the defendant: (a) With the purpose of causing death or serious bodily injury, provoked the use of deadly force against the person; or (b) Knew how to or could avoid the necessity of using deadly force by retreating or by surrendering possession of a item or by complying with a demand that the defendant abstain from an action which is not a duty the defendant is bound to perform by law.
Penal Code of Bhutan 2004, s 102
A defendant is not obliged to retreat from an abode or place of work except: (a) When the defendant is the initial trespasser; or (b) The defendant is attacked in the defendant’s place of work by another person.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • The Penal Code of Bhutan, 2004 (English version) (Judiciary of the Kingdom of Bhutan)
  • Acts list (includes Penal Code Amendment Acts 2011 and 2021) (Judiciary of the Kingdom of Bhutan)

9d388c5d92d6acb9.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Israel

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Under Israel's Penal Law, 5737-1977, a person bears no criminal responsibility for an act that was immediately necessary to repel an unlawful attack posing a real danger of harm to their own or another's life, liberty, body or property, unless they brought on the attack by their own wrongful conduct while foreseeing how things might develop (s. 34J). The defence does not apply where the act was not reasonable in the circumstances for preventing the harm (s. 34P). The statute does not mention retreat, and the sources found do not say whether a safe chance to escape defeats the defence; an Israel Democracy Institute commentary (2024) says the defence does not apply where using a weapon was not needed, or where less harmful alternatives such as calling the police existed. In 2008 a separate home, business and farm defence was added (s. 34J1).

At home

Section 34J1, added in 2008 (known as the 'Dromi Law'), removes criminal responsibility for an act immediately necessary to repel someone breaking into or entering, or trying to, one's own or another's dwelling, business or fenced farm with intent to commit an offence, unless the act was 'clearly unreasonable' in the circumstances or the person's own wrongful conduct brought about the break-in while foreseeing it. An Israel Democracy Institute commentary (2024) notes that lethal fire after a break-in by a defender who prepared for it in advance, or an incident in a stairwell outside the shooter's own flat, has been held not covered.

What the law says
חוק העונשין, התשל״ז–1977 (Penal Law 5737-1977), s. 34J (34י) הגנה עצמית
לא יישא אדם באחריות פלילית למעשה שהיה דרוש באופן מיידי כדי להדוף תקיפה שלא כדין שנשקפה ממנה סכנה מוחשית של פגיעה בחייו, בחירותו, בגופו או ברכושו, שלו או של זולתו; ואולם, אין אדם פועל תוך הגנה עצמית מקום שהביא בהתנהגותו הפסולה לתקיפה תוך שהוא צופה מראש את אפשרות התפתחות הדברים.
Penal Law, s. 34J1 (34י1) הגנת בית מגורים, בית עסק ומשק חקלאי מגודר (amendment 2008)
(א) לא יישא אדם באחריות פלילית למעשה שהיה דרוש באופן מיידי כדי להדוף מי שמתפרץ או נכנס לבית המגורים, בית העסק או המשק החקלאי המגודר, שלו או של זולתו, בכוונה לבצע עבירה, או מי שמנסה להתפרץ או להיכנס כאמור. (ב) הוראת סעיף קטן (א) לא תחול אם – (1) המעשה היה לא סביר בעליל, בנסיבות העניין, לשם הדיפת המתפרץ או הנכנס; (2) האדם הביא בהתנהגותו הפסולה להתפרצות או לכניסה תוך שהוא צופה מראש את אפשרות התפתחות הדברים.
Penal Law, s. 34P (34טז) חריגה מן הסביר
הוראות סעיפים 34י, 34יא ו־34יב לא יחולו כאשר המעשה לא היה סביר בנסיבות הענין לשם מניעת הפגיעה.

6dec5633ec044344.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

El Salvador

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 27(2) of the Penal Code excludes criminal liability for self-defence when there is an unlawful aggression, a "reasonable necessity of the defence used to prevent or repel it", and no sufficient provocation by the defender. Salvadoran appeal chambers (2002 decisions collected by the Supreme Court's jurisprudence centre) explain that the defence must be necessary, meaning the person "was not obliged to carry out another less harmful or harmless conduct" instead, and that there can be no enormous disproportion between defence and attack. The code text quoted does not mention retreat. When the defence was necessary but the defender used disproportionate means or kept going too long, the courts describe this as "excess of defence" rather than full self-defence. The sources opened here did not show a special rule for the home.

What the law says
Código Penal, art. 27 num. 2 (requirements as quoted by the Cámaras de lo Penal)
a) Agresión ilegítima; b) necesidad razonable de la defensa empleada para impedirla o repelerla; ... c) no haber sido provocada la agresión, de modo suficiente, por quien ejerce la defensa
Cámara de la 2ª Sección de Occidente, sentencia de 27/06/2002
Cita la doctrina que la defensa para ser legítima debe ser ante todo necesaria; es decir, que el sujeto no haya estado obligado a realizar otra conducta menos lesiva o inocua en lugar de la conducta típica.

88228f958a7f4b42.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Missouri

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Missouri allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes it is necessary to protect themselves, their unborn child or another against death, serious physical injury or any forcible felony (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 563.031.2(1)), and also against someone unlawfully entering or remaining in a dwelling, residence or vehicle the defender lawfully occupies, or private property the defender owns or leases. A person has no duty to retreat from a dwelling, residence or vehicle where they are lawfully present, from private property they own or lease, or 'in any other location such person has the right to be' (§ 563.031.3). The version history on the Revisor's site shows the steps: in 2007 (S.B. 62 & 41) deadly force against intruders in a dwelling, residence or vehicle and no duty to retreat from them were added; in 2010 (H.B. 1692 et al.) the same was extended to private property the defender owns or leases; and the 'any other location' stand-your-ground rule was added by S.B. 656, enacted in 2016 over the governor's veto (effective 14 October 2016). Self-defence is not available to an initial aggressor unless they withdrew and clearly communicated it and the other person kept attacking, nor to someone attempting, committing or escaping from a forcible felony (§ 563.031.1). The defendant must raise the issue, after which the state bears the burden of proof. Since 2007, justified force is 'an absolute defense to criminal prosecution or civil liability', and a court must award fees and costs to a civil defendant who has that defence (§ 563.074); the statute does not set out a separate pretrial immunity hearing.

At home

Mo. Rev. Stat. § 563.031.2(2)–(3): deadly force may be used against a person who unlawfully enters, remains after unlawfully entering, or attempts to unlawfully enter a dwelling, residence or vehicle lawfully occupied by the defender, or private property owned or leased by the defender (or occupied with the owner's specific authority), without separately showing fear of death or serious injury. If the defendant relies on the dwelling/vehicle rule, the state must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant did not reasonably believe force was necessary (§ 563.031.5). There is no duty to retreat from such a dwelling, residence, vehicle or private property (§ 563.031.3).

What the law says
Mo. Rev. Stat. § 563.031.3
A person does not have a duty to retreat: (1) From a dwelling, residence, or vehicle where the person is not unlawfully entering or unlawfully remaining; (2) From private property that is owned or leased by such individual; or (3) If the person is in any other location such person has the right to be.
Mo. Rev. Stat. § 563.031.2
A person shall not use deadly force upon another person under the circumstances specified in subsection 1 of this section unless: (1) He or she reasonably believes that such deadly force is necessary to protect himself, or herself or her unborn child, or another against death, serious physical injury, or any forcible felony; (2) Such force is used against a person who unlawfully enters, remains after unlawfully entering, or attempts to unlawfully enter a dwelling, residence, or vehicle lawfully occupied by such person ...
Mo. Rev. Stat. § 563.031.1
unless: (1) The actor was the initial aggressor; except that in such case his or her use of force is nevertheless justifiable provided: (a) He or she has withdrawn from the encounter and effectively communicated such withdrawal to such other person but the latter persists ...; (3) The actor was attempting to commit, committing, or escaping after the commission of a forcible felony.
Mo. Rev. Stat. § 563.074.1
a person who uses force as described in sections 563.031, 563.041, 563.046, 563.051, 563.056, and 563.061 is justified in using such force and such fact shall be an absolute defense to criminal prosecution or civil liability.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • Missouri Revised Statutes § 563.031, versions effective 28 Aug 2007 and 28 Aug 2010 (Missouri Revisor of Statutes)

501f926bf23594aa.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Mississippi

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Mississippi makes a homicide justifiable when committed in resisting an unlawful attempt to kill the person or to commit any felony on them, or on or in any dwelling, occupied vehicle, place of business or employment where they are (Miss. Code § 97-3-15(1)(e)), and in lawful defence of oneself or anyone else where there is reasonable ground to fear a design to commit a felony or do great personal injury and imminent danger of it being carried out (§ 97-3-15(1)(f)). A person who is not the initial aggressor and is not engaged in unlawful activity has no duty to retreat before using deadly force, and no judge or jury may treat a failure to retreat as evidence that the force was unnecessary, excessive or unreasonable (§ 97-3-15(4)). These stand-your-ground and presumption provisions were added by Laws 2006, ch. 492, and the section was amended again in 2016 and 2023. In the home, an occupied vehicle, or a business or workplace and its immediate premises, the law presumes reasonable fear when the other person was unlawfully and forcibly entering (§ 97-3-15(3)). A defendant who has been found not guilty by reason of self-defence under these provisions is immune from any civil action for damages from the same conduct (§ 97-3-15(5)(b)), but the sources consulted show no immunity from criminal prosecution and no pretrial immunity hearing.

At home

Miss. Code § 97-3-15(3): a person who uses defensive force is presumed to have reasonably feared imminent death, great bodily harm or a felony when the person against whom it was used was unlawfully and forcibly entering, or had unlawfully and forcibly entered, their dwelling, an occupied vehicle, their business or place of employment, or the immediate premises of the business or workplace. § 97-3-15(1)(e) makes a killing justifiable when resisting an attempt to commit a felony upon or in any dwelling, occupied vehicle, place of business or place of employment (or its immediate premises) where the person is.

What the law says
Miss. Code § 97-3-15(4)
A person who is not the initial aggressor and is not engaged in unlawful activity shall have no duty to retreat before using deadly force under subsection (1)(e) or (f) of this section and no finder of fact shall be permitted to consider the person's failure to retreat as evidence that the person's use of force was unnecessary, excessive or unreasonable.
Miss. Code § 97-3-15(1)(e)–(f)
When committed by any person in resisting any attempt unlawfully to kill such person or to commit any felony upon him, or upon or in any dwelling, in any occupied vehicle, in any place of business, in any place of employment or in the immediate premises thereof in which such person shall be; (f) When committed in the lawful defense of one's own person or any other human being, where there shall be reasonable ground to apprehend a design to commit a felony or to do some great personal injury, and there shall be imminent danger of such design being accomplished;
Miss. Code § 97-3-15(3)
A person who uses defensive force shall be presumed to have reasonably feared imminent death or great bodily harm, or the commission of a felony upon him or another or upon his dwelling, or against a vehicle which he was occupying, or against his business or place of employment or the immediate premises of such business or place of employment, ... was in the process of unlawfully and forcibly entering, or had unlawfully and forcibly entered ...
Miss. Code § 97-3-15(5)(b)
A defendant who has previously been adjudicated 'not guilty' of any crime by reason of subsection (1)(e) or (f) of this section shall be immune from any civil action for damages arising from the same conduct.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Mississippi Code § 97-3-15, Homicide; justifiable homicide; use of defensive force; duty to retreat (Laws 1983 ch. 382; 2006 ch. 492; 2016 ch. 421; 2023 ch. 458) (Justia)

1e579ddd179ec875.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Idaho

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Idaho makes homicide justifiable when resisting an attempt to murder, to commit a felony or to do great bodily injury, and in defence of a home, place of business or employment, occupied vehicle, property or person against someone who clearly intends a violent felony or a violent entry (Idaho Code § 18-4009(1)). A person 'need not retreat from any place that person has a right to be' and may stand their ground using all force that would appear necessary to a reasonable person in the same situation 'without the benefit of hindsight' (§ 19-202A(3)); this rule does not apply to jail or prison inmates dealing with staff. The current wording, including the stand-your-ground sentence and the presumption of reasonable fear in homes, businesses and occupied vehicles, comes from a 2018 amendment (2018 ch. 222). A person may act on appearances as a reasonable person would, without waiting to learn whether the danger is real (§ 19-202A(2)). An assailant or a person who joined in mortal combat must really and in good faith try to decline further fighting before a killing is justified (§ 18-4009(1)(c)). In a criminal case the prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the force was not justified (§ 19-202A(4)); Idaho's statutes do not create immunity from prosecution or a pretrial immunity hearing. A person who used justified force is immune from civil liability (except toward a law enforcement officer they knew or should have known was acting officially), and the court must award fees and costs to a defendant found immune (§ 6-808, added 2006).

At home

Idaho Code § 19-202A(5) (2018): a person using force or deadly force in defence of a habitation, place of business or employment, or occupied vehicle is presumed to have acted reasonably and to have had a reasonable fear of imminent death or serious bodily injury if the other person's entry or attempted entry was unlawful and made by force, in a violent and tumultuous manner, surreptitiously or by stealth, or to commit a felony. § 18-4009(2) also presumes that anyone who unlawfully enters such a place by force or stealth intends to commit a felony. 'Habitation' includes a tent and the curtilage of a dwelling.

What the law says
Idaho Code § 19-202A(3)
In the exercise of the right of self-defense or defense of another, a person need not retreat from any place that person has a right to be. A person may stand his ground and defend himself or another person by the use of all force and means which would appear to be necessary to a reasonable person in a similar situation and with similar knowledge without the benefit of hindsight.
Idaho Code § 19-202A(4)–(5)
the burden is on the prosecution to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the use of force, attempted use of force or threat to use force was not justifiable. (5) A person using force or deadly force in defense of a habitation, place of business or employment or occupied vehicle ... is presumed to have acted reasonably and had a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or serious bodily injury if the force is used against a person whose entry or attempted entry therein is unlawful ...
Idaho Code § 18-4009(1)(a), (c)
Homicide is justifiable when committed by any person in any of the following cases: (a) When resisting any attempt to murder any person, or to commit a felony, or to do some great bodily injury upon any person; ... but such person, or the person in whose behalf the defense was made, if he was the assailant or engaged in mortal combat, must really and in good faith have endeavored to decline any further struggle before the homicide was committed ...
Idaho Code § 6-808(1)
A person who uses force as justified in section 18-4009, Idaho Code, or as otherwise permitted in sections 19-201 through 19-205, Idaho Code, is immune from any civil liability for the use of such force except when the person knew or reasonably should have known that the person against whom the force was used was a law enforcement officer acting in the capacity of his or her official duties.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Idaho Code § 19-202A (added 1974, ch. 238; am. 2018, ch. 222) (Idaho Legislature)
  • Idaho Code § 18-4009 (added 1972, ch. 336; am. 2018, ch. 222) (Idaho Legislature)
  • Idaho Code § 6-808, Civil immunity for self-defense (added 2006, ch. 453) (Idaho Legislature)

008987fb9b00b361.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Montenegro

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Article 10 of Montenegro's Criminal Code says an act committed in necessary defence is not a crime, where the defence is 'absolutely necessary' to repel a simultaneous or imminent unlawful attack on one's own or another's interests. The code does not mention retreat or the home, and no Montenegrin court decision or commentary on whether a person must retreat was found. A person who exceeds the limits of necessary defence may be punished more leniently, or released from punishment if the excess came from strong agitation or fright caused by the attack.

What the law says
Krivični zakonik Crne Gore, član 10
(1) Nije krivično djelo ono djelo koje je učinjeno u nužnoj odbrani. (2) Nužna je ona odbrana koja je neophodno potrebna da učinilac od svog dobra ili dobra drugoga odbije istovremen ili neposredno predstojeći protivpravan napad. (3) Učinilac koji je prekoračio granice nužne odbrane može se blaže kazniti, a ako je prekoračenje učinio usljed jake razdraženosti ili prepasti izazvane napadom, može se i osloboditi od kazne.
Criminal Code of Montenegro, Article 10 (English translation, 2018 version)
(1) An act committed in legitimate self-defence shall not constitute a criminal offence. (2) Legitimate self-defence is such defence which is absolutely necessary for one to avert a concurrent or imminent unlawful attack upon oneself or another. (3) Where a perpetrator exceeds the limits of legitimate self-defence, he may receive a lighter punishment, and where the exceedance was due to strong excitement or fear due to an assault, he may also be released from punishment.

  • Krivični zakonik Crne Gore (consolidated text) (Paragraf Lex Montenegro)
  • Self-defence - national proceedings: Montenegro (University of Nottingham, CJAD database)

d2a426c5aceb48b0.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Indiana

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Indiana allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent serious bodily injury to themselves or a third person or the commission of a forcible felony, and in that case the person 'does not have a duty to retreat' (Ind. Code § 35-41-3-2(c)); the statute does not limit this to particular places. Separately, a person may use deadly force, with no duty to retreat, to prevent or end an unlawful entry into or attack on their dwelling, its curtilage (yard), or an occupied motor vehicle (§ 35-41-3-2(d)). The section was first enacted in 1976 and amended many times; the stand-your-ground wording dates from a 2006 amendment, and later changes came in 2012 (rules on force against public servants, including police), 2013, 2019 and 2024. Force is not justified for a person who is committing or escaping after committing a crime, who provoked unlawful action intending to injure the other person, or who entered into combat or was the initial aggressor, unless they withdrew and communicated that intent and the other person continued (§ 35-41-3-2(g)). Deadly force against a person known (or who should be known) to be a public servant, such as a police officer, is allowed only in narrow listed circumstances (§ 35-41-3-2(i)–(k)). The statute declares that no person 'shall be placed in legal jeopardy of any kind whatsoever' for protecting themselves or others by reasonable means, and refers civil immunity for justified force to Ind. Code 34-30-31 (not opened for this entry); the sources consulted show no pretrial criminal immunity hearing.

At home

Ind. Code § 35-41-3-2(d): a person is justified in using reasonable force, including deadly force, and does not have a duty to retreat, if they reasonably believe the force is necessary to prevent or end another person's unlawful entry into or attack on their dwelling, curtilage or occupied motor vehicle. The statute's policy section recognises 'the unique character of a citizen's home'. Indiana's statute does not state a presumption of reasonable fear; the home rule is instead a separate ground of justification that does not require a threat of serious bodily injury.

What the law says
Ind. Code § 35-41-3-2(c)
a person is justified in using reasonable force against any other person to protect the person or a third person ... is justified in using deadly force; and ... does not have a duty to retreat; if the person reasonably believes that that force is necessary to prevent serious bodily injury to the person ... No person, employer, or estate of a person in this state shall be placed in legal jeopardy of any kind whatsoever ...
Ind. Code § 35-41-3-2(d)
is justified in using reasonable force, including deadly force, against any other person; and ... if the person reasonably believes that the force is necessary to prevent or terminate the other person's unlawful entry ... or attack on the person's dwelling, curtilage, or occupied motor vehicle.
Ind. Code § 35-41-3-2(g)
Notwithstanding subsections (c) through (e), a person is not justified in using force if: ... the person is committing or is escaping after the commission of a crime; ... the person provokes unlawful action by another person with intent to cause bodily injury to the other person; or ... the person has entered into combat with another person or is the initial aggressor unless the person withdraws from the encounter and communicates to the other person the intent to do so ...
Ind. Code § 35-41-3-2(e)
Provisions concerning civil immunity for the justified use of force as defined in this section are codified under IC 34-30-31.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Indiana Code § 35-41-3-2, Use of force to protect person or property (2025 edition; as added by Acts 1976, P.L.148, amended 1977–2024) (Justia)

1b7b990cbc249953.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Lesotho

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Lesotho's Penal Code Act 2010 writes a retreat requirement into the self-defence section itself: force against an unlawful attack on oneself or another is excused only if it was not reasonable to use a means of retreat the defender knew about, and the force was no more than reasonably necessary (s. 20(1)(a)). The explanatory notes printed with the Act say this does not require retreat in every case; the means of escape only has to have been reasonable, so the defender need not take great risks to avoid the harm. The notes also say the drafters chose not to create a plea of 'excessive defence'; instead, where excessive force kills, courts in practice find provocation, which reduces the seriousness of the charge. Murder carries death, but the court must impose a lesser sentence where there are extenuating circumstances (s. 40(3)).

At home

The Penal Code has no separate home or dwelling rule. Force to protect property (s. 20(1)(b)) is allowed only if the means and degree of force are reasonable; the code's explanatory notes say courts would likely not regard lethal force to protect property as reasonable.

What the law says
Penal Code Act 2010 (Act No. 6 of 2012), s. 20 – Self defence
(1) No person shall be criminally responsible for the use of force in repelling an unlawful attack - (a) upon himself or herself or another person if - (i) it was not reasonable to avail himself or herself of any means of retreat of which he or she was aware; and (ii) the degree of force used in repelling the attack was no greater than that which was reasonably necessary in the circumstances; (b) upon his or her property or the property of another provided that the means he or she chooses and the degree of force he or she uses in so doing are reasonable in the circumstances.
Penal Code Act 2010, explanatory notes on s. 20
The accused must have had no means of escaping from the attack. This does not require retreat in every circumstances, as all that is required is that the means of escape should have been reasonable. The accused need not, therefore, take great risks to avoid the threatened harm. The use of excessive force to repel an attack will not be justified. ... where excessive force results in the death of the attacker, in practice the courts will find that there was provocation, and this will reduce the seriousness of the charge. For these reasons it has not been thought appropriate to introduce the plea of excessive defence ... It is likely that the courts would not regard as reasonable the use of lethal force to protect property
Penal Code Act 2010, s. 40(3)
Notwithstanding subsection (2), the court shall in the conviction for murder impose a lesser sentence where it is satisfied that - ... (c) the offence was committed in the presence of extenuating circumstances.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • Self-defence – national proceedings: Lesotho (Cooperation and Judicial Assistance Database (CJAD), University of Nottingham)

32a8c6c39b303d95.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

South Carolina

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

South Carolina's Protection of Persons and Property Act (2006 Act No. 379, in force 9 June 2006) put stand-your-ground and castle rules into statute. A person who is not engaged in unlawful activity and is attacked in any place where they have a right to be, including their place of business, has no duty to retreat and may meet force with force, including deadly force, if they reasonably believe it necessary to prevent death or great bodily injury or a violent crime (S.C. Code § 16-11-440(C)). A person who uses deadly force against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering, or dragging someone out of, a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle is presumed to have had reasonable fear; the presumption does not apply against a lawful resident, a parent or guardian taking their child, a law officer identified as such, or a defender who is engaged in unlawful activity. Someone who forces entry in breach of a protection order or bond condition is presumed to intend an unlawful act even if they live there (§ 16-11-440(E)). A person who uses deadly force as permitted is 'immune from criminal prosecution and civil action', police may not arrest them without probable cause that the force was unlawful, and courts must award fees and lost income to a defendant found immune in a civil suit (§ 16-11-450). In State v. Duncan (2011) the Supreme Court held that immunity is decided at a pretrial hearing on a motion to dismiss, where the defendant must prove it by a preponderance of the evidence. The Act's stated purpose is that no one 'should be required to needlessly retreat in the face of intrusion or attack' (§ 16-11-420(E)).

At home

The 2006 Protection of Persons and Property Act states its intent 'to codify the common law Castle Doctrine' and extend it to an occupied vehicle and place of business (S.C. Code § 16-11-420). A person using deadly force against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering a dwelling (including an attached porch), residence or occupied vehicle is presumed to have reasonable fear of death or great bodily injury (§ 16-11-440(A)); the intruder is presumed to intend a violent crime (§ 16-11-440(D)).

What the law says
S.C. Code § 16-11-440(C) (2006 Act No. 379)
A person who is not engaged in an unlawful activity and who is attacked in another place where he has a right to be, including, but not limited to, his place of business, has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his ground and meet force with force, including deadly force, if he reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent death or great bodily injury to himself or another person or to prevent the commission of a violent crime as defined in Section 16-1-60.
S.C. Code § 16-11-440(A) (presumption)
A person is presumed to have a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or great bodily injury to himself or another person when using deadly force that is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily injury to another person if the person: (1) against whom the deadly force is used is in the process of unlawfully and forcefully entering, or has unlawfully and forcibly entered a dwelling, residence, or occupied vehicle ...
S.C. Code § 16-11-450(A) (immunity)
A person who uses deadly force as permitted by the provisions of this article or another applicable provision of law is justified in using deadly force and is immune from criminal prosecution and civil action for the use of deadly force, unless the person against whom deadly force was used is a law enforcement officer ...
S.C. Code § 16-11-420(A)
It is the intent of the General Assembly to codify the common law Castle Doctrine which recognizes that a person's home is his castle and to extend the doctrine to include an occupied vehicle and the person's place of business.
State v. Duncan (S.C. 2011) (pretrial immunity hearing)
The circuit correctly decided the issue of respondent’s immunity from prosecution by way of a pre-trial hearing on respondent’s motion to dismiss, and the applicable standard of proof was a preponderance of the evidence.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • S.C. Code Title 16 Chapter 11, Article 6 (Protection of Persons and Property Act) (South Carolina Legislature)
  • State v. Duncan case summary (South Carolina Lawyers Weekly)

68800fd6093d9a6c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Massachusetts

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Massachusetts has no general self-defence statute; the rules come from Supreme Judicial Court decisions. To justify deadly force, the defendant must have reasonably believed they were in imminent danger of death or serious bodily harm from which they could save themselves only by using deadly force, and must first have used every reasonable avenue of escape (Commonwealth v. Pike, 428 Mass. 393 (1998)). The court has said this is not 'an absolute duty to retreat regardless of personal safety considerations', but the defendant must have 'availed himself of all means, proper and reasonable under the circumstances, of retreating from the conflict before resorting to the use of deadly force', and a self-defence instruction is not even required unless there is some evidence of this. A mistaken belief in danger can still support self-defence if it was reasonable. The only statutory exception to the retreat rule is the home: under the castle law (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 278, § 8A), an occupant has no duty to retreat from a person unlawfully in the dwelling and has a defence if they reasonably believed the intruder was about to cause death or great bodily injury and used reasonable means. Massachusetts has no workplace or vehicle exception, no stand-your-ground statute, and no statutory immunity from prosecution or civil suit in the sources consulted.

At home

Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 278, § 8A: an occupant charged with killing or injuring someone unlawfully in their dwelling has a defence if they were in the dwelling, acted in the reasonable belief that the intruder was about to inflict great bodily injury or death on them or another person lawfully there, and used reasonable means; and 'there shall be no duty on said occupant to retreat' from the person unlawfully in the dwelling. The statute covers only intruders 'unlawfully in said dwelling', not lawful co-occupants or guests, and creates no presumption of reasonable fear.

What the law says
Commonwealth v. Pike, 428 Mass. 393 (1998)
A self-defense instruction is not required unless there is some evidence that the defendant availed himself of all means, proper and reasonable under the circumstances, of retreating from the conflict before resorting to the use of deadly force. ... This rule does not impose an absolute duty to retreat regardless of personal safety considerations ... He must, however, use every reasonable avenue of escape available to him.
Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 278, § 8A
In the prosecution of a person who is an occupant of a dwelling charged with killing or injuring one who was unlawfully in said dwelling, it shall be a defense that the occupant was in his dwelling at the time of the offense and that he acted in the reasonable belief that the person unlawfully in said dwelling was about to inflict great bodily injury or death upon said occupant or upon another person lawfully in said dwelling, and that said occupant used reasonable means to defend himself or such other person lawfully in said dwelling. There shall be no duty on said occupant to retreat from such person unlawfully in said dwelling.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Commonwealth v. Pike, 428 Mass. 393 (1998) (CourtListener (Free Law Project))
  • Massachusetts General Laws, Part IV, Title II, Chapter 278, Section 8A (Massachusetts Legislature)

0a3de7b3e32ded1a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Burundi

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Burundi's Penal Code (Law No. 1/27 of 29 December 2017) says there is no offence in legitimate defence, defined as the reaction of a person who, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, commits an act that falls under criminal law, provided the means used are proportionate to the seriousness of the attack (art. 31(3°)). The code does not mention retreat or a duty to avoid the attack. No separate rule on excessive self-defence or on defence of the home was found in this article.

What the law says
Code pénal (Loi n°1/27 du 29 décembre 2017), art. 31(3°)
Il n’y a pas d’infraction : ... 3° En cas de légitime défense qui est la réaction de celui qui, devant une agression injustifiée envers elle‐même, ou autrui, accomplit un acte qui tombe sous le coup de la loi pénale, à condition que les moyens utilisés soient proportionnels à la gravité de l’agression.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Code pénal 2017 (Loi n°1/27 du 29 décembre 2017), droit-afrique.com edition (droit-afrique.com (hosted by lemandat.org))

e32750d2e0e673f7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Cook Islands

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

The Cook Islands has its own Crimes Act 1969 (separate from New Zealand's). A person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may repel force with force; they may cause death or grievous bodily harm if acting under reasonable fear of death or grievous bodily harm and believing on reasonable grounds they cannot otherwise preserve themselves (s 50). No retreat is required of someone who did not provoke the attack, but a person who started or provoked the fight may justify force only if, before using it, 'he declined further conflict and quitted or retreated from it as far as was practicable' (s 51). Text is from the 1969 Act as enacted (scanned copy, read by OCR); later amendments were not checked, and no court decisions were opened.

At home

s 57: a person in peaceable possession of a dwellinghouse may use such force as is necessary to prevent its forcible breaking and entering by anyone, if they believe on reasonable and probable grounds there is no lawful justification for it.

What the law says
Crimes Act 1969, s 50 Self-defence against unprovoked assault
(1) Every one unlawfully assaulted, not having provoked the assault, is justified in repelling force by force, if the force he uses - (a) Is not meant to cause death or grievous bodily harm; and (b) Is no more than is necessary for the purpose of self-defence. (2) Every one unlawfully assaulted, not having provoked the assault, is justified in repelling force by force although in so doing he causes death or grievous bodily harm, if - (a) He causes it under reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm from the violence with which the assault was originally made or with which the assailant pursues his purpose; and (b) He believes, on reasonable grounds, that he cannot otherwise preserve himself from death or grievous bodily harm.
Crimes Act 1969, s 51(c) Self-defence against provoked assault
(c) Before the force was used, he declined further conflict and quitted or retreated from it as far as was practicable.
Crimes Act 1969, s 57 Defence of dwellinghouse
Every one in peaceable possession of a dwellinghouse, and every one lawfully assisting him or acting by his authority, is justified in using such force as is necessary to prevent the forcible breaking and entering of the dwellinghouse by any person if he believes, on reasonable and probable grounds, that there is no lawful justification for the breaking and entering.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Crimes Act 1969 No. 20 (scanned original) (Parliament of the Cook Islands, Acts Library)

303bc39fb1d21dc6.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Georgia

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Georgia allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent death or great bodily injury to themselves or a third person, or to prevent the commission of a forcible felony (O.C.G.A. § 16-3-21(a)), and also in defence of a home under the conditions in § 16-3-23. Since Senate Bill 396 in 2006 (Ga. L. 2006, p. 477), a person who uses force lawfully in defence of self, others, home or property 'has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his or her ground' (§ 16-3-23.1); the statute does not limit this to particular places. The justification is not available to someone who provoked the attack as an excuse to hurt the other person, someone attempting, committing or fleeing a felony, or an aggressor or participant in a fight by agreement unless they withdraw, clearly communicate it, and the other person keeps attacking (§ 16-3-21(b)). A person who used force in line with these sections is 'immune from criminal prosecution' (§ 16-3-24.2, enacted 1998 and amended in 2006, 2014 and 2024), but the immunity is lost if, in using deadly force, the person used a weapon they were not legally allowed to carry or possess. The immunity statute itself does not set out the hearing procedure; the sources consulted for this entry did not cover the court-made pretrial procedure or civil immunity, so those are not described here.

At home

O.C.G.A. § 16-3-23: deadly force in defence of a habitation is justified if (1) the entry is made or attempted in a violent and tumultuous manner and the person reasonably believes it is for the purpose of assaulting or offering personal violence to someone inside and that force is necessary to prevent it; (2) the force is used against someone who is not a family or household member and who unlawfully and forcibly enters or has entered the residence, and the person knew or had reason to believe that an unlawful and forcible entry occurred (no separate showing of fear is required); or (3) the person reasonably believes the entry is for the purpose of committing a felony inside and that force is necessary to prevent it. § 16-3-23.1 adds that there is no duty to retreat.

What the law says
O.C.G.A. § 16-3-23.1
A person who uses threats or force in accordance with Code Section 16-3-21, relating to the use of force in defense of self or others, Code Section 16-3-23, relating to the use of force in defense of a habitation, or Code Section 16-3-24, relating to the use of force in defense of property other than a habitation, has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his or her ground and use force as provided in said Code sections, including deadly force.
O.C.G.A. § 16-3-21(a)
a person is justified in using force which is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm only if he or she reasonably believes that such force is necessary to prevent death or great bodily injury to himself or herself or a third person or to prevent the commission of a forcible felony.
O.C.G.A. § 16-3-21(b)
A person is not justified in using force ... if he: (1) Initially provokes the use of force against himself with the intent to use such force as an excuse to inflict bodily harm upon the assailant; (2) Is attempting to commit, committing, or fleeing after the commission or attempted commission of a felony; or (3) Was the aggressor or was engaged in a combat by agreement unless he withdraws from the encounter ...
O.C.G.A. § 16-3-24.2
A person who uses threats or force in accordance with Code Section 16-3-20, 16-3-21, 16-3-23, 16-3-23.1, 16-3-24, or 17-4-20 shall be immune from criminal prosecution therefor unless in the use of deadly force, such person utilizes a weapon the carrying or possession of which is unlawful by such person under Part 2 of Article 4 of Chapter 11 of this title.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

dbb4b7e092fc6863.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Rwanda

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Rwanda's Law No. 68/2018 determining offences and penalties in general (published in the Official Gazette of 27 September 2018, in Kinyarwanda, English and French) exempts from criminal liability a person who acts in self-defence, defends another person in danger, or acts to interrupt damage to property (art. 86). It names two typical self-defence situations: fending off someone who breaks into or enters an inhabited place by force or trickery, and defending oneself against thieves or other wrongdoers. The exemption applies only if the means used 'are proportional to the gravity of the threat'. The law says nothing about retreat, and no Rwandan court decisions on the point were found. Self-defence does not remove civil liability for damages where appropriate (art. 87).

At home

Article 86 lists among acts done in self-defence 'fending off a person who breaks into or enters by force or trickery an inhabited place'. The general proportionality rule in the same article applies.

What the law says
Law No. 68/2018 determining offences and penalties in general, art. 86 (English version)
Grounds for exemption from criminal liability that are inherent to the act are admitted if : 1º a person acts in self-defence in the following cases: a) fending off a person who breaks into or enters by force or trickery an inhabited place; b) defends himself/herself against thieves or other wrongdoers; 2º a person commits the following acts: a) an act of self-defence in case of danger; b) an act of defending another person in danger; c) an act committed to interrupt the commission of an offence of damage to property in order to protect the property. The exemption of criminal liability due to the grounds referred to under Paragraph 2 of this Article is only admitted if the means used by the offender to ensure self-defence or protect himself/herself or another person from danger or interrupt damage to the property he/she protected are proportional to the gravity of the threat.
Law No. 68/2018, art. 86 (French version, extract)
1º une personne agit en état de légitime défense dans les cas suivants: a) repousser quelqu’un qui entre par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité; b) se défendre contre les voleurs ou d’autres malfaiteurs;
Law No. 68/2018, art. 87
Nor do such grounds entail exemption from civil liability, if necessary.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Law determining Offences and Penalties in general (Law No. 68/2018) (RwandaLII (Laws.Africa))
