04c9e69111a6e9ba.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Iowa

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Iowa allows 'reasonable force', which can include deadly force if it is reasonable to believe such force is necessary to avoid injury or risk to one's own or another's life or safety, or to resist a like force or threat (Iowa Code § 704.1(1)). A person may be wrong about the danger or the force needed as long as there was a reasonable basis for the belief and they responded reasonably (§ 704.1(2)). Since 2017 (2017 Acts ch. 69), 'a person who is not engaged in illegal activity has no duty to retreat from any place where the person is lawfully present' before using force (§ 704.1(3)); the same 2017 Act added the presumption of reasonable belief for homes, workplaces and occupied vehicles (§ 704.2A), clarified that merely displaying a weapon is not deadly force (§ 704.2(2)), and added an immunity section. The defence is not available to someone participating in a forcible felony, riot or duel, someone who provoked force as an excuse to injure the other, or someone who provoked force by unlawful acts, unless the response was grossly disproportionate and put them in imminent danger of death or serious injury, or they withdrew and clearly signalled an end to the fight (§ 704.6). Section 704.13 states that a person justified in using reasonable force against an aggressor 'pursuant to section 704.4' is immune from criminal or civil liability for the aggressor's damages; as written it refers to § 704.4 (defence of property), and the sources consulted do not show a pretrial immunity hearing procedure.

At home

Iowa Code § 704.2A (2017 Acts ch. 69): a person is presumed to reasonably believe deadly force is necessary when the other person is unlawfully entering by force or stealth (or has entered and remains in) the defender's dwelling, place of business or employment, or occupied vehicle, or is unlawfully removing someone from it, and the defender knows or has reason to believe this. The presumption does not apply if the defender is engaged in a criminal offence or using the place to further one, against a parent or guardian taking their own child, against a peace officer lawfully entering, or against a lawful resident with no protective or no-contact order.

What the law says
Iowa Code § 704.1(3)
A person who is not engaged in illegal activity has no duty to retreat from any place where the person is lawfully present before using force as specified in this chapter.
Iowa Code § 704.1(1)–(2)
“Reasonable force” means that force and no more which a reasonable person, in like circumstances, would judge to be necessary to prevent an injury or loss and can include deadly force if it is reasonable to believe that such force is necessary to avoid injury or risk to one’s life or safety or the life or safety of another ... 2. A person may be wrong in the estimation of the danger or the force necessary to repel the danger as long as there is a reasonable basis for the belief of the person and the person acts reasonably in the response to that belief.
Iowa Code § 704.2A(1)
a person is presumed to reasonably believe that deadly force is necessary to avoid injury or risk to one’s life or safety or the life or safety of another in either of the following circumstances: a. ... (1) Unlawfully entering by force or stealth the dwelling, place of business or employment, or occupied vehicle of the person using force ...
Iowa Code § 704.6
The defense of justification is not available to the following: 1. One who is participating in a forcible felony, or riot, or a duel. 2. One who initially provokes the use of force against oneself, with the intent to use such force as an excuse to inflict injury on the assailant. 3. One who initially provokes the use of force against oneself by one’s unlawful acts, unless ...
Iowa Code § 704.13
A person who is justified in using reasonable force against an aggressor in defense of oneself, another person, or property pursuant to section 704.4 is immune from criminal or civil liability for all damages incurred by the aggressor pursuant to the application of reasonable force.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Iowa Code 2026, §§ 704.1, 704.2, 704.2A, 704.3, 704.6, 704.13 (Iowa Legislature)

d20c3e94c1f76a77.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Puerto Rico

Part of United States, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Puerto Rico has its own Penal Code (Act 146-2012). Under Article 25, a person who defends life, dwelling, property or rights, their own or another's, under a reasonable fear of imminent harm is not criminally liable if there was a reasonable need for the means used, there was no provocation by the defender, and no more harm than necessary was inflicted; to justify a killing, the defender must have reasonably believed they were in imminent or immediate danger of death or serious bodily harm. Article 25 itself does not mention retreat, so outside homes, vehicles and workplaces the test is necessity and proportionality. Act 92-2018 (S.B. 39, approved 17 April 2018) added Article 25A, which creates rebuttable presumptions in favour of a person who uses force, including deadly force, against someone unlawfully entering an occupied dwelling, vehicle, place of business or employment, or kidnapping someone there. The presumptions do not apply against someone with a legal right to be there, a parent or guardian taking their own child, a law enforcement officer, or when the defender provoked the other or was committing a crime. Article 25A(e) says the trier of fact 'shall not take into consideration the possibility of the actor could have avoided the confrontation'; because it sits in the article on dwellings, vehicles and workplaces, whether it reaches public places is not settled by the text. A person who acts in self-defence under Article 25A is not criminally or civilly liable for the harm or death caused to the aggressor; no pretrial immunity hearing procedure was found.

At home

Article 25A of the Penal Code (added by Act 92-2018, approved 17 April 2018) presumes reasonable belief of imminent harm, no provocation and reasonable need for the means used when the actor knew or had reason to believe the other person was unlawfully entering, or trying to enter, the occupied dwelling, vehicle, place of business or employment, or kidnapping someone inside; a parallel presumption covers killings where the actor faced imminent risk of death or serious harm. The fact-finder may not consider whether the actor could have avoided the confrontation, and the defender is not criminally or civilly liable.

The separate country-level file PRI.json classifies Puerto Rico as 'statute'; this entry uses 'proportional' because the no-retreat sentence is confined to Article 25A (dwelling, vehicle, business or workplace) and Article 25's general rule rests on reasonable necessity and proportionality.

What the law says
Puerto Rico Penal Code (Act 146-2012), art. 25, as amended by Act 92-2018 (official English translation)
Any person who defends his life, dwelling, property or rights, or the life, dwelling, property, or rights of another under circumstances where there is a reasonable fear of imminent harm shall not be criminally liable, provided that there was a reasonable need for the means used to prevent or avoid harm, there was no provocation by the party claiming self-defense, and that no more harm than necessary is inflicted to avoid or prevent harm. When alleging self-defense to justify causing death to a human being, it is necessary to have reasonable belief that when causing death to the aggressor, the aggrieved or defending person was in imminent or immediate danger of death or serious bodily harm.
Penal Code art. 25A(e) (Act 92-2018)
In order to determine the validity of self-defense, the trier of fact shall not take into consideration the possibility of the actor could have avoided the confrontation.
Penal Code art. 25A(a) (presumption)
It shall be presumed that the actor had a reasonable belief that he or another person was at risk of suffering imminent physical harm, that there was no provocation by the actor, and that there was a reasonable need for the means used and for the harm caused to prevent or avoid harm if: (1) the actor knew or had reason to believe that the person against whom force or violence was used: (i) unlawfully entered or was attempting to unlawfully enter the dwelling, vehicle, place of business or employment occupied at that moment by the actor or the person the actor protects ...
Penal Code art. 25A(g) (immunity)
A person who acting in self-defense uses force against or causes death to a human being in accordance with the provisions of this Article shall not be criminally or civilly liable for the harm or death caused to the aggressor.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Act No. 92-2018 (S.B. 39), official English translation (Oficina de Gerencia y Presupuesto, Puerto Rico (Biblioteca Virtual))

97439df998592f38.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Hong Kong S.A.R.

Part of China, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Hong Kong keeps its own criminal law, separate from mainland China. The Criminal Procedure Ordinance (Cap. 221, s 101A, added 1971 and modelled on the UK Criminal Law Act 1967) allows 'such force as is reasonable in the circumstances' in preventing crime or making an arrest, replacing the common-law rules for those purposes. Self-defence itself remains a common-law defence; no Hong Kong court decision or official direction on retreat could be opened from here (the official e-Legislation site and HKLII judgments were not reachable), so the retreat question is left unsettled in this entry.

At home

No home-specific statutory rule found.

What the law says
Criminal Procedure Ordinance (Cap. 221), s 101A
(1) A person may use such force as is reasonable in the circumstances in the prevention of crime or in effecting or assisting in the lawful arrest of offenders or suspected offenders or of persons unlawfully at large. (2) Subsection (1) shall replace the rules of the common law on the question when force used for a purpose mentioned in the subsection is justified by that purpose.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Criminal Procedure Ordinance, Cap. 221 (version of 14 May 2026) (Hong Kong Legal Information Institute (HKLII))

b74549256403ec86.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

East Timor

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Timor-Leste's Penal Code (2009) defines legítima defesa (art. 44) as action by the defender that is necessary to repel an unlawful, imminent or current aggression against any legally protected interest of the defender or a third party. The article contains no proportionality wording and does not mention retreat; no court decision on retreat was opened, so the retreat question is left unsettled here. Under art. 48, using means that are excessive in kind or degree may lead to an extraordinary reduction of the sentence, and excess caused by non-blameworthy disturbance, fear or fright excludes guilt entirely.

At home

No specific home-defence rule; art. 44 covers defence of any legally protected interest of the defender or a third party.

What the law says
Código Penal (Timor-Leste), art. 44 Legítima defesa
Considera-se legítima defesa a actuação do agente necessária ao afastamento de uma agressão ilícita, iminente ou actual, a quaisquer interesses juridicamente protegidos do agente ou de terceiro.
Código Penal (Timor-Leste), art. 48 Excesso de legitima defesa
1. Os meios que, pela sua espécie ou grau de utilização, forem excessivos para a acção defensiva do agente podem determinar a atenuação extraordinária da pena que caberia ao crime. 2. O excesso de meios utilizados na legítima defesa devido a perturbação, medo ou susto, não censuráveis, exclui a culpa do agente.

c5f841582451ea1c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

United States Minor Outlying Islands

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

The Minor Outlying Islands (such as Wake, Midway, Johnston, Palmyra, Baker, Howland, Jarvis, Kingman Reef and Navassa) have no local criminal code found here. Federal criminal law reaches places within the 'special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the United States', which 18 U.S.C. § 7 defines to include lands reserved for federal use and guano islands considered as appertaining to the United States; whether each island falls under a given clause was not checked. Federal self-defence law comes from the courts, not a statute: in Brown v. United States (1921) the Supreme Court rejected a jury instruction that a person attacked must always retreat if he safely can. It held that failure to retreat is only 'a circumstance to be considered' and that 'Detached reflection cannot be demanded in the presence of an uplifted knife', so a person who reasonably believes he faces death or grievous bodily harm may stand his ground.

What the law says
18 U.S.C. § 7(3)-(4)
(3) Any lands reserved or acquired for the use of the United States, and under the exclusive or concurrent jurisdiction thereof, or any place purchased or otherwise acquired by the United States by consent of the legislature of the State in which the same shall be, for the erection of a fort, magazine, arsenal, dockyard, or other needful building. (4) Any island, rock, or key containing deposits of guano, which may, at the discretion of the President, be considered as appertaining to the United States.
Brown v. United States, 256 U.S. 335 (1921)
Detached reflection cannot be demanded in the presence of an uplifted knife. Therefore in this Court, at least, it is not a condition of immunity that one in that situation should pause to consider whether a reasonable man might not think it possible to fly with safety or to disable his assailant rather than to kill him ... Rationally the failure to retreat is a circumstance to be considered with all the others in order to determine whether the defendant went farther than he was justified in doing; not a categorical proof of guilt.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • 18 U.S. Code § 7 - Special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the United States defined (Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School)
  • Brown v. United States, 256 U.S. 335 (1921) (Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School)

9bb2eef6d4d2851c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Oregon

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Oregon's Criminal Code, largely unchanged since 1971, lets a person use the degree of force they reasonably believe necessary to defend themselves or a third person against imminent unlawful force (ORS 161.209). Deadly force is allowed only if the person reasonably believes the other is committing or attempting a felony involving force against a person, a burglary in a dwelling, or is using or about to use unlawful deadly force (ORS 161.219). The statutes say nothing about retreat. In State v. Sandoval (2007) the Oregon Supreme Court read the 1971 code and held that 'the legislature did not intend to require a person to retreat before using deadly force against the imminent use of deadly physical force by another', so there is no duty to retreat anywhere the person is, by court ruling rather than a stand-your-ground statute. Force is not justified for someone who provoked the other with intent to injure or kill, or who was the initial aggressor unless they withdrew and effectively communicated that (ORS 161.215). A person in lawful possession of premises may use force to stop a criminal trespass, but deadly force only in defence of a person or to prevent arson or a violent felony (ORS 161.225). No statutory presumption of reasonable fear, civil immunity or pretrial immunity hearing was found; the official pattern jury instruction text was not located online.

At home

Deadly force is allowed against someone the defender reasonably believes is committing or attempting a burglary in a dwelling (ORS 161.219(2)). A person in lawful possession of premises may use force to stop a criminal trespass, and deadly force only in defence of a person or to prevent arson or a violent felony by the trespasser (ORS 161.225). No separate castle presumption or immunity statute was found.

What the law says
ORS 161.209 (1971 c.743 §22)
... a person is justified in using physical force upon another person for self-defense or to defend a third person from what the person reasonably believes to be the use or imminent use of unlawful physical force, and the person may use a degree of force which the person reasonably believes to be necessary for the purpose.
ORS 161.219
Notwithstanding the provisions of ORS 161.209, a person is not justified in using deadly physical force upon another person unless the person reasonably believes that the other person is: (1) Committing or attempting to commit a felony involving the use or threatened imminent use of physical force against a person; or (2) Committing or attempting to commit a burglary in a dwelling; or (3) Using or about to use unlawful deadly physical force against a person.
State v. Sandoval, 342 Or 506, 513-14, 156 P3d 60 (2007) (leading case)
The legislature did not intend to require a person to retreat before using deadly force against the imminent use of deadly physical force by another.
ORS 161.215(1)
Notwithstanding ORS 161.209, a person is not justified in using physical force upon another person if: (a) With intent to cause physical injury or death to another person, the person provokes the use of unlawful physical force by that person. (b) The person is the initial aggressor, except that ... the person withdraws from the encounter and effectively communicates to the other person the intent to do so ...
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • ORS Chapter 161 (Oregon State Legislature)
  • Stand Your Ground in Oregon (Giffords Law Center)

62cb22b818609842.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Ohio

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Ohio law allows a person to act in self-defence, defence of another or defence of their residence, and once there is evidence supporting that, the prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the person did not act in self-defence (ORC 2901.05(B)(1), burden shifted by HB 228 effective 28 March 2019). Before 2021 Ohio required retreat outside the home and vehicle; Senate Bill 175, effective 6 April 2021, changed ORC 2901.09 so that a person has no duty to retreat before using force 'if that person is in a place in which the person lawfully has a right to be', which covers public places, workplaces and vehicles. The same law bars juries from considering the possibility of retreat when deciding whether the person reasonably believed force was necessary. Since 2008 there has been a presumption of self-defence when deadly force is used against someone unlawfully entering or inside the residence or vehicle the defender occupies; it can be rebutted by a preponderance of the evidence and does not apply against a lawful resident or to a defender who is unlawfully present. The 2021 law added the same no-retreat rule and the same bar on considering retreat to civil lawsuits (ORC 2307.601), but no separate civil immunity or pretrial immunity hearing was found in these sections. The statutes do not themselves define who may claim self-defence; the 'lawfully has a right to be' condition limits the no-retreat rule.

At home

Since 2008 (SB 184) a person is presumed to have acted in self-defence when using deadly force against someone unlawfully entering, or who has unlawfully entered, the residence or vehicle they occupy (ORC 2901.05(B)(2)). 'Residence' includes a dwelling where one lives or is a guest, including an attached porch and tents. The presumption does not apply against a lawful resident or if the defender is unlawfully there.

What the law says
ORC 2901.09(B)-(C) (amended by SB 175, eff. 6 April 2021)
(B) For purposes of any section of the Revised Code that sets forth a criminal offense, a person has no duty to retreat before using force in self-defense, defense of another, or defense of that person's residence if that person is in a place in which the person lawfully has a right to be. (C) A trier of fact shall not consider the possibility of retreat as a factor in determining whether or not a person who used force in self-defense, defense of another, or defense of that person's residence reasonably believed that the force was necessary to prevent injury, loss, or risk to life or safety.
ORC 2901.05(B)(1) (burden on prosecution, HB 228, 2019)
... the prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused person did not use the force in self-defense, defense of another, or defense of that person's residence, as the case may be.
ORC 2901.05(B)(2) (presumption)
... a person is presumed to have acted in self-defense or defense of another when using defensive force that is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm to another if the person against whom the defensive force is used is in the process of unlawfully and without privilege to do so entering, or has unlawfully and without privilege to do so entered, the residence or vehicle occupied by the person using the defensive force.
ORC 2307.601(B) (civil cases)
... the person has no duty to retreat before using force in self-defense, defense of another, or defense of that person's residence if that person is in a place in which the person lawfully has a right to be.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

7e10803ce9428780.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Montana

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Montana allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent imminent death or serious bodily harm to themselves or another, or to prevent a forcible felony (Mont. Code § 45-3-102), and in defence of an occupied structure against an unlawful entry or attack (§ 45-3-103). Since 2009 (Ch. 332, L. 2009), a person who is lawfully in a place and is threatened with bodily injury or loss of life 'has no duty to retreat from a threat or summon law enforcement assistance prior to using force' (§ 45-3-110). The same 2009 law requires the state, once the defendant has offered evidence of justified force, to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant's actions were not justified (§ 46-16-131), even though the code still labels justification an 'affirmative defense' (§ 45-3-115). Justification is not available to a person attempting, committing or escaping from a forcible felony, or to one who purposely or knowingly provoked the force, unless they faced imminent deadly danger and had exhausted every reasonable means of escape, or withdrew in good faith and clearly signalled it (§ 45-3-105). Since 2001 a person who used force allowed by these sections is immune from civil damages for injury to the person or property of the one they used it against, and the winning party gets costs and attorney fees (§ 27-1-722). The sources consulted show no immunity from criminal prosecution and no pretrial immunity hearing.

At home

Mont. Code § 45-3-103: force is justified to prevent or end another's unlawful entry into or attack on an occupied structure, and deadly force is justified if the entry is made or attempted and the person reasonably believes the force is necessary to prevent an assault on someone inside, or to prevent a forcible felony in the structure. Montana's statutes consulted here contain no presumption of reasonable fear; the occupied-structure rule is a separate ground for force that does not require a threat of death.

What the law says
Mont. Code § 45-3-110
Except as provided in 45-3-105, a person who is lawfully in a place or location and who is threatened with bodily injury or loss of life has no duty to retreat from a threat or summon law enforcement assistance prior to using force. The provisions of this section apply to a person offering evidence of justifiable use of force under 45-3-102, 45-3-103, or 45-3-104.
Mont. Code § 45-3-102
However, the person is justified in the use of force likely to cause death or serious bodily harm only if the person reasonably believes that the force is necessary to prevent imminent death or serious bodily harm to the person or another or to prevent the commission of a forcible felony.
Mont. Code § 45-3-103(2)
is justified in the use of force likely to cause death or serious bodily harm only if: (a) the entry is made or attempted and the person reasonably believes that the force is necessary to prevent an assault upon the person or another then in the occupied structure; or (b) the person reasonably believes that the force is necessary to prevent the commission of a forcible felony in the occupied structure.
Mont. Code § 45-3-105
The justification described in 45-3-102 through 45-3-104 is not available to a person who: (1) is attempting to commit, committing, or escaping after the commission of a forcible felony; or (2) purposely or knowingly provokes the use of force against the person, unless ...
Mont. Code § 46-16-131
In a criminal trial, when the defendant has offered evidence of justifiable use of force, the state has the burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant's actions were not justified.
Mont. Code § 27-1-722(1)
A use of force allowable under the provisions of Title 45, chapter 3, part 1, provides immunity to the person using the force from civil damages for injury to any person or property arising from injury to the person, or damage to the property of the person, against whom the force was used.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • Montana Code Annotated § 46-16-131 (En. Ch. 332, L. 2009) and § 27-1-722 (En. Ch. 445, L. 2001) (Justia)

e4f74a01176a0960.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

New Jersey

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

New Jersey's Code of Criminal Justice (N.J.S.A. 2C:3-4) allows deadly force only when the person reasonably believes it is necessary to protect against death or serious bodily harm. It keeps a duty to retreat: deadly force is not justified if the person knows they can avoid the need for it with complete safety by retreating, or by surrendering property to someone claiming a right to it, or by complying with a demand to stop doing something they have no duty to do. The duty does not apply in one's own dwelling, unless the person was the initial aggressor; it does apply in vehicles, workplaces and public places. The model jury charge tells jurors to judge whether a safe retreat was known by the total circumstances, including the excitement of the moment. A separate rule for intruders in a dwelling (added 1987, amended 1999, L.1999, c.73) lets the occupant use force or deadly force when they reasonably believe it is immediately necessary against an intruder's unlawful force. The State must disprove self-defence beyond a reasonable doubt, and a valid claim fully exonerates the defendant of offences against the aggressor (State v. Rodriguez, 195 N.J. 165 (2008), cited in the charge). Deadly force is not justified for someone who provoked the use of force against themselves in the same encounter with the purpose of causing death or serious harm. No statutory presumption of reasonable fear, civil immunity provision or pretrial immunity hearing was found in the sources checked.

At home

A person is not obliged to retreat from their own dwelling (which the model jury charge says includes the porch) unless they were the initial aggressor (N.J.S.A. 2C:3-4b(2)(b)(i)). Under a 1987 amendment (L.1987, c.120), force or deadly force against an intruder who is unlawfully in a dwelling is justifiable when the occupant reasonably believes it is immediately necessary to protect themselves or others in the dwelling from unlawful force by the intruder (2C:3-4c).

The actor is not obliged to retreat from his dwelling, unless he was the initial aggressor
N.J.S.A. 2C:3-4c(1) (intruder in dwelling; L.1987, c.120)
...the use of force or deadly force upon or toward an intruder who is unlawfully in a dwelling is justifiable ...
Model Criminal Jury Charge, Justification - Self Defense in Self Protection (rev. 8/18/25)
If you find that the defendant knew that they could avoid the necessity of using deadly force by retreating, provided that the defendant knew they could do so with complete safety, then the defense is not applicable to them.
Model Criminal Jury Charge, Justification - Use of Force upon an Intruder (2C:3-4c)
The law exonerates a defendant who uses force (or deadly force) upon or toward an intruder who is unlawfully in a dwelling when the defendant reasonably believes that the force is immediately necessary for the purpose of protecting himself/herself or other person(s) in the dwelling against the use of unlawful force by the intruder on the present occasion.

North Macedonia

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Article 9 of North Macedonia's Criminal Code says an act committed in necessary defence is not a crime, where the defence is 'absolutely necessary' for the person to repel a simultaneous unlawful attack on themselves or another. The code does not mention retreat or the home, and no Macedonian court decision or commentary on whether a person must retreat was found. A person who exceeds the limits of necessary defence may be punished more leniently, or released from punishment if the excess came from strong irritation or fear caused by the attack. A working draft of a new Criminal Code has been circulated for comment on the government's ENER portal; it was not checked here.

What the law says

(1) Не е кривично дело она дело што е сторено во нужна одбрана. (2) Нужна е онаа одбрана што е неопходно потребна сторителот да одбие од себе или од друг, истовремен противправен напад. (3) Сторителот кој ги пречекорил границите на нужната одбрана може да се казни поблаго, а ако пречекорувањето го сторил поради силна раздразнетост или уплав предизвикан со нападот, може и да се ослободи од казна.

(2) Self-defense is that defense, which is necessary for the offender to avert a simultaneous unlawful attack upon himself or upon another. (3) The offender who has exceeded the limits of self-defense may be punished more leniently, and if the exceeding was done because of a strong irritation or fear caused by the attack, he may be acquitted from punishment.

1a86a5eb7dbe13e6.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Arkansas

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Arkansas allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes the other person is committing or about to commit a felony involving force or violence, is using or about to use unlawful deadly force, or is imminently endangering the person's life as part of a continuing pattern of domestic abuse (Ark. Code § 5-2-607(a)). Until 2021 Arkansas had a duty to retreat outside the home: deadly force was not allowed if the person knew they could avoid it by retreating with complete safety, unless they were in their dwelling or its curtilage and not the original aggressor. Act 250 of 2021 (Senate Bill 24) struck that rule and replaced it with a rule that a person is not required to retreat before using deadly force if they are lawfully present, reasonably believe the other person is imminently threatening death or serious injury, are not the initial aggressor or provoker, are not a felon illegally carrying the gun used (except at home), and are not engaged in crime or gang activity that gave rise to the need for force. The same Act added a matching no-retreat rule for non-deadly force (§ 5-2-606(c)). Force is not justified for a person who provoked the other with the purpose of injuring or killing them, for an initial aggressor who has not withdrawn in good faith and communicated it, or in a fight by agreement (§ 5-2-606(b)). In the home, a 1981 statute presumes any force used against an unlawful intruder was lawful and necessary unless the prosecution or plaintiff overcomes it by clear and convincing evidence (§ 5-2-620). The sources consulted show no statutory immunity from prosecution or pretrial immunity hearing in Arkansas.

At home

Ark. Code § 5-2-620 (Acts 1981, No. 880) declares the right to defend oneself, others and property in the home against a person unlawfully entering or trying to enter a 'fundamental right', and creates a legal presumption that any force used for that purpose was lawful and necessary unless overcome by clear and convincing evidence. Before 2021, the dwelling and its curtilage were the main exception to Arkansas's duty to retreat; a felon in possession of a firearm keeps the no-retreat protection only in or at their own dwelling or curtilage (§ 5-2-607(b)(4) as amended 2021).

What the law says
Ark. Code § 5-2-607(b) (as amended by Act 250 of 2021)
A person is not required to retreat before using deadly physical force if the person: (1) Is lawfully present at the location where deadly physical force is used; (2) Has a reasonable belief that the person against whom the deadly physical force is used is imminently threatening to cause death or serious physical injury to the person or another person; (3) Except as provided under § 5-2-606(b)(2)(B), is not the initial aggressor and has not provoked the person against whom the deadly physical force is used; ... (5) Is not engaged in criminal activity that gives rise to the need for the use of deadly physical force at the time the deadly physical force is used; and (6) Is not engaged in any activity in furtherance of a criminal gang, organization, or enterprise ...
Ark. Code § 5-2-607(a)
A person is justified in using deadly physical force upon another person if the person reasonably believes that the other person is: (1) Committing or about to commit a felony involving physical force or violence; (2) Using or about to use unlawful deadly physical force; or (3) Imminently endangering the person's life or imminently about to victimize the person as described in § 9-15-103 from the continuation of a pattern of domestic abuse.
Ark. Code § 5-2-606(b)
A person is not justified in using physical force upon another person if: (1) With purpose to cause physical injury or death to the other person, the person provokes the use of unlawful physical force by the other person; (2)(A) The person is the initial aggressor. ... (3) The physical force involved is the product of a combat by agreement not authorized by law.
Ark. Code § 5-2-620(b)
There is a legal presumption that any force or means used to accomplish a purpose described in subsection (a) of this section was exercised in a lawful and necessary manner, unless the presumption is overcome by clear and convincing evidence to the contrary.

4b529f2b301e42d4.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Tennessee

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Tennessee's self-defence statute (Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-11-611) says that a person who is not engaged in conduct that would be a felony or Class A misdemeanor, and is in a place where they have a right to be, has no duty to retreat before threatening or using force, including force likely to cause death or serious bodily injury, if they reasonably believe there is imminent danger of death or serious bodily injury, the danger is real or honestly believed, and the belief is founded on reasonable grounds. The no-retreat rule therefore applies in public, at work and in vehicles. A rebuttable presumption of reasonable fear applies when deadly force is used against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering a residence, business, dwelling or vehicle (§ 39-11-611(c)). In State v. Perrier (2017) the Supreme Court held that the 'not engaged in unlawful activity' wording then in the statute was a condition on the no-retreat privilege, that the trial judge decides whether it applies, and that a person engaged in unlawful activity must retreat; the current text now refers to conduct constituting a felony or Class A misdemeanor. Self-defence is not available to someone who provoked the other's use of unlawful force, unless they abandon the encounter or clearly communicate an intent to do so (§ 39-11-611(e)). A person whose use of force is justified is immune from civil liability (§ 39-11-622), and a separate law (§ 39-17-1322) limits arrest for justified use of a weapon, but no general criminal immunity or pretrial immunity hearing was found. In 2026, Public Chapter 1100 widened deadly force to protect property against arson, burglary, robbery and aggravated animal cruelty.

At home

A person using deadly force within a residence, business, dwelling or vehicle is presumed to have held a reasonable belief of imminent death or serious bodily injury when the person against whom force was used was unlawfully and forcibly entering or had entered (Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-11-611(c)). Public Chapter 1100 of 2026 (in force 1 July 2026) amended § 39-11-614 to allow deadly force in defence of property against arson, burglary, robbery, aggravated robbery and aggravated cruelty to animals, for people in a place where they lawfully reside and not engaged in a felony or Class A misdemeanor.

The official Tennessee Code (LexisNexis) could not be opened; statute quotes are short verbatim excerpts obtained through a summarising fetch tool, with bracketed words as connectors. The year the no-retreat rule was first enacted (commonly given as 2007) was not confirmed from a primary source.

Notwithstanding § 39-17-1322, a person who is not engaged in conduct ... [that would constitute] a felony or Class A misdemeanor and is in a place where the person has a right to be ... has no duty to retreat before threatening or using force intended or likely to cause death ...
Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-11-611(c) (presumption)
Any person using force intended or likely to cause death or serious bodily injury within a residence ...
State v. Perrier, 536 S.W.3d 388 (Tenn. 2017) (leading case)
... a person who is not engaged in unlawful activity … has no duty to retreat before threatening or using force against another person[.] ... [The Court held a defendant is entitled to a no-retreat instruction] only when the person was not engaged in unlawful activity and was in a place the person had a right to be.
Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-11-622(a) (civil immunity)
is justified in using such force and is immune from civil liability for the use of such force, unless:

ea5a5b2ac0bddfc2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Oklahoma

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Oklahoma's self-defence law is in statute (21 O.S. § 1289.25). A person who is not engaged in an unlawful activity and is attacked in any place where they have a right to be has no duty to retreat and may meet force with force, including deadly force, if they reasonably believe it necessary to prevent death or great bodily harm to themselves or another, or to prevent a forcible felony (subsection D). Inside a dwelling, residence, occupied vehicle, place of business or place of worship, a person using deadly force against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering is presumed to have acted from reasonable fear; the presumption does not apply against a lawful resident without a protective order, against a parent or guardian taking their own child, or if the defender is engaged in unlawful activity. A person who uses force as the section permits 'is justified' and 'immune from criminal prosecution and civil action', which includes being charged; police may not arrest without probable cause that the force was unlawful, and a court must award fees and lost income to a defendant found immune in a civil suit. The Court of Criminal Appeals allows a pretrial immunity hearing at which the defendant must prove justification by a preponderance of the evidence (State v. Bradford, 2024 OK CR 3, affirming a grant of immunity). In Dawkins v. State (2011 OK CR 1) the court held the 'unlawful activity' bar covers people actively committing a crime at the time (for example using an illegal weapon or an ongoing assault), not people with minor past infractions. Pointing a weapon to deter a forcible felony is not a crime under the section. The stand-your-ground jury instruction (OUJI-CR 8-15A) is used for attacks outside a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle.

At home

21 O.S. § 1289.25 (the 'Physical or Deadly Force Against Intruder' law) declares that citizens have a right to expect absolute safety in their homes, places of business and places of worship. A person is presumed to have held reasonable fear of death or great bodily harm when using deadly force against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering (or who has entered) a dwelling, residence, occupied vehicle, place of business or place of worship, or trying to remove someone from it; the intruder is presumed to intend violence. 'Dwelling' includes an attached porch and tents.

Statute text was read from a 2023 bill that reprints § 1289.25 with proposed amendments (committee bold not visible in extracted text); the quoted subsections D and F match the wording cited in OUJI-CR 8-15A and the 2024 OCCA opinion. Year of original enactment of subsection D was not confirmed from a primary source.

What the law says
21 O.S. § 1289.25(D)
A person who is not engaged in an unlawful activity and who is attacked in any other place where he or she has a right to be has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his or her ground and meet force with force, including deadly force, if he or she reasonably believes it is necessary to do so to prevent death or great bodily harm to himself or herself or another or to prevent the commission of a forcible felony.
21 O.S. § 1289.25(F) (immunity)
A person who uses defensive force, as permitted pursuant to the provisions of subsections A, B, D and E of this section, is justified in using such defensive force and is immune from criminal prosecution and civil action for the use of such defensive force. As used in this subsection, the term "criminal prosecution" includes charging or prosecuting the defendant.
21 O.S. § 1289.25(A)
The Legislature hereby recognizes that the citizens of the State of Oklahoma have a right to expect absolute safety within their own homes, places of business or places of worship ...
OUJI-CR 8-15A, Defense of Person - Right to Stand Your Ground
A person has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his/her ground and meet force with force, including deadly force, if he/she is not engaged in an unlawful activity and is attacked in any place where he/she has a right to be ...
State v. Bradford, 2024 OK CR 3 (pretrial immunity)
... whether the trial court committed error in an abuse of discretion in finding that the Appellee seeking pre-trial immunity proved by a preponderance of the evidence that his use of deadly force was legally justified ... We affirm the trial court's order finding immunity pursuant to Title 21, Section 1289.25(F).

Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Jordan

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Jordan's Penal Code (No. 16 of 1960, as amended to Law 8 of 2011 in the version found) treats as the exercise of a right any act required by a present necessity to repel an unjustified and unprovoked attack on oneself, another person, or property (art. 60). For killing or wounding in defence of oneself or one's honour, article 341 adds that the defence must happen during the attack, the attack must be unjust, and the person attacked must be unable to escape or rid themselves of the attack except by killing, wounding or effective force. At home

Article 342 makes it legitimate defence to kill, wound or use any force to protect life, honour or property against a person who enters or tries to enter a dwelling, by night or by day, by climbing its fence or walls, being in its yard inside the fence without justification, or forcing its entrances or doors by breaking them or using keys or special tools.

9005ea7744a53689.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Djibouti

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Djibouti's Penal Code says a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves, another person or property, they act at the same moment in a way necessary for legitimate defence, unless the means used or the result obtained were disproportionate to the seriousness of the attack. The code does not mention retreat. Defence is presumed when repelling forced or tricked entry into an inhabited place, or against violent robbery. No specific rule on excessive self-defence was found in these articles.

At home

Article 30 presumes legitimate defence for a person who acts to repel entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place (with no night-time condition), or to defend against violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 30
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, face à une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même, autrui ou un bien, accomplit dans le même temps un acte nécessaire à la défense légitime d'elle-même, d'autrui ou du bien, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés ou le résultat obtenu et la gravité de l'atteinte. Est présumé avoir agi en état de défense légitime celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1 ° pour repousser l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité. 2° pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

1e882db485d85857.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bahrain

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Bahrain's Penal Code (Decree-Law No. 15 of 1976) says the right of self-defence arises when a person faces, or reasonably believes they face, imminent danger to their person or property and there is no time to seek the protection of the public authorities (art. 17). No one may inflict more harm than necessary for defence (art. 18). The code does not mention retreat; the stated limits are the time to call the authorities and necessity. Killing is justified only against an act feared to cause death or serious injury, rape or attack on personal freedom, arson, damage or theft, or breaking into an inhabited house (art. 20). Going beyond the limits of a justified act in good faith is an extenuating circumstance, and the judge may exempt the person from punishment (art. 21).

At home

Article 20 allows killing in defence of self or property against, among other acts, 'breaking into an inhabited house or appurtenances thereof'.

What the law says
Penal Code (Decree-Law No. 15 of 1976), arts. 17–18 (official English translation)
Article 17: The right of self-defence commences when the following two factors are present: 1. If the person is in imminent danger of a threat to his own person or property or if he reasonably believes in the imminence of such danger. 2. If there is no time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities. ... Article 18: In the exercise of the right of self-defence, no person may inflict more harm than is necessary for the purpose of defence.
Penal Code (Decree-Law No. 15 of 1976), arts. 20–21
Article 20: Murder in self-defence or in defence of property shall not be justified except in the following cases: 1. An act from which death or serious injury is feared. 2. An act of rape, assault or attack against personal freedom. 3. An act of setting fire, causing damage or theft. 4. An act of breaking into an inhabited house or appurtenances thereof. Article 21: Bypassing the extent of a justified act in good faith shall be deemed as an extenuating circumstance. A judgement for exemption may be passed if the judge finds grounds for such exemption.

7552eeb195e0317c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Guadeloupe

An overseas region of France, part of France itself. Shown with the entry for France, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 122-5 of the Penal Code, a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same time in a way required by the necessity of self-defence, unless the means used are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack. The defence must be simultaneous with the attack; a blow struck after the attacker has left is treated as ordinary violence. Neither art. 122-5 nor art. 122-6 mentions retreat, and the sources opened here did not address whether flight is expected. Defence of property can never justify intentional homicide. Judges decide whether the defence was disproportionate; Encyclopaedia Universalis notes that an excessive response may lead to mitigating circumstances or a conviction for a lesser offence rather than full exoneration.

At home

Art. 122-6 of the Penal Code presumes self-defence for a person who acts "to repel, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place", and against perpetrators of violent theft or looting. The presumption is rebuttable and does not cover daytime intrusions, which fall under the general rule of art. 122-5.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 122-5
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal, art. 122-6
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

a231d91e2575bf9d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Nebraska

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Nebraska's self-defence statute, enacted in 1972 (Laws 1972, LB 895) and modelled on the Model Penal Code, allows deadly force only when the actor believes it is necessary to protect themselves against death, serious bodily harm, kidnapping, or sexual intercourse compelled by force or threat (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-1409(4)). Nebraska keeps a duty to retreat: deadly force is not justified if the actor knows they can avoid it with complete safety by retreating, by handing over a thing to someone claiming a right to it, or by complying with a demand to refrain from something they have no duty to do (§ 28-1409(4)(b)). There is no duty to retreat from one's own dwelling or place of work, except for an initial aggressor or a person attacked at work by a co-worker; police and people lawfully helping them need not abandon an arrest. Deadly force is also not justified if the actor, intending to cause death or serious bodily harm, provoked the use of force in the same encounter, and force may not be used to resist a known arrest by a peace officer even if the arrest is unlawful. The Nebraska Supreme Court requires a reasonable and good-faith belief in the need for force, though a defendant may be mistaken about the extent of the danger (State v. Miller, 281 Neb. 343 (2011); State v. Graham, 234 Neb. 275 (1990)); if the belief was reckless or negligent, the justification is unavailable for offences requiring only recklessness or negligence (§ 28-1414(2)). The sources consulted show no stand-your-ground law, no statutory immunity from prosecution or civil suit, and no pretrial immunity hearing.

At home

Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-1409(4)(b)(i): the actor is not obliged to retreat from their dwelling or place of work, unless they were the initial aggressor or are attacked at work by a co-worker (someone whose place of work the actor knows it to be). There is no statutory presumption of reasonable fear for home intrusions.

What the law says
Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-1409(4)
The use of deadly force shall not be justifiable under this section unless the actor believes that such force is necessary to protect himself against death, serious bodily harm, kidnapping or sexual intercourse compelled by force or threat, nor is it justifiable if: (a) The actor, with the purpose of causing death or serious bodily harm, provoked the use of force against himself in the same encounter; or (b) The actor knows that he can avoid the necessity of using such force with complete safety by retreating or by surrendering possession of a thing to a person asserting a claim of right thereto or by complying with a demand that he abstain from any action which he has no duty to take, except that: (i) The actor shall not be obliged to retreat from his dwelling or place of work, unless he was the initial aggressor or is assailed in his place of work by another person whose place of work the actor knows it to be ...
Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-1414(2)
When the actor believes that the use of force upon or toward the person of another is necessary ... but the actor is reckless or negligent in having such belief ..., the justification afforded by those sections is unavailable in a prosecution for an offense for which recklessness or negligence, as the case may be, suffices to establish culpability.
State v. Miller, 281 Neb. 343 (2011) (annotation to § 28-1409)
A defendant's use of deadly force in self-defense is justified if a reasonable ground existed under the circumstances for the defendant's belief that he or she was threatened with death or serious bodily harm, even if the defendant was actually mistaken about the extent of the danger.

fe980bcf84c9674c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Jamaica

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Self-defence in Jamaica is common law, set out by the Privy Council in two Jamaican appeals: Palmer v R (1971) and Beckford v R (1987). A person may use such force as is reasonable in the circumstances as they honestly believe them to be, may strike first if an attack is imminent, and the prosecution must disprove self-defence once it is raised. The judges' Criminal Bench Book says there is no general duty to retreat; whether the accused could have retreated is only one factor the jury may weigh in deciding whether the force was reasonably necessary. There is no 'excessive self-defence' halfway house: if the force was excessive and the intent for murder is proved, the defence fails completely and the verdict is murder, not manslaughter.

At home

The Supreme Court of Jamaica's Criminal Bench Book states that at common law a householder may use reasonable force in defence of property, citing R v Hussey (1925), where defence of property (unlike self-defence at that time) did not require retreat; there is no statutory castle doctrine in the sources found.

What the law says
Supreme Court of Jamaica, Criminal Bench Book, ch. 18-1 (Self-Defence), para. 3, citing R v Stanley Brooks (1987) 24 JLR 166 and R v Garnett Shand SCCA 2/93
There is now no general duty to retreat in all cases where self-defence is raised. The question whether the accused's retreat is an element which the jury may consider in deciding whether the force was reasonably necessary.
Criminal Bench Book, ch. 18-1, para. 4 (excessive force), citing R v Wayne Campbell and Mark Lahoo SCCA 119/00
Where a person kills another with the requisite intent for murder in circumstances in which he would have been entitled to an acquittal on the ground of self-defence but for the use of excessive force the defence fails altogether and he is guilty of murder not manslaughter.
Beckford v R [1988] AC 130 (PC Jamaica), Lord Griffiths, as quoted in the Criminal Bench Book
the test to be applied for self-defence is that a person may use such force as is reasonable in the circumstances as he honestly believes them to be in the defence of himself or another.

  • Laing (Delroy) v R [2016] JMCA Crim 11 (Court of Appeal of Jamaica)

974e513a1a7477d7.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Palestine

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Palestinian territory has two different penal codes. In Gaza, the British Mandate Criminal Code Ordinance 1936 excuses an act done 'only in order to avoid consequences which could not otherwise be avoided' and which would have caused grievous harm to the person, honour or property of oneself or others one must protect, provided the person did no more than reasonably necessary and the harm caused was not disproportionate (s. 18). In the West Bank, the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960 applies; in the Jordanian text opened, killing or wounding in defence of oneself, one's honour or another person is legitimate only if done during the attack, the attack is unjust, and the person 'is unable to rid himself of this attack except by killing, wounding or the effective act' (art. 341(1)), and excess in defence may lead to exemption from punishment under the conditions of art. 89 (art. 60(3)). Both texts therefore make the defence depend on there being no other way out. The Jordanian copy opened is Jordan's own text amended to 2011; the West Bank applies the 1960 code without Jordan's post-1967 amendments, so the exact West Bank wording could not be confirmed. No court decisions on retreat were found for either territory.

At home

In the Jordanian Penal Code text opened (art. 342), killing or wounding to protect life, honour or property against a person entering or trying to enter a dwelling by night or day, by climbing a fence or wall, being in its yard without reason, or forcing doors or using keys or tools, counts as legitimate defence. Whether this wording is the version in force in the West Bank could not be confirmed (see summary). No home rule was found in the Gaza code text.

What the law says
Criminal Code Ordinance 1936 (Gaza), s. 18
An act or omission which would otherwise be an offence may be excused if the person accused can show that it was done or omitted to be done only in order to avoid consequences which could not otherwise be avoided, and which if they had followed would have inflicted grievous harm or injury to his person or to his honour or his property or to the person or honour of others whom he was bound to protect or to property placed in his charge: Provided that in so acting he did no more than was reasonably necessary for that purpose, and that the harm inflicted by the act or omission was not disproportionate to the harm avoided.
Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960 (applied in the West Bank), art. 341(1) – text as in Jordan's 2011-amended edition
تعد الأفعال الآتية دفاعا ً مشروعاً: 1 فعل من يقتل غيره او يصيبه بجراح او بأي فعل مؤثر دفاعا ً عن نفسه او عرضه او نفس غيره او عرضه ،بشرط أن: أ -يقع الدفع حال وقوع الاعتداء. ب -أن يكون الاعتداء غير محق. ج -أن لا يكون في استطاعة المعتدى عليه التخلص من هذا الاعتداء الا بالقتل او الجرح او الفعل المؤثر.
Jordanian Penal Code 1960, art. 60 (Jordan's 2011-amended edition)
1 يعد ممارسة للحق: كل فعل قضت به ضرورة حالية لدفع تعرض غير محق ولا مثار عن النفس أو المال أو نفس الغير أو ماله. 2 يستوي في الحماية الشخص الطبيعي والشخص المعنوي. 3 اذا وقع تجاوز في الدفاع أمكن إعفاء فاعل الجريمة من العقوبة في الشروط المذكورة في المادة 89.

4062acebad23962d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Brunei

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Brunei's Penal Code (Chapter 22, 2021 edition) contains a 'right of private defence' chapter. Deadly force in defence of the body is allowed against an assault reasonably causing fear of death or grievous hurt, and against assaults intended to rape, kidnap, abduct or wrongfully confine (s 100). The right never extends to more harm than necessary for defence, and there is no right where there is time to seek protection from the public authorities (s 99). The code does not mention retreat and no Brunei court decision on retreat was opened. A person who in good faith exceeds the right of private defence and kills without premeditation commits culpable homicide, not murder (Exception 2 to murder).

At home

s 103: the right of private defence of property extends to causing death against robbery, house-breaking by night, arson of a building, tent or vessel used as a human dwelling, and theft, mischief or house-trespass that reasonably causes fear of death or grievous hurt.

What the law says
Penal Code (Cap. 22), s 99(3)–(4) [official PDF is an OCR scan; s 99(3) is garbled in the text layer and is given here as printed in the scan's readable form]
(3) There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities. (4) The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence.
Penal Code (Cap. 22), s 100
The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions mentioned in section 99, to the voluntary causing of death, or of any other harm, to the assailant if the offence which occasions the exercise of the right is of any of the following descriptions - (a) such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that death will otherwise be the consequence of the assault; (b) such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of the assault; (c) an assault with the intention of committing rape; ...
Penal Code (Cap. 22), murder, Exception 2
Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law, and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation, and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.

02f95fbf5c6b15af.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Alabama

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Alabama allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes another is using or about to use unlawful deadly force, or is committing or about to commit kidnapping, first- or second-degree assault, burglary, robbery, forcible rape or forcible sodomy, and in those listed situations the law presumes the force was justified (Ala. Code § 13A-3-23(b)). A person who is justified, not engaged in unlawful activity, and in any place they have a right to be has no duty to retreat and may stand their ground (§ 13A-3-23(c)); this rule was added by Act 2006-303, and the statute was amended again in 2013, 2016 and 2023. The home, workplace and car are covered by a presumption: deadly force is presumed justified against someone unlawfully and forcefully entering a dwelling, residence, business property or occupied vehicle, and since Act 2023-493 also against someone attacking a person on business property while the business is closed. Force is not justified for someone who provoked the attack intending to hurt the other person, for an initial aggressor who has not withdrawn and clearly communicated it, or in a fight by mutual agreement. A person who used justified force is immune from both criminal prosecution and civil suit, and the defendant may ask for a pretrial hearing where they must prove immunity by a preponderance of the evidence; if they fail, they can still argue self-defence at trial, where the state must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Since 2023, if the defendant hid, altered or destroyed the weapon (rather than handing it unaltered to police without undue delay), the law presumes the force was not justified, though this can be rebutted. Police may investigate but may not arrest without probable cause that the force was unlawful.

At home

Ala. Code § 13A-3-23(b)(1): deadly force is legally presumed justified against a person who is unlawfully and forcefully entering (or has entered) a dwelling, residence, business property or occupied vehicle, or is trying to remove someone from one, or is using force against an occupant while committing a burglary of a dwelling. The presumption does not apply against another lawful resident (unless there is a domestic-violence protective order or no-contact order), a parent or guardian taking their own child, an on-duty police officer, or where the defender is engaged in unlawful activity.

What the law says
Ala. Code § 13A-3-23(c)
A person who is otherwise justified under this section in using physical force, including deadly physical force, and who is not engaged in an unlawful activity, and who is in any place where he or she has the right to be has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his or her ground.
Ala. Code § 13A-3-23(b)(1)
A person may use deadly physical force, and is legally presumed to be justified in using deadly physical force in self-defense or defense of another pursuant to this subdivision, if the person reasonably believes that another person is doing any of the following: a. Using or about to use unlawful deadly physical force. ...
Ala. Code § 13A-3-23(d)
a person is not justified in using physical force if any of the following apply: (1) With intent to cause physical injury or death to another, he or she provoked the use of unlawful physical force by the other person. (2) He or she was the initial aggressor, except that his or her use of physical force upon another person is justifiable if he or she withdraws from the encounter and effectively communicates to the other person his or her intent to do so ... (3) The physical force involved was the product of a combat by agreement not specifically authorized by law.
Ala. Code § 13A-3-23(f)(1)–(2)
A person who uses force, including deadly physical force, as justified and permitted in this section, is immune from criminal prosecution and civil action for the use of such force, unless the force was determined to be unlawful. ... During any pretrial hearing to determine immunity, the defendant must show by a preponderance of the evidence that he or she is immune from criminal prosecution.

193e1f88e5a6ed5c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Arizona

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Arizona allows deadly force when a reasonable person would believe it is immediately necessary to protect against another's use or attempted use of unlawful deadly force (Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-405(A)), and also to prevent a list of serious crimes including arson of an occupied structure, first- or second-degree burglary, kidnapping, murder, manslaughter, sexual assault, child molestation, armed robbery and certain aggravated assaults (§ 13-411). There is no duty to retreat if the person is in a place where they may legally be and is not engaged in an unlawful act (§ 13-405(B)); the crime-prevention section adds that this covers a home, business, land, vehicle 'or any other place in this state where a person has a right to be', and presumes a person acting to prevent one of the listed crimes is acting reasonably. The current wording of § 13-405 including subsection B was enacted by House Bill 2629, signed 11 May 2010. In a home or occupied vehicle, the law presumes the defender reasonably believed force was necessary and that an unlawful intruder posed a deadly threat (§ 13-419). Force is not justified in response to words alone, to resist a known arrest by police (unless the officer uses unlawful force), or by a person who provoked the fight, unless they withdrew or clearly signalled withdrawal and the other person kept attacking (§ 13-404(B)). Self-defence is not an affirmative defence in Arizona: once the defendant presents evidence of justification, the state must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant did not act with justification (§ 13-205); Arizona has no statutory pretrial immunity hearing. In civil suits by a plaintiff harmed while committing a felony, a person who used force to protect themselves or others is presumed to have acted reasonably (§ 12-716).

At home

Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-418 allows physical or deadly force, with no duty to retreat, against a person unlawfully or forcefully entering (or who has entered) a residential structure or occupied vehicle, or removing someone from it, if the defender reasonably believes someone is in imminent peril of death or serious injury. § 13-419 presumes the defender's belief was reasonable and presumes the intruder poses an imminent threat of deadly harm, except against a lawful resident with no protective order, a parent or guardian taking their own child, an on-duty police officer, or where the defender is engaged in unlawful activity.

What the law says
Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-405
A. A person is justified in threatening or using deadly physical force against another: 1. If such person would be justified in threatening or using physical force against the other under section 13-404, and 2. When and to the degree a reasonable person would believe that deadly physical force is immediately necessary to protect himself against the other's use or attempted use of unlawful deadly physical force. B. A person has no duty to retreat before threatening or using deadly physical force pursuant to this section if the person is in a place where the person may legally be and is not engaged in an unlawful act.
Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-411(B)–(D)
B. There is no duty to retreat before threatening or using physical force or deadly physical force justified by subsection A of this section. C. A person is presumed to be acting reasonably for the purposes of this section if the person is acting to prevent what the person reasonably believes is the imminent or actual commission of any of the offenses listed in subsection A of this section. D. This section includes the use or threatened use of physical force or deadly physical force in a person's home, residence, place of business, land the person owns or leases, conveyance of any kind, or any other place in this state where a person has a right to be.
Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-419(A)–(B)
A person is presumed to reasonably believe that the threat or use of physical force or deadly force is immediately necessary ... if the person knows or has reason to believe that the person against whom physical force or deadly force is threatened or used is unlawfully or forcefully entering or has unlawfully or forcefully entered and is present in the person's residential structure or occupied vehicle.
Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-404(B)
The threat or use of physical force against another is not justified: 1. In response to verbal provocation alone; or ... 3. If the person provoked the other's use or attempted use of unlawful physical force, unless: (a) The person withdraws from the encounter or clearly communicates to the other his intent to do so reasonably believing he cannot safely withdraw from the encounter; and (b) The other nevertheless continues or attempts to use unlawful physical force against the person.

Justification defenses under chapter 4 of this title are not affirmative defenses. ... If evidence of justification pursuant to chapter 4 of this title is presented by the defendant, the state must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant did not act with justification.

bcafd513fb4badaf.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

British Indian Ocean Territory

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

The British Indian Ocean Territory has its own Penal Code (1981, revised to 2020). Section 17 says criminal responsibility for force used in defence of person or property is decided by the principles of English common law, subject to any express provisions. Under English law there is no duty to retreat: the possibility that the defender could have retreated is a factor in judging whether the force was reasonable, not a duty, and force that was disproportionate in the circumstances as the defender believed them to be is not reasonable (Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, s. 76, which says it clarifies the existing common-law defences). The Territory has no permanent civilian population.

At home

English law has a separate 'householder case' rule (Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, s. 76(8A) and related subsections) for force used by a non-trespasser inside a dwelling against someone believed to be a trespasser; whether that statutory rule applies in the Territory, as opposed to common-law principles, was not confirmed.

What the law says
BIOT Penal Code 1981 (Ch. C.2, revised edition to 1 September 2020), s. 17
Subject to any express provisions in the Code or any other law in operation in the Territory, criminal responsibility for the use of force in the defence of person or property shall be determined according to the principles of English common law.
Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008 (England and Wales), s. 76(6A) and (9)
(6A) In deciding the question mentioned in subsection (3), a possibility that D could have retreated is to be considered (so far as relevant) as a factor to be taken into account, rather than as giving rise to a duty to retreat. ... (9) This section, except so far as making different provision for householder cases, is intended to clarify the operation of the existing defences mentioned in subsection (2).

af5baeb5882846bd.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Trinidad and Tobago

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Self-defence in Trinidad and Tobago is common law. The Court of Appeal (La Roche v The State, 2011) applies the Privy Council's statement in Palmer v R: a person who reasonably believes their life is in danger or that they face serious bodily harm may use the force they believe on reasonable grounds is necessary, and is not guilty even if they kill intentionally. There is no fixed duty to retreat: the possibility of retreating without danger is one of the circumstances the jury considers when judging whether the force was reasonably necessary. A case cited in Robley v Placide held that no legal duty to retreat arises for a police officer acting in the execution of duty. No statute on home defence and no source on how excessive force is treated were found for this entry.

What the law says
La Roche v The State, Court of Appeal of Trinidad and Tobago, Cr. App. No. 32 of 2009 (20 April 2011), quoting Palmer v R [1971] AC 814 at 823
A man who is attacked in circumstances where he reasonably believes his life to be in danger or that he is in danger of serious bodily harm, may use such force as on reasonable grounds he believes is necessary to prevent and resist the attack and if in using such force he kills his assailant he is not guilty of any crime even if the killing was intentional, and in deciding in a particular case whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as in fact was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything that he is entitled to protect.
Robley v Placide (Trinidad and Tobago), citing a 1966 decision reported at 11 W.I.R. 58
no legal duty to retreat could arise in circumstances where a police officer acted in exec[ution of his duty]
