c6a5d0bc53a844fd.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Pennsylvania

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Pennsylvania's no-retreat rule is partial. The Crimes Code allows deadly force when a person believes it immediately necessary to protect against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping or forcible sexual intercourse, but keeps the older rule that deadly force is not justified if the person knows they can avoid it with complete safety by retreating, except from their dwelling or place of work (18 Pa.C.S. § 505(b)(2)). Act 10 of 2011 (signed 28 June 2011) added that outside the home a person has no duty to retreat and may 'stand his ground' only if they are not engaged in criminal activity, are not illegally possessing a firearm, have a right to be where they were attacked, and the attacker displays or uses a firearm, replica firearm or other weapon capable of lethal use (§ 505(b)(2.3)); if the attacker is unarmed, the retreat duty still applies in public places and vehicles. The same law created a rebuttable presumption of reasonable belief when deadly force is used against someone unlawfully and forcefully entering a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle; it does not apply against a lawful resident, a parent taking their own child, a peace officer known to be one, or a defender engaged in criminal activity. Deadly force is not justified for someone who, intending to cause death or serious injury, provoked the use of force in the same encounter. A person who uses force justified under §§ 505 to 509 is immune from civil liability for the perpetrator's injuries, and a court must award fees and costs if a perpetrator's suit fails (42 Pa.C.S. § 8340.2, 2011). No statutory pretrial criminal immunity hearing was found.

At home

No duty to retreat from one's dwelling or place of work unless the person was the initial aggressor (or, at work, is attacked by a co-worker in their shared workplace) (18 Pa.C.S. § 505(b)(2)(ii)). Since 2011 a person is presumed to reasonably believe deadly force is necessary against someone unlawfully and forcefully entering, or present after forcibly entering, a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle, or trying to drag someone out (§ 505(b)(2.1)); the intruder is presumed to intend death, serious injury, kidnapping or rape (§ 505(b)(2.5)).

Category 'statute' reflects the 2011 stand-your-ground provision, but it applies only when the attacker displays or uses a firearm or other lethal weapon; otherwise a duty to retreat (outside home and workplace) remains.

What the law says
18 Pa.C.S. § 505(b)(2)(ii) (retreat)
the actor knows that he can avoid the necessity of using such force with complete safety by retreating, except the actor is not obliged to retreat from his dwelling or place of work, unless he was the initial aggressor or is assailed in his place of work by another person whose place of work the actor knows it to be.
18 Pa.C.S. § 505(b)(2.3) (Act 10 of 2011)
An actor who is not engaged in a criminal activity, who is not in illegal possession of a firearm and who is attacked in any place where the actor would have a duty to retreat under paragraph (2)(ii) has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his ground and use force, including deadly force, if: (i) the actor has a right to be in the place where he was attacked; (ii) the actor believes it is immediately necessary to do so to protect himself against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping or sexual intercourse by force or threat; and (iii) the person against whom the force is used displays or otherwise uses: (A) a firearm or replica of a firearm ...; or (B) any other weapon readily or apparently capable of lethal use.
18 Pa.C.S. § 505(b)(2.1) (presumption)
... an actor is presumed to have a reasonable belief that deadly force is immediately necessary to protect himself against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping or sexual intercourse compelled by force or threat if both of the following conditions exist: (i) The person against whom the force is used is in the process of unlawfully and forcefully entering, or has unlawfully and forcefully entered and is present within, a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle ...
42 Pa.C.S. § 8340.2(a) (civil immunity)
... is justified in using such force and shall be immune from civil liability for personal injuries sustained by a perpetrator which were caused by the acts or omissions of the actor as a result of the use of force.

  • 42 Pa.C.S. § 8340.2 Civil immunity for use of force (Pennsylvania General Assembly)

019f596245bff81a.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

South Dakota

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

South Dakota rewrote its self-defence law in 2021 (SL 2021, ch 93), repealing the older justifiable-homicide sections (22-16-34 and 22-16-35) and replacing them with a new set of statutes; a 2006 amendment had already added no-retreat language to the defence-of-person section. A person may use or threaten deadly force if they reasonably believe it necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to themselves or another, or a forcible felony, and has no duty to retreat and may stand their ground if they are not engaged in criminal activity and are in a place where they have a right to be (SDCL 22-18-4.1). In a dwelling or residence there is no duty to retreat, and a presumption of reasonable fear applies against someone unlawfully entering or inside a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle (22-18-4.2, 4.3). Deadly force to protect property other than a dwelling is allowed only to prevent a forcible felony (22-18-4.7). The justification is not available to someone committing or escaping from a forcible felony, or to someone who provoked the force, unless they then faced deadly danger and had exhausted every reasonable means of escape, or withdrew in good faith and clearly said so (22-18-4.9). A person who used force as permitted is immune from criminal prosecution (which includes arrest, detention and charging) and from civil suits by the attacker or their heirs, and courts must award fees and lost income to a defendant found immune (22-18-4.8). Since a 2022 amendment, once the defendant raises a prima facie claim of immunity, the prosecution must overcome it by clear and convincing evidence.

At home

A person in a dwelling or residence where they have a right to be has no duty to retreat, may stand their ground, and may use deadly force if they reasonably believe it necessary to prevent imminent death, great bodily harm or a forcible felony (SDCL 22-18-4.2, 2021). They are presumed to have held reasonable fear when using deadly force against someone unlawfully entering or inside a dwelling, residence or occupied vehicle, or dragging someone out (22-18-4.3).

What the law says
SDCL 22-18-4.1 (SL 2021, ch 93, § 3)
A person who uses or threatens to use deadly force in accordance with this section does not have a duty to retreat and has the right to stand his or her ground, if the person using or threatening to use the deadly force is: (1) Not engaged in a criminal activity; and (2) In a place where the person has a right to be.
SDCL 22-18-4.2 (dwelling)
A person who is in a dwelling or residence, in which the person has a right to be: (1) Has no duty to retreat; (2) Has the right to stand his or her ground; and (3) Has the right to use or threaten to use: ... (b) Deadly force, if the person reasonably believes that using or threatening to use deadly force is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to himself, herself, or another, or to prevent the imminent commission of a forcible felony.
SDCL 22-18-4.3 (presumption)
For purposes of § 22-18-4.2, a person is presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or great bodily harm, to himself, herself, or another, when using or threatening to use defensive force that is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm if: (1) The person against whom the defensive force was used or threatened: (a) Was in the process of unlawfully entering a dwelling, residence, or occupied vehicle ...
SDCL 22-18-4.8 (immunity; amended 2022)
In a criminal prosecution, once a prima facie claim of self-defense immunity has been raised by the defendant, the burden of proof, by clear and convincing evidence, is on the party seeking to overcome the immunity from criminal prosecution ...
SDCL 22-18-4.9 (aggressor)
Any justification for the use or the threatened use of either force or deadly force is not available to a person who: (1) Is attempting to commit, committing, or escaping after the commission of a forcible felony; or (2) Initially provokes the use or threatened use of force against himself or herself, unless: ...

7aaf8acb0f0ab1cb.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

New Hampshire

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

New Hampshire's Criminal Code allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes another is about to use unlawful deadly force against them or a third person, or is likely to use unlawful force during a burglary, or is committing a kidnapping or forcible sex offence, or a felony inside the defender's dwelling or curtilage (RSA 627:4, II). The general rule still says deadly force is not justified if the person knows they and any third person can retreat with complete safety, but a 2011 amendment (SB 88, chapter 268) added that there is no duty to retreat within the dwelling, its curtilage, or anywhere the person has a right to be, provided they were not the initial aggressor. Deadly force is also not justified if the person could safely surrender property to someone asserting a claim to it, or could comply with a demand to refrain from an act they are not obliged to do. A person who provoked the use of deadly force with the purpose of causing death or serious bodily injury, or who was the initial aggressor, loses the justification (an initial aggressor can regain it only by withdrawing and clearly communicating that). Displaying a firearm or other means of self-defence to warn off a threat is not a criminal act (RSA 627:4, II-a). The 2011 law also gave civil immunity: a person who used force justified under the code is immune from civil liability for injuries to the perpetrator (RSA 627:1-a). New Hampshire has no statutory pretrial immunity hearing; justification is raised at trial. No statutory presumption of reasonable fear was found.

At home

Deadly force is allowed against a person likely to use any unlawful force in committing a felony against the defender within the defender's dwelling or its curtilage (RSA 627:4, II(d)); a 2026 act (2026, 323:1, effective 1 January 2027) extends this to a third person. There is no duty to retreat within the dwelling or curtilage. Deadly force is also allowed against someone likely to use unlawful force against a person present during a burglary (II(b)).

Official site was read through a summarising fetch tool that only returns short verbatim excerpts; quotes are assembled from those excerpts. Words in square brackets are paraphrase.

What the law says
RSA 627:4, II (lead-in)
A person is justified in using deadly force upon another person when he reasonably believes that such other person:
RSA 627:4, III(a) (retreat; amended 2011)
...if he or she knows that he or she and the third person can, with complete safety: (a) Retreat from the encounter, except that he or she is not required to retreat if he or she is within his or her dwelling, its curtilage, or anywhere he or she has a right to be [and was not the initial aggressor]
RSA 627:4, II(d) (version in force until 1 Jan 2027)
Is likely to use any unlawful force in the commission of a felony against the actor within such actor's dwelling ...
RSA 627:1-a (civil immunity; 2011, 268:3)
...shall be immune from civil liability for personal injuries sustained by a perpetrator which were caused by the acts or omissions of the person as a result of the use of force.

No text or court decision was found that says whether a person must retreat, so the retreat question is not settled by the sources found. No rule on defence of the home or on excessive self-defence was found in the sources opened.

There is neither crime nor misdemeanour, where homicide, wounds or blows are commanded by an actual necessity of the lawful defence of oneself or of another person.

A person shall, not be regarded as having been deprived of his life in contravention of this section, if he dies as the result of the use, to such extent and in such circumstances as are permitted by law, of such force as is reasonably justifiable - (a) for the defence of any person from violence or for the defence of property;

52129c3e04ba6df0.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Rhode Island

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Rhode Island has no stand-your-ground law; its rules on deadly force come mainly from Supreme Court decisions. A person may use deadly force only when they reasonably believe it necessary to avoid death or great bodily harm, and outside the home they must retreat or attempt to retreat when they actually and reasonably believe a safe retreat is available (State v. Guillemet, State v. Fetzik, and more recently State v. Garrett, 2014, and State v. Guerrero, 2019, as cited by the Giffords Law Center). There is no exception for vehicles, workplaces or public places. In the home, a person attacked by a trespasser has no duty to retreat, including where the attacker first came in as a social guest (State v. Ordway; State v. Walton, 1992), but a person attacked by someone who lives in the same home must retreat if they know of a safe way out (State v. Quarles, 1986). By statute (§ 11-8-8), when a burglar or intruder is killed or hurt during a burglary or breaking and entering, the occupant is presumed in civil and criminal proceedings to have acted reasonably in self-defence and has no duty to retreat from them. Rhode Island has no official pattern criminal jury instructions; the instruction summarised here comes from an Attorney General series last updated around 2000. No civil immunity provision beyond the § 11-8-8 presumption, and no pretrial immunity hearing, was found.

At home

R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-8-8 (1976, amended 1977 and 1984): if a burglar or housebreaker is killed or injured while committing a burglary or breaking-and-entering offence (§§ 11-8-2 to 11-8-6), the owner, tenant or occupier is rebuttably presumed, in civil and criminal proceedings, to have acted by reasonable means in self-defence, and has no duty to retreat from that person. Case law (State v. Ordway; State v. Walton) also frees an occupant attacked by a trespasser in the home from retreating, but an occupant attacked by a co-occupant must retreat if aware of a safe avenue (State v. Quarles).

Case quotes were read through a summarising fetch tool limited to short excerpts; the cases themselves were not opened.

What the law says
R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-8-8 (P.L. 1976, ch. 216; 1977, ch. 17; 1984, ch. 212)
... it shall be rebuttably presumed as a matter of law in any civil or criminal proceeding that the owner, tenant, or occupier of the place where the offense was committed acted by reasonable means in self-defense and in the reasonable belief that the person engaged in the criminal offense was about to inflict great bodily harm or death upon that person or any other individual lawfully in the place where the criminal offense was committed. There shall be no duty on the part of an owner, tenant, or occupier to retreat from any person engaged in the commission of any criminal offense enumerated in §§ 11-8-2 — 11-8-6.
Rhode Island Attorney General model instruction X.L, Self-Defense (citing State v. Martinez, State v. Fetzik, State v. Guillemet)
The law requires a person to retreat or attempt to retreat when he or she actually and reasonably believes ...
Same instruction (citing State v. Quarles, 1986) – co-occupant
The person attacked is obligated to attempt retreat if he or she is aware of a safe available avenue of retreat

19fffe7194282699.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Vermont

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Vermont has no stand-your-ground statute. Its justifiable-homicide law (13 V.S.A. § 2305) says a person who kills or wounds another is 'guiltless' when acting in the just and necessary defence of their own life or another's, or when they reasonably believed that they or another were in imminent peril and deadly force was necessary to repel someone attempting murder, sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, burglary or robbery. The statute does not mention retreat, and it expressly preserves common-law defences (§ 2305(b)). According to the Giffords Law Center, the Vermont Supreme Court in State v. Hatcher, 167 Vt. 338, 348 (1997), held that there is no duty to retreat before using force in public, so the no-retreat rule is judicial. The section was amended in 2021 and 2022 (Acts 2019 No. 165, 2021 No. 27 and 2021 No. 95) mainly to tie police use of force to the standards in 20 V.S.A. § 2368. No statutory presumption of reasonable fear, civil immunity or pretrial immunity hearing was found. The Hatcher opinion itself and Vermont's model jury instruction could not be opened for this entry, so the exact limits (for example on initial aggressors) are not stated here.

At home

13 V.S.A. § 2305(a)(2) makes a killing or wounding guiltless when the person reasonably believed that they or another were in imminent peril and that deadly force was necessary to repel someone attempting murder, sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, burglary or robbery. No separate castle-doctrine presumption was found.

The no-retreat characterisation relies on a secondary source (Giffords) citing State v. Hatcher; the opinion was not opened.

What the law says
13 V.S.A. § 2305(a)
If a person kills or wounds another under any of the circumstances enumerated below, the person shall be guiltless: (1) in the just and necessary defense of the person’s own life or the life of any other person; (2) if the person reasonably believed that the person, or any other person, was in imminent peril and that it was necessary to repel that peril with deadly force in the forceful or violent suppression of a person attempting to commit murder, sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, burglary, or robbery ...
13 V.S.A. § 2305(b)
This section shall not be construed to limit or infringe upon defenses granted at common law.
State v. Hatcher, 167 Vt. 338, 348 (1997) (leading case, as cited by Giffords)
Though Vermont does not have a stand your ground statute, the state supreme court has held that there is no duty to retreat before using force in public. [Giffords summary, citing Hatcher]

5f65281edf5fec36.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

American Samoa

Part of United States, or under it.

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

American Samoa has its own criminal code, enacted in 1979 (PL 16-43) and modelled on Missouri's criminal code (the annotation points to Missouri § 563.031). Under A.S.C.A. § 46.3305 a person may use physical force on another when and to the extent they reasonably believe it necessary to defend against what they reasonably believe is the use or imminent use of unlawful force. Deadly force is allowed only if the person reasonably believes it necessary to protect themselves or another against death, serious physical injury, rape, sodomy or kidnapping. An initial aggressor can claim self-defence only after withdrawing from the encounter and effectively communicating that withdrawal. The section, as read for this entry, says nothing about retreat, and no American Samoa court decision on retreat or any castle-doctrine, immunity or stand-your-ground provision was found. A case note says a finding of self-defence is a complete defence to third-degree assault (Galea'i v. Atofau, 16 A.S.R.2d 76 (1990)). Whether a person must retreat before using deadly force is therefore not settled by the sources found.

6b4505731975ad5d.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Martinique

An overseas region of France, part of France itself. Shown with the entry for France, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 122-5 of the Penal Code, a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same time in a way required by the necessity of self-defence, unless the means used are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack. The defence must be simultaneous with the attack; a blow struck after the attacker has left is treated as ordinary violence. Neither art. 122-5 nor art. 122-6 mentions retreat, and the sources opened here did not address whether flight is expected. Defence of property can never justify intentional homicide. Judges decide whether the defence was disproportionate; Encyclopaedia Universalis notes that an excessive response may lead to mitigating circumstances or a conviction for a lesser offence rather than full exoneration.

At home

Art. 122-6 of the Penal Code presumes self-defence for a person who acts "to repel, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place", and against perpetrators of violent theft or looting. The presumption is rebuttable and does not cover daytime intrusions, which fall under the general rule of art. 122-5.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 122-5
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal, art. 122-6
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.

0caf64c948f51f5f.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Comoros

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

In the 1981 Penal Code of the Comoros (as amended, the version found), there is no crime when killing, wounding or blows were required by the 'present necessity of legitimate defence' of oneself or another. The article does not mention proportionality or retreat; its test is present necessity. Night-time defence against climbing or break-in into a home, and defence against violent theft or looting, are named as cases of such necessity. Whether a newer penal code has since replaced this text could not be confirmed.

At home

Article 316 counts as legitimate defence killing or wounding while repelling at night the climbing or breaking of fences, walls or entrances of a house, inhabited flat or their outbuildings, and defence against violent theft or looting.

What the law says
Code pénal (1981, as amended), arts. 315–316
ART.315.- Il n'y a ni crime ni délit lorsque l'homicide, les blessures et les coups étaient commandés par la nécessité actuelle de la légitime défense se soi même ou d'autrui. ART.316. - Sont compris dans les cas de nécessité actuelle de défense, les deux cas suivants : 1°)- Si l'homicide a été commis et si des blessures ont été faites, ou si les coups ont été portés en repoussant pendant la nuit, l'escalade ou l'effraction, des clôtures, murs ou entrées d'une maison , d'un appartement habité ou de leurs dépendances, 2°)- Si le fait a eu lieu en se défendant contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violences.

3679022b7abe7d51.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Saint Helena

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Saint Helena, a British Overseas Territory, has no criminal code of its own on self-defence found in its published laws; under the English Law (Application) Ordinance 2005 (in force 1 January 2006), the common law of England and the Acts of Parliament in force in England at that date apply in Saint Helena, so far as suitable to local circumstances. Self-defence there is therefore governed by English common law. Under that common law, as quoted from the practitioners' text Archbold by the Seychelles Court of Appeal in 2015, 'the old rule of law that a man attacked must retreat as far as he can has disappeared', and whether the person retreated is only one factor in judging whether the force was reasonable. The later English statute on this point (Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, s. 76(6A), added in 2013) post-dates the 2006 cut-off and was not shown to apply in Saint Helena. No Saint Helena court decision on self-defence was found. Ascension and Tristan da Cunha have separate law lists and were not checked.

What the law says
English Law (Application) Ordinance 2005 (Ord. 10 of 2005), ss. 2–3
In this Ordinance, “Adopted English Law” means: the common law of England, including the rules of equity; and the Acts of Parliament which are in force in England at the time of commencement of this Ordinance. ... 3. (1) Subject to subsection (2) and other provisions of this Ordinance, the Adopted English Law applies in St Helena. ... (2) The Adopted English Law applies to St Helena only in so far as it is applicable and suitable to local circumstances, and subject to such modifications, adaptations, qualifications and exceptions as local circumstances render necessary.
English common law as stated in Archbold, quoted in Freminot v Republic (Seychelles Court of Appeal, 2015), para. 9
The old rule of law that a man attacked must retreat as far as he can has disappeared. ... Whether the accused did retreat is only one element for the jury to consider

37b76498b4b6c445.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Bermuda

Part of United Kingdom, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Bermuda has its own Criminal Code Act 1907. A person unlawfully assaulted who did not provoke it may use reasonably necessary force, and may use force causing death or grievous bodily harm only if the attack causes reasonable fear of death or grievous bodily harm and they believe on reasonable grounds "that he cannot otherwise preserve" the person defended (s. 257). The Code does not impose a general duty to retreat on an innocent victim, but the "cannot otherwise preserve" test means other ways of avoiding the danger are relevant. A person who started the fight or provoked the assault may use deadly force only if, before the need arose, they "declined and quitted conflict or retreated from conflict as far as was practicable" (s. 258). Anyone authorised to use force is criminally responsible for any excess (s. 269), and a killing caused by good-faith but excessive defensive force, without premeditation, is manslaughter rather than murder (s. 296).

At home

Section 253 makes it lawful for a person in peaceable possession of a dwelling-house, and anyone helping them, to use such force as they believe on reasonable grounds to be necessary to prevent the forcible breaking and entering of the house, by night or day, by someone they reasonably believe intends to commit an indictable offence inside.

What the law says
Criminal Code Act 1907, s. 257
(1) When a person is unlawfully assaulted, and has not provoked the assault, it is lawful for him to use such force to the assailant as is reasonably necessary to make effectual defence against the assault, if the force used is not intended, and is not such as is likely, to cause death or grievous bodily harm. (2) If the nature of the assault is such as to cause reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm, and the person using force by way of defence believes, on reasonable grounds, that he cannot otherwise preserve the person defended from death or grievous bodily harm, it is lawful for him to use any such force to the assailant as is necessary for defence, even though such force may cause death or grievous bodily harm.
Criminal Code Act 1907, s. 258 proviso (c)
Provided that the foregoing provisions of this section shall not have effect so as to excuse or justify— ... (c) the use by any person of force which causes death or grievous bodily harm where such person has not before the necessity to use such force arose declined and quitted conflict or retreated from conflict as far as was practicable.
Criminal Code Act 1907, s. 253
It is lawful for any person who is in peaceable possession of a dwelling-house, and for any person lawfully assisting him or acting by his authority, to use such force as he believes, on reasonable grounds, to be necessary in order to prevent the forcible breaking and entering of the dwelling-house, either by night or day, by any person whom he believes, on reasonable grounds, to be attempting to break and enter the dwelling-house with intent to commit any indictable offence therein.
Criminal Code Act 1907, s. 296
An unlawful killing by a person of another person is manslaughter and not murder if the offender while in the exercise in good faith of any right to use force against another person uses more force than that allowed to him by law in relation to the exercise of that right and causes the death of the person against whom the force is used without premeditation and without any intention of doing more bodily harm than he honestly believes is necessary for the purpose of exercising that right.

69d336c5cabe3772.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Australian Capital Territory

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

The ACT Criminal Code 2002 (s 42) follows the Commonwealth model: conduct is self-defence if the person believes it is necessary to defend themselves or someone else (or for listed property and trespass purposes) and it is a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceive them. The section does not mention retreat and no duty to retreat is stated. Intentionally inflicting death or serious harm only to protect property or deal with a trespasser is excluded.

At home

No home-specific rule in s 42; force intended to cause death or serious harm may not be used only to protect property or to prevent or remove a criminal trespasser (s 42(3)).

What the law says
Criminal Code 2002 (ACT), s 42 Self-defence
(1) A person is not criminally responsible for an offence if the person carries out the conduct required for the offence in self-defence. (2) A person carries out conduct in self-defence only if— (a) the person believes the conduct is necessary— (i) to defend himself or herself or someone else; or (ii) to prevent or end the unlawful imprisonment of himself or herself or someone else; or (iii) to protect property from unlawful appropriation, destruction, damage or interference; or (iv) to prevent criminal trespass to land or premises; or (v) to remove from land or premises a person committing criminal trespass; and (b) the conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as the person perceives them. (3) However, the person does not carry out conduct in self-defence if— (a) the person uses force that involves the intentional infliction of death or serious harm— (i) to protect property; or (ii) to prevent criminal trespass; or (iii) to remove a person committing criminal trespass; ...
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Criminal Code 2002 (ACT), republication R58 effective 23/02/26 (ACT Legislation Register, ACT Parliamentary Counsel)
Australia as a whole

Most criminal law in Australia is made by the six states and two territories, each with its own self-defence rule; this national entry describes the Commonwealth Criminal Code, which covers federal offences. Under s 10.4 a person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them. No Australian statute found imposes a duty to retreat; in jury directions (NSW Criminal Trial Courts Bench Book) the availability of retreat is listed as one matter the jury may weigh in deciding whether the response was reasonable. Deadly or really serious force cannot be justified solely to protect property or deal with trespassers. Whether excessive force reduces murder to manslaughter depends on the state or territory (e.g. NSW s 421, WA s 248(3), SA s 15(2)).

4e7da1136c5a7344.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

US Virgin Islands

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

The US Virgin Islands has its own criminal code (Title 14, V.I. Code). It allows 'the use of force to protect oneself, one's family, or one's property from a real or threatened attack' (14 V.I.C. § 43, as quoted by the V.I. Supreme Court), and lists violence used in self-defence against unlawful violence as lawful (§ 293(a)(6)). A killing is justified as self-defence if the defendant actually and reasonably believed they were in imminent danger of death or great bodily harm, and once self-defence is raised the prosecution must disprove it beyond a reasonable doubt (Viera v. People, 2019 VI 22). The right 'does not extend to the infliction of more harm than is necessary', and force greater than needed to stop the harm is unlawful (Marcelle v. People, 2011). No statute on retreat was found. In Gov't of the V.I. v. Fonseca (2001) the federal Third Circuit held that a trial instruction did not impose a duty to retreat; that instruction told jurors that a person who reasonably believed deadly force was needed was 'not required to retreat' and could stand their ground, but that a failure to retreat safely could be weighed in deciding whether the force went further than justified. In Viera the court relied partly on the fact that the defendant kept shooting after he had retreated to his car and was getting away. No castle-doctrine presumption, civil immunity or pretrial immunity hearing was found.

At home

The Virgin Islands Code lists as lawful violence used in self-defence or defence of another against unlawful violence offered to one's person or property (14 V.I.C. § 293(a)(6)), and a separate clause about preventing entry into a home was discussed in Gov't of the V.I. v. Fonseca (3d Cir. 2001), which held it did not apply where the other person never tried to get inside. The text of that home clause was not opened for this entry.

The V.I. Code text itself was not opened; statutory wording is as quoted in court opinions. Category is 'judicial' because the no-retreat rule appears only in an approved jury instruction; the instruction also lets jurors weigh a safe retreat, which overlaps with 'proportional'.

What the law says
Gov't of the V.I. v. Fonseca, Nos. 00-3628/3877/3878 (3d Cir. 2001) – trial instruction held not to impose a duty to retreat
If the defendants had a reasonable ground to believe and actually did believe that they were in imminent danger of death or serious bodily harm, and that deadly force was necessary to repel such danger, they were not required to retreat or to consider whether they could safely retreat. They were entitled to stand their grounds and use such force as was reasonable under the circumstances ... However, if the Defendant could have safely retreated but did not do so, their failure to retreat is circumstances under which you may consider, together with all the other circumstances, in determining whether they went further in repelling the danger, real or apparent, than they were justified in doing under the circumstances.
14 V.I.C. § 43, as quoted in Viera v. People, 2019 VI 22, ¶ 30
Virgin Islands law allows “the use of force to protect oneself, one’s family, or one’s property from a real or threatened attack.” See 14 V.I.C. § 43
Viera v. People, 2019 VI 22, ¶ 30 (excessive force)
Notably, “[t]he right of self-defense does not extend to the infliction of more harm than is necessary for the purpose of defense.” ... “The force used to deflect an aggressor’s threatened harm must be merely sufficient to stop the harm, and application of a greater force than that which is necessary is unlawful.” Marcelle v. People, 55 V.I. 536, 544-45 (V.I. 2011)
14 V.I.C. § 293(a)(6), as quoted in Fonseca
in self-defense or in defense of another against unlawful violence offered to his person or property

80c95efe8dc53e8b.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Connecticut

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Connecticut allows deadly force only when a person reasonably believes the other person is using or about to use deadly force, or is inflicting or about to inflict great bodily harm (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-19(a)). Connecticut keeps a duty to retreat: deadly force is not justified if the person knows they can avoid it with complete safety by retreating, by handing over property to someone claiming a right to it, or by complying with a demand to stop doing something they are not obliged to do (§ 53a-19(b)). The duty to retreat does not apply in the person's own dwelling or place of work if they were not the initial aggressor, or to a police officer (or a person assisting one at the officer's direction) making an arrest. The retreat rule dates to the 1969 penal code (P.A. 69-828) and has been amended several times since, most recently in 2022 (P.A. 22-117), without adopting a stand-your-ground rule. Force is not justified for someone who provoked the other with intent to injure or kill, for an initial aggressor who has not withdrawn and clearly communicated it, or in a fight by agreement not authorised by law (§ 53a-19(c)). The sources consulted show no statutory immunity from prosecution or civil suit and no pretrial immunity hearing.

At home

Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-19(b): a person who was not the initial aggressor need not retreat in their own dwelling (as defined in § 53a-100) or place of work. Under § 53a-20 a person in possession or control of premises may also use deadly force when they reasonably believe it necessary 'to prevent or terminate an unlawful entry by force into his dwelling', and only for that purpose. Connecticut has no statutory presumption of reasonable fear for home intrusions.

What the law says
Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-19(b)
Notwithstanding the provisions of subsection (a) of this section, a person is not justified in using deadly physical force upon another person if he or she knows that he or she can avoid the necessity of using such force with complete safety (1) by retreating, except that the actor shall not be required to retreat if he or she is in his or her dwelling, as defined in section 53a-100, or place of work and was not the initial aggressor, or if he or she is a peace officer or a private person assisting such peace officer at his or her direction, and acting pursuant to section 53a-22, or (2) by surrendering possession of property to a person asserting a claim of right thereto, or (3) by complying with a demand that he or she abstain from performing an act which he or she is not obliged to perform.
Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-19(a)
except that deadly physical force may not be used unless the actor reasonably believes that such other person is (1) using or about to use deadly physical force, or (2) inflicting or about to inflict great bodily harm.
Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-19(c)
a person is not justified in using physical force when (1) with intent to cause physical injury or death to another person, he provokes the use of physical force by such other person, or (2) he is the initial aggressor, except that his use of physical force upon another person under such circumstances is justifiable if he withdraws from the encounter and effectively communicates to such other person his intent to do so ... or (3) the physical force involved was the product of a combat by agreement not specifically authorized by law.

to prevent or terminate an unlawful entry by force into his dwelling as defined in section 53a-100,

d5d8084bdbf4b3b2.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Delaware

Part of United States, or under it.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Delaware allows deadly force when the defendant reasonably believes it is necessary to protect against death, serious physical injury, kidnapping or sexual intercourse compelled by force or threat (11 Del. C. § 464(c)). Delaware keeps a duty to retreat for deadly force: it is not justified if the defendant knows the need can be avoided with complete safety by retreating, by handing over a thing to someone claiming a right to it, or by complying with a demand to stop doing something they are not legally obliged to do (§ 464(e)(2)). There is no duty to retreat in or from one's own dwelling, nor from one's place of work unless the defendant was the initial aggressor; for non-deadly force there is no retreat requirement (§ 464(b)). Deadly force is also not justified if the defendant, intending to cause death or serious injury, provoked the use of force in the same encounter, and force may not be used to resist a known arrest by a police officer, lawful or not. In the home, § 469 (added by 63 Del. Laws c. 276) gives an occupant a specific defence for killing or injuring an unlawful intruder in a sudden encounter, on a reasonable belief the intruder would cause injury, or after the intruder refused to surrender. If the defendant's belief in the need for force was reckless or negligent, the justification is not available for offences that require only recklessness or negligence (such as manslaughter or criminally negligent homicide) (§ 470(a)). The sources consulted show no statutory immunity from prosecution or civil suit and no pretrial immunity hearing.

At home

11 Del. C. § 464(e)(2)(a)–(b): a defendant is not obliged to retreat in or from their own dwelling, and is not obliged to retreat in or from their place of work unless they were the initial aggressor. § 469 gives an occupant charged with killing or injuring an intruder unlawfully in the dwelling a defence if the encounter was sudden and unexpected and forced instant action, or the occupant reasonably believed the intruder would injure someone in the dwelling, or the intruder refused a demand to disarm or surrender.

What the law says
11 Del. C. § 464(e)(2)
The use of deadly force is not justifiable under this section if: ... (2) The defendant knows that the necessity of using deadly force can be avoided with complete safety by retreating, by surrendering possession of a thing to a person asserting a claim of right thereto or by complying with a demand that the defendant abstain from performing an act which the defendant is not legally obligated to perform except that: a. The defendant is not obliged to retreat in or from the defendant’s dwelling; and b. The defendant is not obliged to retreat in or from the defendant’s place of work, unless the defendant was the initial aggressor ...
11 Del. C. § 464(c)
The use of deadly force is justifiable under this section if the defendant reasonably believes that such force is necessary to protect the defendant against death, serious physical injury, kidnapping or sexual intercourse compelled by force or threat.
11 Del. C. § 469
In the prosecution of an occupant of a dwelling charged with killing or injuring an intruder who was unlawfully in said dwelling, it shall be a defense that the occupant was in the occupant’s own dwelling at the time of the offense, and: (1) The encounter between the occupant and intruder was sudden and unexpected, compelling the occupant to act instantly; or (2) The occupant reasonably believed that the intruder would inflict personal injury upon the occupant or others in the dwelling; or (3) The occupant demanded that the intruder disarm or surrender, and the intruder refused to do so.
11 Del. C. § 470(a)
but the defendant is reckless or negligent in having such belief ... the justification afforded by those sections is unavailable in a prosecution for an offense for which recklessness or negligence, as the case may be, suffices to establish culpability.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)
  • Delaware Code, Title 11, Chapter 4 – Defenses to Criminal Liability (§§ 464, 469, 470) (State of Delaware, Legislative Council)

768ddd92e0b87052.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Nevada

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Nevada allows a killing in necessary self-defence or defence of another, or of an occupied home or occupied motor vehicle, against someone who manifestly intends to commit a violent felony (NRS 200.120). Since 2011 a person need not retreat before using deadly force if they are not the original aggressor, have a right to be at the place, and are not engaged in criminal activity; this applies anywhere the person lawfully is, not only at home. Bare fear is not enough: the circumstances must be enough to frighten a reasonable person and the person must have acted from that fear, not revenge (NRS 200.130(1)). A 2015 amendment added a rebuttable presumption of reasonable fear when the person killed was forcibly entering an occupied home or vehicle or committing a violent felony, as long as the defender did not provoke them (NRS 200.130(2)). The older NRS 200.200 still requires that the danger was urgent and that the person killed was the assailant or that the slayer had in good faith tried to decline further struggle, which limits initial aggressors. Civil suits against a person who used force against an armed burglar, home invader or car thief are barred unless the presumption of reasonable fear is overcome by clear and convincing evidence (NRS 41.095). Nevada has no statutory pretrial immunity hearing; a justified killing leads to acquittal at trial (NRS 200.190). Excessive force is not excused and can be prosecuted as manslaughter or murder.

At home

Killing is justifiable in defence of an occupied habitation or occupied motor vehicle against someone who violently or surreptitiously tries to enter to assault anyone inside (NRS 200.120(1)). Since 2015 a rebuttable presumption of reasonable fear applies when the person killed was unlawfully and forcibly entering an occupied home or vehicle (NRS 200.130(2)); civil presumption and immunity for force against armed burglars, home invaders or car thieves in a residence, transient lodging or vehicle (NRS 41.095).

What the law says
NRS 200.120(2) (no duty to retreat, added 2011, amended 2015)
A person is not required to retreat before using deadly force as provided in subsection 1 if the person: (a) Is not the original aggressor; (b) Has a right to be present at the location where deadly force is used; and (c) Is not actively engaged in conduct in furtherance of criminal activity at the time deadly force is used.
NRS 200.120(1)
Justifiable homicide is the killing of a human being in necessary self-defense, or in defense of an occupied habitation, an occupied motor vehicle or a person, against one who manifestly intends or endeavors to commit a crime of violence...
NRS 200.130 (presumption, added 2015)
There is a rebuttable presumption that the circumstances were sufficient to excite the fears of a reasonable person and that the person killing really acted under the influence of those fears and not in a spirit of revenge if the person killing: (a) Knew or reasonably believed that the person who was killed was entering unlawfully and with force, or attempting to enter unlawfully and with force, the occupied habitation or occupied motor vehicle, of another; (b) Knew or reasonably believed that the person who was killed was committing or attempting to commit a crime of violence; and (c) Did not provoke the person who was killed.
NRS 200.200
If a person kills another in self-defense, it must appear that: 1. The danger was so urgent and pressing that, in order to save the person’s own life, or to prevent the person from receiving great bodily harm, the killing of the other was absolutely necessary; and 2. The person killed was the assailant, or that the slayer had really, and in good faith, endeavored to decline any further struggle before the mortal blow was given.
NRS 41.095 (civil immunity)
An action to recover damages for personal injuries to or the wrongful death of the person who committed burglary, invasion of the home or grand larceny of the motor vehicle with the use or threatened use of a deadly weapon may not be maintained against the person who used such force unless the presumption is overcome by clear and convincing evidence to the contrary.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

bee553b61647799c.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

North Dakota

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

North Dakota's Century Code allows deadly force in lawful self-defence or defence of others when necessary to protect against death, serious bodily injury or a violent felony, and never more force than is necessary and appropriate (NDCC 12.1-05-07). The code still contains the older Model Penal Code rule that deadly force is not justified if it can be avoided safely by retreat, but HB 1498, signed on 20 April 2021 and in force from 1 August 2021, added that a person who is not engaged in unlawful activity that gave rise to the need for force and did not provoke the attacker 'is not required to retreat within or from any place the individual otherwise is legally allowed to be'. In a dwelling, place of work, motor vehicle or occupied motor home or travel trailer, deadly force may be used to prevent arson, burglary, robbery or a violent felony there. A person who uses deadly force against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering (or dragging a person out of) a dwelling, workplace or occupied motor home is presumed to have had a reasonable fear of death or serious injury; the prosecution can rebut this only by proof beyond a reasonable doubt, and it does not apply against lawful residents, officers lawfully entering, and similar cases (12.1-05-07.1). Anyone who uses force as permitted by the chapter is immune from civil liability to the person they used it against, and a court must award lost income, attorney's fees and costs to a defendant found immune (12.1-05-07.2, amended 2021). A mistaken but honest belief in the need for force is an excuse, but if the belief was held negligently or recklessly it is no defence to crimes of negligence or recklessness (12.1-05-08). No statutory pretrial criminal immunity hearing was found.

At home

Deadly force is justified for a person in possession or control of (or licensed to be in) a dwelling, place of work, motor vehicle, or occupied motor home or travel trailer when needed to prevent arson, burglary, robbery or a violent felony there and lesser force would expose someone to substantial danger of serious injury (NDCC 12.1-05-07(2)(c)). A rebuttable presumption of reasonable fear applies against someone unlawfully and forcibly entering, or removing a person from, a dwelling, workplace or occupied motor home or travel trailer (12.1-05-07.1).

What the law says
NDCC 12.1-05-07(2)(b) (as amended by HB 1498, 2021)
However, the duty to retreat or avoid force does not apply under the following circumstances: ... (2) An individual who is not engaged in an unlawful activity that gives rise to the need for the use of deadly force and has not provoked the individual against whom the deadly force is used, unless the circumstances in subdivision b of subsection 2 of section 12.1-05-03 apply, is not required to retreat within or from any place the individual otherwise is legally allowed to be.
NDCC 12.1-05-07(1)
An individual is not justified in using more force than is necessary and appropriate under the circumstances.
NDCC 12.1-05-07.1 (presumption)
An individual is presumed to have held a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or serious bodily injury to that individual or another when using deadly force if: a. The individual against whom the deadly force was used was in the process of unlawfully and forcibly entering, or had unlawfully and forcibly entered and remains within a dwelling, place of work, or occupied motor home or travel trailer ...
NDCC 12.1-05-07.2 (civil immunity)
An individual who uses force as permitted under this chapter is immune from civil liability for the use of the force to the individual against whom force was used or to that individual's estate ...
NDCC 12.1-05-08 (excuse)
However, if his belief is negligently or recklessly held, it is not an excuse in a prosecution for an offense for which negligence or recklessness, as the case may be, suffices to establish culpability.
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

  • House Bill 1498 (2021), enrolled (North Dakota Legislative Branch)

cb9a6adcdd994a2f.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Malta

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Article 223 of Malta's Criminal Code says no offence is committed when a homicide or bodily harm is 'imposed by actual necessity' in lawful defence of oneself or another person, and Article 224 lists cases that count as such necessity, including repelling a night-time break-in to a home and defending against violent theft. The code does not mention retreat, and no Maltese court judgment or commentary on retreat was opened during this search, so whether a person must escape when they safely can is not settled here. A person who exceeds the limits set by law or necessity commits only an 'excusable' homicide with a reduced penalty (Article 227(d), punishment in Article 228), and the excess is not punishable at all if it was due to being taken unawares, or to fear or fright. Malta's Constitution (Article 33(2)) also allows deprivation of life by force 'reasonably justifiable' for the defence of any person from violence or of property.

At home

Article 224 treats as cases of 'actual necessity of lawful defence' homicide or bodily harm committed while repelling, at night, the scaling or breaking of enclosures, walls or entrance doors of a house or inhabited apartment (or connected appurtenances), and defence against theft or plunder with violence. The same act during the daytime makes a wilful homicide 'excusable' (reduced punishment) rather than justified (Article 227(b)).

What the law says
Criminal Code (Cap. 9), articles 223-224
223. No offence is committed when a homicide or a bodily harm is ordered or permitted by law or by a lawful authority, or is imposed by actual necessity either in lawful self-defence or in the lawful defence of another person. 224. Cases of actual necessity of lawful defence shall include the following: (a) where the homicide or bodily harm is committed in the act of repelling, during the night-time, the scaling or breaking of enclosures, walls, or the entrance doors of any house or inhabited apartment, or of the appurtenances thereof having a direct or an indirect communication with such house or apartment; (b) where the homicide or bodily harm is committed in the act of defence against any person committing theft or plunder, with violence, or attempting to commit such theft or plunder; (c) where the homicide or bodily harm is imposed by the actual necessity of the defence of one's own chastity or of the chastity of another person.
Criminal Code (Cap. 9), article 227(b) and (d)
Wilful homicide shall be excusable - ... (b) where it is committed in repelling, during the day-time, the scaling or breaking of enclosures, walls, or the entrance of any house or inhabited apartment, or the appurtenances thereof having a direct or an indirect communication with such house or apartment; ... (d) where it is committed by any person who, acting under the circumstances mentioned in article 223, shall have exceeded the limits imposed by law, by the authority, or by necessity: Provided, moreover, that any such excess shall not be liable to punishment if it is due to the person being taken unawares, or to fear or fright.
Constitution of Malta, article 33(2)(a) (English text in CJAD database)
a person shall not be regarded as having been deprived of his life in contravention of this article if he dies as the result of the use of force to such extent as is reasonably justifiable in the circumstances of the case - (a) for the defence of any person from violence or for the defence of property;
Sources (read 2026-10-17)

16a8ddcbca7fb400.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

São Tomé and Principe

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

São Tomé and Príncipe's Penal Code (approved by Law 6/2012, on the Portuguese model) treats self-defence as a ground that removes unlawfulness (art. 31). Self-defence is an act carried out 'as a necessary means' to repel a current and unlawful aggression against any legally protected interests of the defender or a third party (art. 32). The code does not mention retreat or flight, and no court decisions from São Tomé on the point were found. If the means used in self-defence are excessive, the act is unlawful but the penalty may be specially reduced; if the excess came from disturbance, fear or fright that is not blameworthy, the person is not punished (art. 33).

What the law says
Código Penal (Lei n.º 6/2012), art. 32.º – Legítima defesa
Constitui legítima defesa o facto praticado, como meio necessário, para repelir a agressão actual e ilícita de quaisquer interesses juridicamente protegidos do agente ou de terceiro.
Código Penal, art. 33.º – Excesso de legítima defesa
1. Se houver excesso nos meios empregados em legítima defesa, o facto é ilícito, mas a pena pode ser especialmente atenuada. 2. Se o excesso resultar de perturbação, medo ou susto não censuráveis, o agente não é punido.

c217ce7b84ec6933.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Kansas

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, written in the law

Kansas allows deadly force when a person reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to themselves or a third person (Kan. Stat. § 21-5222(b)). Nothing requires a person to retreat when using force to protect themselves or another (§ 21-5222(c)), and a person who is not engaged in unlawful activity and is attacked in a place where they have a right to be 'has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand such person's ground' (§ 21-5230). These rules were carried over from former K.S.A. 21-3211 and 21-3218 into Kansas's recodified criminal code (L. 2010, ch. 136, effective July 2011). In a home, workplace or occupied vehicle the law presumes the defender reasonably believed deadly force was necessary when facing an unlawful or forceful intruder (§ 21-5224). The justification is not available to a person attempting, committing or escaping a forcible felony, a person who provoked force as an excuse to injure, or another initial provoker unless they reasonably faced imminent deadly danger and exhausted every reasonable means of escape, or withdrew in good faith and clearly said so (§ 21-5226). A person who used justified force is immune from criminal prosecution (which includes arrest, detention and charging) and from civil action, unless the person they used force against was an identified or recognisable on-duty law enforcement officer (§ 21-5231). Kansas courts decide immunity before trial at an evidentiary hearing like a preliminary examination, where the judge weighs all the evidence without deference to the state and the case continues only if the state shows probable cause that the force was not justified (State v. Hardy (2015); State v. Macomber, 309 Kan. 907 (2019)).

At home

Kan. Stat. § 21-5224: a person is presumed to reasonably believe deadly force is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm when the other person is unlawfully or forcefully entering, or has entered and is present in, the defender's dwelling, place of work or occupied vehicle, or is removing someone from it against their will, and the defender knows or has reason to believe this. The presumption does not apply against a lawful resident not barred by a protective order, a parent or guardian taking their own child, a law enforcement officer lawfully entering whom the defender knows or should know is an officer, or if the defender is committing a crime or using the place to further one.

What the law says
Kan. Stat. § 21-5230
A person who is not engaged in an unlawful activity and who is attacked in a place where such person has a right to be has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand such person's ground and use any force which such person would be justified in using ...
Kan. Stat. § 21-5222(b)–(c)
A person is justified in the use of deadly force under circumstances described in subsection (a) if such person reasonably believes that such use of deadly force is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to such person or a third person. (c) Nothing in this section shall require a person to retreat if such person is using force to protect such person or a third person.
Kan. Stat. § 21-5224(a)
a person is presumed to have a reasonable belief that deadly force is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to such person or another person if: (1) The person against whom the force is used, at the time the force is used: (A) Is unlawfully or forcefully entering, or has unlawfully or forcefully entered, and is present within, the dwelling, place of work or occupied vehicle of the person using force ...
Kan. Stat. § 21-5226
is not available to a person who: (a) Is attempting to commit, committing or escaping from the commission of a forcible felony; (b) initially provokes the use of any force against such person or another, with intent to use such force as an excuse to inflict bodily harm upon the assailant; or (c) otherwise initially provokes the use of any force against such person or another, unless ...
Kan. Stat. § 21-5231(a)
A person who uses force which, subject to the provisions of K.S.A. 21-5226, and amendments thereto, is justified pursuant to K.S.A. 21-5222, 21-5223 or 21-5225, and amendments thereto, is immune from criminal prosecution and civil action for the use of such force ... As used in this subsection, "criminal prosecution" includes arrest, detention in custody and charging or prosecution of the defendant.

c92a00fb487678c3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Heard Island and McDonald Islands

Part of Australia, or under it.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Heard Island and McDonald Islands is an uninhabited Australian external territory. Section 5 of the Heard Island and McDonald Islands Act 1953 is headed 'Laws of Australian Capital Territory to be in force' (its full wording could not be opened), so the self-defence rule is taken to be that of the ACT Criminal Code 2002, s. 42, and this entry follows the ACT entry. Under s. 42 conduct is self-defence if the person believes it is necessary to defend themselves or someone else (or for listed property and trespass purposes) and it is a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceive them; the section does not mention retreat. Intentionally causing death or serious harm only to protect property or deal with a trespasser is not self-defence.

What the law says

(2) A person carries out conduct in self-defence only if— (a) the person believes the conduct is necessary— (i) to defend himself or herself or someone else; or ... and (b) the conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as the person perceives them. (3) However, the person does not carry out conduct in self-defence if— (a) the person uses force that involves the intentional infliction of death or serious harm— (i) to protect property; or (ii) to prevent criminal trespass; or (iii) to remove a person committing criminal trespass;

976123f19b22f774.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Jan Mayen

A Norwegian island. Shown with the entry for Norway, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

A duty to retreat or avoid the attack where it can safely be done

Under section 18 of the Norwegian Penal Code (2005), an otherwise punishable act is lawful when it is done to avert an unlawful attack, goes no further than necessary, and does not 'obviously' go beyond what is justifiable given how dangerous the attack is, what interest it violates and the attacker's guilt. The statute does not mention retreat, but because force must be 'necessary', a lawyer answering for the state youth-information service ung.no wrote in 2023 that if there were other ways to avert the attack, 'such as calling for help or running away', a killing cannot be claimed as self-defence; the Supreme Court's appeals committee has also upheld a conviction where the defendant had 'several alternative courses of action' and had partly provoked the fight (HR-2022-1377-U). Someone who goes too far can still be acquitted where 'special reasons' justify it, and the sentence can in any case be reduced (sections 80 and 81, as described by the national encyclopedia). Lawful self-defence is not just unpunished but lawful, so the Supreme Court held in 2018 (HR-2018-2427-A) that the defender cannot be ordered to pay damages when the attack was real.

At home

No separate home-defence rule was found; section 18 applies to attacks on persons and on property alike.

What the law says
Straffeloven (Penal Code 2005), § 18 første ledd (as quoted by the Supreme Court in HR-2022-1377-U)
En handling som ellers ville være straffbar, er lovlig når den a. blir foretatt for å avverge et ulovlig angrep, b. ikke går lenger enn nødvendig, og c. ikke går åpenbart ut over hva som er forsvarlig under hensyn til hvor farlig angrepet er, hva slags interesse som angrepet krenker, og angriperens skyld.

10192ec4d520bcd3.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Andorra

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Article 27(1) of the Penal Code (Law 9/2005, consolidated text 2014) excludes criminal liability for acting in defence of oneself, one's rights or another person when four conditions are met: an unlawful aggression; rational necessity of the means used to prevent or repel it; harm that is not disproportionate to the seriousness of the aggression and the circumstances of the aggressor; and no sufficient provocation by the defender. The code does not mention retreat, and no Andorran court ruling on retreat was found. If not all the requirements are met (incomplete self-defence), the penalty is reduced in a 'qualified' way under articles 28 and 54.

At home

Article 27(1)(a): when defending one's home or domicile, unlawful entry ('l'entrada indeguda') counts as an unlawful aggression, so defence may begin from the intrusion itself; the other requirements (rational necessity of the means, no disproportionate harm, no provocation) still apply.

What the law says
Codi penal (Llei 9/2005, text refós 2014), art. 27(1)
Són circumstàncies que exclouen la responsabilitat criminal: 1. Actuar en defensa de la persona o de drets propis o d'altri, si hi concorren els requisits següents: a) Agressió il·legítima. En cas de defensa de béns, es considera agressió il·legítima l'acció constitutiva de delicte o contravenció penal que els posi en perill de deteriorament o pèrdua imminent. En cas de defensa de la llar o del domicili, es considera agressió il·legítima l'entrada indeguda. b) Necessitat racional del mitjà emprat per impedir-la o repel·lir-la. c) Que el mal causat per l'acció de defensa no sigui desproporcionat en relació amb la gravetat de l'agressió i amb les circumstàncies de l'agressor. d) No haver-hi hagut provocació suficient per part del defensor.
Codi penal, art. 28
Les circumstàncies expressades en l'article anterior, quan no hi concorrin tots els requisits necessaris per eximir de responsabilitat, atenuen de manera qualificada la pena d'acord amb el que disposa l'article 54.

4e9227ab655e14e4.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Grenada

Law found, but it does not settle whether one must retreat

Grenada's Criminal Code (s. 62) allows a person to use "necessary force" to prevent or defend themselves or others against crime, with graded limits: force extending to killing is allowed only "in case of extreme necessity" against listed serious crimes such as murder, robbery, burglary, housebreaking, rape, and dangerous or grievous harm. Force used in an unlawful fight cannot be justified. The Code section does not mention retreat, and no Grenadian court decision on retreat was found, so the question is not settled here. The Constitution (s. 2) says a death caused by force reasonably justifiable for the defence of any person from violence, to the extent permitted by law, is not a breach of the right to life. The rule on excessive force was not found in the sources opened.

At home

Killing may be justified in case of extreme necessity to prevent or defend against burglary, housebreaking, or arson of a dwelling-house, among other listed crimes (Criminal Code s. 62(4)).

What the law says
Criminal Code (1987, rev. 2007), s. 62
(1) For the prevention of, or for the defence of himself or herself or any other person against any crime, a person may justify the use of necessary force, not extending to a blow, wound or grievous harm. ... (4) For the prevention of, or for the defence of himself or herself or any other person against any of the following crimes, a person may justify any necessary force or harm, extending, in case of extreme necessity, even to killing, namely— (a) treason; (b) piracy; (c) murder; (d) manslaughter, except manslaughter by negligence; (e) robbery; (f) burglary; (g) housebreaking; (h) arson of a dwelling-house or vessel; (i) rape; (j) forcible unnatural crime; (k) dangerous or grievous harm. ... (6) No force used in an unlawful fight can be justified under any provision of this Code; and every fight is an unlawful fight in which a person engages, or which he or she maintains, otherwise than solely in pursuance of some of the matters of justification specified in this Title.
Constitution of Grenada, s. 2(2)(a)
A person shall not be regarded as having been deprived of his life in contravention of this section if he dies as the result of the use, to such extent and in such circumstances as are permitted by law, of force such as is reasonably justifiable- a. for the defence of any person from violence or for the defence of property

d3c08123554743cd.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Saint Kitts and Nevis

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

Self-defence in Saint Kitts and Nevis is governed by the common law as stated by the Privy Council in Palmer v R (1971), which the Eastern Caribbean Court of Appeal applies. A person who reasonably believes their life is in danger, or that they face serious bodily harm, may use the force they believe on reasonable grounds is necessary, and is not guilty even if the killing was intentional. There is no fixed rule that one must retreat: the chance to retreat without danger is one of the circumstances the jury weighs in deciding whether the force was reasonably necessary. An older Court of Appeal case (Michaud v R, 1969) records a trial direction that a person facing a felonious attack has no duty to retreat and may stand their ground. No statute on retreat, home defence or excessive self-defence was found.

What the law says
Palmer v R [1971] AC 814 (PC), at p. 823, as quoted in Spencer v Director of Public Prosecutions (Court of Appeal, Saint Kitts and Nevis)
A man who is attacked in circumstances where he reasonably believes his life to be in danger or that he is in danger of serious bodily harm, may use such force as on reasonable grounds he believes is necessary to prevent and resist the attack. And if in using such force he kills his assailant he is not guilty of any crime even if the killing was intentional. And in deciding in a particular case whether it was reasonably necessary to have used such force as in fact was used regard must be had to all the circumstances of the case including the possibility of retreating without danger or yielding anything he is entitled to protect.
Michaud v R (West Indies Associated States Court of Appeal, Saint Kitts and Nevis), trial judge's direction quoted in the judgment
If the attack is a felonious one, the victim is under no duty to retreat but may stand his ground and repel

c42b22d859fcf0d9.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

New Mexico

Part of United States, or under it.

No duty to retreat, from the courts or jury instructions

New Mexico has no stand-your-ground statute; its no-retreat rule comes from the courts. The justifiable-homicide statute, unchanged in substance since 1963 (NMSA 30-2-7), allows a killing in the necessary defence of one's life, family or property, or in lawful defence of oneself or another when there are reasonable grounds to believe someone intends to commit a felony or great personal injury and the danger is imminent. In State v. Horton (1953) the Supreme Court held it was wrong to tell a jury that the defendant could not kill his assailant if he could yield without being killed, and the pattern instruction UJI 14-5190 now tells jurors that an attacked person 'need not retreat' and may stand their ground, at home or anywhere. The committee commentary adds that a person may still use no more force than is reasonably necessary, and that the person need not retreat even though they could do so safely. In State v. Anderson (2016-NMCA-007) the Court of Appeals held that leaving out UJI 14-5190 when the evidence supported it was fundamental error. The instruction was most recently amended by Supreme Court order effective 31 December 2025. A 2017 bill (HB 168) proposed a statutory presumption of reasonable belief, but the compiled statute contains no presumption and no 'deadly force' wording. No civil immunity statute or pretrial immunity hearing was found.

At home

NMSA 30-2-7(A) makes homicide justifiable in the necessary defence of one's life, family or property. The pattern instruction UJI 14-5190 says a person defending against an attack, defending another or defending property 'need not retreat' and may stand their ground and defend 'the person's habitation'. No separate castle statute or home-intruder presumption was found.

What the law says
NMSA 1978, § 30-2-7(A) (Laws 1963, ch. 303, § 2-8)
when committed in the necessary defense of his life, his family or his property, ...
UJI 14-5190 NMRA, Self defense; assailed person need not retreat (as amended eff. 31 Dec 2025)
A person who is [defending against an attack] [defending another from an attack] [or] [defending property] need not retreat. In the exercise of the right of [self defense] [defense of another] [or] [defense of property], [a person] may stand [the person’s] ground and defend [[herself] [himself]] [themselves] [another] [the person’s habitation] [or] [property].
State v. Horton, 1953-NMSC-044, 57 N.M. 257, 258 P.2d 371 (leading case)
Certainly the italicized sentence is erroneous in telling the jury the defendant could not kill his assailant if he could yield without being killed
UJI 14-5190 committee commentary
A person need not, however, retreat even though the person could do so safely.

be528a1c6440ff75.h:
Self-defense and the duty to retreat

Réunion

An overseas region of France, part of France itself. Shown with the entry for France, whose law it shares; it has no entry of its own here.

No general duty to retreat, but force must be necessary and proportionate

Under art. 122-5 of the Penal Code, a person is not criminally responsible if, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, they act at the same time in a way required by the necessity of self-defence, unless the means used are out of proportion to the seriousness of the attack. The defence must be simultaneous with the attack; a blow struck after the attacker has left is treated as ordinary violence. Neither art. 122-5 nor art. 122-6 mentions retreat, and the sources opened here did not address whether flight is expected. Defence of property can never justify intentional homicide. Judges decide whether the defence was disproportionate; Encyclopaedia Universalis notes that an excessive response may lead to mitigating circumstances or a conviction for a lesser offence rather than full exoneration.

At home

Art. 122-6 of the Penal Code presumes self-defence for a person who acts "to repel, at night, entry by break-in, violence or trickery into an inhabited place", and against perpetrators of violent theft or looting. The presumption is rebuttable and does not cover daytime intrusions, which fall under the general rule of art. 122-5.

What the law says
Code pénal, art. 122-5
N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, devant une atteinte injustifiée envers elle-même ou autrui, accomplit, dans le même temps, un acte commandé par la nécessité de la légitime défense d'elle-même ou d'autrui, sauf s'il y a disproportion entre les moyens de défense employés et la gravité de l'atteinte. N'est pas pénalement responsable la personne qui, pour interrompre l'exécution d'un crime ou d'un délit contre un bien, accomplit un acte de défense, autre qu'un homicide volontaire, lorsque cet acte est strictement nécessaire au but poursuivi dès lors que les moyens employés sont proportionnés à la gravité de l'infraction.
Code pénal, art. 122-6
Est présumé avoir agi en état de légitime défense celui qui accomplit l'acte : 1° Pour repousser, de nuit, l'entrée par effraction, violence ou ruse dans un lieu habité ; 2° Pour se défendre contre les auteurs de vols ou de pillages exécutés avec violence.
